pools.title: A Small Warm Animal, and What Has to Be Known
pools.covers: reading §9.0, §9.1.1, §9.1.2 · lecture 9.1 slides getting_home_without_a_signal, a_small_warm_animal, what_has_to_be_known

items.stem: A small animal is foraging far from its nest, well out of sight, smell, and hearing of it. Why can steering not get the animal home?

options.text: Steering works only while the goal can be sensed, and nothing at the nest reaches the animal where it is now.
options.why: Correct. Steering means moving forward, turning, and letting what the front end detects affect which way to turn. With no signal from the nest, there is nothing to turn toward, so there is nothing to steer by.

options.text: Steering works only in daylight, when the goal can be seen, and this animal is foraging long after dark.
options.why: Steering does not depend on sight. A worm steers toward a smell that grows stronger as it turns toward the source. Steering fails here because nothing at the nest reaches the animal at all, by any sense.

options.text: Steering works only along a path the animal has traveled before, and each night’s trip out takes a new path.
options.why: Steering does not follow a remembered path. It turns the animal toward whatever the front end detects from the goal. Steering fails here because nothing at the nest reaches the animal where it is now.

options.text: Steering works only once the animal knows how far it has gone, and its body provides no information about distance.
options.why: The animal’s vestibular system and proprioception do provide information about how far, and in which direction, it has gone. Steering needs none of that. It needs a signal from the goal, and nothing at the nest reaches the animal.

items.stem: Steering means moving forward, turning, and letting what the front end detects affect which way to turn. Which of these tasks could an animal accomplish by steering alone?

options.text: A shark swimming up a trail of blood in the water that grows stronger toward the injured fish.
options.why: Correct. The blood can be sensed all along the way, and it grows stronger toward its source. Steering works while the goal can be sensed, so turning toward the stronger signal is enough.

options.text: A squirrel crossing a wide field to nuts it buried weeks ago, which it cannot smell from the far side.
options.why: The squirrel cannot sense the nuts from where it starts, so there is nothing to steer by. It has to work out where the nuts are from other information, such as what it learned about the field before.

options.text: A pigeon flying home to its loft from hundreds of kilometers away, where nothing at the loft can be sensed.
options.why: Nothing at the loft reaches the pigeon, so there is nothing to steer by. Steering works only while the goal can be sensed, and the pigeon has to reach a place it cannot sense.

options.text: A person walking back to a house several streets away, which can be neither seen nor heard from there.
options.why: The house cannot be sensed from where the person starts, so steering has nothing to turn toward. Getting back needs information of other kinds, such as how far and which way the walk went.

items.stem: Far from its nest, with nothing at the nest to sense, the small animal in the dark still has two kinds of information. How do the two kinds differ?

options.text: Signals of its own movement provide information on how far, and which way, it has gone tonight; what it learned on earlier nights is about the ground itself.
options.why: Correct. The vestibular system and proprioception provide information about this trip: how far, and in which direction, the animal has gone. What it learned on earlier nights is about features of the ground, such as a fallen log or a slope down to a stream.

options.text: Signals of its own movement provide information on the features of the ground it passes; what it learned on earlier nights is how far, and which way, it went then.
options.why: That swaps the two. The vestibular system and proprioception provide information about the animal’s own movement, how far and which way it has gone. Features of the ground, such as a fallen log, are what it learned on earlier nights.

options.text: Signals of its own movement report the direction of the nest directly, as a smell from the nest would; what it learned on earlier nights is where beetles were plentiful.
options.why: A spot where beetles were plentiful is part of what the animal learned on earlier nights, but nothing reports the direction of the nest directly. Signals of its own movement provide information on how far, and which way, the animal has gone. From that information, the animal has to work out where the nest is.

options.text: Signals of its own movement provide information on how far it has gone but not which way; what it learned on earlier nights fills in the direction.
options.why: The vestibular system and proprioception provide information about both how far and in which direction the animal has gone. What it learned on earlier nights is about the ground, such as a fallen log or a slope down to a stream.

items.stem: A cat leaves its house at night to roam a neighborhood it has prowled for years. An hour later the cat is several streets away, where nothing at the house can be seen, heard, or smelled. Which information could the cat still use to work out the way home?

options.text: Signals of its own movement, about how far and which way it has gone, and what it learned about the streets on earlier nights.
options.why: Correct. Signals of its own movement and what it learned on earlier nights are the same two kinds of information the small animal in the dark still has. The cat’s vestibular system and proprioception provide information about how far, and in which direction, it has gone, and its earlier nights gave it knowledge of the ground.

options.text: A smell of the house that grows stronger as it turns toward home, and what it learned about the streets on earlier nights.
options.why: Nothing at the house can be smelled from where the cat is, so there is no growing smell to steer by. What the cat still has is information from its own movement and from what it learned on earlier nights.

options.text: Signals of its own movement, about how far and which way it has gone, and the direction that the sun high overhead gives it.
options.why: The cat’s own movement does provide information about how far and which way it has gone. But it is night, so there is no sun to use. Its other source is what it learned about the streets on earlier nights.

options.text: What it learned about the streets on earlier nights, and the sight of its house, which a cat can pick out in quite dim light.
options.why: The cat did learn about the streets on earlier nights. But the house cannot be seen from where it is. Its other source is its own movement, which provides information about how far and which way it has gone.

items.stem: The Arctic tern finds its way to feeding grounds it has never seen. A honeybee’s dance communicates to the hive which way to fly to a patch of flowers, and how far. What do the tern and the bee have in common with a small animal trying to get home to its nest?

options.text: Each acts on information about a place it cannot sense from where it is.
options.why: Correct. The same problem appears at far larger scales. The tern, the bee, and the small animal all have to reach a place they cannot sense from where they start.

options.text: Each follows a signal from the place that grows stronger as it gets closer.
options.why: A signal that grows stronger toward its source is what steering uses, and steering works only while the goal can be sensed. The tern, the bee, and the small animal all act on information about a place they cannot sense from where they are.

options.text: Each returns to a place it has already visited many times on earlier trips.
options.why: The tern reaches feeding grounds it has never seen, so having been there before is not what the three share. What they share is acting on information about a place they cannot sense from where they are.

options.text: Each passes on what it knows about the place to other animals of its kind.
options.why: Only the bee’s dance communicates a place to others. What the tern, the bee, and the small animal share is acting on information about a place they cannot sense from where they are.

items.stem: How is a living fish related to an early mammal, and what can living fish help show?

options.text: A fish is a distant cousin of the early mammal, and living fish help show what their shared ancestor could already do.
options.why: Correct. The fish is not the early mammal’s ancestor. Fish and mammals share an older ancestor, and what living fish can do helps show what that shared ancestor could already do.

options.text: A fish is an ancestor of the early mammal, and living fish help show what early mammals inherited unchanged from them.
options.why: Living fish are not ancestors of mammals. They are distant cousins, whose brains have kept changing too. What they help show is what the ancestor shared by fish and mammals could already do.

options.text: A fish is unrelated to the early mammal, and living fish help show only how one problem can be solved in unrelated ways.
options.why: Fish and mammals are related, as distant cousins that share an ancestor. That shared ancestry is why living fish help show what the common ancestor could already do.

options.text: A fish is a descendant of the early mammal, and living fish help show which abilities were lost on the return to water.
options.why: Fish are not descended from mammals. They are distant cousins, and living fish help show what the ancestor shared by fish and mammals could already do.

items.stem: Rats and mice, and living fish, both help in understanding how an early mammal found its way, but in different ways. How do their roles differ?

options.text: Rats and mice are small animals that forage at night and return to a nest, probably as early mammals did. Fish are distant cousins that help show what an older shared ancestor could do.
options.why: Correct. Most of what is known about the brain cells involved in finding the way comes from rats and mice, which probably live much as their distant ancestors did. Living fish are cousins rather than ancestors, and help show what the ancestor shared by fish and mammals could already do.

options.text: Rats and mice are distant cousins that help show what an older shared ancestor could do. Fish are small animals that forage at night and return to a nest, probably as early mammals did.
options.why: That swaps the two roles. Rats and mice, as small mammals that forage at night and return to a nest, serve as models for early mammals. Fish are the distant cousins whose living relatives help show what an older shared ancestor could do.

options.text: Rats and mice are unchanged survivors of the early mammals, so they show exactly how early mammals lived. Fish are the ancestors from which those early mammals came.
options.why: Neither half is right. Rats and mice are good models because they probably live much as their distant ancestors did, not because they are unchanged survivors. And fish are distant cousins of mammals, not their ancestors.

options.text: Rats and mice serve only for studying behavior, since little is known about their brain cells. Fish are the main source of what is known about the brain cells involved.
options.why: It is the other way around. Most of what is known about the brain cells involved in finding the way comes from rats and mice. Living fish help show what the ancestor shared by fish and mammals could already do.

items.stem: Why does a small, warm insect-eater have to cover a lot of ground?

options.text: Making its own body heat has an energy cost, and its brain cannot go without fuel even briefly, so it must find a lot of food, often.
options.why: Correct. A mammal’s cells burn fuel five to seven times faster than those of a same-sized reptile, and the brain cannot go without fuel even for a short time. For an eater of insects, finding that much food means covering a lot of ground.

options.text: Its cells burn fuel more slowly than a reptile’s, so it eats over a longer stretch of the day and wanders farther while it does so.
options.why: That reverses the comparison. A mammal’s cells burn fuel five to seven times faster than those of a reptile of the same size. It covers a lot of ground because it needs a lot of food, often.

options.text: Its body heat lets it go without food for long stretches, so it can travel far between meals to reach the richest spots.
options.why: Making body heat makes food more urgent, not less. The brain cannot go without fuel even for a short time, so a warm animal has to find a lot of food, and find it often.

options.text: A lizard of its size uses roughly ten times as much energy over a day, so the mammal has to race lizards to the insects.
options.why: That reverses the comparison. Over a whole day, a mammal uses roughly ten times as much energy as a lizard. The mammal covers a lot of ground because its own warm body needs a lot of food.

items.stem: A shrew and a lizard of about the same size hunt insects in the same leaf litter. How should their needs for food compare over a whole day?

options.text: The shrew needs far more energy over a day, so it has to find much more food, find it often, and cover more ground.
options.why: Correct. A mammal makes its own body heat, and over a whole day a mammal uses roughly ten times as much energy as a lizard. So the shrew has to find a lot of food, often, which for an insect-eater means covering a lot of ground.

options.text: The lizard needs far more energy over a day, so it has to find much more food, find it often, and cover more ground.
options.why: That reverses the comparison. It is the mammal that makes its own body heat, and over a whole day a mammal uses roughly ten times as much energy as a lizard.

options.text: The two need about the same energy, since animals of the same size need the same food whether or not they are warm.
options.why: Size alone does not set the need. A mammal’s cells burn fuel five to seven times faster than those of a reptile of the same size, so the warm animal needs far more food.

options.text: The shrew needs only a little more energy than the lizard, and its warm body lets it go longer between its meals.
options.why: The shrew needs far more energy, and a mammal’s brain cannot go without fuel even for a short time. A warm body makes meals more urgent, not less frequent.

items.stem: Two small, warm insect-eaters each forage out from a nest at night. One lives where insects are plentiful, and the other where insects are scarce. Which animal faces the harder problem of getting back home, and why?

options.text: The one where insects are scarce, since it must cover more ground to find enough food, and so ends up farther from home.
options.why: Correct. A warm body needs a lot of food, often, and for an eater of insects that means covering a lot of ground. Where insects are scarce, finding enough food means covering still more ground, and each meal draws the animal farther from its nest.

options.text: The one where insects are plentiful, since it eats more each night, and so its warm body comes to need more food and more ground.
options.why: Eating more where food is plentiful does not mean needing more. Both warm bodies need a lot of food. Where insects are scarce, finding that food means covering more ground, which leaves the animal farther from home.

options.text: Neither one, since a warm body needs little food, so either animal can find enough without leaving the sight or smell of its nest.
options.why: A warm body needs a lot of food, not a little: over a whole day, a mammal uses roughly ten times as much energy as a lizard. Covering a lot of ground to find that food is what takes the animal out of reach of its nest.

options.text: Both equally, since how far each animal travels depends only on its body heat, and not on whether insects are plentiful or scarce.
options.why: Body heat sets how much food the animal needs. How much ground it covers also depends on how hard that food is to find. Where insects are scarce, the animal covers more ground and ends up farther from home.

items.stem: A student says that because no one ever observed early mammals, nothing at all can be said about whether they were active at night. According to the reading, what is wrong with the student’s claim?

options.text: No one can know for sure, but activity at night can be inferred from indirect evidence: bones, genes, and comparisons with living animals.
options.why: Correct. The idea that early mammals were active mainly at night, or in dim light, is a long-standing hypothesis. It cannot be known for sure, and it is inferred from indirect evidence that converges on it.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since without observation the question lies outside science, and any claim about it is a guess with no evidence behind it.
options.why: The question cannot be settled for sure, but that does not leave it without evidence. Bones, genes, and comparisons with living animals provide indirect evidence, and much of it converges on activity at night or in dim light.

options.text: The question was settled once fossils showed that early mammals foraged only after dark, so it no longer rests on inference of any kind.
options.why: No fossil settles the question. The claim that early mammals were active at night, or in dim light, remains a hypothesis inferred from indirect evidence, and it has weak points.

options.text: The question is settled by living mammals, since every living mammal lineage is active at night and so must have inherited the habit.
options.why: Most living lineages of mammals are active at night, not every one, and even a majority would be evidence rather than proof. The claim remains a hypothesis inferred from several kinds of indirect evidence.

items.stem: Consider two claims about mammals. One is that a mammal uses roughly ten times as much energy as a lizard over a day. The other is that early mammals were active mainly at night. According to the reading, how firmly does each claim stand?

options.text: The energy comparison is stated as a fact. Activity at night in early mammals is a hypothesis, inferred from indirect evidence.
options.why: Correct. The energy comparison is stated as a fact about living mammals and lizards. Activity at night, or in dim light, is a long-standing hypothesis about early mammals, inferred from indirect evidence because no one observed them.

options.text: The energy comparison is a hypothesis, inferred from indirect evidence. Activity at night in early mammals is stated as a fact.
options.why: That reverses the two. The energy comparison is stated flatly, as a fact about living mammals and lizards. Activity at night is a hypothesis about early mammals, inferred from indirect evidence.

options.text: Both are stated as facts, since each rests on what is known about the bodies of the mammals living today.
options.why: The energy comparison is stated as a fact, but no one observed what early mammals did at night. The claim about early mammals is a hypothesis, and “probably active at night, or in dim light” is as far as the evidence goes.

options.text: Both are hypotheses, since neither one can be checked without observing animals that lived long ago.
options.why: Activity at night in early mammals is indeed a hypothesis. But the energy comparison is about living mammals and lizards, and it is stated flatly, as a fact.

items.stem: A biologist describes a living mammal with eyes suited to dim light, long whiskers, a keen sense of smell, and good hearing of high-pitched sounds. On the reasoning used for early mammals, which way of life would those features fit?

options.text: Activity at night, or in dim light, the way of life the same features are taken to fit in the first mammals.
options.why: Correct. Eyes suited to dim light, a keener sense of smell, hearing of high-pitched sounds, and whiskers are part of the converging evidence that early mammals were active at night, or in dim light. They are features that would be adaptive for a nocturnal way of life.

options.text: Activity by day, which cold-blooded animals need in order to stay warm, and which keeps the eyes in good light.
options.why: Cold-blooded animals do have to be active by day to stay warm. But a mammal makes its own body heat, and eyes suited to dim light, whiskers, keen smell, and high-pitched hearing fit activity at night, or in dim light.

options.text: Activity only in full darkness, since eyes suited to dim light could not work in any light at all.
options.why: Eyes suited to dim light fit dim light as well as darkness. The lost cones fit a long period of dim light as well as full darkness, so these features cannot single out full darkness.

options.text: No particular way of life, since the features of living mammals give no evidence about when they are active.
options.why: Features like these are part of the converging evidence about when animals are active. For early mammals, they are taken to fit activity at night, or in dim light.

items.stem: Which pairing correctly sorts one piece of evidence for the hypothesis that early mammals were active at night, and one weak point of that hypothesis?

options.text: For: mammals have whiskers and hear high-pitched sounds. Against: predatory dinosaurs with eyes suited to the dark appeared later.
options.why: Correct. Whiskers and hearing of high-pitched sounds fit an animal active in the dark. Predators with eyes suited to the dark meant the night was not entirely safe, which weakens the case.

options.text: For: predatory dinosaurs with eyes suited to the dark appeared later. Against: mammals have whiskers and hear high-pitched sounds.
options.why: That swaps the two. Whiskers and hearing of high-pitched sounds are part of the converging evidence for activity at night. Predatory dinosaurs with eyes suited to the dark are a weak point, since they made the night less safe.

options.text: For: some dinosaurs were probably partly warm-blooded. Against: most living lineages of mammals are active at night.
options.why: Both are misplaced. Partly warm-blooded dinosaurs are a weak point, since they make the night less safe. That most living lineages of mammals are active at night is evidence for the hypothesis.

options.text: For: mammals lost two of their four kinds of cone. Against: mammals have a keener sense of smell.
options.why: The cone losses do count as evidence. But a keener sense of smell counts for the hypothesis too, since it fits an animal active at night, so it is not a weak point.

items.stem: A classmate argues that because mammals lost two of their four kinds of cone, early mammals must have lived in full darkness. What is the problem with the argument?

options.text: The lost cones fit a long period of dim light as well as full darkness, so they give no reason to prefer darkness.
options.why: Correct. The cone losses are part of the converging evidence, but they fit dim light as well as darkness. The fit with dim light is one reason “probably active at night, or in dim light” is as far as the evidence goes.

options.text: The lost cones point the other way, since an animal active in darkness would need more kinds of cone, not fewer of them.
options.why: The cone losses do fit activity in poor light, and they count as evidence for it. The trouble is only that they fit a long period of dim light as well as full darkness.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since the cone losses settle when early mammals were active, with no need for other evidence.
options.why: The cone losses do not settle the question. They fit dim light as well as darkness, and the hypothesis as a whole is inferred from several kinds of indirect evidence.

options.text: The lost cones fit an animal active by day as well as one active at night, so they give no reason to prefer the night.
options.why: The cone losses are evidence for poor light, not for activity by day. What they cannot separate is a long period of dim light from full darkness.

items.stem: Cold-blooded animals have to be active by day to stay warm. Suppose it turned out that no dinosaur was even partly warm-blooded, and that none had eyes suited to the dark. How would that change the case that early mammals were active at night?

options.text: Two weak points would fall away, making the night look safer for a warm animal, but the case would still rest on inference.
options.why: Correct. The reasoning is that cold-blooded animals active by day would leave the night safer for an animal that keeps itself warm. Partly warm-blooded dinosaurs and predators with eyes suited to the dark are what weaken that reasoning. Without them the case is stronger, though it is still a hypothesis inferred from indirect evidence.

options.text: The case would be proven, since nothing would then stand against it, and early mammals would be known to be active at night.
options.why: Removing two weak points would strengthen the case, but it would not prove it. The claim would still be a hypothesis inferred from indirect evidence, and the lost cones would still fit dim light as well as darkness.

options.text: The case would be weaker, since cold-blooded dinosaurs would then have hunted at night, when prey was easier to catch.
options.why: Cold-blooded animals have to be active by day to stay warm, so cold-blooded dinosaurs would have left the night safer, not more dangerous. The case would be stronger.

options.text: The case would not change, since it rests only on the eyes of living mammals and not on anything about dinosaurs.
options.why: The case rests on several kinds of evidence, and some of its weak points come from what dinosaurs were like. Removing those weak points would strengthen it.

items.stem: Which observation supports the guess that early mammals had a home to return to?

options.text: Rats put on a bare laboratory platform settle on a home base within minutes, even with nothing there to hide in.
options.why: Correct. Rats settle on a home base readily, and small mammals living today forage out from a nest and come back to it. The rats and the small mammals living today together make it a reasonable guess that the earliest mammals did the same.

options.text: Mammals lost two of the four kinds of cone the earliest vertebrates had, and their eyes are suited to the dim light.
options.why: The lost cones and eyes suited to dim light are evidence that early mammals were active at night, or in dim light. They are not evidence about whether early mammals returned to a fixed spot.

options.text: A mammal’s cells burn fuel five to seven times faster than the cells of a reptile of the same size.
options.why: That supports the claim that a warm animal needs a lot of food, and so covers a lot of ground. It is not evidence about whether the animal returned to a fixed spot.

options.text: Most living lineages of mammals are active at night, and have whiskers and a keen sense of smell.
options.why: Nocturnal living lineages, whiskers, and a keen sense of smell are evidence that early mammals were active at night, or in dim light. The support for a place to return to comes from small mammals today, which forage out from a nest and come back to it.

items.stem: A student writes that because rats put on a bare platform settle on a home base within minutes, the first mammals must have had nests. How should the student’s claim be corrected?

options.text: The rats, like small mammals living today, make a home for the earliest mammals a reasonable guess, not a proven fact.
options.why: Correct. Living animals that settle on a home base and forage out from it make a home for early mammals likely. That the earliest mammals did the same is a reasonable guess, and no more.

options.text: The rats show the opposite, since they settled where there was nothing to hide in, so early mammals did without shelter.
options.why: The bare platform shows that rats settle on a home base even with nothing to hide in. That makes a home more likely for early mammals, not less, though only as a reasonable guess.

options.text: The rats are no evidence at all, since what living animals do cannot bear on how animals long extinct lived.
options.why: Comparisons with living animals are one of the main sources of evidence about early mammals, along with bones and genes. The rats make a home a reasonable guess, though not a proven fact.

options.text: The claim is correct as it stands, since what living rats do shows directly what the early mammals did long ago.
options.why: Rats are good models for early mammals, but what they do now does not show directly what early mammals did. A home for the earliest mammals is a reasonable guess.

items.stem: On the best reconstruction of how early mammals lived, what was one of the main problems they faced?

options.text: Covering a lot of ground in poor light to find food, and then getting back home again.
options.why: Correct. A warm body needed a lot of food, which meant covering a lot of ground. That ground was probably covered at night or in dim light, and probably with a home to return to. The whole picture is a reconstruction, inferred from indirect evidence.

options.text: Finding a little food close to home in daylight, while keeping out of sight of the dinosaurs.
options.why: Early mammals needed a lot of food, not a little, and were probably active at night or in dim light, not by day. The problem was covering a lot of ground in poor light and getting back home.

options.text: Staying warm through cold nights in the nest, and foraging only in the warmth of the day.
options.why: A mammal makes its own body heat, and early mammals were probably active at night or in dim light. On the reconstruction, the problem was covering a lot of ground in poor light and getting back home.

options.text: Wandering widely in poor light with no fixed home, and settling wherever the food ran out.
options.why: Early mammals probably had a home to return to, as small mammals today do. The problem, as reconstructed, included getting back home after covering a lot of ground in poor light.

items.stem: To reach a place that is out of reach of its senses, what four things does an animal need to know?

options.text: Which place is worth going to now, where it is now, where that place is, and which way to go.
options.why: Correct. One of the four, which place is worth going to now, depends on the animal’s state as well as on what it knows. The other three are where the animal is, where the goal is, and which way to go.

options.text: Where it is now, where that place is, which way to go, and how far it traveled on its last trip there.
options.why: How far a past trip ran is not among the four. The missing item is which place is worth going to now, which depends on the animal’s state as well as on what it knows.

options.text: Which place is worth going to now, where that place is, which way to go, and what the place smells like up close.
options.why: What a place smells like up close helps only once the animal is near enough to steer. The missing item is where the animal is now.

options.text: Which place is worth going to now, where it is now, where that place is, and how it got there the first time.
options.why: How the animal first got there is not among the four. The missing item is which way to go from where it is now.

items.stem: A hiker who knows a mountain well wants to get back to a cabin at the north end of its lake. After hours in thick fog, the hiker has no idea where on the mountain they now stand. Of the four things needed to reach a place out of reach of the senses, which one does the hiker lack?

options.text: Where they are now.
options.why: Correct. The hiker knows which place is worth going to and where that place is. Without knowing where they are now, the hiker cannot work out which way leads to the cabin.

options.text: Which place is worth going to now.
options.why: The hiker has a goal, the cabin, and wants to reach it. What is missing is where the hiker is now.

options.text: Where that place is.
options.why: The hiker knows the mountain well and knows the cabin sits at the north end of the lake. What is missing is where the hiker is now.

options.text: What that place looks like up close.
options.why: What the cabin looks like up close is not among the four things, and it would help only near the cabin. What is missing is where the hiker is now.

items.stem: Places matter to an animal largely because many valuable things stay where they are. Which of these gives an animal the least reason to remember the spot where it came upon it?

options.text: A swarm of gnats that drifts with the wind from one evening to the next.
options.why: Correct. A swarm that drifts does not stay where it was, so remembering the spot is of little use. Shelter, stores of food, and young in a nest stay put, which is why their places are worth knowing.

options.text: A burrow that the animal dug in a bank and sheltered in last winter.
options.why: Shelter stays put, so a burrow is exactly the kind of place worth remembering. The drifting swarm, which does not stay where it was, gives the least reason.

options.text: A store of seeds that the animal hid away under a fallen log in the autumn.
options.why: Stores of food hidden away stay where they are, so their places are worth knowing. The drifting swarm is the one that does not stay put.

options.text: A nest where the animal left its young while it went out to forage for food.
options.why: Young left in a nest stay where they are, which is one of the reasons places matter. The drifting swarm, which moves on, gives the least reason to remember a spot.

items.stem: A squirrel knows where it buried a store of nuts and where a small pond lies, and both are well out of sight and smell. After a long dry spell, having eaten its fill but gone without water all day, it heads for the pond. What follows from the squirrel’s choice?

options.text: Which remembered place is worth going to depends on the animal’s state as well as on what it knows.
options.why: Correct. The squirrel knows both places. Its thirst, an internal state, sets which remembered place is the worthy goal right now, just as hunger or thirst sets it for rats in a Y-shaped maze.

options.text: Knowing where the pond lies has replaced knowing where the nuts are, since an animal can know only one goal at a time.
options.why: The squirrel still knows where the nuts are; it simply does not need them now. An animal can know many places at once, and its state picks which one is worth going to.

options.text: The squirrel steered toward the pond, since a goal that can be sensed draws an animal more strongly than one it recalls.
options.why: Both places are out of sight and smell, so there is nothing to steer by. The squirrel went to the pond because its thirst made the pond the place worth going to.

options.text: Which place an animal goes to depends only on how recently it last visited each place it knows, and not on what it needs.
options.why: What the animal needs does matter. Which place is worth going to depends on the animal’s state, and the squirrel’s thirst is what made the pond its goal.

items.stem: An animal needs to know four things to reach a place out of reach of its senses. How does knowing which place is worth going to differ from knowing where that place is?

options.text: Which place is worth going to changes with the animal’s state, such as hunger or thirst; where the place is stays the same either way.
options.why: Correct. Hunger or thirst sets which remembered place is a worthy goal right now. The place itself does not move when the animal’s needs change. Rats learned where food and water were while needing neither, and later went to whichever they needed.

options.text: Which place is worth going to stays the same whatever the animal needs; where the place is changes with its state, such as hunger or thirst.
options.why: That swaps the two. The animal’s state, such as hunger or thirst, changes which place is worth going to. Where a place is does not change with what the animal needs.

options.text: Which place is worth going to is learned only while the animal is hungry or thirsty; where the place is can be learned at any time.
options.why: Learning does not have to wait for the need. Rats that ran a maze while neither hungry nor thirsty still went to the side they needed once they were made hungry or thirsty.

options.text: Which place is worth going to is fixed by what the animal has learned alone; where the place is depends on what it can sense now.
options.why: Which place is worth going to depends on the animal’s state as well as on what it knows. And where a place is can be known even when the place is out of reach of the senses.

items.stem: Rats ran a Y-shaped maze, with food in one branch and water in the other, while neither hungry nor thirsty. Once made hungry or thirsty, they went more often to the side they needed on their very first test. Why do those first choices count as goal-directed?

options.text: A change in what an outcome was worth changed the choice at once, on the first test after the need changed.
options.why: Correct. In goal-directed choice, changing what an outcome is worth changes the choice immediately. The rats had learned where things were, and on the first test their present need picked the side.

options.text: The rats had been trained many times while hungry or thirsty, so each choice repeated what had been rewarded before.
options.why: The rats were trained while neither hungry nor thirsty. Their choices changed on the very first test after they were made hungry or thirsty, which is what makes them goal-directed.

options.text: The rats came to prefer the side they needed only gradually, over many tests in their new state of need.
options.why: The preference appeared on the first test, not gradually. A choice that changes at once when an outcome’s worth changes is what goal-directed means.

options.text: The rats repeated whichever turn they had made most often in training, whatever they needed on the test.
options.why: The hungry and thirsty rats chose differently, so their choices did depend on what they needed. Repeating a trained turn regardless of need would not be goal-directed.

items.stem: Visitors tour a large zoo on a cool morning, passing a water fountain in one corner and a snack stand in another while neither thirsty nor hungry. That afternoon, hot and thirsty, and out of sight and earshot of both, several of them walk straight to the fountain, though they never drank from it. What follows from their choice?

options.text: They learned where things were before needing them, and their present need picked the goal at once.
options.why: Correct. The case parallels the rats in the Y-shaped maze. Where things were was learned without any need for them, and a change in what water was worth changed the choice immediately, which is goal-directed choice.

options.text: They learned the way to the fountain only once they became thirsty, since places are learned only when needed.
options.why: They walked straight to the fountain without searching, so they had learned where it was in the morning, while not thirsty. Learning where things are does not wait for the need.

options.text: They repeated a habit built up by drinking at the fountain many times, which their thirst then set off.
options.why: They never drank from the fountain, so no habit could have been built by drinking there. Their choice changed at once with their need, which is what makes it goal-directed.

options.text: They followed the sound of the running water, since a goal that can be sensed needs no knowledge of where it is.
options.why: Steering toward a sound would need no knowledge of where the goal is, but the fountain was out of earshot. With nothing to steer by, the visitors relied on where they had learned the fountain was.

items.stem: A wood mouse leaves its burrow at dusk and forages for an hour, until nothing at the burrow can be seen, smelled, or heard. In a few sentences, explain why steering cannot bring the mouse home, and name the two kinds of information it still has to work with.
items.answer: Steering means moving forward and turning according to what the front end detects, so it works only while the goal can be sensed. Nothing at the burrow reaches the mouse where it is now, so there is no signal to turn toward and nothing to steer by. What the mouse still has is information of other kinds. Its vestibular system and proprioception provide information about how far, and in which direction, it has gone. It also has whatever it learned about this ground on earlier nights, such as a fallen log or a slope down to a stream. From these two kinds of information, it has to work out where the burrow is and which way to go.
rubric: Says steering works only while the goal can be sensed.
Says nothing at the burrow reaches the mouse, so there is nothing to steer by.
Names signals of the mouse’s own movement (the vestibular system, proprioception) as providing how far and in which direction it has gone.
Names what the mouse learned about the ground on earlier occasions as the second kind of information.

items.stem: In one study, rats ran a Y-shaped maze with food at the end of one branch and water at the end of the other. They ran it while neither hungry nor thirsty. In a short paragraph, say what the rats did on their first test after being made hungry or thirsty. Then explain what we can conclude from their choices about how an animal picks which place to go to.
items.answer: On their first test, the hungry rats went to the food side more often than to the water side, and the thirsty rats did the reverse. So the rats had learned where the food and the water were, even though they needed neither while learning. Which place they went to depended on what they needed now. Which place is worth going to depends on the animal’s state, such as hunger or thirst, as well as on what it knows. The choice was also goal-directed: changing what an outcome was worth changed the choice immediately, on the very first test.
rubric: Says the hungry rats went more often to the food side and the thirsty rats more often to the water side.
Says the rats had learned where things were while needing neither.
Says which place is worth going to depends on the animal’s state (hunger or thirst) as well as on what it knows.
Says the choice changed immediately, on the first test, which makes it goal-directed.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe one of the main problems early mammals faced, as it is reconstructed. Then take two parts of that reconstruction: when early mammals were active, and whether they had a home. For each, say what the evidence is and how firmly it supports the claim.
items.answer: On the best reconstruction, early mammals had to cover a lot of ground in poor light to find enough food, and then get back home again. That they were active mainly at night, or in dim light, is a long-standing hypothesis. No one observed them, so the hypothesis is inferred from indirect evidence. Most living mammal lineages are active at night. Mammals also lost two kinds of cone, and they have eyes suited to dim light, a keen sense of smell, hearing of high-pitched sounds, and whiskers. The hypothesis also has weak points, so “probably active at night, or in dim light” is as far as the evidence goes. That they had a home to return to rests on small mammals today, which forage out from a nest and come back to it. The claim of a home also rests on rats, which settle on a home base within minutes even on a bare platform. That the earliest mammals did the same is a reasonable guess, not a known fact.
rubric: States the problem as covering a lot of ground in poor light and getting back home again.
Says activity at night or in dim light is a hypothesis inferred from indirect evidence, because no one observed early mammals.
Gives at least one piece of that evidence (most living mammal lineages active at night; lost cones and eyes suited to dim light; keen smell, high-pitched hearing, or whiskers).
Says the home rests on what living small mammals do (foraging out from a nest and back, or rats settling on a home base).
Says a home for the earliest mammals is a reasonable guess, not a known fact.

pools.title: Knowing Where a Goal Is, and How Each Cue Fails
pools.covers: reading §9.1.3, §9.1.4, §9.1.5 · lecture 9.1 slides six_kinds_of_knowledge, cues_and_how_each_fails, tolmans_test

items.stem: What is a beacon?

options.text: Something at or beside a goal that can be sensed from farther away than the goal, which an animal can head for knowing only that it is near the goal.
options.why: Correct. A beacon, like a lighthouse marking a harbor that sailors cannot see, can be sensed from farther away than the goal itself. Using one needs only the knowledge that it is near the goal, and it helps only from where it can be sensed.

options.text: Knowledge of what the goal’s surroundings look like, which lets an animal recognize the goal’s neighborhood once it is close, even when nothing at the goal can be sensed.
options.why: That describes knowing what the goal’s surroundings look like, which works only near the goal. A beacon is something at or beside the goal that can itself be sensed from farther away.

options.text: A smell or other signal that grows stronger toward its source, which an animal can follow by turning toward wherever the signal is stronger, until the signal runs out.
options.why: That describes a gradient, which leads to its source only as far as it reaches. A beacon is a marker at or beside a goal, sensed from farther away than the goal itself.

options.text: Knowledge of where the goal lies relative to other places, which lets an animal head straight for the goal from a starting point it has never used before.
options.why: That describes the highest kind of knowledge about location, knowing where places lie relative to one another. A beacon needs none of that, only the knowledge that the beacon is near the goal.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Something sensed at or beside a goal, which an animal can approach directly without knowing where the goal lies relative to anything else”.

options.text: beacon
options.why: Correct. A beacon, such as a lighthouse marking a harbor or a tall tree beside a nest, is sensed from farther away than the goal. Using one needs only the knowledge that it is near the goal.

options.text: landmark
options.why: A landmark is a recognizable feature of the surroundings, such as a large tree, a rock, or a building. The definition describes something an animal approaches directly, knowing only that it is near the goal.

options.text: place learning
options.why: Place learning is learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes. Place learning names a kind of learning, not something an animal senses at or beside a goal.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it. Latent learning is not something sensed at a goal.

items.stem: A camper pitches a tent at the foot of a tall radio mast whose red light can be seen from far across the surrounding fields. Coming back after dark, the camper cannot see the tent, but walks toward the red light and reaches it. What does the camper need to know for the light to lead back to the tent?

options.text: Only that the mast stands beside the tent, since heading for the mast then brings the camper to the tent.
options.why: Correct. The mast is a beacon, something beside the goal that can be sensed from farther away. Using a beacon needs only the knowledge that it is near the goal.

options.text: Where the tent and the mast lie relative to the other features of the fields, so that a way between them can be worked out.
options.why: That is the highest kind of knowledge, where places lie relative to one another. Heading for a beacon needs none of that knowledge. Knowing that the mast is beside the tent is enough.

options.text: The path walked out from the tent, turn by turn, so that the camper can follow the same path back again to the tent.
options.why: That would be a familiar path, which works only along its own path. Heading for the light works from anywhere the light can be seen, and needs only the knowledge that the mast is beside the tent.

options.text: How far, and in which direction, the camper has walked since leaving the tent, all combined into one estimate.
options.why: That is what the camper’s own movement provides, and it points back to the start. Heading for a light beside the tent needs none of that estimate, only the knowledge that the mast is next to the tent.

items.stem: Six kinds of knowledge about where a goal is can be ranked from lowest to highest. On what basis are they ranked?

options.text: By how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, each kind of knowledge still works.
options.why: Correct. What matters for the problem is what each kind of knowledge lets an animal do, and from where. Sensing the goal itself works only close by, while knowing where places lie relative to one another works from a new starting point to any place the animal knows.

options.text: By how much detail and accuracy each kind of knowledge contains about the goal and the places near it.
options.why: The kinds do vary in detail and accuracy, but that is not what ranks them. What matters is what each lets an animal do, and from where: how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, it still works.

options.text: By the order in which an animal acquires each kind of knowledge as it learns its way around a new place.
options.why: The kinds are not stages that an animal passes through as it learns, and an animal can have several at once. Instead, the kinds are ranked by how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, each still works.

options.text: By how long ago each kind of knowledge first appeared in the evolution of the lineage that led to mammals.
options.why: The kinds are not stages that a lineage passed through as it evolved. Instead, the kinds are ranked by what each lets an animal do: how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, each still works.

items.stem: A researcher wants to find out how high a rat’s knowledge about where its food is ranks among the six kinds. Which test would best separate the higher kinds from the lower ones?

options.text: Start the rat from a place it has never used, beyond where it can sense the food or anything beside it, and see if it heads for the food.
options.why: Correct. The kinds are ranked by how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, each still works. A test from a new and distant start is where the lower kinds stop leading to the food.

options.text: Start the rat from its usual place, on its familiar path, and time how quickly it reaches the food over many trials in a row, day after day.
options.why: On a familiar path, several kinds of knowledge produce the same behavior, so speed there cannot rank them. The kinds differ in how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, each still works.

options.text: Start the rat close enough to smell the food, and measure how directly it heads for the food when it is started from each side in turn.
options.why: Close enough to smell the food, even the lowest kind, sensing the goal itself, works. The kinds differ only farther away and from new starting points, which a test from close by never reaches.

options.text: Start the rat from its usual place, and count how many trials it takes before it can reach the food without making a wrong turn.
options.why: How fast the rat learns does not show which kind of knowledge it ends up with. The kinds are ranked by how far from the goal, and from how new a starting point, each still works.

items.stem: What does knowing what a goal’s surroundings look like let an animal do?

options.text: Recognize the goal’s neighborhood once close, even when nothing at the goal can be sensed from afar, but only near the goal.
options.why: Correct. A person who cannot see their car in a large parking lot may still recognize the corner where they left it. Knowing the surroundings helps only near the goal, where they still look much as they did.

options.text: Head for a marker beside the goal from anywhere the marker can be sensed, though only from within the range at which it can be sensed.
options.why: That describes using a beacon, something at or beside the goal sensed from farther away. Knowing the surroundings works even when nothing at the goal can be sensed from afar, but only close to the goal.

options.text: Reach the goal from far away by following a path already known, though only by staying on that path.
options.why: That describes a familiar path, like a set of directions. Knowing what the goal’s surroundings look like works only near the goal, where the surroundings still look much as they did.

options.text: Head straight for the goal from any starting point at all, though only for goals the animal has visited before.
options.why: That describes knowing where places lie relative to one another, the highest kind. Knowing the goal’s surroundings helps only near the goal, where they still look much as they did.

items.stem: A swimmer leaves a towel on a crowded beach. Coming back from the water, the swimmer cannot pick out the towel among hundreds of others. But the swimmer recognizes the lifeguard stand and a striped umbrella as they looked from the towel, and so finds the towel. What would that knowledge do for the swimmer from the far end of the beach?

options.text: Little or nothing, since from that far away the stand and the umbrella no longer look as they did from the towel.
options.why: Correct. Knowing what a goal’s surroundings look like helps only near the goal, where the surroundings still look much as they did.

options.text: Lead straight to the towel from anywhere on the beach, since knowing how the stand and the umbrella looked from the towel shows where the towel lies.
options.why: Knowing how the stand and the umbrella looked from the towel does not show where the towel lies from far away, where they look different. Knowing a goal’s surroundings helps only near the goal.

options.text: Lead back along the path the swimmer walked from the towel down to the water, and from there to the towel.
options.why: Following a known path is a different kind of knowledge, which works only along that path. Recognizing the towel’s surroundings helps only near the towel, where they still look much as they did.

options.text: Lead straight back to the spot where the swimmer first arrived on the beach that morning, from anywhere at all.
options.why: Getting back to the start from anywhere is a different kind of knowledge, and it leads only to the start. Recognizing the towel’s surroundings helps only near the towel.

items.stem: Where does knowing a familiar path, like a set of directions, stop working?

options.text: A familiar path leads much farther than any beacon can be sensed, but only along its own path, so straying leaves nothing to get back on course.
options.why: Correct. Directions such as “past the park, left at the gas station” can lead far beyond where any beacon can be seen, heard, or smelled. But someone who misses the turn has nothing in the directions to get back on course.

options.text: A familiar path leads to the goal from anywhere that a marker beside the goal can be sensed, but no farther than the marker can be sensed.
options.why: That is the limit of a beacon, which helps only from where it can be sensed. A familiar path leads much farther, but only along its own path.

options.text: A familiar path leads straight back to the start from anywhere at all, but gives no information about how to reach any other place.
options.why: That is the limit of knowing the way back to the start. A familiar path does lead to its goal, but only for an animal that stays on the path.

options.text: A familiar path leads to the goal once the goal’s surroundings come into view, but only near the goal, where the surroundings still look the same as before.
options.why: That is the limit of recognizing the goal’s surroundings, which helps only near the goal. A familiar path leads much farther, but only along its own path.

items.stem: A driver new to a town has directions from the depot to a customer: right at the church, left at the bakery, fourth house on the right. Past the church, the road is closed, and the driver turns down a side street the directions never mention. What can the directions do for the driver now?

options.text: Nothing more until the driver finds the way back onto the roads they name, since directions work only along their own path.
options.why: Correct. Directions can lead much farther than any beacon can be sensed, but only along their own path. Someone who has left the path has nothing in the directions to get back on course.

options.text: Point the driver toward the customer’s house from the side street, since the directions name every turn between the depot and the house.
options.why: Naming every turn on one path is not the same as knowing where places lie relative to one another. Off the path, the directions give no direction to the house at all.

options.text: Lead the driver straight back to the depot, since anyone who can follow directions out can also follow them home from anywhere.
options.why: Getting back to the start from anywhere is a different kind of knowledge. Directions work only along their own path, and the driver has left it.

options.text: Help the driver choose the shortest detour, since the church and the bakery both lie along the way to the customer’s house.
options.why: Knowing which places lie along one path does not show where they lie relative to the side street. Working out a detour needs knowledge of where places lie relative to one another, which directions do not provide.

items.stem: Knowing a familiar path and knowing the way back to the start can each lead an animal far beyond where it can sense its goal. How do the two kinds of knowledge differ?

options.text: A familiar path leads to its goal but only along its own path; the way back to the start works from anywhere but leads only to the start.
options.why: Correct. Directions lead far, but someone who misses a turn has nothing to get back on course. A hiker who knows the trailhead lies a mile east can head straight there from anywhere, but that gives no information about reaching a lake to the north.

options.text: A familiar path works from anywhere but leads only to the start; the way back to the start leads to any goal but only along a path walked before.
options.why: That swaps the two. A familiar path works only along its own path, and the way back to the start works from anywhere, with no path, but leads only to the start.

options.text: A familiar path works only near the goal, where its surroundings look the same; the way back to the start works from anywhere and leads to any place.
options.why: Working only near the goal is the limit of recognizing its surroundings, not of a familiar path. And the way back to the start leads only to the start, not to any place.

options.text: A familiar path leads to its goal but only along its own path; the way back to the start leads to any known place, but only from the start itself.
options.why: A familiar path does work only along its own path. But the way back to the start works from anywhere, and it leads to one place only, the start.

items.stem: A kayaker zigzags among islands on a foggy lake for an hour, and knows that the launch dock, where the trip began, now lies about two kilometers to the southwest. The kayaker then decides to paddle to a café on the far shore instead. What does knowing the way back to the dock give the kayaker?

options.text: A straight course to the dock from where the kayak is now, but no information on how to reach the café.
options.why: Correct. Knowing the way back to the start works from anywhere, without following a path. But it leads to one place only, so it gives no information about reaching a third place such as the café.

options.text: A straight course to the café as well, since knowing where the dock lies from here is enough to work out where any place lies.
options.why: Knowing where one place lies from here does not show where other places lie. Reaching a third place from a new position needs knowledge of where places lie relative to one another.

options.text: No course to the dock at all until the kayaker paddles back along the same zigzag path taken among the islands.
options.why: Knowing the way back to the start does not depend on retracing a path. Knowing the way back leads straight to the start from anywhere.

options.text: A course to the dock only once the dock comes into view through the fog, from close enough to make it out.
options.why: Reaching a goal only once it can be sensed is the lowest kind of knowledge. Knowing the way back to the start leads there from anywhere, even while the dock cannot be seen.

items.stem: Knowing the way back to the start and knowing where places lie relative to one another can both lead an animal straight to a place it cannot sense. Neither kind needs a path to follow. What can knowing where places lie do that knowing the way back to the start cannot?

options.text: Lead from a new starting point to any place the animal knows, including by a route it has never taken.
options.why: Correct. Knowing the way back to the start leads to one place only. Knowing where places lie relative to one another lets the way between any two of them be worked out, which is what a detour or a shortcut needs.

options.text: Lead to a goal from very far away, well beyond the reach of any marker, smell, or sound from the goal.
options.why: Both kinds work far beyond the reach of anything sensed at the goal. What only knowing where places lie can do is lead to any known place, not just the start.

options.text: Lead to a goal while nothing at the goal, or beside it, can be sensed from the place where the animal now is.
options.why: Both kinds work while nothing at the goal can be sensed. What only knowing where places lie can do is lead to any known place, not just the start.

options.text: Lead back to the start from anywhere, where knowing the way back works only along a path walked before.
options.why: That reverses the case. Knowing the way back to the start already works from anywhere, without a path. The limit of knowing the way back is that it leads only to the start.

items.stem: A city resident usually rides a bus to work, and the office building cannot be seen until the last block. One morning the bus is canceled. The resident walks instead, cuts through a neighborhood never walked before, and arrives at the office directly. Of the six kinds of knowledge about where a goal is, which does the walk call for?

options.text: Knowing where places lie relative to one another, so that the way between home and the office can be worked out.
options.why: Correct. Only the highest kind can lead to a known place by a route never taken. In the same way, a person who knows a town well can cut across a park to reach a shop by a way never walked before.

options.text: Knowing a familiar path, so that the turns the bus takes every morning can be followed on foot instead.
options.why: The walk did not follow the bus’s turns. The walk crossed a neighborhood the resident had never walked, and a familiar path works only along its own path.

options.text: Knowing the way back to the start, so that the resident can head straight for the office from anywhere in the city.
options.why: Knowing the way back to the start leads to one place only, the start. The resident was heading away from home, to the office.

options.text: Knowing what the office’s surroundings look like, so that the resident can recognize the right block once it is near.
options.why: Recognizing the office’s surroundings helps only near the office. That knowledge could guide the last block, but not the walk through a neighborhood the resident had never crossed.

items.stem: Are the six kinds of knowledge about where a goal is stages that an animal passes through as it learns a place?

options.text: No. The kinds are ranked by what each lets an animal do, and an animal can have several kinds at once.
options.why: Correct. The six kinds are not stages that an animal passes through as it learns, or that a lineage passed through as it evolved. An animal can have several kinds of knowledge at once.

options.text: Yes. An animal first senses the goal itself, then learns a beacon, and works up one kind at a time to the highest.
options.why: The ranking is by what each kind lets an animal do, not by when it is learned. An animal can have several kinds at once.

options.text: No. The kinds are stages that a lineage passed through as it evolved, rather than stages in one animal’s learning.
options.why: The kinds are not evolutionary stages either. Instead, the kinds are ranked by what each lets an animal do, and an animal can have several at once.

options.text: No. An animal can have only one kind at a time, and it switches from one kind to another as its setting changes.
options.why: An animal can have several kinds of knowledge at once. The kinds are ranked by what each lets an animal do, and they are not stages in learning.

items.stem: On a first day on a new campus, a student comes to recognize the surroundings of the library. The student also follows one way from a dorm to a lecture hall, and cuts across a lawn never crossed before to reach the dining hall. A friend says this is impossible. People learn particular spots first, the friend says, then the paths between them, and only later where places lie relative to one another. Which reply fits the reading?

options.text: There is little evidence for that order, and many people learn all three kinds of knowledge on their first visit to a new place.
options.why: Correct. Researchers once proposed that order, but there is little evidence for it. The six kinds are ranked by what each lets a person or animal do, not stages, and a person or animal can have several at once.

options.text: The order holds for other animals, which learn new places slowly, but people skip the early stages because they learn new places much faster.
options.why: The kinds are not stages for other animals either. Instead, the kinds are ranked by what each lets an animal do, and an animal can have several at once.

options.text: The order holds, so the student must have learned the dining hall’s surroundings first, before crossing the lawn toward it.
options.why: Recognizing a goal’s surroundings helps only near the goal, and the order itself has little evidence behind it. Many people learn all three kinds on a first visit.

options.text: The order holds for evolution, since the kinds of knowledge arose in that sequence in the lineage leading to humans.
options.why: The kinds are not stages that a lineage passed through as it evolved, any more than they are stages of learning. There is little evidence for the order the friend describes.

items.stem: In finding the way, how does a cue differ from knowledge?

options.text: A cue is something in the world, or in the animal’s own movement, that its senses detect; knowledge is what it has learned about how a cue relates to its goal.
options.why: Correct. A smell, a tree, or the sun is a cue, not knowledge. The knowledge is what the animal has learned about how that cue relates to its goal.

options.text: A cue is what the animal has learned about how a feature relates to its goal; knowledge is the feature itself, just as the animal’s senses detect it as it moves.
options.why: That swaps the two. The feature its senses detect, such as a tree, is the cue. What the animal has learned about how the tree relates to its goal is the knowledge.

options.text: A cue is something in the world that the animal’s senses detect; knowledge includes the animal’s own movement, which it senses from within.
options.why: The animal’s own movement is a cue too, one of several the world provides. Knowledge is what the animal has learned about how a cue relates to its goal.

options.text: A cue is used only while an animal first learns an area; knowledge then replaces it, so that cues are no longer needed once the animal’s learning is done.
options.why: Cues are how an animal learns its knowledge, and also how it keeps that knowledge up to date. The cue is what the senses detect, and the knowledge is what has been learned about how it relates to the goal.

items.stem: A squirrel buries an acorn near a large oak and comes back for it a week later. Which of these is knowledge, rather than a cue?

options.text: That the acorn lies a few steps north of the oak.
options.why: Correct. Knowledge is what the animal has learned about how a cue relates to its goal. The relation between the oak and the buried acorn is something the squirrel has learned.

options.text: The sight of the oak as the squirrel comes toward it.
options.why: The oak as the squirrel sees it is a cue, a feature its senses detect. Knowledge is what it has learned about how the oak relates to the acorn.

options.text: The smell of the acorn in the soil, once it is close.
options.why: A smell is a cue, something the senses detect. Knowledge is what the squirrel has learned about how a cue relates to its goal.

options.text: The squirrel’s own steps and turns as it moves along.
options.why: The animal’s own movement is a cue, one its senses detect as it moves. Knowledge is what it has learned about how a cue relates to its goal.

items.stem: Why does an estimate of position built only from an animal’s own steps and turns drift?

options.text: Every small estimate of a step or turn has some error, the estimate includes them all, and nothing in the signals shows how far it has drifted.
options.why: Correct. Each step and turn has to be combined into one estimate of position, so every small error stays in it. Nothing in the signals themselves shows how large the error has grown.

options.text: Each step and turn is sensed without any error, but the animal can combine them only over a short distance before it loses count of them all.
options.why: The trouble is not a limit on how many steps can be combined. Every small estimate of a step or turn has some error, and all of those errors stay in the estimate.

options.text: The errors in the steps cancel out over a long path, but each turn adds an error that nothing in the signals can show.
options.why: Errors from steps stay in the estimate just as errors from turns do. The estimate includes every small error, and nothing in the signals shows how far it has drifted.

options.text: An animal’s own movement gives only the direction it has gone, not how far, so the distance has to be guessed from elapsed time.
options.why: An animal’s own movement gives both how far and which way it has gone. The trouble is that every small error in either stays in the estimate.

items.stem: A walker in thick fog keeps track of position only from steps and turns. Early on, the walker misjudges one turn by a few degrees, and then walks straight ahead for a long way, judging every later step correctly. What happens to the error in the walker’s estimate of position as the walk goes on?

options.text: The error grows larger and larger, since the misjudged turn sends each step that follows it in the wrong direction.
options.why: Correct. An error in heading does particular harm, because it becomes a growing error in position as the path goes on.

options.text: The error stays the same size, since it was made only once, at one turn, and every step after the turn was judged correctly.
options.why: One misjudged turn is enough. Each later step is taken in the wrong direction, so the error in position grows as the walk goes on.

options.text: The error shrinks, since the many correctly judged steps that follow the turn gradually average out the one misjudged turn.
options.why: Later steps do not average away an error in heading. Each one is taken in the wrong direction, so the error in position grows.

options.text: The error disappears once the walker stops, since the steps and turns themselves show the walker how far the estimate has drifted.
options.why: Nothing in the signals from steps and turns shows how far the estimate has drifted. And an error in heading grows into a larger error in position the farther the walker goes.

items.stem: A mouse foraging along a creek steps onto a floating leaf, drifts a few meters downstream on it, and climbs off onto the bank. If the mouse kept track of its position only from its own steps and turns, what would its estimate be once it climbed off?

options.text: Off by about the distance it drifted, since the leaf moved it without any steps for it to register.
options.why: Correct. An animal that is swept along or carried has moved without stepping, which its own steps cannot register.

options.text: Accurate, since the leaf’s drift jostled the mouse, and the jostling registered as steps in the direction it drifted.
options.why: Being carried moves an animal without stepping, so its own steps cannot register the drift. The estimate is off by about the distance the leaf carried it.

options.text: Off by twice the distance it drifted, since the drift registered as steps taken in the opposite direction.
options.why: The drift does not register as steps in any direction. Being carried moves an animal without stepping, so the estimate is off by about the distance it drifted.

options.text: Accurate, since the drift lasted only a few seconds, too short a time for any error in the estimate to build up.
options.why: How long the drift lasted does not matter. The mouse moved without stepping, so its own steps registered none of the drift.

items.stem: What is a landmark?

options.text: A recognizable feature of the surroundings, such as a large tree, a rock, or a building.
options.why: Correct. A landmark is a recognizable feature of the surroundings, and an animal can learn where it lies relative to a goal or a route. Landmarks have shortcomings too: one can move, change with the seasons, or look like another.

options.text: Something at or beside a goal that can be sensed from farther away, which an animal heads for knowing only that it is near the goal.
options.why: That describes a beacon. A landmark is any recognizable feature of the surroundings, and what matters is its position relative to a goal or a route.

options.text: A smell or other signal that grows stronger toward its source, which an animal can follow until the signal runs out somewhere.
options.why: That describes a gradient, which leads toward its source only as far as it reaches. A landmark is a recognizable feature of the surroundings, such as a tree, a rock, or a building.

options.text: What an animal has learned about how a feature of its surroundings relates to the place it is trying to reach.
options.why: That is knowledge, not a landmark. The landmark is the feature itself, a cue the senses detect. The knowledge is what the animal has learned about how the landmark relates to the goal.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A recognizable feature of the surroundings, such as a large tree, a rock, or a building”.

options.text: landmark
options.why: Correct. A landmark is a recognizable feature of the surroundings, such as a large tree, a rock, or a building. An animal can learn where a landmark lies relative to a goal or a route.

options.text: place learning
options.why: Place learning is learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes. Place learning names a kind of learning, not a feature of the surroundings.

options.text: homology
options.why: Homology is a resemblance between two species that both inherited from a common ancestor. Homology is not a feature of the surroundings.

options.text: response learning
options.why: Response learning is learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to. Response learning names a kind of learning, not a feature of the surroundings.

items.stem: A landmark and the shape of the surroundings are both parts of the world that an animal can use to find its way. How do they differ in the ways they fail?

options.text: A landmark can move, change with the seasons, or look like another; shape stays the same across seasons, but a symmetric space gives two answers.
options.why: Correct. Walls, banks, and the edges of a clearing stay the same while colors and plants change. Shape fails in another way: in a rectangular room, a corner and the corner diagonally opposite it look the same by shape alone.

options.text: A landmark stays the same across the seasons, but it can look like another one; shape changes with the seasons, as the plants grow and the colors change.
options.why: That swaps the seasonal half. Plants and colors change, but walls, banks, and edges stay the same from season to season. It is a landmark that can change with the seasons.

options.text: A landmark can move or change with the seasons; shape never fails, since walls and edges stay the same in every kind of space.
options.why: Shape fails too. A symmetric space gives two equally good answers, and an open plain has no shape to use at all.

options.text: A landmark gives only a direction, never a position; shape gives a position, but only on open ground with no walls or edges.
options.why: A nearby landmark pins down position closely. And open ground is where shape fails, since an open plain has no shape to use.

items.stem: How does a nearby landmark differ from a distant one in what it gives an animal?

options.text: A nearby one changes with every step, so it pins down position closely but only nearby; a distant one barely changes, giving a direction but little about position.
options.why: Correct. How useful a landmark is depends on its distance. A nearby object changes its appearance with every step, while a distant one barely changes as the animal moves.

options.text: A nearby one gives a direction but little about position; a distant one pins down position more closely, since it can be seen from so much farther away.
options.why: That swaps the two. A distant landmark barely changes as the animal moves, so it gives a direction and indicates little about position. A nearby one pins down position closely.

options.text: A nearby one pins down position closely, but only nearby; a distant one gives no steady direction at all, since it barely changes as the animal moves.
options.why: A nearby landmark does pin down position closely, but only nearby. A distant landmark’s barely changing is exactly what lets it give a direction. What a distant landmark indicates little about is position.

options.text: A nearby one changes with every step, so it is of no use until the animal stops; a distant one barely changes, so it pins down position anywhere.
options.why: A nearby landmark’s changing appearance is what makes it useful, since it pins down position closely. A distant one barely changes, so it gives a direction but little about position.
