items.stem: A sailor anchored offshore can see a mountain peak far inland and a buoy a few dozen meters from the boat. The anchor slips, and the boat drifts a hundred meters. From which of the two landmarks can the sailor better judge how far the boat has moved, and why?

options.text: The buoy, since a nearby landmark changes a great deal with movement, while the peak barely changes and gives mainly a direction.
options.why: Correct. A nearby landmark changes its appearance with every movement, so it pins down position closely, but only nearby. A distant one barely changes, so it gives a direction but indicates little about position.

options.text: The peak, since a distant landmark stays steady while the boat moves around it, which makes it the more reliable guide to position.
options.why: Staying steady is exactly why a distant landmark indicates little about position. The peak barely changes as the boat drifts, while the buoy changes a great deal, which pins down position closely.

options.text: The peak, since a landmark that can be seen from much farther away pins down position over a much larger area.
options.why: Being visible from far away does not make a landmark good for position. A distant landmark barely changes as the observer moves, so it gives a direction but little about position.

options.text: Neither, since any landmark gives only a direction to follow and never any information about the observer’s position.
options.why: A nearby landmark does pin down position closely, because its appearance changes with every movement. Only a distant landmark is limited mainly to giving a direction.

items.stem: The sun and a distant landmark can each give an animal a direction. How do their shortcomings differ?

options.text: The sun moves through the day and the season, and is gone at night; a distant landmark barely changes as the animal moves, so it indicates little about position.
options.why: Correct. The sun gives a direction, but it moves through the day and the season, and there is none at night or under cover. A distant landmark also gives a direction, and its shortcoming is that it indicates little about where the animal is.

options.text: The sun pins down position closely but moves through the day; a distant landmark gives a direction, but its appearance changes with every single step the animal takes.
options.why: Changing with every step is true of a nearby landmark, not a distant one. And the sun gives a direction, not a close fix on position.

options.text: The sun keeps the same path across the sky in every season; a distant landmark changes its appearance with every step, so it gives no steady direction.
options.why: The sun’s path across the sky changes with the season. And a distant landmark barely changes as the animal moves, which is why it gives a steady direction but little about position.

options.text: The sun and a distant landmark fail in the same way, at night, when neither can be seen, and by day they give equally good information about position.
options.why: They do not fail in the same way. The sun also moves through the day and changes its path with the season, and a distant landmark indicates little about position at any hour.

items.stem: A mouse learns that food is always in one corner of a plain rectangular box with no other features. If the mouse relies on the shape of the box alone, which corners would look right to it?

options.text: The correct corner and the corner diagonally opposite it, since the two look the same by shape alone.
options.why: Correct. A symmetric space gives two equally good answers. In a rectangular room, a corner and the corner diagonally opposite it look the same by shape alone.

options.text: The correct corner alone, since each corner of a rectangle meets its long wall and its short wall in its own way.
options.why: In a rectangle, the corner diagonally opposite the correct one looks the same by shape alone. A symmetric space gives two equally good answers.

options.text: Any of the four corners, since the shape of a closed box gives no information at all about which corner is which.
options.why: Shape does narrow the choice. Shape rules out two corners, and leaves the correct corner and its diagonal twin, which look the same by shape alone.

options.text: The correct corner and the corner beside it along the same long wall, since both corners lie on that one wall.
options.why: The corner beside the correct one along a long wall is its mirror image, not its twin. By shape alone, the corner diagonally opposite looks the same.

items.stem: The shape of the surroundings stays the same from season to season, while colors and plants change. For which of these animals would shape give nothing to go on?

options.text: An animal crossing a wide, flat plain, with no walls, slopes, or edges of any kind anywhere nearby.
options.why: Correct. An open plain has no shape to use. Shape helps only where there are walls, banks, or edges for it to come from.

options.text: An animal in a long, rectangular burrow chamber, whose diagonally opposite corners look the same by shape.
options.why: A rectangular space gives two equally good answers, which is a limit but not nothing. Shape gives nothing only where there is none, as on an open plain.

options.text: An animal in a forest clearing whose plants and colors change completely between summer and winter.
options.why: The plants and colors change, but the clearing’s edges stay the same across seasons, so shape still gives something to go on.

options.text: An animal on a riverbank, where the water’s edge curves in a long, gentle arc past its nest.
options.why: A bank is part of the shape of the surroundings, which stays the same from season to season. Shape gives nothing only where there is none, as on an open plain.

items.stem: Even an animal with several cues to find its way faces two further problems. What are they?

options.text: Deciding, when cues disagree, whether they point to the same place and how far to rely on each; and recovering a lost heading before anything else is used.
options.why: Correct. Several cues do not settle everything. Cues that disagree raise the question of whether they point to the same place at all. And an animal that has lost its heading has to recover which way it is facing first.

options.text: Deciding, when cues disagree, whether they point to the same place and how far to rely on each; and finding the way to a place by a route it has never taken.
options.why: Deciding what to do when cues disagree is one of the two problems. The other is recovering a lost heading, after a fright or a tumble. Nothing else the animal knows can be used until it knows which way it is facing.

options.text: Telling which of its cues are knowledge and which are not; and recovering a lost heading before anything else it knows can be used.
options.why: Recovering a lost heading is one of the two problems. But a cue is never knowledge, so there is nothing to sort. The other problem is deciding what to do when cues disagree.

options.text: Combining every step and turn into a single estimate of position; and finding which way the sun lies at night or under cover.
options.why: Those are shortcomings of single cues, the animal’s own movement and the sun. The two problems that remain with several cues are cues that disagree and a lost heading.

items.stem: A field mouse fleeing an owl tumbles down a bank in the dark and comes to rest among roots it knows well. What does the mouse have to do first, before anything it knows about where its nest lies can be used?

options.text: Recover which way the mouse is facing, since a tumble can leave an animal with no sense of its heading.
options.why: Correct. An animal that has lost its heading, after a fright or a tumble, has to recover which way it is facing before anything else it knows can be used.

options.text: Relearn where the mouse’s nest lies relative to the roots, since a fright wipes out what an animal has learned about places.
options.why: What the mouse knows about its nest is still there. The trouble is that it cannot be used until the mouse has recovered which way it is facing.

options.text: Wait for daylight, since no cue for finding the way can be sensed in the dark until the sun rises again.
options.why: The mouse has cues in the dark: its own movement, smells, and nearby landmarks it can smell or touch. What it must do first is recover which way it is facing.

options.text: Find the smell of its nest, since after a tumble sensing the goal itself is the only kind of knowledge that works.
options.why: The tumble does not leave the mouse with only the lowest kind of knowledge. The mouse has to recover which way it is facing, and then what it knows can be used again.

items.stem: Every cue for finding the way fails in some way when used alone. How well do animals find their way all the same?

options.text: Remarkably well: many animals, from desert ants to taxi drivers, reach places they cannot sense from where they start.
options.why: Correct. For all the cues’ shortcomings, animals find their way remarkably well. Each of them reaches a place it cannot sense from where it starts.

options.text: Poorly: most animals cannot reach a place until they can sense the goal itself, or some marker standing right beside it.
options.why: Many animals do far better than that. Desert ants, orchid bees, wild rats, goldfish, and taxi drivers all reach places they cannot sense from where they start.

options.text: Well, but only where landmarks are plentiful, since without landmarks every other cue drifts too far to be of any use.
options.why: Desert ants forage over flat ground with almost no landmarks, and still run home in a straight line once they find food.

options.text: Well, but just along paths they have traveled before, and not from starting points they have not used before.
options.why: Goldfish trained to swim to one place in a tank head for it from starting points they have never used.

items.stem: A desert ant forages over flat ground with almost no landmarks, on an outward path that winds back and forth. What does the ant do once it finds food?

options.text: The ant runs home in a straight line, rather than retracing the winding path it took outward.
options.why: Correct. Desert ants run home in a straight line once they find food, though their outward paths wind back and forth over ground with almost no landmarks.

options.text: The ant retraces its winding outward path, step by step, back to the nest it started from.
options.why: Desert ants run home in a straight line, rather than retracing the winding path. That straight run is part of what makes their homing remarkable.

options.text: The ant searches back and forth at random until it comes close enough to smell its nest.
options.why: Searching at random until the nest can be sensed would be the lowest kind of knowledge at work. Desert ants run home in a straight line instead.

options.text: The ant heads for the nearest landmark and waits there until other ants pass on their way home.
options.why: The ground desert ants forage over has almost no landmarks. Once an ant finds food, it runs home in a straight line on its own.

items.stem: Desert ants, orchid bees, wild rats, goldfish, and taxi drivers each reach a place they cannot sense from where they start. Why is it hard to say whether they all know the same kind of thing?

options.text: Some cues and kinds of knowledge are very difficult to tell apart, and experiments built to separate them have not always succeeded.
options.why: Correct. Scientists have tried to devise experiments to work out which cues animals use and which kinds of knowledge they have. Those experiments have not always succeeded, because some cues and kinds of knowledge are incredibly difficult to tell apart.

options.text: Each animal can have only one kind of knowledge at a time, and no experiment yet devised can show which kind that single one happens to be.
options.why: An animal can have several kinds of knowledge at once. The difficulty is that some cues and kinds of knowledge are hard to tell apart, and experiments have not always managed it.

options.text: Scientists have not yet tried to test what these animals know, so only their behavior in the wild has been described.
options.why: Scientists have tried to devise such experiments. The experiments have not always succeeded, because some cues and kinds of knowledge are very difficult to tell apart.

options.text: Each of these animals was studied only in a laboratory, where the cues from outside a maze or a tank can never be controlled.
options.why: Several of these animals find their way outside any laboratory, such as desert ants foraging over flat ground and wild rats in a large outdoor pen. The difficulty is that some cues and kinds of knowledge are very hard to tell apart.

items.stem: Goldfish trained to swim to one place in a tank head for it from starting points they have never used. Why does that result, on its own, not settle which kind of knowledge about the place the goldfish have?

options.text: Different kinds of knowledge, such as a marker beside the place that is visible from every start, could produce the same behavior.
options.why: Correct. Some cues and kinds of knowledge are very difficult to tell apart. If a marker beside the goal could be seen from every starting point, the marker would lead the fish there just as knowing where places lie would. Heading for the place from a new start does not, by itself, separate the two.

options.text: Heading for a place from a new start shows only that the fish knows a familiar path, which no experiment could ever tell apart from other kinds.
options.why: A familiar path works only along its own path, so it could not lead the fish from starting points it has never used.

options.text: Heading for a place from a new start shows only that the fish knows the way back to the start, which can lead to every place.
options.why: The way back to the start leads only to the start, not to a trained place elsewhere in the tank.

options.text: Fish cannot have any kind of knowledge about places, so their behavior must come from something other than knowledge.
options.why: Goldfish do learn places. Goldfish learn to swim to a place defined by cues around a room, and they reach it from starting points they have never used.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the difference between a cue and knowledge in finding the way, and describe the two problems that remain even for an animal with several cues.
items.answer: A cue is something in the world, or in the animal’s own movement, that its senses can detect as it moves, such as a smell, a tree, or the sun. Knowledge is what the animal has learned about how a cue relates to its goal. So the tree is a cue, and knowing that the nest lies beside the tree is knowledge. Having several cues does not solve everything. When the cues disagree, the animal has to decide whether they point to the same place at all, and how far to rely on each one. And an animal that has lost its heading, after a fright or a tumble, has to recover which way it is facing before anything else it knows can be used.
rubric: Says a cue is something in the world, or in the animal’s own movement, that its senses can detect.
Says knowledge is what the animal has learned about how a cue relates to its goal, with an example or a contrast between the two.
Says that when cues disagree, the animal has to decide whether they point to the same place and how far to rely on each.
Says an animal that has lost its heading has to recover which way it is facing before anything else it knows can be used.

items.stem: An animal is set down at a spot in its home area where it has never stood before. The spot is far from a feeding place it knows well, beyond where it can sense the feeding place or anything beside it. In a short paragraph, explain what knowing what the feeding place’s surroundings look like would let the animal do from there. Then explain what knowing where places lie relative to one another would let it do instead.
items.answer: Knowing what the feeding place’s surroundings look like helps only near the goal, where the surroundings still look much as they did. From a distant spot, the surroundings would look quite different, so knowing them would give the animal no direction to the feeding place until it somehow got close. Knowing where places lie relative to one another is the highest of the six kinds. Knowing where places lie lets the way between any two known places be worked out. So the animal could head for the feeding place from the new starting point, even by a route it has never taken. Knowing where places lie is the only kind that can lead from a new starting point to any place the animal knows.
rubric: Says knowing the surroundings helps only near the goal, where the surroundings still look much as they did.
Says that from the distant new spot, knowing the surroundings gives no direction to the feeding place.
Says knowing where places lie relative to one another lets the way between any two known places be worked out.
Says the animal could then head for the feeding place from the new spot, even by a route it has never taken.
Says knowing where places lie is the only one of the six kinds that can lead from a new starting point to any place the animal knows.

items.stem: A small animal keeps track of where it is only from its own steps and turns. In a few sentences, give two different reasons its estimate of position can end up wrong, and say why an error in heading does particular harm. Then explain why the animal cannot find the error from those same signals.
items.answer: Every step and turn has to be combined into one estimate of position, and each small estimate of a step or a turn has some error. The estimate includes all of those errors, so it drifts. An error in heading does particular harm, because a heading error becomes a growing error in position as the path goes on. A second reason is that an animal that is swept along or carried has moved without stepping, and its own steps cannot register that movement. The animal cannot find the error from its steps and turns, because nothing in those signals shows how far the estimate has drifted.
rubric: Says each small estimate of a step or turn has some error, and the estimate of position includes all of those errors.
Says an animal that is swept along or carried has moved without steps it can register.
Says nothing in the signals from its own movement shows how far the estimate has drifted.
Says an error in heading does particular harm, because it becomes a growing error in position as the path goes on.

items.stem: In a few sentences, say which cues an early mammal foraging on a dark night probably had for finding its way. Then give the one caution that this inference needs, and what follows from the caution.
items.answer: We infer, from what we know of its senses, that on a dark night the early mammal had its own movement, gradients of smell, and nearby landmarks it could smell or touch. The early mammal had few distant landmarks it could see. The caution is that land animals see much farther at night than fish do by day. So the early mammal was not blind, and some distant landmarks would still have been in view.
rubric: Names at least two of the cues: the animal’s own movement, gradients of smell, and nearby landmarks it could smell or touch.
Says the early mammal had few distant landmarks it could see.
Treats the list as an inference from the early mammal’s senses, not an observation.
Gives the caution that land animals see much farther at night than fish do by day.
Concludes that the early mammal was not blind, and that some distant landmarks would still have been in view.

pools.title: Places, Responses, and Routes Never Taken
pools.covers: reading §9.1.6, §9.1.7 · lecture 9.1 slides tolmans_test, place_or_response, routes_never_taken

items.stem: What is latent learning?

options.text: Learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it.
options.why: Correct. Rats that wandered a maze with no food in it seemed to learn little. Once food appeared, they reached it about as efficiently as rats rewarded from the start, so they had been learning all along.

options.text: Learning to go to one particular location, whatever movements it takes to get there from where the animal starts.
options.why: That is place learning, which is defined by what is learned, a location. Latent learning is defined by timing: it does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it.

options.text: Learning to repeat one movement, such as a turn, whatever location that movement happens to lead the animal to.
options.why: That is response learning, which is defined by what is learned, a movement. Latent learning is defined by timing: it does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it.

options.text: Learning that happens only once a reward appears, and that fades again soon after the reward is taken away.
options.why: The rats that showed latent learning had no reward while they learned. Their learning did not show at the time, and appeared later, once food gave them a reason to use it.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Correct. Rats that wandered a maze with no food in it learned its layout without showing it. The learning appeared once food gave them a reason to use it.

options.text: place learning
options.why: Place learning is learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes. It is defined by what is learned, not by when the learning shows in behavior.

options.text: response learning
options.why: Response learning is learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to. It is defined by what is learned, not by when the learning shows in behavior.

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Cue combination is combining estimates from several sources of evidence, each weighted by how reliable it is. The definition here is about learning that shows in behavior only later, which is latent learning.

items.stem: A student rides the same bus to campus every morning, looking out of the window as it passes a small café. The student never gets off at that stop. Months later, wanting coffee, the student walks to the café without needing directions. What is the best account of what happened?

options.text: The student learned the way to the café on the bus rides, though the learning did not show in behavior until there was a reason to use it.
options.why: Correct. That is latent learning. The rats that wandered a maze with no food in it also learned without showing it. In both cases, the learning appeared once there was a reason to use it.

options.text: The student learned the way to the café on the day the coffee was wanted, since learning that does not show in behavior has not happened.
options.why: Learning can happen without showing at the time. Once food appeared, the rats that had wandered a maze with no food in it reached the food about as efficiently as rats rewarded from the start. So they had learned during the unrewarded runs.

options.text: The student could not have learned anything about the café on the bus rides, since nothing rewarded the student for passing it every day.
options.why: Learning does not need a reward at the time it happens. Rats that ran a maze with no food in it learned its layout anyway, and the learning appeared once food gave them a reason to use it.

options.text: The student learned the way to the café by response learning, the kind of learning that does not show in behavior until there is a reason to use it.
options.why: Response learning is defined by what is learned, a movement repeated wherever it leads, not by when the learning shows. Learning that does not show when it happens, and appears once there is a reason to use it, is latent learning.

items.stem: Some rats ran a maze once a day for several days with no food in it, and seemed to learn little. Other rats were rewarded at the end of the maze from the start. Once food began appearing for the unrewarded rats, how did they compare with the rewarded rats?

options.text: The unrewarded rats reached the food about as efficiently as the rats that had been rewarded from the start.
options.why: Correct. The unrewarded rats had learned something about the maze during their runs, and the learning showed only once food gave them a reason to use it. That is latent learning.

options.text: The unrewarded rats reached the food far less efficiently, needing as many days as the rewarded rats had needed at the start.
options.why: If the rats had learned nothing on the unrewarded runs, they would have had to start over. Instead, they reached the food about as efficiently as the rewarded rats, so they had learned without showing it.

options.text: The unrewarded rats reached the food more efficiently, since running without food had let them try every path in the maze.
options.why: The unrewarded rats did not do better than the rewarded rats. They reached the food about as efficiently, so learning had happened during the unrewarded runs without showing at the time.

options.text: The unrewarded rats never reached the food reliably, since running a maze with no reward in it leaves nothing learned at all.
options.why: Running a maze with no reward did leave something learned. Once food appeared, the unrewarded rats reached it about as efficiently as the rewarded rats, which is latent learning.

items.stem: A rat has learned the way through a maze to food. Why can watching it run the familiar path not show whether it learned a sequence of moves or where the food is?

options.text: On the familiar path both kinds of knowledge produce the same behavior, so only a change, such as a blocked path or a new start, separates them.
options.why: Correct. Go left, then right, then right again leads to the food just as surely as knowing where the food is. The two can be distinguished only when something changes.

options.text: On the familiar path the two kinds of knowledge produce slightly different behavior, but the differences are too small to measure in any single run.
options.why: On the familiar path the two kinds of knowledge produce exactly the same behavior, not slightly different behavior. They can be distinguished only when something changes, such as the start or the open route.

options.text: A rat running a familiar path shows only latent learning, which by definition never appears in behavior while the rat is running.
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it. A rat running to food has a reason, and its behavior on the familiar path fits either kind of knowledge.

options.text: A rat learns a sequence of moves first and where the food is only later, so its early runs can reveal only the moves it has learned.
options.why: Kinds of knowledge are not stages learned in a fixed order, and an animal can have several at once. The trouble is that on the familiar path both kinds produce the same behavior.

items.stem: A commuter drives the same roads to work every day. An observer wants to know whether the commuter has learned only a sequence of turns, or where the office lies relative to other places. Which observation gives the observer a chance to tell the two apart?

options.text: What the commuter does on a morning when the usual road is closed and a new way to work has to be found.
options.why: Correct. On the familiar route the two kinds of knowledge produce the same behavior, so only a change can separate them. Even then, the observer would have to rule out simpler knowledge, such as a tall building beside the office used as a beacon.

options.text: How much faster the commuter now makes the usual trip, compared with how long the same trip took in the first week of the job.
options.why: Getting faster on the usual trip fits both kinds of knowledge equally well. On the familiar route they produce the same behavior, so only a change, such as a closed road, can separate them.

options.text: Whether the commuter ever misses a turn on the usual trip, counted across a whole month of ordinary mornings without any closures.
options.why: A commuter who never misses a turn could know either a sequence of turns or where the office lies. On the familiar route the two produce the same behavior, so only a change can separate them.

options.text: How many times the commuter has made the usual trip in all, counted from the first morning of the job to the present day.
options.why: Counting the trips cannot separate the two kinds of knowledge. On the familiar route both kinds produce the same behavior, so only a change, such as a closed road, can separate them.

items.stem: Two rats are trained on the same route through a maze to food. One knows only that familiar path. The other knows where places in the maze lie relative to one another. When would the behavior of the two rats differ?

options.text: Only when the start or the route changes, as when the trained path is blocked or the rat is started from somewhere new.
options.why: Correct. On the trained route the two rats behave the same way. Only the rat that knows where places lie could reach the food by a route it has never taken, so a change is needed to reveal the difference.

options.text: From the first trials onward, since the rat that knows where places lie would run the trained route faster and with fewer errors.
options.why: Knowing where places lie does not show on the trained route. Both rats behave the same way there, and they differ only when the start or the route changes.

options.text: Only once the food is removed from the maze, since the rat that knows only the familiar path would then stop running it.
options.why: Removing the food leaves the start and the route as they were, so it does not separate the two rats. They differ only when the start or the route changes.

options.text: Never, since both kinds of knowledge produce the same behavior wherever the rat starts and whichever paths are left open.
options.why: The two kinds of knowledge produce the same behavior only on the trained route. When the start or the route changes, only the rat that knows where places lie could take a route it has never taken.

items.stem: On the strength of latent learning and other demonstrations, researchers proposed that rats learn more than a familiar path through a maze. On that proposal, what do rats learn?

options.text: Where places lie relative to one another, so that a rat can reach a goal by a route it has never taken.
options.why: Correct. On the proposal, a rat learns how places are laid out relative to one another. Knowledge of that kind lets it reach a goal by a new route, such as a shortcut or a detour.

options.text: A sequence of moves that leads to the goal, so that a rat can repeat it from the same start on every trial.
options.why: A sequence of moves is the familiar path the proposal went beyond. Knowing a familiar path works only from its own start and along that path, so it cannot lead a rat by a route never taken.

options.text: Something at or beside the goal that can be sensed from afar, so that a rat can head straight for it.
options.why: That describes a beacon, which helps only from where it can be sensed. The proposal was that rats learn where places lie relative to one another, so that they can reach a goal by a route never taken.

options.text: The way back to where it started from anywhere, so that a rat can return there across the whole maze.
options.why: Knowing the way back to the start leads to one place only. The proposal was broader: that rats learn where places lie relative to one another, so that they can reach any goal by a route never taken.

items.stem: What is the test of knowing where places lie relative to one another, and why does passing it not settle the matter on its own?

options.text: Taking a route never taken, such as a shortcut or a detour; a beacon, or knowing the way back to the start, can produce the same result.
options.why: Correct. A new route is still the test, but it is not proof by itself. An animal could reach the goal by a new route by heading for a beacon, or, if the goal is the start, by knowing the way back to it.

options.text: Running a trained route without errors; a well-practiced sequence of moves can produce the same result with no knowledge of places at all.
options.why: Running a trained route cannot be the test, because on the familiar path a sequence of moves and knowing where places lie produce the same behavior. The test is a route never taken.

options.text: Taking a route never taken, such as a shortcut or a detour; following a familiar path a little farther than usual can produce the same result.
options.why: The test is right, but knowing a familiar path works only along that path and cannot produce a new route. The simpler kinds of knowledge that can produce a new route are a beacon and knowing the way back to the start.

options.text: Finding the goal again after the food has been removed; an animal that searches where food used to be may only be repeating its last turn.
options.why: Searching where food used to be is not the test named for knowing where places lie. That test is a route never taken, which a beacon or knowing the way back to the start can also produce.

items.stem: A dog is trained to run a winding path through a park to a food bowl that sits behind a low hedge, at the foot of a tall flagpole. One day the winding path is fenced off, and the dog runs straight across the grass to the bowl. Why is the straight run, on its own, not proof that the dog knows where places in the park lie relative to one another?

options.text: The flagpole stands beside the goal and can be seen from afar, so the dog could have reached the bowl by heading for the flagpole.
options.why: Correct. A new route is the test of knowing where places lie, but it is not proof on its own. A tall flagpole beside the bowl can serve as a beacon, and a beacon can produce a new route with no knowledge of where places lie.

options.text: The straight run is a shortcut rather than a detour, and only a detour counts as a route never taken in a test of knowing where places lie.
options.why: A shortcut and a detour both count as routes never taken. The trouble is that the flagpole beside the bowl could have served as a beacon, which can also produce a new route.

options.text: The dog had run toward the bowl and its flagpole many times, so the straight run only repeats a movement it had already learned.
options.why: The straight run is a new route, not a repeated movement. It is not proof on its own because the flagpole beside the bowl could have served as a beacon.

options.text: The dog could have been going back to where it started, since knowing the way back to the start can also produce a new route.
options.why: Knowing the way back to the start can produce a new route, but only to the start. The dog was running away from its start, to the bowl. The simpler explanation here is the flagpole beside the bowl, which could have served as a beacon.

items.stem: In the radiating-paths test, rats were trained on a roundabout route to food and then offered a fan of new paths with the old route blocked. The room’s only light was a desk lamp just behind the old food box, in training and in the test. Why does the lamp matter for interpreting the result?

options.text: Heading for the light and heading for the goal were nearly the same thing, so the lamp could have served the rats as a beacon.
options.why: Correct. A new route is not proof on its own, because a beacon can produce one. The lamp stood just behind the old food box throughout, so a rat could head for it without knowing where places lie. The authors raised that problem themselves, and argued against it.

options.text: The lamp was moved to a new spot between training and the test, so the rats had to find the old food box without its light.
options.why: The lamp stayed where it was, just behind the old food box, in training and in the test. That is why it matters: heading for the light and heading for the goal were nearly the same thing.

options.text: The lamp guided most rats in the later repetitions of the test, which is why a preference for the shortcut appeared in those repetitions.
options.why: In a later review of 47 experiments, a preference for the shortcut appeared in only 17%, and the lamp rarely guided choices in the later studies. The lamp matters for the original test, where it stood just behind the old food box and could have served as a beacon.

options.text: The lamp lit only the entrance to the fan of paths, so the rats could see which paths were open but not where any of them led.
options.why: The lamp stood just behind the old food box, at the far end from where the rats entered, in training and in the test. So heading for the light and heading for the goal were nearly the same thing, and the lamp could have served as a beacon.

items.stem: In the original radiating-paths test, 19 of 53 rats, or 36%, took the path ending nearest where the food box had been. In a later review, the original study and a dozen later ones were gathered, 47 experiments in all. How did the later experiments compare with the original?

options.text: A preference for the shortcut appeared in only 17% of the experiments, and in most of the rest subjects preferred paths next to the old route, or none.
options.why: Correct. The result has proved hard to repeat. And although the lamp was the most criticized feature of the original test, it rarely guided choices in the later studies.

options.text: A preference for the shortcut appeared in about 36% of the experiments, and in the rest subjects spread over the other paths, as the rats had in the original.
options.why: In the original test, 19 of 53 rats, or 36%, took the path ending nearest the old food box, and the rest spread over the other paths. Across the 47 experiments, a preference for the shortcut appeared in only 17%.

options.text: A preference for the shortcut appeared in most of the experiments, but only in those where a desk lamp stood just behind the old food box, as in the original.
options.why: A preference for the shortcut appeared in only 17% of the experiments. The lamp rarely guided choices in the later studies, although it was the most criticized feature of the original test.

options.text: A preference for the shortcut appeared in nearly every experiment, so the original result has since been repeated many times over by others.
options.why: The original result has proved hard to repeat. A preference for the shortcut appeared in only 17% of the experiments. In most of the others, subjects preferred paths next to the old route, or showed no preference.

items.stem: In later repetitions of the radiating-paths test, subjects often chose paths right beside the blocked old route. Why might such a choice be sensible rather than a mistake?

options.text: A path beside the blocked one could lead past the blocked stretch and rejoin the old route farther on, toward the goal.
options.why: Correct. A rat taking a path beside the blocked one, to rejoin its old route, would have been acting sensibly too. That is one reason the radiating-paths test is weak evidence, on its own, that rats know where places lie relative to one another.

options.text: A path beside the blocked one is the shortest way to the goal, so it is the route a rat that knew where places lie should take.
options.why: The shortcut in the test was the path ending nearest where the food box had been, not a path beside the blocked one. A path beside it is sensible for another reason: it could rejoin the old route farther on.

options.text: A path beside the blocked one leads toward the lamp, so a rat taking it was sensibly heading for a beacon near the goal.
options.why: The lamp stood just behind the old food box, near where the shortcut ended, and it rarely guided choices in the later studies. A path beside the blocked one is sensible because it could rejoin the old route farther on.

options.text: A path beside the blocked one leads back toward the start, so a rat taking it was sensibly using the way back to the start.
options.why: Going back to the start would not bring a rat any closer to the food. A path beside the blocked one is sensible because it could rejoin the old route farther on, toward the goal.

items.stem: What is place learning?

options.text: Learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes to get there from the starting point.
options.why: Correct. A place learner started from a new side of a maze takes whatever turns lead to the same location. What is learned is the location, not a movement.

options.text: Learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location that movement ends up leading to.
options.why: That is response learning, the reverse of place learning. A response learner repeats the movement, while a place learner goes to the location, whatever movements it takes.

options.text: Learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and that appears later once there is a reason to use it.
options.why: That is latent learning, which is defined by when learning shows in behavior. Place learning is defined by what is learned: a location, reached by whatever movements it takes.

options.text: Learning which way leads back to the starting point from anywhere, without following any familiar path to get there.
options.why: That describes knowing the way back to the start, which leads to one place only. Place learning is learning to go to a location, any location, whatever movements it takes.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes to get there from the starting point.

options.text: place learning
options.why: Correct. A rat that has learned a place, started from the other side of a maze, makes whatever turns lead to the same location. What is learned is the location, not a movement.

options.text: response learning
options.why: Response learning is the reverse: learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to. The definition here is about reaching a location by any movements.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later. It is defined by timing, not by whether a location or a movement is learned.

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: Exploration versus exploitation is the trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better or worse. The definition here is about learning a location, reached by whatever movements it takes.

items.stem: What is response learning?

options.text: Learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to.
options.why: Correct. A response learner started from a new side of a maze makes the same turn as before, and so ends up in a different place. What is learned is the movement, not the location.

options.text: Learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes to reach it from the start.
options.why: That is place learning, the reverse of response learning. A place learner goes to the location by whatever movements it takes, while a response learner repeats the movement.

options.text: Learning that appears in behavior only after a reward first turns up.
options.why: That describes latent learning, which is defined by when learning shows in behavior. Response learning is defined by what is learned: a movement, repeated wherever it leads.

options.text: Learning something at or beside a goal that can be sensed from afar.
options.why: That describes knowing a beacon, which helps only from where the beacon can be sensed. Response learning is learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location it leads to.

options.text: response learning
options.why: Correct. A rat rewarded for always turning right, wherever it starts, has to learn a response. Started from the other side, it ends up in a different place.

options.text: place learning
options.why: Place learning is the reverse: learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes. The definition here is about repeating a movement wherever it leads.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later. It is defined by timing, not by whether a movement or a location is learned.

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: Exploration versus exploitation is the trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better or worse. The definition here is about repeating a movement, which is response learning.

items.stem: On a plus-shaped maze, rats are started on alternate trials from either side of a path that runs between two food boxes. One group is rewarded for always turning right. The other is rewarded for always going to the same food box. How does what the two groups must learn differ?

options.text: Rats rewarded for turning right must repeat one turn that ends at different places; rats rewarded at one food box must reach it by different turns.
options.why: Correct. Turning right from opposite starts leads to opposite food boxes, so the rats rewarded for turning right learn a response. Reaching the same food box from opposite starts takes opposite turns, so the rats rewarded at one food box learn a place.

options.text: Rats rewarded for turning right must reach one place by different turns; rats rewarded at one food box must repeat one turn that ends at different places.
options.why: That reverses the two groups. Always turning right from opposite starts ends at different food boxes, which is response learning. Always going to one food box takes different turns, which is place learning.

options.text: Both groups must reach one place by different turns, but the rats rewarded for turning right are rewarded on fewer of their trials.
options.why: Only the rats rewarded at one food box must reach one place by different turns. The rats rewarded for turning right repeat one turn, which leads to different places depending on where they start.

options.text: Both groups must repeat one turn, but the rats rewarded at one food box must also learn which of the two boxes has the food in it.
options.why: Only the rats rewarded for turning right repeat one turn. The rats rewarded at one food box go to it from either start, and that takes a right turn from one side and a left turn from the other.

items.stem: In a large, dim room, eight rats were trained on a plus-shaped maze to go to one place, and eight to repeat one turn. How quickly did each group learn?

options.text: All 8 place learners learned within 8 trials, and only 3 of the 8 response learners learned within 72.
options.why: Correct. The response learners that failed kept going to one end of the room, a sign that something outside the maze was playing a role.

options.text: All 8 response learners learned within 8 trials, and only 3 of the 8 place learners learned within 72.
options.why: That reverses the two groups. All 8 place learners learned within 8 trials, while only 3 of 8 response learners learned within 72.

options.text: Both groups learned within 8 trials, though the place learners made slightly fewer errors along the way.
options.why: The groups differed sharply. All 8 place learners learned within 8 trials, but only 3 of 8 response learners learned within 72.

options.text: Neither group learned within 72 trials, and the rats of both groups kept going to one end of the room.
options.why: All 8 place learners learned within 8 trials. It was the response learners that mostly failed, and the ones that failed kept going to one end of the room.

items.stem: In a plus-shaped maze experiment, rats trained to go to one food box learned far faster than rats trained to repeat one turn. A rack of the rats’ home cages stood 15 feet behind that food box. What does the rack mean for the result?

options.text: A rat could reach that food box from either start by heading toward the rack. So the result is evidence only that rats readily learn a place marked from outside the maze.
options.why: Correct. The rack could serve much as a beacon would. So the result is evidence that rats readily learn a place when something outside the maze marks it, not that place learning is easier everywhere. The authors drew the same limited conclusion.

options.text: With the rack there, the result is evidence that place learning is easier than response learning everywhere, since rats prefer places near their home cages.
options.why: The rack is the reason the result is not evidence of that. A rat could head toward the rack from either start, so the result is evidence only that rats readily learn a place marked from outside the maze.

options.text: The rack drew the response learners toward their cages, so the result is evidence that rats cannot learn to repeat a turn in any room.
options.why: Three of the eight response learners did learn, and in plainer rooms rats repeated the turn. Because of the rack, the result is evidence only that rats readily learn a place when something outside the maze marks it.

options.text: The rack stood too far from the maze for the rats to use, so the place learners knew where the food box lay relative to other places.
options.why: A rat could reach that food box from either start by heading toward the rack, much as it would head toward a beacon. So the place learners’ success is not evidence that they knew where the food box lay relative to other places.

items.stem: Across repetitions of the plus-maze experiment, rats sometimes went to the trained place and sometimes repeated the trained turn. How did the settings where rats went to the place differ from the settings where they repeated the turn?

options.text: Where the surroundings beyond the two arms looked very different, rats went to the place; in a plain cloth enclosure or a plain, dim room, they repeated the turn.
options.why: Correct. The difference lay in the room, not in the rat. A rack of cages, a window, or a well-lit room full of objects favored the place, while plain surroundings favored the turn. Both tendencies were present every time, and one was stronger.

options.text: Where the surroundings beyond the two arms looked very different, rats repeated the turn; inside a plain cloth enclosure or a plain, dim room, they went to the place.
options.why: That reverses the finding. Distinct surroundings beyond the arms, such as a rack of cages or a window, gave rats something to go to, so they went to the place. In plain surroundings, they repeated the turn.

options.text: Where the rats came from a strain bred to learn places, they went to the place; where they came from a strain bred to learn turns, they repeated the turn.
options.why: The reviewer of these experiments concluded that nothing in the nature of a rat makes it a place or response learner. The difference lay in the room: distinct surroundings beyond the arms favored the place, and plain ones the turn.

options.text: Where the room was well lit, rats went to the place whatever stood in it; in any dim room at all, however full of objects, they repeated the turn.
options.why: Light alone did not decide it. In the original experiment the room was large and dim, yet rats went to the place, with a rack of home cages standing behind one food box. What mattered was whether the surroundings beyond the arms looked different.

items.stem: A plus-shaped maze is set up in a windowless room whose bare walls look the same on every side. Rats are trained from one start to turn toward a food box, then started from the opposite side. Going by what rats did in such settings, what will these rats tend to do?

options.text: Repeat the turn they were trained on, even though that same turn now leads them to the food box at the other end of the maze.
options.why: Correct. In plain surroundings, such as a plain cloth enclosure or a plain, dim room, rats tended to repeat the turn. Where the surroundings beyond the arms looked very different, they tended to go to the place instead.

options.text: Go to the trained food box, since rats are place learners by nature, whatever the setting, and learn turns only with great difficulty.
options.why: Nothing in the nature of a rat makes it a place or response learner. Both tendencies were present every time, and in plain surroundings the tendency to repeat the turn was the stronger.

options.text: Go to the trained food box, since bare walls leave nothing to distract the rats from where the food was, which they then head straight for.
options.why: Plain surroundings did not help rats go to the place. With nothing distinct beyond the arms to mark it, rats tended to repeat the turn instead.

options.text: Choose the two arms about equally often, since rats in plain surroundings learn neither the place nor the turn and must simply guess.
options.why: Rats in plain surroundings did learn something: they tended to repeat the turn. Both tendencies were present every time, and the setting decided which was stronger.

items.stem: In one plus-maze experiment, in a large, dim room, rats learned to go to a place far faster than they learned to repeat a turn. Later repetitions sometimes found the reverse. In a few sentences, explain why the fast place learning in that experiment is not evidence that place learning is easier everywhere. Then say what decided which tendency was stronger across experiments.
items.answer: In that experiment, a rack of the rats’ home cages stood 15 feet behind one food box. A rat could reach that box from either start by heading toward the rack, much as it would head toward a beacon. So the result is evidence only that rats readily learn a place when something outside the maze marks it. Later repetitions did not all agree: of ten experiments gathered in a review, place learning was faster in seven and response learning in two. The difference lay in the room, not in the rat. Where the surroundings beyond the arms looked very different, rats went to the place, and in a plain enclosure or a plain, dim room they repeated the turn. Both tendencies were present every time, and the setting decided which one was stronger.
rubric: Says a rack of home cages behind one food box let rats reach it by heading toward the rack, much as toward a beacon.
Says the original result is therefore evidence only that rats readily learn a place marked from outside the maze, not that place learning is easier everywhere.
Says later experiments did not all agree, with response learning faster in some (place learning faster in seven of ten, response learning in two).
Says distinct surroundings beyond the arms favored going to the place, and plain surroundings favored repeating the turn.
Says both tendencies were present, and the setting, not the nature of the rat, decided which was stronger.

items.stem: A friend reads that, in the radiating-paths test, 19 of 53 rats took the path ending nearest where the old food box had been. The friend concludes that rats know where places lie relative to one another. In a few sentences, explain why the test is weak evidence for that conclusion on its own.
items.answer: The room’s only light was a desk lamp just behind the old food box, there in training and in the test. So heading for the light and heading for the goal were nearly the same thing, and the lamp could have served as a beacon. The authors raised that problem themselves, and argued against it. The result has also proved hard to repeat. In a review of 47 experiments, a preference for the shortcut appeared in only 17%. In most of the others, subjects preferred paths next to the old route, or showed no preference. And a rat taking a path beside the blocked one, to rejoin its old route farther on, would have been acting sensibly too. None of these problems means that rats lack such knowledge. The radiating-paths test, on its own, is simply weak evidence for that knowledge.
rubric: Says the lamp just behind the old food box could have served as a beacon, since heading for the light and heading for the goal were nearly the same thing.
Says the result has proved hard to repeat (a preference for the shortcut in only 17% of 47 experiments).
Says taking a path beside the blocked one, to rejoin the old route, would also have been sensible.
Concludes that the test is weak evidence on its own, without claiming that rats lack such knowledge.

items.stem: In the radiating-paths test, rats could have reached the goal area by heading for a lamp just behind the old food box. A rat trained from a single start could also rely on a fixed sequence of turns. How were both ruled out in the water maze?

options.text: The platform was hidden under cloudy water, so nothing at the goal could be sensed, and rats started from a different place on each trial.
options.why: Correct. The rats could not see, hear, or smell the platform, and the start changed from trial to trial. So neither a beacon nor a fixed sequence of turns could lead them, yet they learned to swim to it directly.

options.text: The platform was lit from under the water on every trial, so that rats could learn to ignore the light and find the platform by the room.
options.why: A lamp at the platform would have been a beacon, which is exactly what had to be ruled out. In the water maze nothing at the platform could be sensed, and rats started from a different place on each trial.

options.text: The platform was moved to a new place on each trial, so that rats could not have learned any single path to it or any single spot.
options.why: The platform stayed in one place, and the cloudy water hid it from the rats’ senses. What changed from trial to trial was where the rats started, so a fixed sequence of turns could not lead them.

options.text: The pool was kept in total darkness, so that rats had no light to head for and had to find the platform by touch alone as they swam about.
options.why: The rats found the platform by where it lay relative to features of the room around the pool, not by touch. Instead, the platform was hidden in cloudy water, and the rats were started from a different place on each trial.

items.stem: A researcher wants to show that mice can find a goal in a large arena by where it lies relative to the room around them. Which training plan would rule out both a beacon and a fixed sequence of turns as the way the mice reach the goal?

options.text: Leave nothing at the goal that the mice can sense from afar, and start each mouse from a different place on every trial.
options.why: Correct. That is the logic of the water maze. With nothing at the goal to sense, no beacon can lead the mice, and with a new start on every trial, no fixed sequence of turns can.

options.text: Leave nothing at the goal that the mice can sense from afar, and start each mouse from the same place on every trial.
options.why: Hiding the goal rules out a beacon, but a fixed start leaves a fixed sequence of turns open. A mouse could reach the goal by repeating the same moves each time.

options.text: Mark the goal with a small flag the mice can see from afar, and start each mouse from a different place on every trial.
options.why: Changing the start rules out a fixed sequence of turns, but a flag at the goal is a beacon. A mouse could reach the goal by heading for the flag.

options.text: Mark the goal with a small flag the mice can see from afar, and start each mouse from the same place on every trial.
options.why: That plan rules out neither. A flag at the goal is a beacon, and a fixed start lets a mouse repeat the same sequence of turns each time.

items.stem: Rats learned to swim to a platform hidden just under the surface of a pool of cloudy water. Later, the platform was taken out, and the rats searched the area where it had been. What does that search indicate?

options.text: The rats had been heading for a spot defined by where it lay relative to features of the room, not for anything at the platform.
options.why: Correct. With the platform gone, nothing at the goal remained to be sensed, yet the rats searched its old position. They had found the platform by where it lay relative to features of the room around the pool.

options.text: The rats had been finding the platform by seeing it through the water, and searched the spot where they had last seen it from the surface.
options.why: The water was cloudy, and the rats could not see, hear, or smell the platform. They found it by where it lay relative to features of the room around the pool.

options.text: The rats had learned a fixed sequence of turns from one start, and their search was simply that same sequence of turns repeated.
options.why: The rats were started from a different place on each trial, so no fixed sequence of turns could have led them. They searched where the platform had been because they knew where it lay relative to the room.

options.text: The rats had learned nothing about the room, and searched in whatever part of the pool they happened to be put into the water.
options.why: The rats searched where the platform had been, not wherever they were put in. That shows they had learned where the platform lay relative to features of the room.

items.stem: Rats exploring in darkness ran straight back to where they had started. Why is running straight back to the start not evidence that the rats knew where places lie relative to one another?
tags: the way back to the start

options.text: The way back to the start leads to one place only, and does not let an animal work out the way between any two others.
options.why: Correct. Running straight back in darkness shows knowing the way back to the start. Knowing where places lie relative to one another is broader, and a run back to the start cannot show that broader knowledge.

options.text: Running straight back retraces the outward path, and knowing a familiar path works only along that path, never along a new one.
options.why: The rats ran straight back, not back along the way they had explored. What they showed was the way back to the start, which leads to one place only.

options.text: Running straight back is response learning, a repeated turn, since the rats always went back to the start in the same way.
options.why: A straight run home from wherever the rat happens to be is not a repeated turn. It shows the way back to the start, which leads to one place only.

options.text: Animals in darkness cannot sense their own movement at all, so the rats must have reached the start by chance on each run.
options.why: From each step and each turn, an animal could sense how far, and which way, it has gone, in darkness as in light. A sense of how far, and which way, it has come points back to one place, the start.

items.stem: A blindfolded volunteer is led along a winding path across a large field and then asked to walk straight back to the start, which the volunteer does well. Asked next to walk to a bench passed along the way, the volunteer heads off in the wrong direction. What kind of knowledge fits the volunteer’s success and failure?
tags: the way back to the start

options.text: Knowing the way back to the start, which leads to one place from anywhere but gives no way to other places.
options.why: Correct. The volunteer could head straight for the start without following the path, which is the way back to the start. That knowledge leads to one place only, so it gives no way to the bench.

options.text: Knowing where places lie relative to one another, since a straight walk back to the start is itself a route never taken.
options.why: A straight walk back is a new route, but the way back to the start can produce it without any knowledge of where places lie. A volunteer who knew where places lie could also have found the bench.

options.text: Knowing a familiar path, since the volunteer had been led along the path and could simply follow it again in reverse.
options.why: The volunteer walked straight back rather than retracing the winding path. Knowing a familiar path works only along that path, and the straight walk was a different way.

options.text: Knowing a beacon at the start, since only a beacon can lead an animal straight back to a place from far away.
options.why: A blindfolded volunteer had no beacon to sense. Heading straight back to the start from anywhere is the way back to the start, which needs no beacon.

items.stem: What does the strongest test of a route never taken require, and why?

options.text: Knowing every route the animal has ever taken, so that a new route can be recognized as truly new.
options.why: Correct. Without a record of every route, a path that looks new may be one the animal has taken before. With every route recorded, a new route can be recognized as truly new.

options.text: Starting the animal from a different place on every trial, so that no fixed sequence of turns can lead it.
options.why: Changing the start rules out a fixed sequence of turns, as in the water maze. Recognizing a route as truly new requires something else: knowing every route the animal has ever taken.

options.text: Blocking the animal’s trained route, so that it has to choose from a fan of paths it has never seen before.
options.why: Blocking a trained route and offering a fan of paths was the design of the radiating-paths test, which is weak evidence on its own. The strongest test requires knowing every route the animal has ever taken.

options.text: Removing every landmark before the test, so that the animal cannot use anything it sees to find the way.
options.why: Using landmarks does not count against knowing where places lie, since that knowledge always needs places to measure from. The strongest test requires knowing every route the animal has ever taken.

items.stem: Young wild Egyptian fruit bats were tracked by GPS from their very first flight outdoors. Why was tracking them from the very first flight important?

options.text: Every route a bat had flown was recorded, so a later route could be recognized as truly new rather than one it had flown before.
options.why: Correct. A route counted as new only if at least half of it lay more than 100 meters from anywhere the bat had been. Every bat later flew shortcuts that met that test.

options.text: The bats could be kept from seeing any landmarks on their first flights, so a later shortcut could not have relied on vision at all.
options.why: The bats did rely on what they could see to fly their shortcuts. Tracking from the first flight mattered because it recorded every route, so a new route could be recognized as truly new.

options.text: From the first flights, the bats could be sorted into place learners and response learners, before any of them had been trained.
options.why: The bats were not trained, and they were not sorted into place and response learners. Tracking from the first flight recorded every route a bat had flown, so a new route could be recognized as truly new.

options.text: Young bats have not yet learned the way back to the roost, so any later return to the roost shows they know where places lie.
options.why: A return to the roost could come from the way back to the start, which leads to one place only. Tracking from the first flight mattered because every route was recorded, so a new route could be recognized as truly new.

items.stem: Wild fruit bats flew shortcuts they had truly never flown, and relied on what they could see to do it. A skeptic argues that relying on sight means the bats did not know where places lie relative to one another. What answers the skeptic?

options.text: Knowing where places lie always requires some places to measure from, so using landmarks does not count against it.
options.why: Correct. Knowing where places lie relates places to one another, so it always needs some places to measure from. The bats’ use of landmarks to fly their shortcuts does not count against it.

options.text: The bats could not have relied on sight, since they flew in the dark, and fruit bats find their way by hearing alone rather than by sight.
options.why: The bats did rely on what they could see. That does not count against knowing where places lie, because such knowledge always needs some places to measure from.

options.text: The skeptic is right, since any landmark the bats used along the way would have served as a beacon and led them straight to the goal.
options.why: A beacon is something at or beside the goal. Landmarks seen along the way are places to measure from, and knowing where places lie always needs some.

options.text: Relying on sight matters only for the way back to the start, not for knowing where places lie relative to one another on a new shortcut.
options.why: The way back to the start does not depend on sight in particular. The skeptic is answered because knowing where places lie always needs some places to measure from, so using landmarks does not count against it.

items.stem: A person who knows a town well cuts across a park to reach a shop by a way never walked before. On the way, the person checks the position of a distant church tower and of the river, neither of which is near the shop. Does steering by these landmarks count against the person knowing where places lie relative to one another?

options.text: No, because knowing where places lie relative to one another always requires some places to measure from.
options.why: Correct. The church tower and the river are places to measure from, and knowledge of where places lie relative to one another always needs some. Steering by them does not count against that knowledge.

options.text: Yes, because the church tower and the river serve as beacons, which lead to a goal without knowledge of where it lies.
options.why: A beacon is something at or beside the goal. The church tower and the river are not near the shop, so they are places to measure from, which knowing where places lie always needs.

options.text: Yes, because any way that depends on landmarks is a familiar path rather than knowing where places lie relative to one another.
options.why: The person took a way never walked before, so it was not a familiar path. Landmarks are places to measure from, and knowing where places lie always needs some.

options.text: No, because landmarks seen from far away give no information at all, so the person must be relying on the way back to the start.
options.why: A distant landmark gives a direction, even though it indicates little about position. And the shop is not the person’s start, so the way back to the start could not lead there.

items.stem: Whether rats know where places lie relative to one another was not settled by the earlier maze experiments. According to later, better-controlled experiments, what can animals do?

options.text: Animals can find a goal that nothing at the goal marks, and some animals take routes they have truly never taken.
options.why: Correct. In the water maze, rats found a hidden platform from changing starts, and young fruit bats tracked from their first flight later flew truly new shortcuts. The verdict is narrow: animals can, and some animals do.

options.text: Animals in general know where places lie relative to one another, and use that knowledge whenever they find a goal.
options.why: That goes beyond the evidence. Animals can find a goal nothing at the goal marks, and some take truly new routes. But whether a particular behavior needs knowledge of where places lie has to be shown one experiment at a time.

options.text: Animals cannot find a goal that nothing at the goal marks, so every apparent shortcut turned out to be guided by a beacon.
options.why: Rats in the water maze found a platform that nothing at the goal marked, from a different start on each trial. So animals can find an unmarked goal, and some take routes they have truly never taken.

options.text: Rats can find a goal that nothing at the goal marks, but no other animal has been shown to take a truly new route.
options.why: Young wild fruit bats, tracked by GPS from their first flight, later flew shortcuts that were truly new. So some animals do take routes they have never taken.

items.stem: A student concludes that, in better-controlled experiments, animals were shown to know where places lie relative to one another. On that view, any shortcut an animal takes is evidence of such knowledge. Which correction is the most accurate?

options.text: Animals can find unmarked goals and some take truly new routes, but whether a given shortcut needs that knowledge must be shown one experiment at a time.
options.why: Correct. The settled part is narrow: animals can find a goal nothing at the goal marks, and some animals take routes they have truly never taken. Skeptics hold that simpler kinds of knowledge working together can produce many such behaviors.

options.text: No animal has been shown to take a truly new route, so a shortcut always shows simpler knowledge, such as a beacon or a familiar path working together.
options.why: That swings too far the other way. Young fruit bats tracked from their first flight flew shortcuts that were truly new. What remains open is whether a particular behavior needs knowledge of where places lie.

options.text: Only rats have been shown to know where places lie relative to one another, so a shortcut taken by any other kind of animal shows simpler knowledge.
options.why: The truly new shortcuts came from wild fruit bats, not from rats. And for any animal, whether a given shortcut needs that knowledge has to be shown one experiment at a time.

options.text: That knowledge has been shown only in animals tested indoors, so a shortcut is evidence of it only when the animal takes it inside a laboratory.
options.why: The fruit bats were wild and flew outdoors. The real limit is different: whether a particular shortcut needs knowledge of where places lie has to be shown one experiment at a time.

items.stem: A bird is seen flying a direct path from one feeder to another, a path no one has seen it fly before. A tall, bright post stands beside the feeder it flies to, and the bird has flown familiar paths around the area for weeks. A skeptic doubts that the flight shows knowledge of where places lie relative to one another. What is the skeptic’s reasoning?

options.text: Simpler kinds of knowledge working together, such as a landmark near the goal and familiar paths, could produce the flight.
options.why: Correct. Skeptics hold that many such behaviors can be produced by simpler kinds of knowledge working together, such as landmarks near the goal, familiar paths, and the way back to the start. Whether a particular flight needs knowledge of where places lie has to be shown one experiment at a time.

options.text: No animal has ever been shown to take a truly new route, so the bird cannot have flown a path that it had never flown before.
options.why: Some animals, such as young fruit bats tracked from their first flight, have been shown to take truly new routes. The skeptic’s point is narrower: simpler kinds of knowledge working together could produce this flight.

options.text: Knowledge of where places lie never makes use of landmarks, so a flight that passes close to a post cannot show that knowledge.
options.why: Using landmarks does not count against knowing where places lie, since that knowledge always needs places to measure from. The skeptic’s point is that the post beside the feeder, with familiar paths, could produce the flight.

options.text: Birds lack knowledge of where places lie, which has been shown in rats running mazes but not in birds flying among familiar paths.
options.why: The skeptic’s doubt is not about birds as such, and the routes shown to be truly new came from wild fruit bats, not from rats in mazes. The skeptic’s point is narrower: simpler kinds of knowledge working together, such as the post beside the feeder and familiar paths, could produce this flight.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say what is now settled, after better-controlled experiments, about whether animals take routes never taken, and what question remains open.
items.answer: In better-controlled experiments, animals were able to find a goal that nothing at the goal marks. In the water maze, for example, rats swam directly to a hidden platform from a different start on each trial. Some animals also took routes they had truly never taken. Young fruit bats tracked by GPS from their first flight later flew shortcuts that were truly new. At least half of each shortcut lay more than 100 meters from anywhere the bat had been. What remains open is narrower. Skeptics hold that many such behaviors can be produced by simpler kinds of knowledge working together, such as landmarks near the goal, familiar paths, and the way back to the start. So whether a particular behavior needs knowledge of where places lie relative to one another has to be shown one experiment at a time.
rubric: Says animals can find a goal that nothing at the goal marks.
Says some animals, not animals in general, take routes they have truly never taken.
Says skeptics hold that simpler kinds of knowledge working together (landmarks near the goal, familiar paths, the way back to the start) can produce many such behaviors.
Says whether a particular behavior needs knowledge of where places lie relative to one another has to be shown one experiment at a time.

pools.title: Whether to Keep Exploring, Wanting to Know, and What the Ancestors Had
pools.covers: reading §9.1.8, §9.1.9, §9.1.10 · lecture 9.1 slides whether_to_keep_exploring, wanting_to_know, what_the_ancestors_had

items.stem: What does exploration versus exploitation mean?

options.text: The trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better and might be worse.
options.why: Correct. Exploiting takes the option already known to be decent. Exploring samples an option whose worth is not yet known, which might turn out better and might turn out worse.

options.text: Choosing in a way that changes at once when what an outcome is worth changes, as when a rat that becomes hungry heads for food.
options.why: That is goal-directed choice, as when rats that had learned where food and water were went to whichever one they now needed. Exploration versus exploitation is a trade-off between a known, decent option and one that might be better and might be worse.

options.text: Learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and that appears later, once there is a reason to use it.
options.why: That is latent learning, which researchers who study curiosity have counted among its signs. Exploration versus exploitation is a trade-off between a known, decent option and one that might be better and might be worse.

options.text: The choice between learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes, and learning to repeat a movement, wherever it leads.
