options.why: That contrasts place learning with response learning. Exploration versus exploitation is a different choice: between an option known to be decent and one that might be better and might be worse.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? The trade-off between taking an option already known to be decent and sampling one that might be better and might be worse.

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: Correct. Exploiting takes the option known to be decent, and exploring samples one that might be better and might be worse. The trade-off between them is exploration versus exploitation.

options.text: goal-directed choice
options.why: Goal-directed choice is choice that changes at once when what an outcome is worth changes, as when hungry rats head for the food side of a maze. It is not a trade-off between a known option and an unknown one.

options.text: place learning
options.why: Place learning is learning to go to a location, whatever movements it takes. It concerns what an animal learns about a goal, not a trade-off between a known option and an unknown one.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show in behavior when it happens and appears later, once there is a reason to use it. It is not a trade-off between a known option and an unknown one.

items.stem: A crow knows a bakery’s dumpster where it reliably finds a decent meal of scraps. It has never visited a park across town, where food might be richer or poorer. What makes the crow’s choice between the two a case of exploration versus exploitation?

options.text: One option is already known to be decent, and the other is unknown and might turn out better or might turn out worse.
options.why: Correct. That pairing is the trade-off. Going back to the dumpster takes the known, decent option, and trying the park samples one that might be better and might be worse.

options.text: The crow’s hunger sets which place is worth going to now, so the choice depends on its state as well as on what it knows.
options.why: Hunger does set which place is worth going to, but that holds for any choice of where to go, even between two places the crow already knows. The trade-off sets an option known to be decent against one that might be better or worse.

options.text: The park is known to offer more food than the dumpster, but the park is farther away, while the decent option lies close by.
options.why: If the park were known to be better, the crow would be weighing distance, not knowledge. The park is unknown and might be better or worse, which is what makes the choice a case of exploration versus exploitation.

options.text: Neither option has ever been tried, so the crow has no idea which is decent and can only pick one of the two at random.
options.why: The crow has tried the dumpster and knows it is decent. The trade-off sets that known option against the park, which is unknown and might be better or worse.

items.stem: Why does knowing where places lie relative to one another lead an animal to a choice about whether to explore?

options.text: That knowledge can be used only once it has been learned, and learning it means going where the animal has not been.
options.why: Correct. An animal cannot use knowledge of where places lie until it has learned it. Learning it means venturing onto unfamiliar ground, which sets exploring against using what is already known.

options.text: That knowledge can be used only close to the goal, so the animal has to keep exploring until it gets near enough to use it.
options.why: Working only near the goal describes knowing what the goal’s surroundings look like. Knowing where places lie works from anywhere, but it has to be learned first, by going where the animal has not been.

options.text: That knowledge works only along a familiar path, so the animal has to explore again whenever it strays from that one path.
options.why: Working only along its own path describes a familiar path. Knowing where places lie lets an animal take routes it has never taken, but it has to be learned first, by going where the animal has not been.

options.text: That knowledge is in place from birth, so the animal explores only to check that places are still where it expects them to be.
options.why: The knowledge is not in place from birth. Knowing where places lie has to be learned before it can be used, and learning it means going where the animal has not been.

items.stem: A mouse moves into a barn and wanders its floors for several nights, finding no food anywhere. Then grain is spilled in a far corner. From the first night after the spill, the mouse reaches the grain about as quickly as a mouse that had found food there from the start. What were the nights of wandering, on this evidence?

options.text: Exploring that built knowledge of the barn’s layout, which showed in behavior only once food gave a reason to use it.
options.why: Correct. Learning where places lie means going where the animal has not been. As with the rats that wandered a maze with no food in it, the knowledge was built during the wandering and showed once food gave a reason to use it.

options.text: Time spent learning nothing, since an animal learns the layout of a place only while food is rewarding it for crossing it.
options.why: The wandering mouse showed no sign of learning, which makes that tempting. But its quick trip to the grain shows that knowledge was built during the wandering, and it showed once there was a reason to use it.

options.text: Practice at one fixed sequence of turns, which happened by chance to be the same sequence that later led to the far corner.
options.why: The mouse wandered all over the barn rather than practicing one sequence, and a single sequence would lead to the grain only by luck. The wandering built knowledge of the layout, which showed once the grain appeared.

options.text: Exploiting a known option, since the mouse kept returning to the parts of the barn that it already knew to be decent.
options.why: Exploiting means taking an option already known to be decent, and the barn had no food at all. The mouse was exploring, and what it learned about the layout showed once the grain appeared.

items.stem: For an animal with a home range, the trade-off between exploring and exploiting takes two forms: leaving a patch of food that is running down, and going somewhere it has never been. How do the two forms differ?

options.text: Leaving a patch means comparing what the animal finds now with what patches around it yield on average; going somewhere new means choosing without knowing what is there.
options.why: Correct. A patch that is running down can be judged against what patches around it yield on average. Ground the animal has never visited offers no such comparison, because nothing is yet known about what is there.

options.text: Leaving a patch means choosing without knowing what any other patch yields; going somewhere new means comparing what the animal finds now with what it found there before.
options.why: That swaps the two. An animal going somewhere new has never been there, so it has found nothing there to compare with. Leaving a patch is the form that compares current finds with what patches around it yield on average.

options.text: Leaving a patch means comparing what the animal finds now with what patches around it yield on average; going somewhere new means comparing those same two things.
options.why: The patch half is right, but going somewhere new cannot be judged that way. The animal does not know what is there at all, and that is how the two forms differ.

options.text: Leaving a patch involves no trade-off, since a patch that is running down is plainly worse; going somewhere new is the only form that sets a known option against an unknown one.
options.why: Leaving a patch is still a trade-off. Staying keeps a known if dwindling supply, and moving to another patch takes time. The forms differ in what can be compared: patches around it on average, or nothing known at all.

items.stem: A squirrel gathering acorns under one oak, in woods it knows well, finds them more and more slowly the longer it stays. Reaching another oak would take time. What does the squirrel have to weigh in deciding when to leave?

options.text: How fast it is finding acorns under this oak now, against what the oaks around it yield on average.
options.why: Correct. The squirrel faces the form of the trade-off that is leaving a patch that is running down. The longer an animal stays, the more slowly it finds more, so the decision compares what it is finding now with what patches around it yield on average.

options.text: Nothing about other oaks, since it cannot know anything about what an oak it has not yet visited will yield.
options.why: That describes going somewhere never visited, where an animal chooses without knowing what is there. Within its home range, the squirrel can compare its current rate with what the oaks around it yield on average.

options.text: Only whether any acorns remain under this oak, since it should stay until the very last one has been found.
options.why: Staying until the last acorn ignores how slowly the last ones come, and moving on takes time as well. The decision sets what the squirrel is finding now against what the oaks around it yield on average.

options.text: How many acorns it has found under this oak today, against how many it found under the same oak on its first visit.
options.why: Comparing this oak with itself leaves out the alternative of moving on. The decision sets what the squirrel is finding now against what the oaks around it yield on average.

items.stem: Sampling an unknown option usually yields less right away than taking a known one. Why is exploring ever worth doing?

options.text: Its value lies in what it teaches, and that value is real only if there will be time to use what is learned.
options.why: Correct. Exploring is worth doing only because of the future. What is learned now can be used later, so its value depends on there being time to use it. Information about a world that will soon change is worth less.

options.text: Its value lies in the extra food it yields right away, since an unknown option is usually richer than a known one.
options.why: An unknown option usually yields less now, not more. Exploring is worth doing only because of the future: its value lies in what it teaches, if there is time to use it.

options.text: Its value lies in what it teaches, and that value is greatest in a world that will soon change, where knowledge is scarce.
options.why: Information about a world that will soon change is worth less, not more, because the change makes it out of date. The value of exploring is real only if there is time to use what is learned.

options.text: Its value lies in finding an option certain to be better, since an animal samples only options sure to beat the known one.
options.why: An unknown option might be better and might be worse, and that uncertainty is what makes the choice a trade-off. Exploring is worth doing for what it teaches, if there will be time to use what is learned.

items.stem: Two birds of the same species land in the same unfamiliar woodland. One will stay there through the winter. The other is migrating and will leave at dawn. For which bird is sampling the woodland’s unknown feeding spots more worth doing, and why?

options.text: The bird that will not migrate, because what sampling teaches is worth something only if time remains to use it.
options.why: Correct. Exploring is worth doing only because of the future. The wintering bird has months to use what it learns, while the migrating bird will be gone before anything sampling teaches it could be used.

options.text: The migrating bird, because it knows less about the woodland and so has more to learn from each spot it samples.
options.why: Both birds know equally little about the woodland. What differs is the time left to use what is learned, and the migrating bird will leave before it can use what sampling teaches.

options.text: The migrating bird, because unknown feeding spots usually yield more right away, and it needs a large meal before its flight.
options.why: Sampling an unknown option usually yields less now, not more. Its value lies in what it teaches, and only the wintering bird will be there long enough to use that.

options.text: Neither bird more than the other, because what sampling teaches about the woodland is worth the same whichever bird learns it.
options.why: Information is worth something only if there will be time to use it. The two birds would learn the same things, but only the wintering bird stays long enough to use them.

items.stem: Why must every animal, and every machine, settle for rules of thumb in choosing between exploring and exploiting?

options.text: No general best answer to the trade-off can be computed in a realistic world, where options are many and much is unknown.
options.why: Correct. With many options and much unknown, no general best answer can be computed, so every animal and every machine has to settle for rules of thumb.

options.text: Rules of thumb are needed by animals with small brains, since a large enough brain can work out the best answer to the trade-off.
options.why: The limit is not the size of a brain. In a realistic world, with many options and much unknown, no general best answer can be computed at all. So every animal, and every machine, has to settle for rules of thumb.

options.text: Rules of thumb always reach the best answer anyway, so working it out by any other means would add nothing to them.
options.why: Settling for rules of thumb means accepting something short of a best answer. No general best answer can be computed in a realistic world, where options are many and much is unknown.

options.text: Exploring never improves on a known option in a realistic world, so a simple rule against exploring is all that is needed.
options.why: An unknown option might be better as well as worse, which is why the choice is a trade-off. The rules of thumb are needed because no general best answer to that trade-off can be computed.

items.stem: An engineer claims to have written a program that computes the single best balance between exploring and exploiting for a cleaning robot. The program is meant to work in any real home, with many rooms, objects that get moved, and corners the robot has never seen. According to the reading, what is wrong with the claim?

options.text: In a realistic world, with many options and much unknown, no general best answer can be computed, so the robot too has to follow rules of thumb.
options.why: Correct. The point holds for machines as well as animals. With many options and much unknown, no program can compute a general best answer, so the robot settles for rules of thumb like any animal.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it in principle, since a machine can compute what an animal cannot, and only animals have to settle for rules of thumb.
options.why: The limit is not a weakness of animals. No general best answer to the trade-off can be computed in a realistic world, so every animal and every machine has to settle for rules of thumb.

options.text: The claim fails because the robot’s sensors are imperfect, and with perfect sensors the single best balance could then be computed.
options.why: Perfect sensors would not reveal corners the robot has never seen, or where objects will be moved next. In a world with many options and much unknown, no general best answer can be computed at all.

options.text: The claim fails because exploring is never worth doing for a machine, which has no later time in which to use what it learns.
options.why: A robot can use later what it learns now, so exploring can be worth doing for a machine as for an animal. The claim fails because no general best answer to the trade-off can be computed in a realistic world.

items.stem: Monkeys offered a gamble will give up about a quarter of a reward’s value to learn early whether the reward is coming. What makes that choice puzzling?

options.text: Learning early leaves what they get unchanged, so they accept less in exchange for information they cannot use.
options.why: Correct. The monkeys seek information that no reward depends on. Whether the reward comes is settled either way, so giving up a quarter of its value gains them nothing they can act on.

options.text: Learning early makes the reward less likely to come, so they lower their own chances of a reward as well as its value.
options.why: Learning early changes nothing about what the monkeys get, including whether the reward comes. The puzzle is that they accept less in exchange for information they cannot use.

options.text: They already know whether the reward is coming, so they give up part of its value for news that adds nothing to what they know.
options.why: The monkeys do not know whether the reward is coming; that is what they pay to learn early. The puzzle is that the early news changes nothing about what they get.

options.text: Learning early lets them back out of a gamble that looks bad, yet they give up more than backing out could ever save.
options.why: If the early news let them back out, it would be information they could use. Learning early changes nothing about what they get, and that is what makes the choice puzzling.

items.stem: Suppose rats in a maze choose between two arms. One arm gives one food pellet on average. In that arm, a tone sounds just after the rat has entered, when it can no longer turn back, signaling whether food is waiting at the end. The other arm gives one and a half pellets on average, with no tone. The rats come to prefer the arm with the tone. Which description fits that choice?

options.text: The rats accept less food on average in exchange for information that changes nothing about what they get.
options.why: Correct. The tone comes too late to change anything, and its arm gives less. Like the pigeons that chose an option averaging two pellets, with a signal, over one averaging three, the rats seek information that no reward depends on.

options.text: The rats are exploring the arm with the tone to learn the maze’s layout, which they can use later to reach food more quickly.
options.why: Exploring to learn a layout yields knowledge an animal can use later. The rats already know both arms, and the tone teaches them nothing they could use, since what waits at the end is already settled.

options.text: The rats choose the arm with the tone because, on average, the tone makes food more likely to be waiting at its end.
options.why: The tone signals whether food is waiting; it does not change whether food is there. The arm with the tone still gives less on average, which is what makes the choice puzzling.

options.text: The rats face open-ended not knowing, since they cannot yet tell what about the maze will turn out to be worth asking.
options.why: The rats know exactly what they are waiting to find out: whether food is at the end. That is the kind of not knowing in which the question is known, not the open-ended kind.

items.stem: A driver searching a large parking lot does not know where the car is. A newcomer who has just arrived in an unfamiliar city does not know which streets lead anywhere. How do the two kinds of not knowing differ?

options.text: The driver knows the question and where its answer will come from; the newcomer does not yet know which questions are even worth asking.
options.why: Correct. The driver knows exactly what is being looked for and will recognize it on sight. The newcomer does not yet know which questions about the city will turn out to matter, which makes that search open-ended.

options.text: The driver does not yet know which questions are even worth asking; the newcomer knows the question and where its answer will come from.
options.why: That swaps the two. The driver knows exactly what is being looked for. It is the newcomer who does not yet know which questions about the city will turn out to matter.

options.text: The driver knows the question and where its answer will come from; the newcomer knows the same things, but has many more places to look.
options.why: The driver half is right, but the newcomer’s problem is not merely a larger search. The newcomer does not yet know which questions about the city will turn out to matter.

options.text: Both lack only the answer to a question they already know; the two differ only in how long finding that answer is likely to take.
options.why: The driver does know the question, but the newcomer does not. Not knowing which questions are worth asking is a different kind of not knowing, not a slower version of the same kind.

items.stem: A child is handed a wrapped present and told it is one of the three toys on their wish list. The child does not know which of the three it is. Which kind of not knowing does the child face?

options.text: Not knowing with a known question, since the child knows what they are waiting to find out and will recognize the answer.
options.why: Correct. Not knowing the answer is not the same as not knowing the question. Like a driver searching a parking lot for a car, the child knows exactly what is being looked for.

options.text: Open-ended not knowing, since the child cannot tell which of the three toys is inside until the paper comes off.
options.why: Being unable to tell the answer yet is true of both kinds. The open-ended kind is not knowing what is even worth asking, and the child knows the question exactly.

options.text: Open-ended not knowing, since no reward is yet in view to guide the child, who has not been given any toy so far.
options.why: A reward is plainly in view: one of three known toys. In open-ended not knowing, no reward is yet in view, because it is not yet known what is worth asking.

options.text: Not knowing with a known question, since the child has opened presents before and remembers what each of them held.
options.why: The kind is right, but past presents are not the reason. The question is known because the child knows exactly what they are waiting to find out, whatever happened with earlier presents.

items.stem: Monkeys give up part of a reward to learn early whether it is coming. Pigeons accept fewer pellets on average in exchange for a signal of what they will get. Which kind of not knowing did these animals face?

options.text: The kind with a known question, since they knew exactly what they were waiting to find out.
options.why: Correct. The monkeys and the pigeons knew exactly what they were waiting to find out. So the open-ended kind of not knowing does not explain why they accept less, and that puzzle is left open.

options.text: The open-ended kind, since they could not tell in advance whether the reward would come or how much it would be.
options.why: Not knowing whether a reward will come is lacking an answer, not lacking a question. The animals knew exactly what they were waiting to find out, which places them in the kind with a known question.

options.text: The open-ended kind, since no reward was in view to guide what they chose, only a signal about one.
options.why: A reward was plainly in view: the gamble’s reward, or the pellets. What the animals sought was early news about it, and they knew exactly what that news would be about.

options.text: Neither kind, since an animal with a reward already on offer is not lacking any knowledge at all.
options.why: The animals did lack knowledge: whether the reward was coming, or how many pellets. They knew exactly what they were waiting to find out, which is the kind of not knowing with a known question.

items.stem: When it is not yet known what is even worth asking, why can reward not guide the search?

options.text: No reward is yet in view, and much time may go into learning before anyone can tell whether it will lead anywhere.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes this kind of not knowing open-ended. With no reward in view, and no way yet to tell whether the learning will lead anywhere, a search guided by reward has nothing to go on.

options.text: The answer is already known, so a reward for finding it would add nothing that the searcher does not already have.
options.why: When even the question is unknown, the answer certainly is not known. The search is open-ended because no reward is yet in view.

options.text: The searcher knows exactly what is wanted, and will recognize it on sight whether or not a reward comes with it.
options.why: Knowing exactly what is wanted describes the other kind of not knowing, like a driver searching a parking lot for a car. Here it is not yet known what is worth asking, so no reward is in view.

options.text: Rewards come only to searchers who know where an answer will come from, so an open-ended search can never be rewarded.
options.why: An open-ended search may still lead somewhere. The trouble is that no reward is yet in view, and much time may go into learning before anyone can tell whether it will.

items.stem: A young otter swims past the farthest bend of the river it knows, into water it has never been in. What kind of not knowing does it face there?

options.text: Something closer to the open-ended kind: it does not yet know what in the new water will matter, and no reward is yet in view.
options.why: Correct. An animal venturing past the edge of the ground it knows faces something closer to the open-ended kind of not knowing. Much time may go into learning before anyone can tell whether it will lead anywhere.

options.text: The kind with a known question: it knows exactly which fish it is looking for, and will recognize them on sight.
options.why: Knowing the question and recognizing the answer on sight fits a driver in a parking lot. Past the edge of its known ground, the otter does not yet know what will be worth looking for.

options.text: Something closer to the open-ended kind: it knows exactly what it is looking for, but has never searched this water before.
options.why: Never having searched the water does not make a search open-ended if the question is known. The search is open-ended because the otter does not yet know what in the new water will be worth asking about.

options.text: No kind of not knowing, since it can follow the river’s banks back to its known water whenever it chooses.
options.why: Being able to get back does not settle what lies ahead. In new water the otter faces something closer to the open-ended kind, with no reward yet in view to guide it.

items.stem: What is homology?

options.text: A resemblance between two species that both inherited from a common ancestor.
options.why: Correct. A homology is a similarity with a shared origin. When distantly related species share a capacity, homology is the simplest reading: their common ancestor very probably had it.

options.text: A resemblance between two species that arose separately because both faced the same problem.
options.why: That is analogy, the counterpart of homology, which attributes a similarity to a shared problem rather than a shared origin. A homology is a resemblance both species inherited from a common ancestor.

options.text: A resemblance between a living species and the ancestor it descends from, kept unchanged ever since.
options.why: A homology is a resemblance between two species, both of which inherited it. A living species is not an unchanged copy of its ancestor, since its brain has kept changing too.

options.text: A resemblance between two individuals of one species, produced because both learned the same skill.
options.why: A homology is a resemblance between species, not individuals, and it is inherited, not learned. Both species inherited it from a common ancestor.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? A resemblance between two species that both inherited from a common ancestor.

options.text: homology
options.why: Correct. Homology attributes a similarity to a shared origin. When distantly related species share a capacity, homology is the simplest reading: their common ancestor very probably had it.

options.text: analogy
options.why: Analogy is the counterpart of homology. It attributes a similarity to a shared problem rather than to a shared origin.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: Convergent evolution is the same problem solved twice from different starting points, as insects’ spatial abilities likely were. Its similarities are not inherited from a common ancestor.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that does not show in behavior when it happens and appears later, once there is a reason to use it. It is not a resemblance between species.

items.stem: One capacity is shared by two closely related kinds of mouse. Another is shared by a mouse and a goldfish. Both resemblances are homologies. Which capacity is likely to be older, and why?

options.text: The one shared by the mouse and the goldfish, since the more distantly related the species that share a capacity, the older it is likely to be.
options.why: Correct. On the homology reading, each capacity comes from a common ancestor. The mouse and the goldfish share a far more ancient ancestor than the two mice do, so their shared capacity is likely the older one.

options.text: The one shared by the two kinds of mouse, since a capacity is likely to be older when the species sharing it are closely related.
options.why: On the homology reading, a shared capacity comes from the species’ common ancestor, and the two mice share a recent one. The more distantly related the species, the older the capacity is likely to be.

options.text: Neither is likely older, since every homology, the mouse and goldfish’s included, comes from the earliest common ancestor of all animals.
options.why: Each homology goes back to the common ancestor of the species that share it, and those ancestors lived at very different times. The more distantly related the species, the older the capacity is likely to be.

options.text: Neither can be dated, since a resemblance between a living mouse and a living goldfish is no evidence of when the capacity arose.
options.why: Comparing living species is how such capacities are dated. How long ago their lines parted indicates how old a shared capacity is likely to be.

items.stem: Goldfish reach a place defined by cues around a room from starting points they have never used. Turtles do the same in a dry maze. Fish, chicks, and pigeons recover their heading from the shape of a space. What conclusion fits these findings?

options.text: Spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates, and are not found only in mammals.
options.why: Correct. Fish, reptiles, and birds all show abilities like those of rats, so spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates. That wide sharing is the starting point for asking how old the abilities are.

options.text: Spatial abilities of this kind are found only in animals that make their own body heat, as mammals do.
options.why: Goldfish and turtles do not make their own body heat as mammals do, yet both reach a place from new starting points. Spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates.

options.text: Animals other than mammals reach a goal only while they can sense the goal or a marker beside it.
options.why: Reaching a place defined by cues around a room, from starting points never used, goes beyond sensing the goal or a marker beside it. Spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates.

options.text: Spatial abilities appear only in animals that live on land, since fish have no fixed places to return to.
options.why: Goldfish learn to swim to a place and reach it from new starting points. Spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates, including fish.

items.stem: Twenty-five small geckos, each living in a single tree, were carried to nearby trees. By the next night, 11 had walked almost straight back to their own tree. What can be concluded from the geckos’ return trips about spatial abilities across vertebrates?

options.text: Reptiles find their way home too, one more sign that spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. The geckos join goldfish, turtles, chicks, and pigeons as vertebrates other than mammals that show spatial abilities. Such abilities are shared widely among vertebrates.

options.text: Reptiles find their way home only by retracing their own outward steps, so the geckos bear on no other vertebrates.
options.why: The geckos were carried, so they had no outward steps to retrace. Their return is one more sign that spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates.

options.text: Geckos are among the ancestors of mammals, so their ability is a direct record of what the early mammal inherited.
options.why: Geckos are living cousins of mammals, not their ancestors, and their brains have kept changing too. Their ability is one more sign that spatial abilities are shared widely among vertebrates.

options.text: Fewer than half returned, so reptiles must lack the spatial abilities that fish and birds have been shown to have.
options.why: Eleven of 25 walked almost straight back to their own tree by the next night, which is a real ability, not its absence. Reptiles find their way home too.

items.stem: Goldfish are not ancestors of mammals. How, then, can comparing goldfish with rats help date a spatial ability that both share?

options.text: How long ago the goldfish line parted from the line leading to mammals indicates how old an ability both share is likely to be.
options.why: Correct. Goldfish are living cousins, not ancestors. What dates a shared ability is the time since their lines parted, since the common ancestor at that split very probably had it.

options.text: Goldfish brains have changed little since their line parted from the others, so a goldfish shows what the ancestor’s brain was like.
options.why: Goldfish brains have kept changing too. Comparison dates an ability by how long ago the lines parted, not by treating a goldfish as a preserved ancestor.

options.text: Goldfish are a recent offshoot of the line leading to mammals, so any ability they share with rats must itself be recent.
options.why: The goldfish line parted from the others more than 400 million years ago, before vertebrates moved onto land. An ability shared with rats is therefore likely to be old, not recent.

options.text: Comparing goldfish with rats cannot date an ability at all, since only fossils of the common ancestor would be evidence of when it arose.
options.why: Abilities can be dated without fossils. How long ago the lines of two living species parted indicates how old an ability they share is likely to be.

items.stem: Suppose a capacity were found in turtles and in rats, but had never been tested in fish. Reasoning by homology, as for the spatial abilities of vertebrates, which ancestor does the simplest reading say very probably had the capacity?

options.text: An early four-legged animal that lived about 320 million years ago, where the lines to reptiles and to mammals parted.
options.why: Correct. The line to mammals and the line to reptiles and birds parted about 320 million years ago, from an early four-legged animal. Without fish, the simplest reading goes back only to that common ancestor of turtles and rats.

options.text: An animal that lived in water more than 400 million years ago, before vertebrates moved onto land, the ancestor of goldfish too.
options.why: That ancestor is the simplest reading only when goldfish share the capacity as well. Turtles and rats alone point back to their own common ancestor, an early four-legged animal about 320 million years ago.

options.text: The first mammal, which lived more than 200 million years ago, since rats are mammals and the capacity is found in rats.
options.why: Turtles are not mammals, so a capacity they share with rats points to an ancestor older than the first mammals. The simplest reading is their common ancestor, an early four-legged animal about 320 million years ago.

options.text: A mammal that lived about 66 million years ago, when mammals became much larger after the dinosaurs other than birds died out.
options.why: Mammals did become larger then, but turtles share the capacity. So the simplest reading points to an ancestor older than mammals themselves: an early four-legged animal about 320 million years ago.

items.stem: Goldfish, turtles, and rats all learn to reach a place from a starting point they have never used. What is the simplest reading of how old that ability is?

options.text: More than 400 million years old, very probably present in their common ancestor, an animal that lived in water.
options.why: Correct. The goldfish line parted from the others more than 400 million years ago, before vertebrates moved onto land. Their common ancestor very probably had the ability.

options.text: About 320 million years old, first present in an early four-legged animal, the ancestor of turtles and rats.
options.why: About 320 million years ago is when the line to mammals parted from the line to reptiles and birds. Including goldfish pushes the date back further, to more than 400 million years.

options.text: More than 200 million years old, first present in the early mammals that lived alongside the dinosaurs.
options.why: Goldfish and turtles are not mammals, so an ability they share with rats did not begin with the first mammals. The simplest reading puts it in a common ancestor that lived in water.

options.text: About 66 million years old, arising once mammals grew larger after the dinosaurs other than birds died out.
options.why: Mammals did grow larger after that extinction, but goldfish and turtles have the ability too. The simplest reading puts its origin more than 400 million years ago.

items.stem: Insects also reach places they cannot sense. Why do the insects’ abilities not make the spatial abilities of vertebrates any older?

options.text: The brain parts that do the work in insects are not counterparts of those in vertebrates, so the abilities likely arose separately.
options.why: Correct. When similar abilities rest on brain parts that were not inherited from a common ancestor, separate origins are the simpler reading. The insects’ abilities are likely a case of convergent evolution, the same problem solved twice from different starting points.

options.text: Insects reach places by steering toward something they can sense, so their abilities cannot be compared with those of vertebrates.
options.why: Insects do more than steer. They reach places they cannot sense, as vertebrates do. Their abilities do not date the vertebrates’ because the brain parts doing the work are not counterparts.

options.text: Insects use counterparts of the vertebrates’ brain parts, but those parts have changed so much that no sign of their age remains in them.
options.why: The brain parts that do the work in insects are not counterparts of the vertebrates’ at all. That is why separate origins are the simpler reading.

options.text: Similar abilities in distantly related animals always arose separately, so no shared ability can ever go back to a common ancestor.
options.why: That would rule out homology altogether. When distantly related species share a capacity, homology is the simplest reading. Separate origins become the simpler reading when the brain parts involved were not inherited from a common ancestor.

items.stem: Suppose researchers found that octopuses can reach a hidden place from starting points they have never used. Suppose also that the brain parts doing this work are not counterparts of any in vertebrates. Reasoning as for insects, what would follow for the age of the vertebrates’ ability?

options.text: The age would stay as it was, since an ability that likely arose separately in octopuses has no bearing on the vertebrates’ ability.
options.why: Correct. As with insects, brain parts that are not counterparts make separate origins the simpler reading. An ability that likely arose separately in octopuses would not make the vertebrates’ ability any older.

options.text: The ability would be older than 400 million years, since the octopus line parted from the vertebrate line earlier than the goldfish line did.
options.why: That would follow only if the shared ability were a homology. With brain parts that are not counterparts, separate origins are the simpler reading, so the octopus would leave the vertebrates’ date unchanged.

options.text: The ability would be younger than thought, since an ability that arose twice cannot be as old as one that arose only once.
options.why: An ability arising separately in another line has no bearing on how old the vertebrates’ own ability is. Comparing vertebrates still puts it at more than 400 million years.

options.text: The octopuses’ ability would very probably be inherited from a common ancestor with vertebrates, since the two share a capacity.
options.why: Sharing a capacity points to a common ancestor unless separate origins are the simpler reading. With brain parts that are not counterparts, separate origins are simpler, as for insects.

items.stem: The spatial abilities of the first mammals were old. What was new for them?

options.text: First of all, the problem: a warm body that needed a great deal of food, found in poor light, and then a trip back home.
options.why: Correct. The abilities were shared with vertebrates whose lines parted long before. What was new for the early mammal was, first of all, the problem its warm body set.

options.text: The ability to reach a place from a starting point never used before, which no animal had shown before the first mammals appeared.
options.why: Goldfish and turtles show that ability too, and the simplest reading puts it in a common ancestor that lived more than 400 million years ago. The ability was old; the problem was new.

options.text: The ability to recover a heading from the shape of a space, which fish, reptiles, and birds all lack, and which mammals alone have.
options.why: Fish, chicks, and pigeons all recover their heading from the shape of a space. The abilities were old; what was new was the problem the warm body set.

options.text: The ability to find the way home after being carried away from it, which no animal before the first mammals had shown.
options.why: Geckos carried to nearby trees walked almost straight back to their own, so reptiles find their way home too. The abilities were old, and what was new for the early mammal was, first of all, the problem.

items.stem: The early mammal’s warm body needed a great deal of food, found in poor light, and then a trip back home. What is one possibility for how that need for food bore on finding the way?

options.text: The need for food may have favored animals that remembered more places and found their way back to them more reliably.
options.why: Correct. The abilities were old, and the warm body’s great need for food was new. That this need favored animals that used the older abilities well is offered as one possibility, a suggestion rather than a finding.

options.text: Fossils show that the need for food favored animals that remembered more places and found their way back to them more reliably.
options.why: The idea is right, but its standing is not. That the need for food favored animals that used the older abilities well is offered only as one possibility, not as something fossils or any other evidence has shown.

options.text: The need for food was met by new spatial abilities that appeared in the first mammals and that no earlier vertebrate had.
options.why: The abilities were not new. Goldfish, turtles, and rats share them, and the simplest reading is that they are more than 400 million years old.

options.text: The need for food made spatial abilities unnecessary, since a warm body could find enough food by smell and touch alone.
options.why: The early mammal still had to get back home after foraging, and the smell of its nest leads it home only once it is close. One possibility is that the need for food favored animals that used the older abilities well.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the two forms that the trade-off between exploring and exploiting takes for an animal with a home range, and say how they differ. Then explain why exploring in either form is worth doing only because of the future.
items.answer: One form is leaving a patch of food that is running down. The longer an animal stays in a patch, the more slowly it finds more, and moving to another patch takes time. Deciding when to leave means comparing what it is finding now with what patches around it yield on average. The other form is going somewhere it has never been, which means choosing without knowing what is there at all. In both forms, sampling an unknown option usually yields less now. Its value lies in what it teaches. That value is real only if there will be time to use what is learned. Information about a world that will soon change is worth less, since the change makes it out of date.
rubric: Names leaving a patch that is running down as one form.
Names going somewhere never visited as the other form.
Says leaving a patch compares what the animal finds now with what patches around it yield on average, while going somewhere new means choosing without knowing what is there.
Says exploring usually yields less now, and that its value lies in what it teaches.
Says that value is real only if there will be time to use what is learned, or that information about a world that will soon change is worth less.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe the two kinds of not knowing, give an example of each, and explain why reward cannot guide the search in one of them.
items.answer: In one kind, the question is known, and so is where its answer will come from. A person looking for their car in a large parking lot does not know where it is. But they know exactly what they are looking for, and will recognize it on sight. In the other kind, it is not yet known what is even worth asking. A person who has just arrived in an unfamiliar city does not know which streets lead anywhere, or which questions about the city will turn out to matter. That second kind is open-ended. No reward is yet in view to guide the search, and much time may go into learning before anyone can tell whether it will lead anywhere.
rubric: Describes a kind of not knowing in which the question, and where its answer will come from, are known.
Describes a kind in which it is not yet known what is even worth asking.
Gives a fitting example of each (a car in a parking lot and a newcomer to a city, or equivalent cases).
Says reward cannot guide the open-ended kind because no reward is yet in view.
Says much time may go into learning before anyone can tell whether it will lead anywhere.

items.stem: Goldfish, turtles, and rats all reach a place from a new starting point, and none of the three is an ancestor of the others. In a short paragraph, explain how comparing them supports dating that ability to more than 400 million years ago. Then explain why the abilities of insects do not push the date back further.
items.answer: Goldfish, turtles, and rats are living cousins, not ancestors, and their brains have kept changing. But how long ago their lines parted indicates how old a shared ability is likely to be. The line to mammals and the line to reptiles and birds parted about 320 million years ago. The goldfish line parted from both more than 400 million years ago, before vertebrates moved onto land. All three reach a place from a new starting point, so the simplest reading is homology. The ability was very probably present in their common ancestor, an animal that lived in water. Insects also reach places they cannot sense, but the brain parts that do the work in insects are not counterparts of those in vertebrates. So separate origins, by convergent evolution, are the simpler reading, and the insects’ abilities do not make the vertebrates’ abilities any older.
rubric: Says the three species are living cousins rather than ancestors, so what dates a shared ability is how long ago their lines parted.
Says the goldfish line parted from the others more than 400 million years ago, before vertebrates moved onto land.
Says the simplest reading is that their common ancestor, an animal that lived in water, very probably had the ability.
Says the brain parts doing the work in insects are not counterparts of those in vertebrates.
Concludes that the insects’ abilities likely arose separately, by convergent evolution, and so do not make the vertebrates’ abilities older.

pools.title: Beacons, Snapshots, Routes, and a Running Sum
pools.covers: reading §9.2.1, §9.2.2, §9.2.3 · lecture 9.2 slides beacons_snapshots_routes, a_running_sum, correcting_the_sum

items.stem: What is a snapshot?

options.text: A stored view of what the surroundings look like from the goal, which an animal can match only near the goal.
options.why: Correct. An animal using a snapshot moves until the scene around it matches the stored view. The match improves as the animal gets closer, but it can be made only near the goal, where the surroundings still look much as they did.

options.text: A fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, leading from one place to another, which works only along its own path.
options.why: That is a route. A route can lead an animal to the goal from much farther away than a snapshot can, but only along its own path. A snapshot is a stored view of the surroundings from the goal.

options.text: Something sensed at or beside a goal, which an animal can reach by steering toward it for as long as it can be sensed.
options.why: That is a beacon, which an animal steers toward. A snapshot is not one thing at the goal but a stored view of the whole surroundings, as seen from the goal.

options.text: The straight-line distance and direction from where an animal is back to its start, which points there from anywhere.
options.why: That is a home vector, the result of path integration. A snapshot is a stored view of the surroundings from the goal, and it can be matched only near the goal.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A stored view of what the surroundings look like from a goal, which an animal can match only near the goal”.

options.text: snapshot
options.why: Correct. A snapshot is a stored view of the surroundings from the goal. An animal moves until the scene matches it, which works only near the goal, where the surroundings still look much as they did.

options.text: route
options.why: A route is a fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, leading from one place to another. A route can lead from much farther away than a snapshot can, but only along its own path.

options.text: beacon
options.why: A beacon is something sensed at or beside the goal, which an animal steers toward. A stored view of the whole surroundings from the goal is a snapshot.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, which points there from anywhere. A stored view of the surroundings from the goal, matched only nearby, is a snapshot.

items.stem: A beachgoer buries a set of keys in the sand, in the middle of three tall striped umbrellas on an otherwise bare stretch of beach, and goes for a swim. While the beachgoer is away, a lifeguard moves all three umbrellas 20 meters down the beach, keeping their arrangement. The beachgoer comes back by moving until the scene looks as it did from the keys. Where does the beachgoer first search?

options.text: In the middle of the three umbrellas at their new spot, where the scene now matches the stored view.
options.why: Correct. Matching a snapshot means moving until the scene matches the stored view, and the umbrellas now make that match 20 meters away. A digger wasp did the same when a ring of pinecones around its nest was moved a short distance. The wasp searched in the middle of the ring rather than at its nest.

options.text: At the spot where the keys are buried, since the stored view of the umbrellas was taken there and still leads back to it.
options.why: The stored view was taken at the keys, but a snapshot leads only to wherever the scene matches it. With the umbrellas moved, that is the middle of the umbrellas at their new spot, as with the wasp that searched in the middle of a moved ring of pinecones.

options.text: Halfway between their old spot and the new one, since a scene matching the view only in part is a compromise.
options.why: Nothing in matching a snapshot averages an old place with a new one. The beachgoer moves until the scene matches the stored view, and the moved umbrellas make that match at their new spot.

options.text: Nowhere in particular, since the middle of the umbrellas matches the view only while every feature is where it was.
options.why: A partial change does not stop the match. When a ring of pinecones around a digger wasp’s nest was moved, the wasp searched in the middle of the ring, where the scene matched its stored view.

items.stem: What is a route?

options.text: A fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, leading from one place to another, which works only along its own path.
options.why: Correct. Directions such as “past the park, then left at the gas station” are a route. A route can lead an animal to the goal from much farther away than a beacon or a snapshot can, but only along its own path.

options.text: A stored view of what the surroundings look like from the goal, which an animal can match only once it is near the goal.
options.why: That is a snapshot. A snapshot works only near the goal, while a route is a fixed sequence of moves or landmarks that can lead from much farther away.

options.text: A running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, kept from heading and distance traveled.
options.why: That is path integration. Its result, the home vector, is not tied to a path at all, while a route works only along its own path.

options.text: Knowledge of where places lie relative to one another, so that the way between any two of them can be worked out.
options.why: That is survey knowledge, the only kind that can lead from a new starting point to any place an animal knows. A route is a fixed sequence of moves or landmarks that works only along its own path.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, leading from one place to another, which works only along its own path”.

options.text: route
options.why: Correct. A route, like directions past the park and left at the gas station, can lead an animal to the goal from much farther away than a snapshot can. But a route works only along its own path.

options.text: snapshot
options.why: A snapshot is a stored view of the surroundings from the goal, matched only near the goal. A fixed sequence of moves or landmarks is a route.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the start. It is not tied to any path, while a route works only along its own.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Path integration is keeping a running estimate of the way back to the start, from heading and distance traveled. A fixed sequence of moves or landmarks is a route.

items.stem: A snapshot and a route can each lead an animal to a goal it cannot sense from where it is. How do the two differ in where they work?

options.text: A snapshot can be matched only near the goal; a route leads from much farther away, but only along its own path.
options.why: Correct. A snapshot depends on the surroundings still looking as they did from the goal, which is true only nearby. A route can lead from much farther away, but someone who misses the turn has nothing in it to get back on course.

options.text: A snapshot can be matched from anywhere its landmarks are in view; a route works only near the goal it leads to.
options.why: Neither half is right. A snapshot can be matched only near the goal, where the surroundings still look as they did, and a route leads from much farther away along its own path.

options.text: A snapshot works from any starting point at all; a route leads from much farther away, but only along its own path.
options.why: The route half is right, but a snapshot does not work from anywhere. Far from the goal the surroundings look different, so the stored view can be matched only nearby.

options.text: A snapshot can be matched only near the goal; a route leads to the goal from any starting point, on its path or off it.
options.why: The snapshot half is right, but a route works only along its own path. An animal that strays off it has nothing in the route to get back on course.

items.stem: Desert ants following a familiar route keep a familiar landmark on the same side as it was in training. Judging by the ants’ behavior, what does following a route require?

options.text: At each point along the route, the ant needs only a sensible direction, as if walking a corridor with signposts.
options.why: Correct. Following a route needs little. Keeping a landmark on the same side gives a sensible direction at that point, and nothing more is needed to keep going.

options.text: At each point along the route, the ant needs to know where that point lies relative to every other place it knows.
options.why: Knowing where places lie relative to one another is the most informative kind of knowledge, but a route does not need it. At each point, a route needs only a sensible direction.

options.text: At each point along the route, the ant needs a stored view of the goal itself, matched against the scene in front of it.
options.why: Matching a stored view of the goal is a snapshot, which works only near the goal. Following a route needs only a sensible direction at each point along it.

options.text: At each point along the route, the ant needs the straight-line distance and direction back to the place where it started.
options.why: That is a home vector, which path integration keeps. Following a route needs much less: only a sensible direction at each point along it.

items.stem: Desert ants were picked up while heading home and set down on their own familiar outward route. They behaved as if they were lost. What can be concluded from the ants’ behavior?

options.text: Separate routes are kept separate, so the outward route did not guide an ant that was on its way home.
options.why: Correct. The ants knew the outward route well, but they were heading home, and the outward route was not the route home. Separate routes are kept separate.

options.text: A route works only near the goal, like a stored view, so the ants were too far from the nest for any route to help them.
options.why: That describes a snapshot, which works only near the goal. A route can lead an animal from much farther away. The ants were lost because the outward route and the route home are kept separate.

options.text: Following a route requires knowing where the nest lies, and the ants lost that knowledge when they were picked up and moved.
options.why: Following a route needs little: at each point, only a sensible direction. The ants were lost because the route they were set down on was the outward one, and separate routes are kept separate.

options.text: Ants keep only one route at a time, so the outward route had been forgotten once the ants turned for home with food.
options.why: The ants had not forgotten the outward route, which was still a familiar one. Ants keep more than one route, and separate routes are kept separate, so knowing the outward route gave the ants nothing for the trip home.

items.stem: How does steering toward a beacon differ from steering toward a goal that can itself be sensed?

options.text: It needs only one more thing, knowing the beacon is near the goal, and it works as long as the beacon can be sensed.
options.why: Correct. Steering toward a beacon is the same steering an animal uses toward any goal it can sense directly. The one extra fact is that the beacon is near the goal, and the procedure works only while the beacon can be sensed.

options.text: It needs a stored view of the goal’s surroundings as well, and it works only once the goal itself comes into view.
options.why: A stored view of the surroundings is a snapshot, a different procedure. Steering toward a beacon needs only ordinary steering plus knowing the beacon is near the goal.

options.text: It needs to know where the beacon lies relative to other places, and then it works from any starting point at all.
options.why: Knowing where places lie relative to one another is not needed. Steering toward a beacon needs only ordinary steering plus knowing the beacon is near the goal, and it works only where the beacon can be sensed.

options.text: It needs a running estimate of the way back to the start, and it works even after the beacon can no longer be sensed.
options.why: A running estimate of the way back to the start is path integration, a different procedure. Steering toward a beacon works only as long as the beacon can be sensed.

items.stem: A hiker returning to camp at dusk steers toward a tall radio tower that stands beside the campsite. Partway back, the trail drops into a deep valley, and a ridge hides the tower. Steering toward the tower is the only procedure the hiker is using. What does that procedure offer in the valley?

options.text: No direction at all, because steering toward a beacon works only while the beacon itself can be sensed.
options.why: Correct. A beacon helps only from where it can be sensed. Once the ridge hides the tower, steering toward it gives the hiker nothing to steer by.

options.text: The same direction as before, because knowing the tower is beside camp lets the hiker work out where camp lies.
options.why: Knowing the tower is beside camp is all a beacon needs, but it gives a direction only while the tower can be sensed. Working out where camp lies from elsewhere would take a different kind of knowledge.

options.text: A rougher direction, because a beacon that was in view a little while ago still points weakly toward the goal it marks.
options.why: A beacon does not keep pointing once it is out of view. It helps only from where it can be sensed, so in the valley the procedure gives no direction.

options.text: A direction taken from the hiker’s memory of the scene, because steering toward a beacon includes matching a stored view.
options.why: Matching a stored view is a snapshot, which is a separate procedure. Steering toward a beacon needs only ordinary steering plus knowing the beacon is near the goal, and it stops when the beacon cannot be sensed.

items.stem: Bees and desert ants were each trained to find food in the middle of a set of landmarks, and then tested with the array of landmarks spread wider. How did their searches differ?

options.text: Bees searched where the directions to the landmarks matched what they had seen from the food; ants searched sharply only if the landmarks were enlarged too.
options.why: Correct. The bees matched the directions to the landmarks. The ants searched sharply only when the landmarks themselves were enlarged as well, so that the whole picture matched the stored view.

options.text: Bees searched sharply only if the landmarks were enlarged too; ants searched wherever the directions to the landmarks matched what they had seen from the food.
options.why: That swaps the two findings. The bees searched where the directions matched, and the ants searched sharply only when the landmarks were enlarged as well.

options.text: Bees scattered their search widely across the spread-out array; ants searched sharply only if the landmarks were enlarged too.
options.why: The ant half is right, but the bees did not scatter. They searched where the directions to the landmarks matched the directions they had seen from the food.

options.text: Bees searched where the directions to the landmarks matched what they had seen from the food; ants searched sharply whatever the landmarks’ size.
options.why: The bee half is right, but with ordinary landmarks the ants’ search was scattered. They searched sharply only when the landmarks were enlarged too, so that the whole picture matched.

items.stem: What is path integration?

options.text: Keeping a running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, from heading and distance traveled.
options.why: Correct. Path integration adds up heading and distance as the animal goes, so that at any moment it has an estimate of the way back to the start. The result is a home vector.

options.text: Storing a view of the surroundings at the start, and then moving until the current scene matches that stored view once again.
options.why: That describes matching a snapshot, which works only near the goal. Path integration keeps a running estimate of the way back from heading and distance traveled.

options.text: Repeating the moves made on the way out in reverse order, one by one, until the animal arrives back at the place it started.
options.why: Retracing the outward path is not path integration. Desert ants that find food run home in a straight line rather than retracing their winding outward path.

options.text: Combining several estimates of where the start lies, each weighted by how reliable its own source of evidence has proved.
options.why: That is cue combination, one way to correct a running sum that has drifted. Path integration is keeping the running sum itself, from heading and distance traveled.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Keeping a running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the starting point, from the heading and the distance traveled”.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Correct. Path integration is the process of keeping that running estimate. Its result at any moment is a home vector.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, which is the result. Keeping the running estimate that produces it is path integration.

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Cue combination is combining several estimates, each weighted by how reliable it is, which is one way to correct a running sum. Keeping the running sum is path integration.

options.text: simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)
options.why: SLAM is building a map of the surroundings while keeping track of one’s own position on it. A robot doing it keeps a running estimate from its wheels, but the term for keeping that running estimate of the way back is path integration.

items.stem: What is a home vector?

options.text: The straight-line distance and direction from where an animal is back to its start, which points there from anywhere.
options.why: Correct. A home vector is not tied to any path. It points to one place, the start, from wherever the animal is, but gives no information about the way to anywhere else.

options.text: The process of keeping a running estimate of the way back to the start, from the heading and from the distance traveled.
options.why: That is path integration, the process. The home vector is its result: the straight-line distance and direction back to the start.

options.text: A fixed sequence of moves leading from the start out to a goal, which the animal can then follow back again in reverse.
options.why: A fixed sequence of moves is a route, which works only along its own path. A home vector is not tied to a path at all.

options.text: The straight-line distance and direction from where an animal is to any place it knows, read off a map it keeps.
options.why: A home vector points to one place only, the start. It gives no information about the way to anywhere else.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The straight-line distance and direction from where an animal is back to its starting point. It points to one place from anywhere, but gives no information about the way between other places”.

options.text: home vector
options.why: Correct. A home vector is the result of path integration. Like the hiker who knows the trailhead lies about a mile to the east, an animal with one can head straight back to its start from anywhere.

options.text: route
options.why: A route is a fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, which works only along its own path. A home vector is not tied to any path.

options.text: snapshot
options.why: A snapshot is a stored view of the surroundings from the goal, matched only near the goal. A distance and direction back to the start, usable from anywhere, is a home vector.

options.text: survey knowledge
options.why: Survey knowledge is knowing where places lie relative to one another, so that the way between any two of them can be worked out. A home vector points to one place only, the start.

items.stem: How is path integration related to a home vector?

options.text: Path integration is the process of keeping a running estimate, and the home vector is the estimate that the process produces.
options.why: Correct. Path integration keeps a running estimate of the way back to the start, from heading and distance traveled. The result, at any moment, is a home vector.

options.text: The home vector is the process of keeping a running estimate, and path integration is the estimate that the process then produces.
options.why: That reverses the two. Path integration is the process of keeping the running estimate, and the home vector is the estimate itself.

options.text: Path integration works along a familiar path, while a home vector works from anywhere, so the two are rival procedures.
options.why: Path integration is not tied to a path, and it is not a rival to the home vector. The home vector is what path integration produces.

options.text: Path integration measures distance traveled only, and the home vector adds the direction that a landmark or the sun gives.
options.why: Path integration uses both heading and distance traveled. The home vector, its result, is a distance and a direction together.

items.stem: An animal knows a route from its nest to a feeding spot, and it also keeps a home vector. Chasing a beetle, it runs well off the route, into ground it has never crossed. Which of the two still gives it a way back to the nest?

options.text: The home vector, because it is not tied to any path and points back to the start from wherever the animal is.
options.why: Correct. Unlike a route, a home vector is not tied to a path. It points to one place, the start, from anywhere, so it still leads back to the nest.

options.text: The route, because a route leads from much farther away than other procedures, and so it reaches off its own path too.
options.why: A route does lead from far away, but only along its own path. Off the route, it gives nothing to get back on course.

options.text: Both, because a route and a home vector are each a running estimate of the straight-line way back to the start.
options.why: Only the home vector is such an estimate. A route is a fixed sequence of moves or landmarks, and it works only along its own path.

options.text: Neither, because a home vector, like a route, works only along the path that the animal took on its way out.
options.why: A home vector is not tied to a path. That is the difference between it and a route, and it is why the home vector still points to the nest.

items.stem: Desert ants judge the distance home correctly in darkness, and with the lower halves of their eyes covered. What can be concluded about how desert ants measure distance and take their heading?

options.text: Vision is not what measures distance; in desert ants, distance comes from the legs, while heading comes from the sun.
options.why: Correct. Darkness and covered eyes do not disturb the ants’ judgment of distance, so vision is not the measure. Their distance comes from their legs, and their heading from the sun.

options.text: Vision is not what measures distance; in desert ants, distance comes from the sun’s position, while heading comes from the legs.
options.why: The first half is right, but the sources are swapped. The sun gives the ants their heading, and their legs give the distance.

options.text: Vision measures distance only by day; at night, desert ants switch to timing how long they have been walking, and the sun gives heading.
options.why: A timer is ruled out. Ants given longer legs walked slightly more slowly yet went farther, which a timer would not produce. Distance comes from the legs, day or night.

options.text: Vision measures distance with the upper halves of the eyes, which still see landmarks against the sky as the ant walks.
options.why: In darkness, no part of the eye sees landmarks, and the ants still judge distance correctly. Vision is not what measures it; the legs are.

items.stem: Desert ants were trained to walk 10 meters along a channel to a feeder. At the feeder, some had bristles glued to their legs to lengthen them, and some had their legs shortened. Released in a parallel channel to head home, how did each group do?

options.text: Ants with lengthened legs walked past the nest before searching, and ants with shortened legs stopped short of it.
options.why: Correct. Ants on stilts walked past the nest, and ants on stumps stopped short. So the distance an ant judges depends on its strides: something tracks them, though the researchers write that the ants “most probably do not literally count”.

options.text: Ants with lengthened legs stopped short of the nest before searching, and ants with shortened legs walked on past it.
options.why: That reverses the result. Longer legs take longer strides, so ants on stilts walked past the nest, and ants on stumps stopped short.

options.text: Both groups searched at about the right distance, since the ants measured the trip home by the time it took them.
options.why: The altered legs did change where the ants searched. And a timer is ruled out: the ants on stilts walked slightly more slowly, yet they went farther.

options.text: Both groups searched at about the right distance, since the sun gave each ant its distance back to the nest.
options.why: The sun gives desert ants their heading, not their distance. Distance comes from the legs, which is why altering the legs changed where the ants searched.

items.stem: Ants whose legs were lengthened at the feeder overshot the nest on the way home, and ants whose legs were shortened fell short. Which conclusion is supported by these results?

options.text: Something in the ant tracks its strides, although the ant most probably does not literally count them.
options.why: Correct. Changing the length of the strides changed the distance the ants judged, so something tracks strides. The researchers write that the ants “most probably do not literally count”, so the conclusion stops short of counting.

options.text: Something in the ant times its trip, and longer legs probably let each moment of walking cover more ground.
options.why: A timer is ruled out. The ants on stilts walked slightly more slowly than normal ants, and an ant timing its trip would then have gone less far, not farther.

options.text: Something in the ant gauges how fast the ground flows past its eyes, and longer legs probably changed that flow.
options.why: Vision is not what measures distance. Ants judge distance correctly in darkness and with the lower halves of their eyes covered.

options.text: Something in the ant takes its heading from its legs, so altered legs probably threw off its direction.
options.why: Desert ants take their heading from the sun and their distance from the legs. The altered legs changed how far the ants went, not which way.

items.stem: Ants on stilts walked slightly more slowly than normal ants, and yet they walked farther before searching for the nest. Given the slower pace, why is a timer ruled out as the way ants measure distance?

options.text: An ant timing its trip would have gone less far at a slower pace, not farther, so a timer predicts the opposite.
options.why: Correct. A timer would stop the ant after a fixed time, and at a slower pace that covers less ground. The ants on stilts went farther, so they were not timing the trip.

options.text: An ant timing its trip would have gone exactly as far at any pace, so a timer predicts that the stilts change nothing.
options.why: A timer does not give the same distance at every pace. A fixed time at a slower pace covers less ground, which is the opposite of what the ants on stilts did.

options.text: An ant timing its trip would have gone farther at a slower pace, so a timer predicts the result but not its size.
options.why: A slower pace for a fixed time covers less ground, not more. The ants on stilts went farther, which a timer cannot explain at all.

options.text: An ant timing its trip would have been counting a fixed number of strides, so a slower pace would change nothing.
options.why: A timer measures time, not strides. Tracking strides is what the experiment supports, and a fixed time at a slower pace would have covered less ground.

items.stem: What does cue combination mean?

options.text: Combining estimates from several sources of evidence, such as two senses, weighting each by how reliable it is.
options.why: Correct. Cue combination applies to the senses, and it is also one way to correct a running sum: averaging the sum with landmarks, each weighted by how reliable it is.

options.text: Replacing a drifting estimate outright with the one that a recognized landmark gives, especially an estimate of heading.
options.why: That is resetting, a different correction. Cue combination averages several estimates, weighting each by how reliable it is, rather than replacing one with another.

options.text: Following whichever single source of evidence has proved most reliable, and setting every other source of evidence aside.
options.why: Following one source is what people do when two sources disagree by a lot. Cue combination uses several sources at once, each weighted by how reliable it is.

options.text: Adding the seen vector from the animal to a landmark to a stored vector that runs from that landmark to the goal.
options.why: That is converting between frames of reference by adding vectors. Cue combination is combining several estimates, each weighted by how reliable it is.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Combining estimates from several sources of evidence, such as two senses, by weighting each according to how reliable it is”.

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Correct. Cue combination applies to the senses. In finding the way, cue combination is averaging, one of the three ways a drifting running sum can be corrected.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Path integration combines heading and distance into a running estimate of the way back to the start. Weighting several estimates by reliability is cue combination.

options.text: reorientation
options.why: Reorientation is recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented. Weighting several estimates by reliability is cue combination.

options.text: ring attractor
options.why: A ring attractor is a circle of units whose single bump of activity marks the heading. Weighting several estimates by reliability is cue combination.

items.stem: A person walks back to a starting point across a park, using both landmarks and a sense of their own movement. On one day the park is full of large sculptures fixed in place.
