On another, thick fog hides nearly everything. If the person combines the two sources as adults do on average, how does the weighting differ between the two days?

options.text: Landmarks get more weight on the day of the sculptures, and the sense of movement gets relatively more weight in fog.
options.why: Correct. Cue combination weights each source by how reliable it is. Adults give landmarks more weight when landmarks are plentiful and stable, and in fog the landmarks are neither.

options.text: Landmarks get the same weight on both days, since the sculptures stay put and cue combination fixes each source’s weight.
options.why: The weights are not fixed. Each source is weighted by how reliable it is, and adults give landmarks more weight when landmarks are plentiful and stable.

options.text: Landmarks get more weight in the fog, since the few that can be seen there are each more informative than usual.
options.why: That runs the wrong way. Adults give landmarks more weight when landmarks are plentiful and stable, and fog makes them scarce and hard to make out.

options.text: The sense of movement gets all of the weight on both days, since it is the one source that is available everywhere.
options.why: Cue combination uses both sources, weighted by reliability. On the day of the sculptures, adults give the landmarks more weight, not none.

items.stem: A drifting running sum can be corrected by averaging it with a landmark, or by resetting it at a landmark. How do the two corrections differ?

options.text: Averaging blends the estimates, each weighted by how reliable it is; resetting replaces the drifting estimate outright.
options.why: Correct. Averaging is cue combination, which weights each estimate by its reliability. In resetting, a recognized landmark replaces the drifting estimate outright, especially an estimate of heading.

options.text: Averaging replaces the drifting estimate outright; resetting blends the estimates, each weighted by how reliable it is.
options.why: That reverses the two. Averaging is cue combination, which blends weighted estimates, and resetting is the correction that replaces the drifting estimate outright.

options.text: Averaging uses only a landmark that stays put; resetting can use any landmark, including one that moves from night to night.
options.why: All three corrections rest on one principle: a landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is. That holds for resetting as much as for averaging.

options.text: Averaging corrects only an estimate of position; resetting corrects only an estimate of heading, and never one of position.
options.why: Resetting works especially on an estimate of heading, but not only on heading: a fallen log could reset the early mammal’s sense of where it was. The two corrections differ in how they use the landmark.

items.stem: A sailor in a small boat at night keeps a running estimate of the boat’s heading, which has slowly drifted. Then a familiar lighthouse comes into view, and the sailor drops the old estimate and takes the heading straight from the lighthouse. What has the sailor done?

options.text: Reset the estimate, letting a recognized landmark replace the drifting estimate of heading outright.
options.why: Correct. In resetting, a recognized landmark replaces a drifting estimate outright, and an estimate of heading is the usual case. The sailor did not blend the old estimate with the new one.

options.text: Averaged the estimates, combining the drifting estimate and the lighthouse, with each weighted by how reliable it is.
options.why: Averaging would blend the two estimates. The sailor dropped the old estimate entirely, which is resetting.

options.text: Reoriented by shape, letting the outline of the coast settle which way the boat is facing after becoming disoriented.
options.why: Reorientation by shape uses the outline of the surroundings, and the sailor was not disoriented. A recognized landmark replacing a drifting estimate is resetting.

options.text: Integrated the path, adding the boat’s heading and distance traveled into a running estimate of the way back to port.
options.why: Path integration keeps the running sum that drifts. Replacing that drifting estimate with what a recognized landmark gives is resetting.

items.stem: People walking back to a starting point, with both landmarks and their own movement to go on, usually average the two. When do they stop averaging and follow one source instead?

options.text: When the two sources disagree by a lot, people stop averaging them and follow one of the two instead.
options.why: Correct. Following one source is the third way of correcting a running sum. When two sources disagree by a lot, people stop averaging and follow one of them.

options.text: When the two sources agree closely, people stop averaging, since either source alone gives much the same answer.
options.why: Close agreement is when averaging works best. People stop averaging when the two sources disagree by a lot.

options.text: When landmarks are plentiful and stable, people stop averaging and follow the sense of their own movement alone.
options.why: Plentiful, stable landmarks get more weight in the average, not less. People stop averaging when the two sources disagree by a lot.

options.text: When they are still children; adults go on averaging the two sources, however far apart the two sources are.
options.why: Children do follow one source or the other rather than combining them. But adults also stop averaging, and follow one source, when the two sources disagree by a lot.

items.stem: A person walking back to a starting point in a large field has two sources to go on. Their sense of their own movement puts the start straight ahead, but a familiar tree puts it far off to the right, nearly at a right angle. What does the person most likely do?

options.text: The person follows one of the two sources, rather than heading somewhere in between them.
options.why: Correct. When two sources disagree by a lot, people stop averaging and follow one of them. The person does not head for a point in between.

options.text: The person heads somewhere in between, with each source weighted by how reliable it has been.
options.why: Weighting by reliability is averaging, which people do when sources roughly agree. When two sources disagree by a lot, they stop averaging and follow one.

options.text: The person heads exactly halfway between, since sources that disagree get equal weight.
options.why: Disagreeing sources are not given equal weight. When two sources disagree by a lot, people stop averaging altogether and follow one of them.

options.text: The person stops and turns in place until the two sources come back into agreement.
options.why: Turning in place does not bring the two sources back into agreement. When two sources disagree by a lot, people stop averaging and follow one of them.

items.stem: A hiker crossing a wide meadow every morning keeps a running sum of position. Which of these would be worth using to correct that sum?

options.text: A large boulder at the edge of the meadow, passed every morning in the same place.
options.why: Correct. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is, and the boulder does.

options.text: A herd of deer grazing near the trail, seen in that very same spot yesterday morning.
options.why: Deer seen in one spot yesterday may be anywhere today. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is.

options.text: A bright cloud low over the meadow, sitting straight ahead when the hiker first set out.
options.why: A cloud drifts across the sky. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is.

options.text: A parked tractor that the farmer moves to a different field every few days.
options.why: A tractor that keeps being moved would correct the sum toward the wrong place. A landmark is worth using only if it stays where it is.

items.stem: Consider the early mammal foraging at night. Why could a fallen log passed every night reset the animal’s sense of where it was, while a beetle seen in the same spot last week could not?

options.text: A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is, and a log stays put but a beetle moves.
options.why: Correct. All three ways of correcting a running sum rest on that one principle. The log stays where it is, and the beetle does not.

options.text: A landmark is worth using only if it can be smelled from afar, and a log gives off a stronger smell than a beetle does.
options.why: How far a landmark can be smelled is not the issue. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is.

options.text: A landmark is worth using only if it is large, since a large landmark changes its appearance less as the animal moves.
options.why: Size is not the principle. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is, and a log does while a beetle does not.

options.text: A landmark is worth using only if it is close by, since only nearby objects pin down position, and a beetle is too small.
options.why: Nearby objects do pin down position closely, but that is not why the beetle fails. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is.

items.stem: How do children differ from adults in using landmarks and their own movement to walk back to a starting point?

options.text: Children follow one source or the other; combining the two has not been shown in navigation before about age 11.
options.why: Correct. Adults combine landmarks and self-motion close to the ideal on average. Children follow one source or the other, and combining has not been shown in navigation before about age 11, which is not the same as saying it begins then.

options.text: Children combine the two closer to the ideal than adults do, since they have not yet learned to favor one source.
options.why: Children do not combine the two at all, as far as has been shown. They follow one source or the other.

options.text: Children combine the two just as adults do, but they give landmarks more weight than their own movement.
options.why: Children do not combine the sources. They follow one or the other, and combining has not been shown in navigation before about age 11.

options.text: Children begin combining the two at exactly age 11, and before that they rely on their own movement alone.
options.why: Children follow one source or the other, not their own movement alone. And combining “has not been shown” before about age 11, which is not a claim that it begins at that age.

items.stem: A warehouse robot keeps a running estimate of its position from the turning of its own wheels. Halfway across the floor, its camera picks out a fixed pillar whose position is stored, and the robot replaces its estimate with the position the pillar gives. How does the error in the robot’s estimate change over the trip?

options.text: The error grows as the robot travels, and it drops back once the robot resets its drifting estimate at the pillar.
options.why: Correct. Every small error in heading or distance stays in a running sum, so the estimate drifts farther from the truth as the robot travels. Resetting at a recognized landmark replaces the drifting estimate outright, so the error drops back at the pillar.

options.text: The error stays about the same as the robot travels, since each turn of a wheel is measured equally well, and then drops at the pillar.
options.why: Measuring each turn equally well does not keep the error steady. Every small error stays in the sum and adds to the ones before it, so the error grows until the pillar resets the estimate.

options.text: The error shrinks as the robot travels, since each turn of a wheel adds evidence about where the robot is, and the pillar confirms the estimate.
options.why: Each turn of a wheel adds its own small error, not more certainty. The error grows as the robot travels, and resetting at the pillar replaces the drifting estimate.

options.text: The error grows as the robot travels, and it keeps growing after the pillar, since nothing can remove error already in the sum.
options.why: The growth before the pillar is right, but a recognized landmark can replace a drifting estimate outright. That is resetting, and it removes the error built up before the pillar.

items.stem: In one experiment, desert ants trained to a feeder had their legs lengthened or shortened before they set off home. In a short paragraph, say what the altered ants did, what the result suggests about how ants measure distance, and why the result also rules out a timer.
items.answer: Ants given longer legs walked past the nest before searching for it, and ants given shorter legs stopped short. So the distance an ant judges depends on its strides. Something in the ant tracks them, although the researchers write that the ants “most probably do not literally count”. The result also rules out a timer. The ants on stilts walked slightly more slowly than normal ants. An ant timing its trip at a slower pace would have gone less far, but the ants on stilts went farther.
rubric: Says ants with longer legs overshot the nest and ants with shorter legs fell short.
Says something tracks the ants’ strides (or steps, or leg movements), and does not claim the ants literally count them.
Says the ants on stilts walked more slowly than normal ants.
Says an ant timing its trip would then have gone less far, the opposite of what the ants on stilts did.

items.stem: A running sum of position drifts and has to be corrected with landmarks. In a few sentences, explain which landmarks are worth using for that, using a fallen log and a beetle on the early mammal’s nightly rounds as examples. Then give one further example of a landmark that would work and one that would not.
items.answer: A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is. A fallen log that the early mammal passes every night stays put, so seeing it could reset the animal’s sense of where it is. A beetle seen in the same spot last week has probably moved, so it could not. In the same way, a person walking to work could correct a running sum with a stone bridge over a stream, but not with a car parked on the street.
rubric: States that a landmark is worth using only if it stays where it is.
Says the fallen log, passed every night in the same place, could reset the animal’s sense of where it is.
Says the beetle could not, because it does not stay in one place.
Gives a fresh example of a landmark that stays put and one that does not, each correctly classed.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how little following a route requires at each point along it. Then explain why desert ants set down on their own familiar outward route, while they were on their way home, behaved as if they were lost.
items.answer: Following a route needs little. At each point, the animal needs only a sensible direction, as if it were walking a corridor with signposts. Desert ants, for example, keep a familiar landmark on the same side as in training. The ants set down on their outward route knew that route well, but they were heading home, and the outward route does not lead home. Separate routes are kept separate, so knowing the way out gave the ants nothing for the way back.
rubric: Says following a route needs only a sensible direction at each point (the corridor with signposts, or keeping a landmark on the same side).
Says the ants knew the outward route but were on their way home.
Says separate routes are kept separate.
Says the outward route did not help the ants get home (or words to that effect).

pools.title: Keeping a Heading, Frames of Reference, and Reorienting by Shape
pools.covers: reading §9.2.4, §9.2.5, §9.2.6 · lecture 9.2 slides keeping_a_heading, frames_of_reference, reorienting_by_shape

items.stem: What is a ring attractor?

options.text: A circle of units, each standing for one direction, that excite their neighbors and share inhibition, so that one bump of activity marks the heading.
options.why: Correct. Neighboring units excite one another while a shared inhibition holds every unit down, so the circle settles into a single bump. Where the bump sits is the stored heading. A turning signal slides the bump, and a recognized landmark pulls a drifted bump back.

options.text: A running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, built up step by step from a heading and the distance traveled so far.
options.why: That is path integration, which keeps track of position. A ring attractor keeps track of direction alone: a circle of units, each standing for one direction, whose single bump of activity marks the heading.

options.text: A stored view of what the surroundings look like from the goal, which an animal matches by moving until the scene looks the same as before.
options.why: That is a snapshot, which can be matched only near the goal. A ring attractor is a circle of units, each standing for one direction, whose single bump of activity marks the heading.

options.text: A way of combining several estimates of heading into a single estimate, giving each one a weight that depends on how reliable it is.
options.why: That is cue combination, one way of correcting a drifting estimate. A ring attractor is a circle of units, each standing for one direction, whose single bump of activity marks the heading.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A circle of units, each standing for one direction, that excite their neighbors and share inhibition, so that a single bump of activity marks the heading, slides when the animal turns, and is pulled back by recognized landmarks”.

options.text: ring attractor
options.why: Correct. A ring attractor stores a heading as the place of one bump on a circle of units. Turning signals slide the bump, and recognized landmarks pull a drifted bump back.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Path integration keeps a running estimate of the distance and direction back to the start, so it keeps track of position. The circle of units whose single bump marks the heading is a ring attractor, which does the same job for direction alone.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, the result of path integration. The circle of units whose single bump marks the heading is a ring attractor.

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Cue combination combines several estimates, each weighted by how reliable it is. A landmark pulling a drifted bump back is a correction, but the circle of units whose bump marks the heading is a ring attractor.

items.stem: A planetary rover keeps its heading with a ring attractor. In a dark crater, it turns quickly to the left, and a moment later turns slowly back to the right. What happens to the bump of activity on its ring?

options.text: It slides around the ring one way during the first turn, and then back the other way, at a lower speed, during the second turn.
options.why: Correct. A signal for turning, delivered to one side of the bump, slides the bump around the ring, faster for faster turns. The bump turns with the rover, so the quick left turn moves the bump quickly and the slow right turn moves it back slowly.

options.text: It stays where it is through both turns, since with no landmark in view there is nothing that can move the bump from the stored heading.
options.why: The bump stays put only when nothing pushes it. A turning signal does push it, with or without a landmark in view, so the bump slides around the ring as the rover turns.

options.text: It fades away during each turn and forms again once the rover stops, at whichever unit stands for the heading the rover ends up facing.
options.why: The bump does not fade and form again. Neighboring units excite one another and all share inhibition, so the circle keeps a single bump, and a turning signal slides that bump around the ring as the rover turns.

options.text: It slides by one fixed step at the start of each turn, whatever the speed of the turn, and then stays put until the next turn begins.
options.why: The slide is not a fixed step. A turning signal slides the bump faster for faster turns, and keeps sliding it for as long as the turn goes on. So the bump keeps pace with the turn the rover actually makes.

items.stem: A lawn-mowing robot keeps its heading with a ring attractor. After a long stretch in tall grass, where it recognizes nothing, its bump has drifted away from its true heading. Then it recognizes the garden shed, a landmark it has stored. What happens on its ring?

options.text: The shed adds input at the shed’s own place on the ring, and that input pulls the drifted bump back toward the true heading.
options.why: Correct. A recognized landmark adds input at its own place on the ring and pulls a drifted bump back. Pulling the bump back is the correction, much as a recognized landmark can reset a drifting running sum.

options.text: The shed slides the bump around the ring at a speed set by how fast the robot happens to be turning at the moment it sees the shed.
options.why: That describes a turning signal, which slides the bump faster for faster turns. A recognized landmark works differently: it adds input at its own place on the ring and pulls a drifted bump back.

options.text: The shed starts a second bump at the shed’s place on the ring, and the robot keeps both headings until one of the two bumps fades.
options.why: Neighboring units excite one another and all share inhibition, so the circle settles into a single bump. A recognized landmark pulls that one bump back toward its own place rather than starting a second one.

options.text: Nothing happens to the drifted bump, since a heading on the ring can be moved only by turning signals, and the robot is driving straight when it sees the shed.
options.why: Turning signals do move the bump, but they are not its only input. A recognized landmark adds input at its own place on the ring, which pulls a drifted bump back even while the robot drives straight.

items.stem: How does a ring attractor compare with the running sum of path integration and the ways of correcting that sum?

options.text: The ring attractor does for direction alone what the running sum and its corrections do for position: it stores, updates, and corrects a heading.
options.why: Correct. The bump’s place is the stored heading, a turning signal updates it, and a recognized landmark corrects it. The running sum stores, updates, and corrects an estimate of position in the same three ways.

options.text: The ring attractor keeps direction and position together, so that one bump marks both where the animal is and which way it faces, replacing the running sum.
options.why: Each unit on the ring stands for a direction, so the bump marks only the heading. Keeping track of position is the running sum’s job, and the ring attractor does the same job for direction alone.

options.text: The ring attractor keeps direction alone, but unlike the running sum it does not drift, so a heading kept by a ring attractor needs no correction from landmarks.
options.why: A ring attractor’s bump can drift away from the true heading. A recognized landmark corrects the drift: it adds input at its own place on the ring and pulls the drifted bump back.

options.text: The ring attractor keeps direction alone, but unlike the running sum it is not updated by movement, and its heading is set only by landmarks in view.
options.why: A turning signal slides the bump around the ring, faster for faster turns, so the animal’s own movement does update the heading, just as movement updates the running sum. Landmarks correct the bump rather than being the only thing that moves it.

items.stem: Nothing in the description of a ring attractor depends on neurons. What kind of thing does that make a ring attractor?

options.text: A procedure for keeping a heading, which could run in neurons or in something else, and on which robot navigation systems have been built.
options.why: Correct. A ring attractor is a procedure: units on a circle that excite their neighbors and share inhibition. Nothing in that description depends on neurons, and robot navigation systems have been built on the same principle.

options.text: A statement of the problem of keeping a heading, which leaves open which of many possible procedures an animal might use to solve it.
options.why: That would be a description of the problem, at the computational level. A ring attractor is itself one procedure for storing, updating, and correcting a heading, and nothing in that procedure depends on neurons.

options.text: A structure in the mammalian brain, a ring of neurons drawn simply enough that the neurons themselves need not be named in it.
options.why: A ring attractor is not a part of the brain. In the rat, the cells that signal heading are not even laid out in a circle. A ring attractor is a procedure, and nothing in its description depends on neurons.

options.text: A rough analogy for keeping a heading, which describes how a heading behaves without giving any steps that could actually be run.
options.why: A ring attractor is more than an analogy. Robot navigation systems have been built on the same principle, so its steps can actually be run. It is a procedure, and nothing in its description depends on neurons.

items.stem: An engineer writes a drone’s compass as a program. The program has sixty-four numbers arranged in a circle, each standing for one direction, each boosting its neighbors, and all of them pushed down by one shared term. Turning commands slide the peak around the circle, and a recognized radio tower pulls the peak back. A classmate objects that the program cannot be a ring attractor, because the program contains no neurons. Who is right?

options.text: The engineer, because a ring attractor is a procedure, and nothing in its description depends on neurons.
options.why: Correct. A ring attractor is units on a circle that excite their neighbors and share inhibition, with turns sliding the bump and landmarks pulling it back. Nothing in that depends on neurons, and robot navigation systems have been built on the same principle.

options.text: The classmate, because a ring attractor is a structure in the brain made of neurons, which a program can imitate but not be.
options.why: That treats the ring attractor as a part of the brain. It is a procedure, described without reference to neurons, and the drone’s program runs that procedure.

options.text: The classmate, because the drone is corrected by a radio tower, while a ring attractor is corrected by its turning signals.
options.why: Turning signals update the bump; they do not correct it. In a ring attractor, a recognized landmark adds input at its own place on the ring and pulls a drifted bump back, which is what the radio tower does here.

options.text: The engineer, because the numbers lie in a circle, and lying in a circle is all it takes to make a system a ring attractor.
options.why: Lying in a circle is not enough. What makes a ring attractor is how the units interact: neighbors excite one another and all share inhibition. So one bump marks the heading, slides with turns, and is pulled back by landmarks.

items.stem: What does egocentric mean?

options.text: Given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead of the animal or to its left.
options.why: Correct. An egocentric location is measured from the animal’s own body, so it changes whenever the animal moves or turns.

options.text: Given relative to things in the world, such as north of a boulder or beside a stream.
options.why: That is allocentric. An egocentric location is given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead or to the left.

options.text: Centered on the animal’s own needs, so that a place counts only if it serves a present goal.
options.why: That is the everyday sense of the word, meaning self-centered. Here an egocentric location is one given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead or to the left.

options.text: Given only as which places connect to which, with no distances or directions between them.
options.why: That describes a topological map, like a subway map. An egocentric location is one given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead or to the left.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead or to the left.

options.text: egocentric
options.why: Correct. An egocentric location is measured from the animal’s own body, so it changes whenever the animal moves or turns.

options.text: allocentric
options.why: Allocentric is the reverse: given relative to things in the world, such as north of a boulder. The definition here is about a location measured from the animal’s own body.

options.text: frame of reference
options.why: A frame of reference is the origin and directions against which any location is measured. Egocentric names one kind, the frame set by the animal’s own body, which is what the definition here describes.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the starting point, so it points to one place only. The definition here is about how any location is given: relative to the animal itself.

items.stem: What does allocentric mean?

options.text: Given relative to things in the world, independent of where the animal is or which way it faces.
options.why: Correct. An allocentric location, such as north of the boulder or beside the stream, stays the same however the animal moves, because it is measured from things in the world.

options.text: Given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead or to its left, and so changing as the animal moves.
options.why: That is egocentric. An allocentric location is given relative to things in the world, independent of where the animal is or which way it faces.

options.text: Given by what the animal can see, hear, or smell from where it now stands, such as a sound off to one side.
options.why: What the animal senses from where it stands depends on where it is and which way it faces. An allocentric location is given relative to things in the world, independent of both.

options.text: Given by adding up the animal’s own steps and turns into a running estimate of the way back to the start.
options.why: That is path integration, which builds an estimate from the animal’s own movement. Allocentric names a frame of reference: a location given relative to things in the world.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Given relative to things in the world, independent of where the animal is or which way it faces.

options.text: allocentric
options.why: Correct. An allocentric location, such as north of the boulder or beside the stream, stays the same however the animal moves, because it is measured from things in the world.

options.text: egocentric
options.why: Egocentric is the reverse: given relative to the animal itself, such as ahead or to the left, and so changing as the animal moves. The definition here is about a location measured from things in the world.

options.text: frame of reference
options.why: A frame of reference is the origin and directions against which any location is measured. Allocentric names one kind, the frame set by things in the world, which is what the definition here describes.

options.text: landmark
options.why: A landmark is a recognizable feature of the surroundings, such as a large tree or a rock. An allocentric location can be given relative to landmarks, but the definition here names a way of giving locations, not a feature of the world.

items.stem: What is a frame of reference?

options.text: The origin and directions against which a location is measured, such as the animal’s own body or fixed things in the world.
options.why: Correct. An egocentric location is stated in a frame of reference set by the animal’s own body, and an allocentric location in one set by fixed things in the world.

options.text: A stored view of the surroundings from a goal, against which the current scene is compared as the animal moves closer to the goal.
options.why: That is a snapshot, a stored view matched near the goal. A frame of reference is the origin and directions against which a location is measured.

options.text: The single direction an animal is facing at a given moment, which a ring attractor keeps as the place of its bump.
options.why: That is the animal’s heading. Converting between frames of reference needs the heading, but a frame of reference is the origin and directions against which a location is measured.

options.text: The set of cues an animal relies on in a given setting, such as the walls of a room, its colors, and its objects.
options.why: That is the set of cues available for finding the way. A frame of reference is the origin and directions against which a location is measured, such as the animal’s own body or fixed things in the world.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? The origin and directions against which a location is measured, such as the animal’s own body or fixed things in the world.

options.text: frame of reference
options.why: Correct. The animal’s own body sets one frame of reference, the egocentric one, and fixed things in the world set another, the allocentric one.

options.text: allocentric
options.why: Allocentric names one particular frame of reference, the one set by things in the world. The definition here covers any origin and directions a location is measured against, the animal’s own body included.

options.text: reorientation
options.why: Reorientation is recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented. The definition here is of the origin and directions a location is measured against.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the starting point. It is a location stated in a frame, not the frame itself, which is what the definition here describes.

items.stem: An animal walks a long, winding path away from its nest. How do an egocentric code and an allocentric code for the nest’s location fare along the way?

options.text: The egocentric code stays useful only if it is updated for every step and turn, while the allocentric code does not depend on where the animal now stands.
options.why: Correct. A location given relative to the animal changes whenever the animal moves, so it has to be updated step by step. A location given relative to things in the world stays the same wherever the animal goes.

options.text: The allocentric code stays useful only if it is updated for every step and turn, while the egocentric code does not depend on where the animal now stands.
options.why: That reverses the two. A location given relative to the animal itself, which is the egocentric code, changes with every step and turn. A location given relative to things in the world does not.

options.text: Both codes stay useful only if they are updated for every step and turn, since the location of the nest changes in any code as the animal walks farther away.
options.why: Only the egocentric code changes as the animal walks. The allocentric code gives the nest relative to things in the world, which do not move when the animal does, so it needs no updating.

options.text: Neither code needs updating for each step and turn, since the nest itself stays where it is whatever the animal does along the way.
options.why: The nest does stay put, which is why the allocentric code needs no updating. But the egocentric code gives the nest relative to the animal, and that changes with every step and turn.

items.stem: Before getting up from the couch, a person notes two facts about where the TV remote is: “by my right hand” and “on the arm of the couch nearest the window”. The person then walks to the kitchen and back, and sits down at the other end of the couch. Which fact still gives the remote’s location correctly without any updating?

options.text: Only “on the arm of the couch nearest the window”, since it is given relative to things in the room, not to where the person sits.
options.why: Correct. That fact is allocentric, given relative to the couch and the window, so it stays true wherever the person goes. “By my right hand” is egocentric, and it went out of date as soon as the person moved.

options.text: Only “by my right hand”, since it is given relative to the person, who can feel which hand is which wherever the person happens to sit.
options.why: The person does know left from right anywhere, but a location given relative to the body changes when the body moves. At the other end of the couch, the remote is no longer by the right hand.

options.text: Both “by my right hand” and “on the arm of the couch nearest the window”, since the remote has not moved and so needs no updating.
options.why: The remote has not moved, so the fact given relative to the room is still true. But the person has moved, and a location given relative to the person changes whenever the person does.

options.text: Neither “by my right hand” nor “on the arm of the couch nearest the window”, since a stored location goes out of date once the person moves.
options.why: Only a location given relative to the person goes out of date when the person moves. A location given relative to things in the room does not depend on where the person stands.

items.stem: A delivery robot stores the location of its charging dock as “three meters ahead and a little to the left”. It then drives forward and turns a corner before heading back. What must be true for that stored location to still lead it to the dock?

options.text: The robot must have updated the stored location for every move and turn it made, since a location given relative to itself changes whenever it moves.
options.why: Correct. “Three meters ahead and a little to the left” is egocentric. An egocentric code stays useful while the robot moves only if it is updated for every step and turn.

options.text: The robot must have recognized a landmark beside the dock, since a location stored relative to itself can never be used again once the robot has moved.
options.why: An egocentric location does not become useless when the robot moves. It stays useful as long as it is updated for every move and turn, without any landmark.

options.text: Nothing further is needed, since the dock has stayed where it was, and so its location relative to the robot has not changed while the robot drove.
options.why: The dock has not moved, but the robot has. A location given relative to the robot changes whenever the robot moves, so it has to be updated for every move and turn.

options.text: The robot must have stored the dock as a snapshot instead, since only a stored view can still be matched once the robot has moved to a new place.
options.why: A snapshot can be matched only near the goal. A location given relative to the robot can still lead it to the dock from farther away, as long as it is updated for every move and turn.

items.stem: A hiker in light fog can see a fire tower but cannot see camp. The hiker knows which way is east, and remembers that camp lies a short walk east of the tower. How can the hiker work out the straight-line way to camp?

options.text: Add the seen vector from the hiker to the tower and the stored vector from the tower to camp; the sum runs from the hiker to camp.
options.why: Correct. Converting is vector addition. The seen vector to a landmark, plus the stored vector from that landmark to the goal, gives the vector from the hiker to the goal. The sum works even though the goal cannot be seen.

options.text: Walk to the tower first and then a short way east, since those two legs make up the only way to camp that the hiker could work out.
options.why: Those two legs would reach camp, but they are not the straight-line way. Adding the two vectors gives a single vector that runs directly from the hiker to camp.

options.text: Walk a short way east from where the hiker now stands, since the stored vector from the tower to camp gives the way to camp from anywhere.
options.why: The stored vector runs from the tower to camp, not from wherever the hiker happens to be. It has to be added to the seen vector from the hiker to the tower to give the way from the hiker to camp.

options.text: Judge the distance to the tower and to camp separately, then head for whichever is nearer, since a seen vector and a stored one cannot be combined.
options.why: A seen vector and a stored vector can be combined. Added together, the vector to the tower and the vector from the tower to camp give the vector from the hiker to camp.

items.stem: A mouse sees a landmark straight ahead of it, a meter away. It has stored that its food lies half a meter north of that landmark. What else does the mouse need before it can add the two vectors and head for the food?

options.text: Its current heading, because “straight ahead” is given relative to the mouse, while “north of the landmark” is given relative to the world.
options.why: Correct. The seen vector is egocentric and the stored one is not. To add them, the mouse needs to know which way it is facing, which a ring attractor can supply.

options.text: A second landmark beside the food, because a vector to the food can be found only from something the mouse can sense at the goal itself.
options.why: That would be steering to a beacon. Vector addition reaches a goal that nothing at the goal marks: the seen vector to one landmark plus the stored vector to the food. What the mouse lacks is its heading.

options.text: A home vector back to its nest, because the stored vector is measured from the nest and has to be converted before the mouse can use it.
options.why: The stored vector runs from the landmark to the food, not from the nest. What the mouse lacks is its current heading, because the seen vector is given relative to the mouse and the stored one is not.

options.text: Nothing further, because “straight ahead” and “north of the landmark” are already in the same frame of reference, so the mouse can add them as they are.
options.why: The two vectors are in different frames. “Straight ahead” is given relative to the mouse, and “north of the landmark” relative to the world, so the mouse needs its current heading to add them.

items.stem: An animal adds the vector it sees from itself to a landmark and the vector it has stored from that landmark to the goal. Why does it also need its current heading?

options.text: The seen vector is egocentric and the stored vector is not, so the heading is needed to relate the two before they are added.
options.why: Correct. The seen vector is given relative to the animal, and the stored one relative to the world. The animal’s current heading relates the two, and a ring attractor can supply it.

options.text: The stored vector is egocentric and the seen vector is not, so the heading is needed to relate the two before they are added.
options.why: That reverses the two. The vector the animal sees, from itself to the landmark, is egocentric. The stored vector, from the landmark to the goal, is given relative to the world.

options.text: Both vectors are egocentric, but the seen vector drifts as the animal moves, so the heading is needed to correct it before adding.
options.why: Only the seen vector is egocentric, and the problem is not drift. The stored vector is given relative to the world, so the heading is needed to relate the two frames.

options.text: Both vectors are allocentric, but adding them gives only a distance, so the heading is needed to supply a direction for the sum.
options.why: Adding two vectors gives a direction as well as a distance. The heading is needed because the seen vector is egocentric and the stored one is not.

items.stem: In vision, where something falls on the eye is not enough to locate the thing in the world. Finding the way raises the same problem one step further. What do the two cases share?

options.text: In both, a position given relative to the eye or to the animal has to be combined with where the eye or the animal is pointing.
options.why: Correct. A place on the eye locates nothing in the world until it is combined with where the eye was pointing. Likewise, a vector seen from the animal has to be combined with the animal’s heading before it can be added to a vector stored relative to the world.

options.text: In both, a position given relative to the eye or to the animal already gives a location in the world, as long as the scene stays still.
options.why: A still scene does not solve the problem. A position given relative to the eye or the animal changes with where the eye or the animal points, so it has to be combined with that direction.

options.text: In both, a location in the world is found only by moving until the scene looks as before, since the senses give no direction at all.
options.why: That describes matching a snapshot, which works only near a goal. The senses do give a direction, but relative to the eye or the animal, and that direction has to be combined with where the eye or the animal is pointing.

options.text: In both, the trouble is that signals arrive late, so the eye or the animal has already moved on before the signal about the thing arrives.
options.why: Delay is a real problem for a moving body, but it is a different one. The shared problem is that a position given relative to the eye or the animal has to be combined with where the eye or the animal is pointing.

items.stem: What is reorientation?

options.text: Recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented, as after a fright or a tumble.
options.why: Correct. An animal that has lost its heading has to recover it before anything else it knows can be used, and the shape of the surroundings is one cue that can help.

options.text: Keeping a running estimate of the distance and direction back to the start, from the heading and the distance traveled.
options.why: That is path integration. It needs a heading to work, so an animal that has lost its heading needs reorientation first: recovering which way it is facing, and where it is.

options.text: The reorganization of place cells when an animal moves to a new environment, with some cells firing in new places.
options.why: That is remapping, a change in how cells fire. Reorientation is recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented.

options.text: Turning a location given relative to the animal into one given relative to things in the world, by adding vectors.
options.why: That is converting between frames of reference, which needs a heading. Reorientation is recovering that heading, and one’s place, after becoming disoriented.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented”.

options.text: reorientation
options.why: Correct. For an animal that has lost its heading, reorientation has to come first, because nothing else the animal knows can be used until the heading is recovered.

options.text: remapping
options.why: Remapping is the reorganization of place cells when an animal moves to a different environment. Recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented is reorientation.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Path integration keeps a running estimate of the way back to the start from heading and distance traveled. It depends on a heading, and recovering a lost one is reorientation.

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Cue combination weights several estimates by how reliable each is. Recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented is reorientation.

items.stem: A warehouse robot keeps a map of the warehouse, and stored vectors from known landmarks to each loading bay. A forklift bumps the robot and spins it around, and the robot loses its heading. What has to happen before its map and stored vectors can guide it again?

options.text: It has to recover which way it is facing, and where it is, because nothing else in its memory can be used until that recovery is made.
options.why: Correct. That recovery is reorientation. The map and the stored vectors are still correct. But using them means relating what the robot now sees, given relative to itself, to things in the warehouse, and that needs the robot’s heading.

options.text: It has to build a new map of the warehouse, because a map made before the bump stopped matching the warehouse once the robot was spun.
options.why: The warehouse did not change when the robot was spun, so the map still matches it. What the robot lost is its heading, which it has to recover before the map can be used.

options.text: Nothing has to happen first, because neither the map nor the stored vectors depend on which way the robot happens to be facing.
options.why: The map and the vectors are indeed still correct, since they are given relative to things in the warehouse. But using them means relating what the robot sees, given relative to itself, to that map, and that needs the heading it has lost.

options.text: It has to clear its stored vectors to the loading bays, because a vector stored before the spin points the wrong way once the robot has turned.
options.why: The stored vectors run from landmarks to loading bays, relative to things in the warehouse, so the spin did not change them. What the spin took away is the robot’s heading, which it has to recover first.

items.stem: A child watches a toy being hidden in one corner of a plain rectangular room with nothing else in it, and is then gently turned around several times. The child searches in the corner diagonally opposite the right one, which is called a rotational error. Why is that corner such a natural mistake?

options.text: By shape alone, the correct corner and the corner diagonally opposite it look the same, so nothing in the room picks out the correct one.
options.why: Correct. The shape of the surroundings helps, but not completely. In a rectangular room, a corner and its diagonal opposite look the same by shape alone, and choosing that twin is a rotational error.

options.text: By shape alone, all four corners of a rectangular room look the same, so the child was as likely to search that corner as any of the others.
options.why: Shape does narrow the choice. In a rectangular room, a long wall lies on one side of each corner and a short wall on the other, so only a corner and its diagonal opposite look the same.

options.text: Young children do not yet use the shape of a space to reorient, so the child had nothing at all to go on and picked a corner by chance.
options.why: Young children do use shape. Toddlers in a small room searched the correct corner and its twin about equally, which is what using shape alone produces.

options.text: The diagonally opposite corner was the farthest away, and a distant feature gives a direction but indicates little about the searcher’s position.
options.why: That is true of distant landmarks, but a corner of a plain room is not a landmark that sets one corner apart. The diagonal corner is chosen because, by shape alone, it looks the same as the right one.

items.stem: A rescue dog is led, disoriented, into a bare rectangular shed with no markings, and has to find a toy hidden in one corner. What can the shape of the shed alone give the dog?

options.text: It narrows the search to two corners, the toy’s corner and the one diagonally opposite, without settling which of the two is right.
options.why: Correct. In a rectangular space, a corner and its diagonal opposite look the same by shape alone. Shape helps, but a dog relying on it alone will sometimes make a rotational error.

options.text: It picks out the toy’s corner exactly, since the long and short walls meet in a different arrangement at each of the four corners.
options.why: Each corner does have a long wall on one side and a short wall on the other, but a corner and its diagonal opposite share the same arrangement. So shape alone leaves two corners, not one.

options.text: It gives the dog nothing at all, since in a shed with bare walls and no markings, every corner looks just the same as every other.
options.why: Bare walls still have a shape. In a rectangle, only a corner and its diagonal opposite look the same, so shape narrows the search to two corners.

options.text: It narrows the search to two corners, the toy’s corner and the one beside it along the same long wall, without settling which.
options.why: The two corners along one long wall are mirror images, with the long wall on opposite sides. The corners that look the same by shape alone are a corner and its diagonal opposite.

items.stem: Rats searched for food in a rectangular box with a distinct panel in each corner. They chose the correct corner 44% of the time, and the corner diagonally opposite it 25% of the time. Toddlers in a small rectangular room with one blue wall searched the correct corner and its diagonal twin about equally. What do the two results have in common?

options.text: Both include choices of the diagonal twin, the corner that looks the same as the correct one by shape alone.
options.why: Correct. In a rectangular space, a corner and its diagonal opposite look the same by shape alone, and choosing that twin is a rotational error. The rats chose the twin 25% of the time even with a distinct panel in each corner. The toddlers in the small room searched the twin about as often as the correct corner.

options.text: In both, a distinct feature, a panel or a blue wall, picked out the correct corner, so the diagonal twin was never chosen.
options.why: A feature did not settle the matter. The rats chose the twin 25% of the time even with a distinct panel in each corner. The toddlers in the small room ignored the blue wall. Both made rotational errors, choosing the corner that looks the same by shape alone.

options.text: In both, the wrong choices fell on the corner beside the correct one, along the same long wall, rather than on the diagonal twin.
options.why: The corner beside the correct one, along the same long wall, is its mirror image, with the long wall on the opposite side. By shape, the two do not look the same. The rats chose the diagonal twin 25% of the time. The toddlers in the small room searched the twin about as often as the correct corner.

options.text: In both, the searchers ignored the shape of the space altogether, which is why the correct corner was not chosen every time.
options.why: Rats and people both use the shape of a space to reorient. Choosing the diagonal twin is what relying on shape alone produces, since by shape the twin looks the same as the correct corner.

items.stem: Toddlers searched for a hidden toy in rectangular rooms with one blue wall. How did their searching in a small room differ from their searching in a room twice as large?

options.text: In the small room, they ignored the blue wall and searched the correct corner and its twin about equally; in the larger room, they used the wall.
options.why: Correct. In the small room, the toddlers searched as shape alone would lead them to. In the room twice as large, they used the blue wall to pick out the correct corner.

options.text: In the small room, they used the blue wall to pick the correct corner; in the larger room, they ignored it and searched the correct corner and its twin about equally.
options.why: That reverses the two rooms. The toddlers ignored the blue wall in the small room and used it in the room twice as large.

options.text: In both rooms, they ignored the blue wall and searched the correct corner and its twin about equally, relying on the shape of the room alone.
options.why: That fits the small room only. In the room twice as large, the toddlers used the blue wall.

options.text: In both rooms, they used the blue wall to pick out the correct corner, so the size of the room made no difference to how they searched.
options.why: That fits the larger room only. In the small room, the toddlers ignored the blue wall and searched the correct corner and its twin about equally.

items.stem: Researchers once proposed that, in reorientation, a dedicated process matches the shape of the surroundings and ignores everything else. Why has that proposal lost ground?

options.text: Many species reorient using features such as colors and objects, not only the shape of the surroundings.
options.why: Correct. Fish, chicks, pigeons, rats, monkeys, and people all use shape, but many species also use features such as colors and objects. A process that ignores everything but shape does not fit them.

options.text: Few species turn out to use the shape of the surroundings at all, so shape is a rare cue rather than a common one.
options.why: Shape is a common cue: fish, chicks, pigeons, rats, monkeys, and people all use it to reorient. The proposal lost ground because many species use colors and objects as well.

options.text: Shape turns out to give no help in a rectangular room, since every corner of such a room looks the same as every other.
options.why: Shape does help in a rectangular room, narrowing the choice to a corner and its diagonal opposite. The proposal lost ground because many species use colors and objects as well as shape.

options.text: Only people turn out to use features such as colors and objects, and a process that ignores them fits every other species.
options.why: People are not the only ones. Many species use features such as colors and objects as well as shape, which is why a process that ignores everything but shape lost ground.

items.stem: Suppose that disoriented fish in a rectangular tank, with one wall painted red, choose the food corner far more often than its diagonal twin. Is that result evidence for or against the proposal that a dedicated process matches shape and ignores everything else?

options.text: Evidence against the proposal, since shape alone cannot set the food corner apart from its twin, so the fish must be using something else, such as the red wall.
options.why: Correct. By shape alone, the food corner and its diagonal twin look the same. Choosing one far more often than the other needs a feature such as color, which the proposed process would ignore.

options.text: Evidence for the proposal, since the fish found the food corner in a rectangular tank, where shape is what sets that corner apart from the rest of the corners.
options.why: Shape sets the food corner apart from two of the other corners, but not from its diagonal twin. Choosing the food corner over its twin needs something besides shape.

options.text: Evidence for the proposal, since a painted wall is part of the tank’s shape, and so the fish were still matching the shape of the tank alone.
options.why: Paint does not change a tank’s shape. A colored wall is a feature, like an object, and a process that matched shape alone would ignore it.

options.text: Evidence against the proposal, since the fish must have ignored the shape of the tank entirely and relied only on the color of the red wall.
options.why: The result is evidence against the proposal, but not evidence that shape is ignored. Many species use features as well as shape, and fish are among the animals that use shape to reorient.

items.stem: Mice raised in round enclosures, which have no corners or straight walls, fail to use shape at all when they later have to reorient. What does that suggest?

options.text: Which cue an animal relies on depends on its experience, such as the kind of enclosure it was raised in.
options.why: Correct. Mice raised in enclosures with no corners or straight walls fail to use shape at all. That finding is one reason the proposal of a dedicated process that matches shape and ignores everything else has lost ground.

options.text: Mice as a species cannot use shape to reorient, whatever kind of enclosure they happen to grow up in.
options.why: The finding concerns mice raised in round enclosures. The point is that their experience shaped which cue they relied on, not that mice in general lack the ability.

options.text: A dedicated shape process is present from birth and needs no experience, so the mice raised in round enclosures must have used it without showing it.
options.why: A process that needed no experience would have worked in the mice raised in round enclosures too. That they failed to use shape at all is evidence that which cue an animal relies on depends on its experience.

options.text: Being raised in round enclosures teaches mice to average shape with other cues, so they still use shape but give it little weight.
options.why: The mice did not give shape a small weight; they failed to use it at all. Which cue an animal relies on depends on its experience.

items.stem: How does the current view of reorientation differ from the earlier proposal of a dedicated shape process?

options.text: The earlier proposal had shape matched and everything else ignored; on the current view, the cue relied on depends on how reliable and noticeable it has proved.
options.why: Correct. On the current view, which cue an animal relies on depends on how reliable and noticeable that cue has proved. Two findings fit that view: many species use colors and objects as well as shape, and mice raised in round enclosures fail to use shape at all.

options.text: The earlier proposal had shape matched and everything else ignored; on the current view, an animal relies on colors and objects instead, and ignores the shape of its surroundings.
options.why: The current view does not throw shape out. Fish, chicks, pigeons, rats, monkeys, and people all use shape; what matters is how reliable and noticeable a cue has proved.

options.text: The earlier proposal had every cue averaged together; on the current view, shape is matched first and everything else is ignored.
options.why: That reverses the history. Matching shape and ignoring everything else was the earlier proposal, and it has lost ground. On the current view, which cue an animal relies on depends on how reliable and noticeable that cue has proved.

options.text: The earlier proposal had shape matched and everything else ignored; on the current view, an animal relies on whichever cue lies nearest the goal it is searching for.
options.why: Nearness to the goal is not the deciding feature. On the current view, which cue an animal relies on depends on how reliable and noticeable that cue has proved.

items.stem: Two groups of rats search for food in rectangular boxes with one striped wall. For one group, the striped wall always stands beside the food corner. For the other group, the striped wall is moved to a different side on every trial. Later, both groups are disoriented and tested in a box with a striped wall. On the current view, which group is more likely to rely on the stripe?

options.text: The group whose stripe stayed put next to the food, since for those rats the stripe has proved to be a reliable cue.
options.why: Correct. On the current view, which cue an animal relies on depends on how reliable and noticeable that cue has proved. A stripe that kept moving has not proved reliable, so those rats have little reason to rely on it.

options.text: The group whose stripe kept moving away from the food, since for those rats the stripe has been the most noticeable thing in each new box.
options.why: Being noticeable is not enough. A cue that keeps moving has not proved reliable, and on the current view both reliability and noticeability decide which cue an animal relies on.

options.text: Both groups equally, since the two stripes were equally noticeable, and noticeability is what decides which cue gets used.
options.why: Noticeability matters, but so does how reliable a cue has proved. The stripe that stayed beside the food proved reliable, and the stripe that moved did not, so the two groups differ.

options.text: Neither group, since rats reorient by the shape of a box alone, and a striped wall is a feature that shape matching ignores.
options.why: That is the older proposal of a dedicated shape process, which has lost ground. Many species use features such as colors and objects as well as shape.

items.stem: According to the lecture, the way people use cues in reorientation is unlike one of the ways a drifting running sum can be corrected. What is the contrast?

options.text: Averaging cues, each weighted by its reliability, is one way to correct a running sum, while in reorientation people seem to select the most useful cue instead.
options.why: Correct. Adults correcting a running sum combine landmarks and their own movement close to the ideal on average. In reorientation, people seem instead to pick out the single most useful cue. Following one source when two sources disagree by a lot is another way of correcting a running sum, so the contrast is with averaging in particular.

options.text: A running sum can be corrected only by selecting the single most useful cue, while in reorientation people average several cues, each weighted by its reliability.
options.why: That reverses the contrast. A running sum can be corrected in more than one way, and averaging is one of them. In reorientation, people seem to select the most useful cue rather than average.

options.text: A drifting running sum and a lost heading are both handled by averaging cues, each weighted by its reliability, so the two differ only in which cues are averaged.
options.why: Averaging is one way of correcting a running sum. In reorientation, though, people seem to select the most useful cue rather than average several.

options.text: A drifting running sum and a lost heading are both handled by selecting the single most useful cue, so neither one ever involves averaging cues together.
options.why: Selecting fits reorientation, and following one source, when two sources disagree by a lot, is also one way of correcting a running sum. But averaging by cue combination is another way, so correcting a running sum can involve averaging. The contrast is with that averaging.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe how a ring attractor stores a heading, updates it when the animal turns, and corrects it when the animal recognizes a landmark.
items.answer: A ring attractor is a circle of units, each standing for one direction. Each unit excites its near neighbors, and all of them feed a shared inhibition that holds every unit down. So the circle settles into a single bump of activity at one place on the ring. When nothing pushes the bump, it stays where it is, and its place on the ring is the stored heading. When the animal turns, a turning signal delivered to one side of the bump slides it around the ring, faster for faster turns. That is the update. When the animal recognizes a landmark, the landmark adds input at its own place on the ring, which pulls a drifted bump back. That is the correction.
rubric: Says the units lie on a circle, each standing for one direction, with neighbors exciting one another and a shared inhibition.
Says the circle settles into a single bump of activity, whose place on the ring is the stored heading and which stays put when nothing pushes it.
Says a turning signal slides the bump around the ring, faster for faster turns.
Says a recognized landmark adds input at its own place on the ring and pulls a drifted bump back.

items.stem: A squirrel can see a large oak tree, and it has stored where a cache of nuts lies relative to the oak. In a few sentences, explain how the squirrel could work out the direction and distance to the cache from where it sits. Say also what else the squirrel needs to know besides the two vectors.
items.answer: The squirrel can see the vector from itself to the oak, and it has stored the vector from the oak to the cache. Adding the two vectors gives the vector from the squirrel to the cache, which is the direction and distance it needs. But the two vectors are in different frames of reference. The seen vector is egocentric, given relative to the squirrel, while the stored vector is allocentric, given relative to the oak. So the squirrel also needs its current heading to relate the two before adding them. A ring attractor is one procedure that can supply that heading.
rubric: Says the seen vector runs from the squirrel to the oak, and the stored vector from the oak to the cache.
Says adding the two vectors gives the vector from the squirrel to the cache.
Says the seen vector is egocentric and the stored vector is allocentric (or not egocentric).
Says the squirrel also needs its current heading, because of that difference in frames.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the proposal that a dedicated process matches the shape of the surroundings and ignores everything else has lost ground, and say what view has replaced it.
items.answer: The proposal has lost ground for two reasons. Many species use features such as colors and objects to reorient, as well as shape. And mice raised in round enclosures fail to use shape at all, so which cue an animal relies on depends on its experience. On the current view, which cue an animal relies on depends on how reliable and noticeable that cue has proved. In reorientation, people seem to select the most useful cue rather than average several.
rubric: Says many species use features such as colors and objects, as well as shape.
Says mice raised in round enclosures fail to use shape, so which cue is relied on depends on experience.
Says that on the current view, the cue relied on depends on how reliable and noticeable it has proved.
Says people seem to select the most useful cue rather than average several, without stating the selection as settled.

pools.title: What a Map Contains, and Using It

items.stem: What is survey knowledge?

options.text: Knowledge of where places lie relative to one another, so that the way between any two of them can be worked out.
options.why: Correct. Survey knowledge is the kind of knowledge that “would support detouring and shortcutting”. Of all the kinds of knowledge about location, only survey knowledge can lead an animal from a new starting point to any place it knows.

options.text: Knowledge of the straight-line distance and direction back to the starting point, from wherever the animal now happens to be.
options.why: That is a home vector. It points to one place, the start, from anywhere, but gives no information about the way between two other places. Survey knowledge relates places to one another, so the way between any two can be worked out.

options.text: Knowledge of a fixed sequence of moves or landmarks that leads from one particular place to another particular place.
options.why: That is a route. A route can lead far, but only along its own path. Survey knowledge relates places to one another, so the way between any two of them can be worked out, including by a route never taken.

options.text: Knowledge of what the surroundings look like from the goal, which can be matched by moving as the animal draws near.
options.why: That is a snapshot, a stored view that can be matched only near the goal. Survey knowledge relates places to one another, so the way between any two of them can be worked out from anywhere.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? An understanding of where places lie relative to one another, good enough that the way between any two of them, including a shortcut or a detour, can be worked out.

options.text: survey knowledge
options.why: Correct. Survey knowledge is the kind of knowledge that “would support detouring and shortcutting”. A map, in the sense used for finding the way, is what contains it.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is the straight-line distance and direction back to the start. It relates the animal to one place only, so it cannot give the way between two other places, as survey knowledge can.

options.text: route
options.why: A route is a fixed sequence of moves or landmarks from one place to another. It works only along its own path, so it cannot give a shortcut or a detour, as survey knowledge can.

options.text: frame of reference
options.why: A frame of reference is the origin and directions against which a location is measured, such as the animal’s own body. It is not itself knowledge of where places lie. Survey knowledge relates places to one another, so the way between any two can be worked out.

items.stem: A kayaker has spent an hour paddling among the islands of a large lake. The kayaker can point straight back to the launch from anywhere. But the kayaker cannot work out the way from the present spot to a cabin on the far shore. The kayaker has paddled to that cabin from the launch before. Does the kayaker have survey knowledge of the lake?

options.text: No, because pointing back to the launch needs only the way back to the start, and survey knowledge would also give the way from where the kayaker is now to the cabin.
options.why: Correct. The way back to the start, even when it is known from anywhere, leads to one place only. Survey knowledge relates places to one another, so the way between any two of them, the present spot and the cabin included, can be worked out.

options.text: Yes, because a straight line back to the launch across open water is a shortcut, and only survey knowledge supports a shortcut like that.
options.why: Heading straight back to the start is what a home vector does, as desert ants do when they run straight home. The way back to the start leads to one place only, so it is not evidence of survey knowledge.

options.text: No, because survey knowledge comes only after a person has learned the views first and then the routes, and the kayaker’s one hour is too little.
options.why: There is little evidence that people learn views, then routes, then layouts in that order, and many people learn all three on a first visit. The kayaker lacks survey knowledge because only the way back to one place is known.

options.text: No, because survey knowledge relates only places that can be seen from where one is, and the cabin is out of sight across the lake.
options.why: Survey knowledge relates places to one another whether or not they can be sensed. So survey knowledge can lead from a new starting point to any place an animal knows. The kayaker lacks it because the only thing known is the way back to the launch, which points to one place.

items.stem: What is a cognitive map?

options.text: A map animals are proposed to keep, relating places to one another so that a goal can be reached by a route never taken.
options.why: Correct. A map, in the sense used for finding the way, is what contains survey knowledge. The proposal that animals keep such a map, a cognitive map, is a proposal that they can reach a goal by a route they have never taken.

options.text: A stored record of the turns that once led an animal to a goal, which it can repeat from the same starting point as on earlier trips.
options.why: That describes a route, a remembered chain of turns. It works only along its own path. A cognitive map relates places to one another, so a goal can be reached by a route never taken.

options.text: A running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, updated with every step and every turn.
options.why: That is path integration, whose result is a home vector. It points to one place only. A cognitive map relates places to one another, so a goal can be reached from anywhere by a route never taken.

options.text: A stored view of a goal’s surroundings, which an animal matches by moving until the scene in front of it looks the same.
options.why: That is a snapshot, which works only near the goal. A cognitive map relates places to one another, so a goal can be reached from far away by a route never taken.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Something that animals are proposed to keep, which relates places to one another so that an animal can reach a goal by a route it has never taken.

options.text: cognitive map
options.why: Correct. A cognitive map is a map in the sense used for finding the way: it contains survey knowledge. That animals keep one is a proposal, and a route never taken is the test of it.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Path integration keeps a running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the start. Its result points to one place from anywhere, but it does not relate other places to one another, as a cognitive map does.

options.text: route
options.why: A route is a fixed sequence of moves or landmarks from one place to another. It works only along its own path, so it cannot lead to a goal by a route never taken, as a cognitive map can.

options.text: beacon
options.why: A beacon is something sensed at or beside a goal, which an animal can approach directly. It helps only from where it can be sensed. A cognitive map relates places to one another, so a goal can be reached from anywhere.

items.stem: How are survey knowledge and a cognitive map related?

options.text: Survey knowledge is knowledge of where places lie relative to one another, and a cognitive map is a map animals are proposed to keep, which contains it.
options.why: Correct. A map, in the sense used for finding the way, is what contains survey knowledge. The cognitive map is the proposal that animals keep such a map, so that they can reach a goal by a route never taken.

options.text: A cognitive map is the first, rough stage in learning a new place, and survey knowledge is the accurate stage that replaces it after long experience there.
options.why: Neither one is a stage. There is little evidence that people learn a place in stages, and many people learn views, routes, and layout all on a first visit. A cognitive map is a map that contains survey knowledge.

options.text: Survey knowledge is a map that animals are proposed to keep, and a cognitive map is the knowledge of where places lie that such a map contains.
options.why: That reverses the two. Survey knowledge is the knowledge of where places lie relative to one another, and a cognitive map is the map animals are proposed to keep, which contains it.

options.text: A cognitive map is a stored view of the goal’s surroundings, and survey knowledge is what lets an animal match that view from farther away.
options.why: A stored view of the goal’s surroundings is a snapshot, which can be matched only near the goal. A cognitive map is a map that contains survey knowledge, knowledge of where places lie relative to one another.

items.stem: What does a metric map contain?

options.text: The distances and directions between places, like the bearings and miles marked on a sailor’s chart.
options.why: Correct. A metric map contains distances and directions between places. A sailor’s chart is the standard example.

options.text: Only which places connect to which, like the lines joining the stations on a subway map.
options.why: That is a topological map, which contains connections and nothing more. A metric map also contains the distances and directions between places, like a sailor’s chart.

options.text: A single vector: the straight-line distance and direction from the animal back to its starting point, and to no other place.
options.why: That is a home vector, which points to one place only, the start. A metric map contains the distances and directions between many places, like a sailor’s chart.
