options.text: For each place, an expectation of which places will follow it, and how soon, given how the animal moves.
options.why: That is the predictive map, a proposed procedure for valuing places. A metric map contains the distances and directions between places, like a sailor’s chart.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? A map that contains distances and directions between places.

options.text: metric map
options.why: Correct. A metric map contains distances and directions between places. A sailor’s chart is the standard example.

options.text: topological map
options.why: A topological map contains less: only which places connect to which, like a subway map. The definition here includes distances and directions.

options.text: home vector
options.why: A home vector is a distance and a direction, but only from where the animal is back to its starting point. The definition here is of distances and directions between many places.

options.text: route
options.why: A route is a fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, that works only along its own path. The definition here is of a map relating places by distance and direction.

items.stem: What does a topological map contain?

options.text: Only which places connect to which, like the lines and stations of a subway map.
options.why: Correct. A topological map contains connections alone, with no distances or directions. A subway map is the standard example.

options.text: The distances and directions between places, like the bearings and miles on a sailor’s chart.
options.why: That is a metric map. A topological map contains less: only which places connect to which, like a subway map.

options.text: A fixed sequence of moves or landmarks that leads from one place to another along one path.
options.why: That is a route, which works only along its own path. A topological map contains which places connect to which, like a subway map, across a whole network of places.

options.text: A stored view of what the surroundings look like from a goal, which is matched only near the goal.
options.why: That is a snapshot. A topological map contains which places connect to which, like a subway map, and nothing about how the surroundings look.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? A map that contains only which places connect to which, like a subway map.

options.text: topological map
options.why: Correct. A topological map contains connections alone, with no distances or directions. A subway map is the standard example.

options.text: metric map
options.why: A metric map contains more: the distances and directions between places, like a sailor’s chart. The definition here contains connections only.

options.text: route
options.why: A route is a fixed sequence of moves, or of landmarks, leading along one path. A topological map covers a whole network of connected places, not one path.

options.text: snapshot
options.why: A snapshot is a stored view of what the surroundings look like from a goal, matched only near the goal. The definition here is of a map of connections between places.

items.stem: Two delivery robots work in the same warehouse. One robot’s map contains only which aisles connect to which. The other robot’s map contains the distances and directions between places. When a shelf is removed, a gap opens that would let a robot cut straight across floor it has never crossed. Which robot’s map contains what is needed to work out the direction and distance of the cut?

options.text: Only the second robot’s map, since a map of connections alone contains no distances or directions to work the cut out from.
options.why: Correct. The second robot’s map is a metric map, like a sailor’s chart. The first robot’s is a topological map, like a subway map. A topological map contains only which places connect to which, so the direction and distance of a new cut cannot be worked out from it.

options.text: Only the first robot’s map, since the gap is a new connection between aisles, and connections are what that map contains.
options.why: The first robot’s map does contain connections, but only the ones already in it, and connections alone give no direction or distance. Working out the cut needs the distances and directions a metric map contains.

options.text: Both maps equally, since each one relates the same places in the warehouse to one another, which is what any kind of map contains.
options.why: The two maps relate the same places, but they contain different amounts. A topological map contains only which places connect to which, with no distances or directions, so only the metric map gives the cut.

options.text: Neither map, since no map, whatever distances and directions it contains, can give a way across floor the robot has never crossed.
options.why: With the robot’s position and a goal’s in one code, the direction and distance to the goal can be computed directly, even across ground never crossed. That needs the distances and directions of a metric map.

items.stem: Suppose a person judges Montreal to lie north of Seattle, because they think of Canada as lying north of the United States. In fact, Seattle is farther north. What can be inferred from the Montreal error about how people remember where places are?

options.text: People place a city partly by the region it belongs to, so their remembered layout is not perfectly metric.
options.why: Correct. The error matches people judging Reno to be east of San Diego, because Nevada is east of California, though Reno is in fact to the west. Remembered positions also drift toward the centers of the regions they belong to.

options.text: People store only which cities connect to which, so they have no sense of the direction from one city to another at all.
options.why: If people had no sense of direction between cities, they would not judge one city to lie north of another. Human geography is more than connections alone, but it is not perfectly metric either.

options.text: People store exact distances and directions between cities, and the error comes only from misreading a map seen long ago.
options.why: A store of exact distances and directions would not produce errors that follow the regions cities belong to. Human geography is neither perfectly metric nor merely topological.

options.text: People remember east and west accurately, and their errors are confined to judging which of two cities lies farther north.
options.why: The same kind of error happens east and west: people judge Reno to be east of San Diego, though it is to the west. Positions are placed partly by the regions they belong to, in every direction.

items.stem: People can judge roughly which way one city lies from another, yet they judge Reno to be east of San Diego, when Reno is in fact to the west. How does human geography compare with a metric map and a topological map?

options.text: It is neither perfectly metric nor merely topological: people judge directions between places, but with errors that follow the regions places belong to.
options.why: Correct. Judging directions at all is more than a topological map contains. But people make errors that follow regions, such as placing Reno east of San Diego because Nevada is east of California. So human geography is not perfectly metric either.

options.text: It is perfectly metric, since people can judge which way one city lies from another, and an occasional error is only a lapse of memory.
options.why: Judging directions is more than a topological map allows, but the errors are not random lapses. They follow the regions places belong to, so human geography is not perfectly metric.

options.text: It is merely topological, since people store only which places connect to which, and their judgments of direction are no better than guesses.
options.why: People’s judgments of direction follow the regions places belong to, so they are not mere guesses. Human geography is more than topological, though not perfectly metric.

options.text: It is metric in distance but topological in direction, since people judge how far apart places are accurately but not which way they lie.
options.why: Distances are distorted too, since remembered positions drift toward the centers of the regions they belong to. Human geography is neither perfectly metric nor merely topological.

items.stem: On one proposal, a map keeps track of where the animal is with a pattern that repeats across the floor, like tiles, and slides along as the animal moves. A robot uses one such pattern, which repeats every 2 meters. The pattern currently puts the robot half a meter into a repeat. What does that one pattern fix about the robot’s position?

options.text: Its position within one repeat, but not which of the many repeats across the floor it is standing in.
options.why: Correct. On its own, a repeating pattern fixes position only within one repeat, much as a clock’s minute hand gives the minute but not the hour. Several patterns of different sizes, combined, would pin down a single place.

options.text: Its exact position on the floor, since a pattern that slides with every movement fixes a single place.
options.why: The pattern does slide with every movement, but it repeats, so the same reading occurs once in every repeat. Like a minute hand, which gives the minute but not the hour, one pattern fixes position only within one repeat.

options.text: Nothing about its position, since a pattern that repeats gives the same reading in every repeat across the floor.
options.why: The same reading does recur once in every repeat. But the pattern’s value changes from point to point within a repeat, so one pattern does fix position within one repeat. What one pattern cannot fix is which repeat the robot is in, much as a minute hand gives the minute but not the hour.

options.text: Its distance from the start, but not its direction, since the pattern slides with speed alone.
options.why: The pattern slides with a signal for both speed and direction. What one pattern cannot fix is which repeat the robot is in, much as a minute hand gives the minute but not the hour.

items.stem: A robot keeps track of its position along a hallway with three patterns that repeat along the floor, each with a different repeat size. Each pattern on its own gives the robot’s position only within one of its own repeats. On the proposal of codes that repeat across space, what does combining the three readings give?

options.text: A single place, since only one position fits all three of the readings at once, though each fits many positions alone.
options.why: Correct. On the proposal, several patterns of different sizes, combined, pin down a single place, though each on its own fixes position only within one repeat.

options.text: Position within the smallest repeat only, since the smallest pattern is the most precise and the larger ones add nothing to it.
options.why: The smallest pattern fixes position finely, but only within one of its many repeats. The larger patterns settle which of those repeats the robot is in, so together the three pin down a single place.

options.text: Position within the largest repeat only, since the larger patterns override the readings of the smaller ones when they are combined.
options.why: No pattern overrides another. Each fixes position within its own repeat, and combining patterns of different sizes pins down a single place.

options.text: No position at all, since three patterns of different sizes give readings that conflict, and they cancel one another out.
options.why: Patterns of different sizes do not conflict. Each fixes position within one of its own repeats, and only one position fits all three readings, so combined they pin down a single place.

items.stem: Suppose a fox keeps a map that contains its own position and the position of a stream. The fox has reached the stream before, but only from the far side of a hill. It has never crossed the ground between where it now stands and the stream. With both positions in one code, what can the fox work out?

options.text: The direction and distance straight to the stream, computed directly, even across the ground it has never crossed.
options.why: Correct. With the animal’s position and the goal’s in one code, the direction and distance to the goal can be computed directly, even across ground the animal has never crossed.

options.text: Only the way along paths it has used before, since a map never gives a way over ground the animal has not crossed.
options.why: That is the limit of a route, which works only along its own path. With both positions in one code, the direction and distance to the stream can be computed directly, even across new ground.

options.text: Only the direction back to its den, since a straight-line direction from a running sum points to the start and nowhere else.
options.why: A running sum gives a home vector, which points only to the start. A code that contains both the fox’s position and the stream’s gives the direction and distance to the stream itself.

options.text: Nothing until it comes near enough to recognize the stream’s surroundings, since the stream cannot be sensed from where it stands.
options.why: Recognizing a goal’s surroundings works only near the goal. A code that contains both positions gives the direction and distance to the stream from where the fox stands.

items.stem: A home vector, and a code that contains both the animal’s position and a goal’s, can each give a straight-line direction. How do the two differ?

options.text: A home vector points only back to the start, while the code gives the direction and distance to any goal whose position the code includes, even across new ground.
options.why: Correct. A home vector points to one place, the start, from anywhere. With the animal’s and a goal’s positions in one code, the direction and distance to that goal can be computed directly, even across ground never crossed.

options.text: A home vector points to any goal the animal has visited before, while the code gives only the direction and distance from the animal’s position back to the start.
options.why: That reverses the two. A home vector points only to the start, and the code gives the direction and distance to any goal whose position it contains.

options.text: A home vector can be followed only along the winding path the animal took out, while the code points straight to a goal from anywhere.
options.why: A home vector is not tied to a path at all. It points straight back to the start from anywhere. The difference is that it points only to the start, while the code points to any goal it contains.

options.text: A home vector gives the distance to the start but not its direction, while the code gives a goal’s direction but not its distance.
options.why: A home vector gives both the distance and the direction back to the start, and the code gives both for a goal. The difference is that a home vector points only to the start.

items.stem: A driver always reaches work by the same chain of turns from home. One morning, after dropping a friend at an unfamiliar address across town, the driver has to get to work from there. Why is a map of the city more useful than the remembered chain of turns?

options.text: The chain of turns starts from home, so it gives no way from somewhere new, while a map lets a way be worked out from anywhere.
options.why: Correct. In finding the way, the map is the model in model-based choice. A remembered chain of turns does not help an animal escape a predator from somewhere new, and a map does. The driver faces the same problem.

options.text: The chain of turns works from anywhere, but only to the one place it was learned for, while a map gives the way to many places.
options.why: A chain of turns does not work from anywhere. Like any route, it works only along its own path, from the place it starts. A map lets a way be worked out from a new starting point.

options.text: The chain of turns is a running sum of the trip, which drifts with every turn, while a map is corrected by every landmark passed.
options.why: A running sum keeps track of the way back to the start, and it is what drifts. A chain of turns is a route, which fails the driver because it starts from home, not because it drifts.

options.text: A map is simpler to follow than a chain of turns, which is why it does better from every starting point, familiar or new.
options.why: A map is more complicated than a chain of turns, and early in learning it can do worse than habit. The map does better for the driver because the driver is starting from somewhere new.

items.stem: In choosing a way, how does following a map compare with following a remembered chain of turns that once led to food?

options.text: A map gives a way from a new starting point, which the turns cannot, but early in learning, while the map is still wrong, it can do worse than habit.
options.why: Correct. In finding the way, the map is the model in model-based choice, so a way can be worked out from somewhere new. But a map is more complicated, and while it is still wrong, following it can do worse than habit.

options.text: A map does better than the turns from familiar and new starting points alike, as soon as the first parts of the map have been learned.
options.why: A map does give a way from somewhere new, but early in learning it is still wrong. While it is wrong, following it can do worse than following habit.

options.text: The turns give a way from any starting point, while a map gives one only from places already visited, so the turns do better early in learning.
options.why: The turns work only from the place they start. It is the map that gives a way from a new starting point. Habit can do better early on, but because the map is still wrong, not because the turns work from anywhere.

options.text: A map is simpler to follow than the turns, so it wins early in learning, and the turns win only after long practice has made them automatic.
options.why: A map is more complicated than a chain of turns, not simpler. Early in learning, while the map is still wrong, it is habit that can do better.

items.stem: A new nurse is in her first week at a large hospital. She knows one route from the entrance to her ward by heart, and has a rough sense of how the rest of the building is laid out. When she tries to cut through an unfamiliar wing using that rough sense, she gets lost, and has to go back to the route she knows. Why might the route have served her better?

options.text: Early in learning, her map is still wrong, and following a map that is still wrong can do worse than habit.
options.why: Correct. A map is more complicated than a remembered route, and early in learning it is still wrong. While it is wrong, following it can do worse than following habit.

options.text: A route is more reliable than a map in every case, since a route is learned first and a map can never be fully trusted.
options.why: A map does better than a route from a new starting point, where a route gives no help at all. The nurse’s map failed because it was still wrong early in learning.

options.text: Her rough sense of the layout is a home vector, which points back to the entrance and cannot lead her through a wing.
options.why: A home vector is the way back to the start, not a sense of how a building is laid out. Her rough sense of the layout is a map that is still wrong, which can do worse than habit.

options.text: A map works only for places that have been crossed before, so no map could lead her through a wing she has never entered.
options.why: A map can give the way across ground never crossed. Her map failed because, early in learning, it was still wrong, and a map that is still wrong can do worse than habit.

items.stem: On the proposal known as the predictive map, what is stored?

options.text: For each place, an expectation of which places will follow it, and how soon, given the way the animal usually moves.
options.why: Correct. Combined with where food is now, the expectations give every place a value, with no search. The predictive map is a proposed third procedure, between choosing by remembered values and choosing by running a model.

options.text: For each place, the distances and directions to every other place, from which a straight path to the goal can be worked out.
options.why: That is a metric map, which contains distances and directions between places. A predictive map stores, for each place, an expectation of which places will follow it, and how soon.

options.text: For each turn the animal has made, the value it earned on past visits, recalled whenever the animal reaches that turn again.
options.why: That is closer to choosing by values remembered from experience. A predictive map stores, for each place, an expectation of which places will follow it, and how soon, and combines it with where food is now.

options.text: For the goal alone, a view of what its surroundings look like, matched by moving until the scene looks the same again.
options.why: That is a snapshot. A predictive map stores something for every place: an expectation of which places will follow it, and how soon, given how the animal usually moves.

items.stem: Choosing a way can rest on values remembered from experience, or on running a model of what leads to what. The predictive map has been proposed as a third procedure between the two. How would a predictive map give each place a value?

options.text: By combining its stored expectations of which places follow which with where food is now, giving every place a value with no search.
options.why: Correct. The expectations are of which places will follow each place, and how soon, given how the animal usually moves. Combined with where food is now, they value every place at once, without searching a model.

options.text: By running its model forward step by step from the animal’s position, searching the possible routes for the one that ends at food.
options.why: That is choosing by running a model. The predictive map was proposed as something between that and remembered values, and it gives every place a value with no search.

options.text: By recalling the value each place earned on past visits, which changes only as the animal visits the place again and finds food there.
options.why: Recalling values earned on past visits is choosing by values remembered from experience. On the proposal, values come from combining stored expectations with where food is now, so they change at once when food turns up somewhere new.

options.text: By working out the straight-line direction and distance from the animal to the food, and valuing each place by how close it lies to that line.
options.why: Computing a direct vector to a goal is what a code containing both positions allows. A predictive map instead combines expectations of which places follow which with where food is now.

items.stem: What is the standing of the predictive map as an account of finding the way?

options.text: It is a proposal for what the hippocampus does, tested in simulations in which the way the simulated animal moved was supplied rather than learned.
options.why: Correct. The predictive map is a proposal, and its tests have been simulations. In them, how the simulated animal moved was supplied, not learned.

options.text: It is an established account of what the hippocampus does, confirmed by recordings showing that place cells store expectations of which places follow.
options.why: The predictive map remains a proposal for what the hippocampus does. Its tests have been simulations, in which the way the simulated animal moved was supplied.

options.text: It is an illustration made up for the early mammal, not drawn from research, of how insects swarming along its usual circuit could be valued.
options.why: The swarming insects are an illustration offered for the early mammal, not a finding. The predictive map itself is a proposal from researchers, tested in simulations.

options.text: It is a proposal tested in simulations in which the simulated animal learned both how to move and where food was, with nothing supplied.
options.why: The predictive map is a proposal tested in simulations, but in those simulations the way the simulated animal moved was supplied, not learned.

items.stem: A simulated animal values places by the predictive-map procedure. It usually runs a loop that passes through five places, and food has always been at the third. On one trial, the animal finds food at the fifth place instead, still on the loop. On the proposal, what happens to the values of the places?

options.text: They change at once, since the expectations of which places follow which are unchanged, and only the food’s place is new.
options.why: Correct. The expectations depend on how the animal usually moves, which has not changed. Combining them with the food’s new place changes the values at once, which is the quick side of the procedure.

options.text: They change only slowly, since the expectations of which places follow which were built from trips that ended with food at the third place.
options.why: The expectations depend on how the animal moves, not on where food was. When food turns up somewhere new, the values change at once. The procedure is slow only when the best route changes.

options.text: They stay close to what they were until the animal has been fed at the fifth place many times, since each value builds up slowly over rewarded visits.
options.why: Building values up slowly over visits that end in food is closer to choosing by values remembered from experience. On the proposal, values come from combining expectations with where food is now, so they change at once.

options.text: They change at once, but only after the animal has searched every route around the loop to find which of them now reaches the food.
options.why: The values do change at once, but with no search. Combining the stored expectations with where food is now is enough to give every place a value.

items.stem: A simulated animal values places by the predictive-map procedure. A barrier is put across its usual route to food, so that a route it has rarely taken becomes the best one. On the proposal, how well does the procedure handle the change?

options.text: Poorly at first, since the expectations of which places follow which were built from the routes the animal has been taking, and they lag behind.
options.why: Correct. The procedure is quick, and only partly flexible. A change in where food is changes the values at once, but a change in the best route leaves the expectations, built from old routes, lagging behind.

options.text: Well and at once, since the values change immediately whenever anything about the surroundings changes, just as they do when food moves.
options.why: Values do change at once when food turns up somewhere new. But when the best route changes, the expectations, built from the routes already taken, lag behind.

options.text: Well and at once, since the procedure searches its model of the surroundings for a new route each time the animal has to choose.
options.why: Searching for a new route at each choice is closer to running a model. The predictive map gives values with no search, and its expectations lag behind when the best route changes.

options.text: Not at all, since the expectations of which places follow which are fixed for good once learned, so the animal can only keep trying the blocked route.
options.why: The expectations lag behind a change in the best route, but they are not fixed for good. The procedure is described as quick, and only partly flexible, not as rigid.

items.stem: An animal that knows many places has to choose which of its maps it is on. Choosing a map is a case of which more general choice, made for whole places?

options.text: The choice between generalizing, treating similar inputs alike, and discriminating, telling them apart.
options.why: Correct. A familiar place seen in new light has to be matched to its stored map. A new place that resembles an old one has to get a map of its own. Choosing a map is generalizing against discriminating, for whole places.

options.text: The choice between exploring, sampling an option that might be better, and exploiting one already known to be decent.
options.why: That is exploration versus exploitation, the choice of whether to look for something new. Choosing a map is deciding whether a place is one already known, which is generalizing against discriminating.

options.text: The choice between learning a place, whatever the movements, and learning a movement, whatever place it leads to.
options.why: That is place learning against response learning. Choosing a map is deciding whether a place should be treated like a known one or told apart from it, which is generalizing against discriminating.

options.text: The choice between running a model of what leads to what, and repeating a chain of moves that once led to food.
options.why: That is model-based choice against habit, a choice about how to pick a way. Choosing a map is deciding which place the animal is in, which is generalizing against discriminating.

items.stem: A person moves from an apartment on the third floor of a building to one on the sixth floor. The new apartment has the same floor plan, but different furniture and a different view. In terms of choosing a map, what does the new apartment call for?

options.text: Discriminating: although the new apartment resembles the old one, it is another place, and it needs a map of its own.
options.why: Correct. A new place that resembles an old one has to get a map of its own. Telling the two apart is discriminating, applied to whole places.

options.text: Generalizing: since the new apartment resembles the old one, the stored map of the old apartment should be used for it.
options.why: Generalizing is right for a familiar place seen in new light. The sixth-floor apartment is a different place that only resembles the old one, so it calls for discriminating and a map of its own.

options.text: Generalizing: any two places with the same floor plan are the same place on a map, whatever their furniture and view.
options.why: A shared floor plan makes two places alike, not the same. A new place that resembles an old one calls for discriminating, and a map of its own.

options.text: Discriminating: the old apartment’s map has to be erased first, since a person can keep only one map of a building at a time.
options.why: Discriminating is right, but nothing needs erasing. An animal that knows many places has a map for each, so the new apartment gets a map of its own beside the old one.

items.stem: A shopper visits a branch of a grocery chain in a new city. The store looks much like the branch at home. The shopper walks straight to where the milk is at home, but in the new store that aisle is full of cereal. In terms of choosing a map, what went wrong?

options.text: The shopper generalized where discriminating was called for, matching a look-alike place to the stored map of a different one.
options.why: Correct. A new place that resembles an old one has to get a map of its own. The shopper treated the new store as the familiar one, generalizing where discriminating was needed, and so used the wrong map.

options.text: The shopper discriminated where generalizing was called for, giving a familiar place a new map of its own that it did not need.
options.why: That reverses the error. The new store was a different place that only looked familiar. The shopper treated it as the home store, which is generalizing where discriminating was needed.

options.text: The shopper’s map of the home store contained only which aisles connect, so it had no position for the milk at all.
options.why: The shopper walked straight to where the milk is at home, so the home store’s map did contain its position. The error was using that map in a different store.

options.text: The shopper’s running sum of position drifted on the way in, so the shopper lost track of where the milk aisle lay.
options.why: The shopper reached exactly the spot where the milk is at home, so position was tracked well. The error was being on the wrong map, by treating a look-alike store as the familiar one.

items.stem: Old rats sometimes swim straight to a platform hidden under the water of a familiar pool, and sometimes seem lost. According to the reading, what may be happening on the trials where they seem lost?

options.text: They may be calling up the wrong map, locating themselves on the map of a different place, not on the pool’s own.
options.why: Correct. The rats seem lost as if they had called up the wrong map. As one group of researchers put it, “Proper navigation requires not only locating oneself correctly but also locating oneself on the correct map”.

options.text: They may not have learned where the platform lies, so that their straight swims on other trials were a matter of luck.
options.why: On other trials the rats swim straight to the platform, so they have learned where it lies. The lost trials look instead as if they had called up the wrong map.

options.text: They may be steering by sight, which works on the trials when the platform happens to show above the water.
options.why: The platform is hidden under the water, so there is nothing to steer toward by sight. The lost trials look as if the rats had called up the wrong map.

options.text: They may be too slow with age to reach the platform, though they swim toward it on every trial in the pool.
options.why: Rats that swam toward the platform every time would not seem lost. On the lost trials, they behave as if they had called up the wrong map.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what part a map plays in model-based choice. Then explain when finding the way by a map does better than following a remembered chain of turns, and when it can do worse.
items.answer: In finding the way, the map serves as the model in model-based choice: a way is chosen by working out what leads to what. A remembered chain of turns works only from the place where it starts, so it does not help an animal escape a predator, or reach a goal, from somewhere new. A map relates places to one another, so a way can be worked out from a new starting point. But a map is more complicated. Early in learning it is still wrong, and while it is wrong, following it can do worse than following habit.
rubric: Says a remembered chain of turns works only from its own starting point.
Says a map lets a way be worked out from a new starting point, as in escaping a predator from somewhere new.
Says the map plays the part of the model in model-based choice.
Says early in learning, while the map is still wrong, following it can do worse than habit.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe what the proposed predictive map stores, how it gives places a value, and why it is quick but only partly flexible. Give one change it would handle at once and one it would be slow to handle.
items.answer: On the proposal, the procedure stores, for each place, an expectation of which places will follow it, and how soon, given the way the animal usually moves. Combined with where food is now, those expectations give every place a value with no search. So when food turns up somewhere new, the values change at once, because only the food’s position has changed. But the expectations were built from the routes the animal has been taking. If a barrier blocks the usual route, and a route the animal rarely takes becomes the best one, the expectations lag behind, and so do the values. The predictive map is a proposal for what the hippocampus does, tested in simulations.
rubric: Says the predictive map stores, for each place, which places will follow it and how soon, given how the animal usually moves.
Says those expectations are combined with where food is now to value every place without search.
Gives a change handled at once, such as food turning up somewhere new.
Gives a change handled slowly, such as the best route changing, because the expectations were built from routes already taken.
Treats the predictive map as a proposal, tested in simulation, not as an established finding.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how, on one proposal, patterns that repeat across space could keep track of where an animal is on a map. Then explain what having the animal’s position and a goal’s in one code would let the animal do.
items.answer: On one proposal, a pattern repeats across the floor, like tiles, and slides along as the animal moves, driven by a signal for speed and direction. One such pattern fixes the animal’s position only within one repeat, much as a clock’s minute hand gives the minute but not the hour. But several patterns of different sizes, combined, pin down a single place. With the animal’s position and the goal’s in one code, the direction and distance to the goal can be computed directly, even across ground the animal has never crossed.
rubric: Says a single repeating pattern slides as the animal moves and fixes position only within one repeat.
Says several patterns of different sizes, combined, pin down a single place.
Says that with the animal’s and the goal’s positions in one code, the direction and distance to the goal can be computed directly.
Says the direct computation works even across ground the animal has never crossed.
Treats repeating codes as one proposal, not as an established finding.

pools.title: Ways to Explore, Curiosity, and Machines That Map
pools.covers: reading §9.2.9, §9.2.10, §9.2.11 · lecture 9.2 slides ways_to_explore, curiosity, machines_that_map

items.stem: What is random exploration?

options.text: Choosing the better-looking option most of the time and another option some of the time, with a setting for how often.
options.why: Correct. Random exploration mostly takes the option that looks best so far, and now and then takes another, at a rate given by a setting. It adds no bonus for being less known.

options.text: Adding a bonus to the value of options that are less known, so that uncertainty itself makes such an option attractive.
options.why: That is directed exploration, which favors the less-known option because it is less known. Random exploration picks another option at a set rate, with no bonus for being less known.

options.text: Giving extra value to an option simply for being new, a value that fades as the option is seen.
options.why: That is a novelty bonus, which fades with seeing an option. Random exploration mostly takes the better-looking option and sometimes another, with a setting for how often.

options.text: Leaving a patch once its rate of finding food has fallen to the average rate for the habitat as a whole.
options.why: That is the patch-leaving rule, which concerns when to leave a patch that is running down. Random exploration concerns choosing among options, mostly the better-looking one and sometimes another.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Choosing the better-looking option most of the time and another option some of the time, with a setting for how often.

options.text: random exploration
options.why: Correct. Random exploration mostly takes the option that looks best so far, and now and then takes another, at a rate given by a setting.

options.text: directed exploration
options.why: Directed exploration adds a bonus to options that are less known, so it favors less-known options. The procedure described picks another option at a set rate, with no such preference, which is random exploration.

options.text: novelty bonus
options.why: A novelty bonus values a thing more simply for being new, and fades with seeing it. The procedure described picks another option at a set rate, which is random exploration.

options.text: exploration versus exploitation
options.why: Exploration versus exploitation is the trade-off itself, between a known decent option and one that might be better or worse. The procedure described is one way of handling that trade-off, random exploration.

items.stem: A commuter has tried four coffee shops near work and has a clear favorite. Most mornings the commuter goes to the favorite. On about one morning in ten, the commuter goes to one of the other three instead, picked with no preference for whichever is least known. Which procedure for exploring fits?

options.text: Random exploration, since the commuter mostly takes the better-looking option and sometimes another, at a set rate.
options.why: Correct. The commuter takes the best-looking shop most of the time and another at a fixed rate, without favoring the least-known one. That is random exploration.

options.text: Directed exploration, since the commuter adds a bonus to the shops that are less known, so their uncertainty draws the commuter in.
options.why: Directed exploration would favor whichever shop is least known. The commuter picks among the other shops with no such preference, which is random exploration.

options.text: A novelty bonus, since the commuter values each of the other three shops more simply for being new to the commuter.
options.why: All four shops have been tried, so none is new, and a novelty bonus fades with seeing an option. Mostly taking the favorite and sometimes another, at a set rate, is random exploration.

options.text: The patch-leaving rule, since the favorite’s rate of good coffee has fallen to the average rate for all the shops nearby.
options.why: The patch-leaving rule concerns leaving a patch that is running down, and the commuter keeps returning to the favorite. Taking the favorite most mornings and another at a set rate is random exploration.

items.stem: What is directed exploration?

options.text: Adding a bonus to the value of options that are less known, so that uncertainty itself makes an option attractive.
options.why: Correct. Directed exploration favors an option because less is known about it. The bonus for uncertainty fades only as the option is sampled.

options.text: Choosing the better-looking option most of the time and another option some of the time, with a setting for how often.
options.why: That is random exploration, which picks another option at a set rate with no preference for the less-known one. Directed exploration adds a bonus to options that are less known.

options.text: Giving extra value to an option simply for being new, a value that fades as the option is seen.
options.why: That is a novelty bonus, which fades with seeing an option. Directed exploration adds a bonus for being less known, which fades only with sampling.

options.text: A drive to gain information for its own sake, even when no reward depends on the information gained.
options.why: That is curiosity, a drive rather than a procedure for choosing among options. Directed exploration adds a bonus to the value of options that are less known.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Adding a bonus to the value of options that are less known, so that uncertainty itself makes an option attractive.

options.text: directed exploration
options.why: Correct. Directed exploration favors an option because less is known about it, and its bonus fades only as the option is sampled.

options.text: random exploration
options.why: Random exploration picks another option at a set rate, with no preference for the less-known one. A bonus for being less known is directed exploration.

options.text: novelty bonus
options.why: A novelty bonus values a thing for being new and fades with seeing it. A bonus for being less known fades only with sampling, and adding it is directed exploration.

options.text: curiosity
options.why: Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake, not a bonus added to particular options. Adding a bonus to less-known options is directed exploration.

items.stem: A diner walks past two restaurants every day, so both are familiar sights. The diner has eaten twenty times at one and twice at the other, and the meals at both have been about equally good. Over the next weeks, the diner picks the less-tried restaurant more often, and its pull weakens only as the diner eats there more. Which procedure fits?

options.text: Directed exploration, since a bonus for the less-sampled restaurant makes its uncertainty attractive, and the bonus fades only with sampling.
options.why: Correct. The diner favors the restaurant that is less known, and the pull weakens only with eating there. A bonus for uncertainty that fades only with sampling is directed exploration.

options.text: A novelty bonus, since the less-tried restaurant is valued more simply for being new to the diner, and that value fades only with eating there.
options.why: The diner sees both restaurants every day, so neither is new, and a novelty bonus fades with seeing an option. A pull that weakens only with eating there is a bonus for uncertainty, which is directed exploration.

options.text: Random exploration, since the diner mostly takes the better-looking restaurant and picks the other one some of the time, at a set rate.
options.why: Random exploration picks another option at a set rate, with no preference for the less-known one. The diner favors the less-tried restaurant because it is less known, which is directed exploration.

options.text: The patch-leaving rule, since the restaurant tried twenty times has run down until its rate of good meals fell to the average.
options.why: The patch-leaving rule concerns leaving a patch that is running down, and there is no sign that the familiar restaurant has gotten worse. Favoring the less-known option for being less known is directed exploration.

items.stem: What is a novelty bonus?

options.text: Extra value given to an option simply for being new, which fades as the option is seen.
options.why: Correct. A novelty bonus makes a thing attractive because it is new. Once the option has been seen, it is no longer new, and the bonus fades.

options.text: Extra value given to an option for being less known, which fades only as the option is sampled.
options.why: That is the bonus added in directed exploration, a bonus for uncertainty. It fades only with sampling, while a novelty bonus fades with seeing.

options.text: Choosing the better-looking option most of the time, and another option now and then, at a set rate.
options.why: That is random exploration, which picks another option at a set rate. A novelty bonus is extra value for being new, which fades as the option is seen.

options.text: A drive to gain information for its own sake, even when no reward depends on that information.
options.why: That is curiosity, a drive rather than a value attached to an option. A novelty bonus is extra value for being new, which fades as the option is seen.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Extra value given to an option simply for being new, which fades as the option is seen.

options.text: novelty bonus
options.why: Correct. A novelty bonus values a thing for being new, so it fades once the thing has been seen.

options.text: directed exploration
options.why: Directed exploration adds a bonus for being less known, which fades only with sampling. Extra value for being new, which fades with seeing, is a novelty bonus.

options.text: random exploration
options.why: Random exploration picks another option at a set rate and adds no value to any option. Extra value for being new is a novelty bonus.

options.text: curiosity
options.why: Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake, not a value attached to one option. Extra value for being new, which fades with seeing, is a novelty bonus.

items.stem: A novelty bonus and a bonus for uncertainty can both make an unfamiliar option attractive. How do they differ in what makes each one fade?

options.text: A novelty bonus fades with seeing an option, while a bonus for uncertainty fades only with sampling it.
options.why: Correct. An option stops being new once it has been seen. It stops being uncertain only once it has been tried, so seeing an option leaves a bonus for uncertainty in place.

options.text: A novelty bonus fades only with sampling an option, while a bonus for uncertainty fades with merely seeing it.
options.why: That reverses the two. Seeing an option is enough to make it no longer new, while only sampling it reduces how uncertain its value is.

options.text: Both fade with seeing an option, but a bonus for uncertainty fades more slowly because it starts out larger.
options.why: Only the novelty bonus fades with seeing. A bonus for uncertainty fades only with sampling, because seeing an option does not reveal what it is worth.

options.text: Both fade only with the passing of time, whether or not the option has been seen or sampled.
options.why: Each bonus fades with something the animal does. A novelty bonus fades with seeing an option, and a bonus for uncertainty fades only with sampling it.

items.stem: Monkeys and people were offered options they had never seen. The pull of such options could come from a fixed bonus for being new, or from the value of what could still be learned about each option. Which predicted their choices better?

options.text: The value of what could still be learned about an option, in monkeys and in people alike.
options.why: Correct. In both species, the value of what could still be learned about an option predicted choices better than a fixed bonus for being new.

options.text: A fixed bonus for being new, in monkeys and in people alike, since every option offered was unseen.
options.why: Every option was unseen, so a novelty bonus might seem enough. But in both species, the value of what could still be learned about an option predicted choices better.

options.text: The value of what could still be learned about an option for people, and a fixed bonus for being new for monkeys.
options.why: The result did not split by species. In monkeys and in people alike, the value of what could still be learned predicted choices better than a fixed bonus for being new.

options.text: Neither one better than the other, since an option never seen is both new and unknown.
options.why: An unseen option is both new and unknown, which is why the comparison could be made at all. The value of what could still be learned predicted choices better, in both species.

items.stem: In a two-option game, people had been shown one option more often than the other. When six choices were still ahead rather than one, their choices changed in two ways. How does each change line up with a procedure for exploring?

options.text: Choosing the less-sampled option more often reflects directed exploration, and choosing more noisily reflects random exploration.
options.why: Correct. A shift toward the less-known option fits a bonus for uncertainty, which is directed exploration. Noisier choices, with the better-looking option taken less consistently, fit random exploration. People use both.

options.text: Choosing the less-sampled option more often reflects random exploration, while choosing more noisily reflects directed exploration.
options.why: That reverses the two. Random exploration adds noise without favoring the less-known option. Directed exploration adds a bonus for uncertainty, which shifts choices toward the less-sampled option.

options.text: Choosing the less-sampled option more often reflects a novelty bonus, and choosing more noisily reflects directed exploration.
options.why: Both options had been seen in the forced choices, so neither was new, and a novelty bonus fades with seeing. The shift toward the less-sampled option is directed exploration, and the added noise is random exploration.

options.text: Both changes reflect directed exploration, since each is a bonus added to the value of the less-sampled option.
options.why: Only the shift fits a bonus for the less-known option. Noisier choices mean whichever option looks better is taken less consistently, with no bonus added to either, which fits random exploration.

items.stem: A traveler has two weeks in a city full of restaurants, and has already eaten at some of them more than others. Recall how people played a two-option game with one choice or six choices still ahead. How are the traveler’s choices on the first night likely to differ from those on the last night?

options.text: On the first night, the traveler is more likely to try a less-sampled restaurant and to choose less consistently than on the last night.
options.why: Correct. With many choices ahead, people chose the less-sampled option more often and chose more noisily. What is learned early can still be used later, so exploring is worth more at the start of the trip.

options.text: On the first night, the traveler is more likely to stick with the best-known restaurant, saving the trying of others for the last nights.
options.why: That reverses the pattern. Exploring is worth doing only because of the future, so people explore more with many choices ahead, not with few.

options.text: On the first night, the traveler chooses less consistently, but is no more likely to try a less-sampled restaurant than on the last night.
options.why: More choices ahead made people noisier, which is random exploration. They also chose the less-sampled option more often, which is directed exploration, so both effects should appear.

options.text: On both nights, the traveler chooses the same way, since how good each restaurant has seemed so far is the same on both nights.
options.why: What the traveler knows may be the same, but the number of meals still ahead is not. With more choices ahead, people chose the less-sampled option more often and chose more noisily.

items.stem: A bear is eating berries from one bush on a hillside of scattered bushes. The longer it stays, the more slowly it finds berries, and walking to another bush takes time. According to the rule from the study of foraging, when is the best time to leave this bush?

options.text: When its rate of finding berries at this bush has fallen to the average rate for the hillside as a whole, counting the walking time.
options.why: Correct. The rule compares the rate in the current patch with the average rate for the whole habitat. The time taken to travel between patches is counted in that average.

options.text: When the bush has no berries left at all, since any berries still on it are food the bear would give up by walking away.
options.why: Staying until a patch is empty means a long stretch of finding food very slowly. On the rule, the best time to leave comes earlier, once the patch’s rate has fallen to the habitat’s average rate, counting travel.

options.text: When its rate of finding berries at this bush has fallen below the rate at the single best bush it remembers on the hillside.
options.why: The rule compares the current patch with the average for the habitat, not with the best patch. The average includes poorer bushes and the time taken walking between them.

options.text: When its rate of finding berries at this bush has fallen to the average rate for the hillside, but leaving the walking time out of it.
options.why: The comparison with the habitat’s average is right, but travel time is part of that average. Leaving it out would make the average too high, and the bear would leave too soon.

items.stem: Two groups of the same bird feed on similar patches of seeds. In one area, the patches are close together. In the other, they are far apart, so flying between them takes much longer. According to the patch-leaving rule, which birds should stay longer in each patch?

options.text: The birds whose patches are far apart, since longer travel lowers their habitat’s average rate, and a patch’s falling rate reaches it later.
options.why: Correct. Travel time is part of the habitat’s average rate. Longer flights between patches lower that average, so a patch running down reaches it later, and the best time to leave comes later.

options.text: The birds whose patches are close together, since nearby patches leave them more time to search each one, so they can stay longer before moving on.
options.why: Close patches mean short travel, which raises the habitat’s average rate. A patch’s falling rate reaches that higher average sooner, so these birds should leave sooner, not later.

options.text: Neither group, since the rule compares a patch’s rate with the habitat’s average, and travel between patches plays no part in it.
options.why: The comparison with the habitat’s average is right, but the average counts the time it takes to travel between patches. Longer travel lowers the average, so the far-apart birds should stay longer.

options.text: The birds whose patches are far apart, since birds in a poorer area have learned to expect less, and so take longer to notice a patch running down.
options.why: The group is right, but the reason is not. The rule concerns when leaving is best, not how an animal arrives at it. The far-apart birds should stay longer because longer travel lowers the habitat’s average rate.

items.stem: In a test of the patch-leaving rule, chickadees searched blocks of wood for mealworms. They left sooner where food was plentiful, as the rule predicts. Whatever the patch, they waited about the same time after their last find before leaving. What can be concluded about how the birds decide when to leave?

options.text: That their timing fits the rule, but not that they compute an average rate, since the rule concerns the best time to go, not how it is reached.
options.why: Correct. The rule concerns when leaving is best, not how an animal arrives at it. Waiting a similar time after the last find is a simple behavior, and nothing in it shows the birds computing an average.

options.text: That they compute the habitat’s average rate, counting travel time, and compare each patch’s rate with that average, just as the rule is stated.
options.why: The birds left about when the rule predicts, but leaving at about the right time is not evidence that they compute what the rule states. The rule concerns when leaving is best, not how an animal arrives at it.

options.text: That they do not follow the rule, since birds that wait the same time after a find in every patch cannot leave sooner where food is plentiful.
options.why: The chickadees did leave sooner where food was plentiful, as the rule predicts. A similar wait after the last find is how they behaved, which is compatible with leaving at about the best time.

options.text: That they leave each patch at random, with a setting for how often, since their waiting time did not depend on the patch.
options.why: Leaving at a set rate would be something like random exploration, and it would not make the birds leave sooner where food was plentiful. They did leave sooner, about as the rule predicts.

items.stem: A foraging animal moves from a poor stretch of woods into a richer one, where every patch has more food. According to the reasoning given in the lecture about the patch-leaving rule, why should the animal now leave each patch sooner?

options.text: The richer woods raise the average rate for the habitat, so a patch’s falling rate reaches that average sooner.
options.why: Correct. On the rule, the best time to leave is when a patch’s rate has fallen to the habitat’s average rate. A richer habitat raises that average, so the falling rate reaches it sooner, and the best time to leave comes sooner.

options.text: The richer woods lower the average rate for the habitat, so a patch’s falling rate reaches that lower average sooner.
options.why: Richer patches raise the habitat’s average rate, not lower it. A lower average would take longer to reach, which would mean leaving later.

options.text: The richer woods leave the animal less hungry, so any patch it is in becomes less worth staying in.
options.why: How hungry the animal is plays no part in the patch-leaving rule. On the rule, leaving sooner follows because a richer habitat raises the average rate that a patch’s falling rate is compared with.

options.text: The richer woods draw more animals to each patch, so every patch runs down faster than before.
options.why: Nothing in the rule concerns other animals. Leaving sooner follows because a richer habitat raises the average rate that a patch’s falling rate is compared with.

items.stem: An observer films a rat during its first hour on a bare, unfamiliar platform with nothing on it to hide in. The rat makes many trips from one spot and back. Some legs of these trips are slow and broken by many stops, and others are fast with few stops. Based on what rats do on such a platform, which reading of the film is most likely?

options.text: The slow legs are trips out from a home base, which is likely at an edge or corner, where the rat stays longest.
options.why: Correct. Rats settle on a home base within minutes, even with nothing there to hide in. The spot is usually at an edge or corner, where they stay longest, groom most, and return most often. Their trips out are slower and have more stops than their trips back.

options.text: The slow legs are trips back to a home base, which is likely at the center, where the rat can see every edge.
options.why: Both parts are reversed. Trips out from a home base are the slower ones, with more stops, and the home base is usually at an edge or corner rather than at the center.

options.text: The slow legs are trips out from a home base, which is likely at the center, where the rat can see every edge.
options.why: The slow legs are indeed trips out. But the home base is usually at an edge or corner, where the rat stays longest, grooms most, and returns most often, rather than at the center.

options.text: The slow legs are trips back to a home base, which is likely at an edge or corner, where the rat stays longest.
options.why: The home base is indeed usually at an edge or corner. But trips out are the slower ones, broken by more stops, and trips back are faster.

items.stem: Rats explore an unfamiliar place in trips out from a home base and back. One proposal for why they explore this way rests on keeping a running sum of position. What is that proposal?

options.text: The sum drifts, each return to a known place lets it start again, and landmarks encountered on the way can be tied to positions measured from home.
options.why: Correct. A running sum collects every small error, so it drifts. Returning home lets the sum start again from a known place, and landmarks on each trip can be tied to positions measured from home. The link to the running sum is a proposal, not an established finding.

options.text: The sum does not drift at all, so the returns home are for rest, and the landmarks along the way play no part in keeping track of position.
options.why: A running sum does not stay accurate, since every small error in heading or distance stays in it. On the proposal, returning home lets the drifting sum start again, and landmarks are tied to positions measured from home.

options.text: The sum is kept on trips back but not on trips out, so trips out are slower because the rat must find its way by the landmarks it passes.
options.why: A running sum is kept from the start of a trip, which is what lets an animal head home in a straight line. On the proposal, returning home lets the drifting sum start again from a known place.

options.text: The sum drifts, so each return home lets the rat swap it for a route, a fixed sequence of moves that stays accurate however far from home the rat goes.
options.why: The sum does drift, but on the proposal, returning home lets it start again, not be replaced. A route works only along its own path, while the proposal ties landmarks to positions measured from home.

items.stem: A hiker explores an unfamiliar forest in a series of loops out from a campsite and back, rather than in one long walk. On the proposal about exploring from a home base, what does returning to camp between loops do for the hiker’s knowledge of the forest?

options.text: Each return lets the hiker’s drifting estimate of position start again from a known place, so landmarks on the next loop can be placed relative to camp.
options.why: Correct. On the proposal, a running estimate of position drifts, and returning to a known place lets it start again. Landmarks encountered on each loop can then be tied to positions measured from home.

options.text: Each return lets the hiker add one more stretch to a single route, so the forest becomes known as one long, fixed sequence of moves from camp.
options.why: A route works only along its own path, and loops out and back do not join into one route. On the proposal, each return lets a drifting estimate of position start again from a known place.

options.text: Each return lets the hiker rest, since a loop out and back covers the same ground twice and so adds nothing new to the hiker’s knowledge of the forest.
options.why: On the proposal, the loops are how knowledge of the forest is built. Each return resets a drifting estimate of position, so landmarks on the next loop can be placed relative to home.

options.text: Each return lets the hiker view the forest from one fixed spot, so the whole forest can be stored as a single snapshot that is matched near camp.
options.why: A snapshot can be matched only near the place it was taken, so it would not place landmarks far out in the forest. On the proposal, each return resets a drifting estimate of position.

items.stem: What is curiosity?

options.text: A drive to gain information for its own sake, even when no reward depends on the information gained.
options.why: Correct. Curiosity names a drive behind seeking information that no reward depends on. There are two proposed answers to what it rewards: information itself, or progress in predicting.

options.text: A bonus for options that are less known, so that uncertainty itself makes one option more attractive than another.
options.why: That is the bonus added in directed exploration, a procedure for choosing among options. Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake.

options.text: Learning that does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it.
options.why: That is latent learning, which has long been counted among the signs of curiosity but is not curiosity itself. Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake.

options.text: Extra value given to an option simply for being new, which fades as the option is seen by the animal.
options.why: That is a novelty bonus, a value attached to an option. Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake, even when no reward depends on it.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? A drive to gain information for its own sake, even when no reward depends on it.

options.text: curiosity
options.why: Correct. Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake, and two proposals differ over what it rewards: information itself, or progress in predicting.

options.text: novelty bonus
options.why: A novelty bonus is extra value for being new, attached to one option and fading as the option is seen. A drive to gain information for its own sake is curiosity.

options.text: latent learning
options.why: Latent learning is learning that appears only once there is a reason to use it. It has been counted among the signs of curiosity, but the drive itself is curiosity.

options.text: directed exploration
options.why: Directed exploration adds a bonus to options that are less known, a procedure for choosing among options. A drive to gain information for its own sake is curiosity.

items.stem: A student sees three trivia questions: one whose answer the student is sure of, one the student has no idea about, and one the student half remembers. On the account that information is a reward in itself, which question should make the student most curious?

options.text: The half-remembered question, since curiosity is highest when one knows a little, but not enough.
options.why: Correct. On this account, curiosity plotted against confidence rises and then falls, in an inverted U. It peaks in the middle, where one knows a little but not enough.

options.text: The question the student has no idea about, since curiosity rises steadily as confidence falls and peaks with no knowledge at all.
options.why: On this account, curiosity is low with no knowledge at all, as well as with full knowledge. It peaks in the middle, where one knows a little but not enough.

options.text: The question the student is sure of, since curiosity rises steadily with confidence and peaks when the answer is already known.
options.why: When the answer is already known, there is little information left to gain, so curiosity is low. On this account it peaks where one knows a little but not enough.

options.text: All three equally, since on this account information is a reward in itself, whatever the student already knows.
options.why: Information is the reward on this account, but curiosity still depends on confidence. It rises and then falls, peaking where one knows a little but not enough.

items.stem: There are two proposed answers to what curiosity rewards. How do the two accounts differ?

options.text: On one, gaining information is itself the reward; on the other, the reward is getting better at predicting.
options.why: Correct. On one account, information is a reward in itself, and curiosity peaks where one knows a little but not enough. On the other, progress in predicting is the reward, so an agent drops what it cannot learn.

options.text: On one, gaining information is itself the reward; on the other, the reward is the food or water that the information leads to.
options.why: Curiosity is a drive to gain information for its own sake, so neither account makes food or water the reward. On the account that does not make information itself the reward, the reward is getting better at predicting.

options.text: On one, the reward is anything new; on the other, the reward is anything less known, whether sampled or not.
options.why: Those describe a novelty bonus and a bonus for uncertainty, which are procedures for exploring. The two accounts of curiosity make information itself the reward, or progress in predicting.

options.text: On one, the reward is errors in predicting; on the other, the reward is being right every time.
options.why: Rewarding errors in predicting is the pitfall that rewarding progress avoids, and being right every time leaves nothing to learn. The two accounts make information the reward, or progress in predicting.

items.stem: An agent rewards itself for getting better at predicting. It can work on a puzzle it has fully mastered, a spinner that lands at random, or a game it is still learning. On this account, which will the agent work on?

options.text: On the game, since there it can keep improving, while the mastered puzzle and the random spinner offer no progress.
options.why: Correct. An agent rewarded for progress drops what it already predicts well and drops what it cannot learn. It works on whatever it is learning now, so it produces its own curriculum.

options.text: On the spinner, since its errors in predicting the random spinner stay largest, while the mastered puzzle and the game offer fewer errors.
options.why: Large errors are rewarding only to an agent rewarded for errors themselves. Nothing about a random spinner can be learned, so it offers no progress, and an agent rewarded for progress drops it.

options.text: On the puzzle, since being right is what the agent rewards itself for, while the spinner and the game still produce mistakes.
options.why: The agent rewards getting better, not being right. It already predicts the mastered puzzle well, so there is no progress left there, and the agent drops it.

options.text: On the puzzle, the spinner and the game in turn, at a set rate, since each deserves sampling some of the time.
options.why: Sampling at a set rate is closer to random exploration. An agent rewarded for progress drops what it predicts well and what it cannot learn, and works on what it is learning now.

items.stem: A program explores a simulated room and is rewarded simply for errors in predicting the results of its own moves. In one corner, a set of lights flickers at random. What is likely to happen, and how would a reward for progress differ?

options.text: The program keeps returning to the lights, slowing its learning badly; a reward for progress would drop them, since nothing about them can be learned.
options.why: Correct. Random lights can never be predicted, so errors there stay high and keep rewarding a program that is rewarded for errors. Returning to the lights slows learning badly, though not for good. There is no progress to be had at the lights, so a reward for progress drops them.

options.text: The program soon drops the lights, since errors that never shrink stop being rewarding; a reward for progress would keep it there longer.
options.why: That reverses the two. Errors that never shrink keep rewarding a program rewarded for errors, so it keeps returning. A reward for progress is what drops what cannot be learned.

options.text: The program keeps returning to the lights and never learns anything else; a reward for progress would keep it there too, since it also follows errors.
options.why: The program kept returning, but the pitfall slowed its learning badly without stopping it for good. And a reward for progress follows improvement, not errors, so it would drop the lights.

options.text: The program keeps returning to the lights until it learns to predict them; a reward for progress would bring it there sooner.
options.why: Lights that flicker at random can never be learned, which is why errors there never shrink. There is no improvement to be had at the lights, so a reward for progress would drop them.

items.stem: A seven-year-old and an adult each play a two-option game, sometimes with one choice left and sometimes with six. Based on how exploring changes with age, what difference between the two players is most likely?

options.text: The child explores more overall, but adjusts how much to explore to the number of choices left less than the adult does.
options.why: Correct. Children explore more than adults, and partly in a directed way. But tuning how much to explore to how much time remains matures late, at about 11 or 12.

options.text: The child explores less overall, since tuning exploring to the time remaining matures early and makes children cautious.
options.why: Children explore more than adults, not less. And tuning how much to explore to how much time remains matures late, at about 11 or 12, not early.

options.text: The child explores more overall, but only at random, since children do not yet explore in a directed way.
options.why: Children do explore more, but partly in a directed way, not only at random. What matures late is tuning how much to explore to how much time remains.

options.text: The child explores more overall, and adjusts how much to explore to the number of choices left more closely than the adult does.
options.why: Children do explore more, but tuning exploring to the time remaining matures late, at about 11 or 12. A seven-year-old is likely to adjust less than an adult.

items.stem: On one proposal, a long, protected childhood is a period of broad search before narrowing. What is the standing of the further claim that a young mammal, fed and protected while it explores, has such a period too?

options.text: It is an extension that the reading itself offers, not a finding, of a proposal about long childhoods whose evidence is mixed.
options.why: Correct. The proposal about childhood as broad search has mixed evidence. Applying it to a young mammal is an extension offered in the reading, not a finding.

options.text: It is a finding from studies that tracked young mammals as they explored, showing a broad search that narrows as the animals grow older.
options.why: No such studies are reported. The claim about young mammals is an extension offered in the reading, of a proposal whose evidence is mixed.

options.text: It is a result shown in simulated robots, while whether young mammals actually explore this way is still open.
options.why: Simulated robots are where learning by rewarding progress has been shown, which is a different idea. The claim about young mammals is an extension offered in the reading, of a proposal with mixed evidence.

options.text: It is a claim that has been ruled out, since in many species juveniles are warier of new things than adults are.
options.why: In many species, juveniles are less wary of new things than adults, not more. And the proposal has mixed evidence rather than having been ruled out.

items.stem: What is simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)?

options.text: Building a map of the surroundings while keeping track of one’s own position on it, when each depends on the other.
options.why: Correct. A robot needs a map to work out its position, and it needs its position to add what it detects to the map. SLAM is doing both at once.

options.text: Keeping a running estimate of the straight-line distance and direction back to the start, from heading and distance traveled.
options.why: That is path integration, which gives a home vector. A robot doing SLAM keeps a running estimate of its position from its wheels, but SLAM is building a map while keeping track of position on it.

options.text: Pulling a whole drifted path estimate back into line, once a place that was visited before has been recognized.
options.why: That is loop closure, one step a robot doing SLAM can take. SLAM itself is building a map while keeping track of one’s own position on it.

options.text: Matching the current view to a stored view of the surroundings from a goal, moving until the two views agree.
options.why: That is matching a snapshot, which works only near the goal. SLAM is building a map of the surroundings while keeping track of one’s own position on it.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? Building a map of the surroundings while keeping track of one’s own position on it, when each depends on the other.

options.text: simultaneous localization and mapping
options.why: Correct. Each half depends on the other: a map is needed to find the position, and the position is needed to add to the map.

options.text: path integration
options.why: Path integration keeps a running estimate of the way back to the start, much as a robot’s wheels give a running estimate of position. Building a map while tracking one’s position on it is SLAM.

options.text: loop closure
options.why: Loop closure pulls a drifted path back into line when a place is recognized, and it is one step within the larger job. Building a map while tracking one’s position on it is SLAM.

options.text: cognitive map
options.why: A cognitive map is knowledge that relates places to one another, not the job of building a map while tracking one’s position. That job is SLAM.

items.stem: A small rover is sent into a cave that no one has mapped, with no signal from outside to give its position. It must record the cave’s layout as it goes and also keep track of where it is in that layout. Why is this harder than either job alone?

options.text: Each job depends on the other: placing what the rover detects needs its position, and finding its position needs the map.
options.why: Correct. The rover faces the problem of simultaneous localization and mapping. Neither the map nor the position can be finished first, because each is needed to build the other.
