options.text: The rover’s estimate of position from its wheels never drifts, so the hard part is only recognizing places it has been before.
options.why: A wheel-based estimate does drift, which is why recognizing a place matters. The deeper difficulty is that the map and the position each depend on the other.

options.text: Recording the layout needs just a stored view from the cave’s entrance, so keeping track of position adds a job nothing else needs.
options.why: A stored view from one spot can be matched only near that spot, so it cannot record a whole cave. And placing anything on a map requires knowing the rover’s position.

options.text: Keeping track of position needs just a home vector back to the entrance, and a home vector points to each place in the cave.
options.why: A home vector points to one place, the start, and gives no information about the way to anywhere else. The difficulty is that map and position each depend on the other.

items.stem: In a robot that builds a map as it moves, what is loop closure?

options.text: When the robot recognizes a place it has been before, it pulls the whole loop of its estimated path back into line.
options.why: Correct. The robot’s estimate of its position from its wheels drifts as it travels. Recognizing a place it has visited lets it correct the whole loop of its path at once.

options.text: When the robot’s wheel estimate drifts, it retraces its path in reverse until it reaches the place where it started.
options.why: Retracing a path does not correct an estimate that has drifted. Loop closure uses a recognized place to pull the whole estimated path back into line.

options.text: When the robot’s path crosses itself, it discards the map built so far and begins a new one from that place.
options.why: Loop closure keeps the map and corrects it. Recognizing a place pulls the whole estimated path back into line, rather than starting over.

options.text: When the robot finishes a loop, it adds the length of each stretch to a running sum of position that never needs correcting.
options.why: A running sum from wheels does need correcting, because it drifts. Loop closure is that correction, made when the robot recognizes a place it has been before.

items.stem: A robot pulls its drifted path estimate back into line when it recognizes a place it has been before. Which thing an animal does is the direct parallel?

options.text: Correcting a drifting running sum of position when a stable landmark comes into view, as a fallen log passed each night could do.
options.why: Correct. In both cases, an estimate built from the body’s or the wheels’ own movement drifts, and a recognized, stable place corrects it. A fallen log could reset the early mammal’s sense of where it was.

options.text: Matching the current view to a stored view from the goal, moving on while the mismatch shrinks, as a digger wasp does near its nest.
options.why: Snapshot matching guides an animal to a goal from nearby. It does not correct a drifting estimate of position built from the animal’s own movement, which is what loop closure does.

options.text: Following a fixed sequence of landmarks along a familiar trail, as wild rats keep to their trails even under snow.
options.why: Following a route needs only a sensible direction at each point along it. Loop closure corrects a drifting estimate of position when a known place is recognized.

options.text: Steering toward a tall tree beside the goal, approaching it directly as a beacon until the goal can be sensed.
options.why: Steering toward a beacon needs no estimate of position at all. Loop closure corrects a drifting estimate when a known place is recognized, as a landmark can correct a running sum.

items.stem: A program learned a video game of many rooms, in which random actions almost never find a reward. It was given an extra reward measured by how unlike the screens it had already seen the current screen was, and that reward shrank as similar screens recurred. What happened?

options.text: It scored much higher than it did without the extra reward, and higher than an average human player.
options.why: Correct. Its average score rose from 2,497 without the extra reward to 8,152 with it, against 4,753 for an average human player. Machines need help to explore too.

options.text: It scored about the same as without the extra reward, since screens unlike the earlier ones earned no points in the game.
options.why: The unlike screens earned no game points themselves, yet the program’s average score rose from 2,497 without the extra reward to 8,152 with it.

options.text: It kept returning to a screen that changed at random, and its score fell below what it reached without the extra reward.
options.why: Returning to a random screen was the pitfall of a different program, one rewarded for errors in predicting. With the reward for unlike screens, this program scored much higher than without it.

options.text: It scored higher, and the extra reward helped most with choices whose reward came much later, such as saving keys for the last doors.
options.why: It did score higher, but the extra reward helped only with what lay just ahead. Choices whose reward came much later, such as saving keys for the last doors, were where it did not help.

items.stem: A program playing a game is given an extra reward for screens unlike those it has already seen, a reward that shrinks as similar screens recur. In this game, a rope picked up early is needed only at the last cliff. Which part of the game is the extra reward least likely to help with?

options.text: Deciding early to keep the rope, since the extra reward helped with what lay just ahead, not with choices whose reward came much later.
options.why: Correct. The extra reward helped only with what lay just ahead. A choice that is rewarded only much later, like saving keys for the last doors, was where it did not help.

options.text: Reaching rooms it has never entered, since the extra reward shrank as similar screens recurred and so stopped working after the first few rooms.
options.why: The reward did shrink as similar screens recurred. But in Montezuma’s Revenge, the program given it still often reached 22 of the 24 rooms of the first level, so it kept helping with rooms not yet entered.

options.text: Finding the first reward in the first room early on, since an extra reward for unlike screens does nothing until the game’s own score has started to rise.
options.why: In Montezuma’s Revenge, even with no game score at all, the extra reward alone took the program through more than half the rooms. It helped with what lay just ahead.

options.text: Moving on through the next few rooms, since the extra reward made the program avoid any screen that it had not already seen before.
options.why: The extra reward did the opposite, rewarding screens unlike those already seen. It helped with what lay just ahead, and not with choices rewarded much later.

items.stem: In one study, a network trained to keep track of its position from its own movement developed units that fired in repeating triangular patterns. Later researchers trained more than 11,000 networks the same way. In light of the later networks, what can be concluded from the first network’s triangular units?

options.text: Triangular units appeared only when training targets were coded with grid cells in mind, so self-motion training is not shown to produce them.
options.why: Correct. Almost all the networks came to keep track of position, but the triangular units depended on how the training targets were coded. So such a code can serve an artificial agent, without showing that self-motion training produces it.

options.text: Almost none of the networks came to keep track of position, so the first network’s success was a lucky exception that the others did not repeat.
options.why: Almost all of the networks did come to keep track of position. What depended on the coding of the training targets was whether triangular units appeared.

options.text: Triangular units appeared in almost every network, however the targets were coded, so the code turns out to follow from training on self-motion.
options.why: Triangular units appeared only when the training targets were coded in one particular way, chosen with grid cells in mind. So the code does not follow from self-motion training alone.

options.text: Triangular units appeared in every network that kept track of position, so the code turns out to be needed for keeping track of position at all.
options.why: Almost all the networks kept track of position, but triangular units appeared only with one coding of the training targets. So the code is not needed for keeping track.

items.stem: Someone argues: “Networks trained to keep track of their own movement develop triangular units, and an agent using one takes shortcuts. So brains must have grid cells because keeping track of movement produces them”. Which reply fits the network studies?

options.text: In the studies, such a code served an artificial agent, but it was not shown that self-motion training produces it, or that brains have it for that reason.
options.why: Correct. An agent using such a network did take newly opened shortcuts, so the code can serve an agent. But the triangular units appeared only with targets coded with grid cells in mind, so the argument’s conclusion does not follow.

options.text: In the studies, the networks failed to keep track of their own position at all, so nothing about the networks bears on why brains have grid cells.
options.why: Almost all the networks did come to keep track of position. The trouble is that triangular units appeared only with one coding of the targets, so the argument’s conclusion does not follow.

options.text: In a follow-up of more than 11,000 networks trained the same way, it turned out that self-motion training produces the code whatever the training targets were.
options.why: In the follow-up, triangular units appeared only when training targets were coded with grid cells in mind. So self-motion training was not shown to produce the code.

options.text: In the studies, an agent using such a network failed to take shortcuts through newly opened passages, so the code is of little use to an artificial agent.
options.why: An agent using the network did take shortcuts through newly opened passages, so the code can serve an agent. What was not shown is that self-motion training produces the code, or that brains have it for that reason.

items.stem: An agent was given nothing but its own change of position and heading, with no vision and no touch, and was rewarded only for progress toward goals. What happened in houses it had never been in?

options.text: It reached the goal on 95.1% of trials, and a decoder trained to find a layout of the free space could read one from its memory.
options.why: Correct. The agent reached goals along paths that followed the walls, and a layout including walls it had not passed was decoded from its memory. Three cautions go with the result. The layout was read out by a decoder trained to find it. A second agent given that memory took a more direct route, but mostly by cutting out detours rather than crossing new ground. And the change of position and heading was supplied, not computed.

options.text: It reached the goal on 95.1% of trials by direct routes across open rooms, ignoring the walls, since it had built a complete map of each house.
options.why: The agent’s paths followed the walls rather than cutting across rooms. A layout was decoded from its memory, but only by a decoder trained to find it.

options.text: It rarely reached the goal, since with no vision and no touch it had no way to register where the walls of a house were.
options.why: The agent reached the goal on 95.1% of trials. A layout including walls it had not passed was decoded from its memory, by a decoder trained to find it.

options.text: It reached the goal on 95.1% of trials, computing its own change of position and heading from its movements as it went.
options.why: The success rate is right, but the agent was given its change of position and heading rather than computing it from its movements. That is one of the cautions on the result.

items.stem: In one line of machine work, triangular units appeared in networks trained to keep track of position. In another, an agent given its change of position and heading reached goals in new houses, and a layout was decoded from its memory. What sets the house agent’s result apart from the triangular units?

options.text: No spatial training target was used, though the layout still had to be read out by a decoder trained to find it.
options.why: Correct. The triangular units depended on training targets coded with grid cells in mind. The house agent had no spatial target, so its layout was not built into what it was trained to produce. Three cautions still go with the result. The layout was read out by a decoder trained to find it. The second agent’s more direct route mostly cut out detours. And the change of position and heading was supplied.

options.text: The agent computed its own change of position and heading from its movements, while the networks had theirs supplied.
options.why: The house agent was given its change of position and heading rather than computing it, which is one caution on that result. What sets it apart is that no spatial training target was used.

options.text: The agent’s second trip crossed ground it had never covered, while the networks’ agent only cut out detours on familiar ground.
options.why: That reverses them. The agent using the triangular units took newly opened shortcuts, while the house agent’s more direct route was a second agent’s, and mostly cut out the first agent’s detours.

options.text: The agent’s layout was read directly from its memory with no trained decoder, while the networks’ units had to be decoded first.
options.why: The house agent’s layout was read out by a decoder trained to find it, which is one caution on the result. What sets it apart is that no spatial training target was used.

items.stem: A news story about the agent that reached goals in houses it had never been in runs under the headline “Brains navigate just as this AI does”. What conclusion is supported by the machine studies instead?

options.text: That such a procedure can work in a machine, which is evidence of what the procedure can do, not of how brains explore or find the way.
options.why: Correct. No program in the machine studies shows how brains explore or find the way. Each shows what a procedure can do in a machine. The house agent’s result also comes with three cautions. A trained decoder read out the layout. A second agent’s more direct route mostly cut out detours. And the change of position and heading was supplied.

options.text: That brains find their way by the same procedure, since the agent succeeded using only the kinds of input that an animal also has.
options.why: The agent’s success is evidence of what the procedure can do in a machine, not of what brains do. And it was given its change of position and heading, rather than computing it from its movements.

options.text: That brains cannot be using such a procedure, since the agent needed its change of position and heading to be supplied.
options.why: Being supplied its change of position is a caution on the machine result, not evidence about brains. Each machine study is evidence of what a procedure can do in a machine, not of how brains find the way.

options.text: That the agent built a map just like a rat’s, since a layout including walls it had not passed was found in the machine’s memory.
options.why: The layout was read out by a decoder trained to find it, and a machine result is evidence about a procedure in a machine, not about brains.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe the two ways people’s choices in a two-option game changed when six choices were still ahead rather than one. Say which kind of exploring each change reflects, and how children differ from adults in this respect.
items.answer: With six choices still ahead, people chose the less-sampled option more often, even when it had looked worse. That shift reflects directed exploration, a bonus for options that are less known. Their choices were also noisier, which reflects random exploration, mostly taking the better-looking option and sometimes another. Exploring makes more sense with more choices ahead, because what is learned can still be used. Children explore more than adults, and partly in a directed way. But tuning how much to explore to how much time remains matures late, at about 11 or 12.
rubric: Says that with six choices ahead, people chose the less-sampled option more often.
Links that shift to directed exploration, a bonus for less-known options.
Says choices were noisier with six choices ahead, and links that to random exploration.
Says children explore more than adults, partly in a directed way.
Says tuning how much to explore to the time remaining matures late, at about 11 or 12.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how rewarding progress differs from rewarding errors in predicting, using the case of a screen whose channel changes at random. Then say what is known about whether brains learn by rewarding progress.
items.answer: A program rewarded simply for errors in predicting the results of its own moves is drawn to whatever it predicts badly. A screen whose channel changes at random can never be predicted, so the errors there stay high, and the program keeps returning to the screen. Returning to the screen slowed its learning badly, though it did not stop the learning for good. An agent rewarded for progress, for getting better at predicting, drops what it already predicts well and also drops what it cannot learn. Nothing about the random screen can be learned, so there is no progress to be had there. The agent works on whatever it is learning now, producing its own curriculum. Learning by rewarding progress has been shown in simulated robots. Whether brains do it is open.
rubric: Says a program rewarded for prediction errors keeps returning to what it cannot learn to predict, such as the random screen.
Says returning to the screen slowed the program’s learning badly, without stopping the learning for good.
Says a reward for progress drops both what is already predicted well and what cannot be learned, so it would drop the random screen.
Says the agent rewarded for progress works on what it is learning now, producing its own curriculum.
Says learning by rewarding progress has been shown in simulated robots, and whether brains do it is open.

items.stem: An agent given only its change of position and heading reached goals in houses it had never been in. A classmate concludes that the agent built a map of each house, and that brains find their way the same way. In a short paragraph, say what was found, and give the cautions that limit each part of the classmate’s claim.
items.answer: The agent reached the goal on 95.1% of trials in houses it had never been in, along paths that followed the walls. A layout of the free space, including walls it had not passed, could be decoded from its memory, and no spatial training target was used. But three cautions go with that result. The layout was read out by a decoder trained to find it. A second agent, given the first agent’s memory, took a more direct route, but mostly by cutting out the first agent’s detours rather than by crossing new ground. And the agent was given its change of position and heading rather than computing it from its movements. Even setting the cautions aside, a machine result is evidence of what a procedure can do in a machine, not of how brains explore or find the way.
rubric: Reports the finding: goals reached on most trials (95.1%) in unfamiliar houses, with a layout decodable from the agent’s memory.
Says the layout was read out by a decoder trained to find it.
Says the more direct route was a second agent’s, and mostly cut out detours rather than crossing new ground.
Says the change of position and heading was supplied rather than computed.
Says machine results are evidence of what a procedure can do in a machine, not of how brains find their way.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe how rats explore a bare, unfamiliar platform. Then explain the proposal that links this way of exploring to keeping a running sum of position.
items.answer: Put on a bare platform, rats settle within minutes on a home base, usually at an edge or corner. The home base is where they stay longest, groom most, and return most often. Their trips out from it are slower and have more stops than their trips back. One proposal ties this pattern to a running sum of position. A running sum drifts, because every small error in heading or distance stays in it. Each return to a known place lets the sum start again, so landmarks encountered along the way can be tied to positions measured from home. The link to the running sum is a proposal rather than an established finding.
rubric: Says rats settle on a home base within minutes, usually at an edge or corner, where they stay longest and return most often.
Says trips out from the home base are slower, with more stops, than trips back.
Says a running sum of position drifts as errors build up.
Says each return to a known place lets the sum start again, so landmarks along the way can be tied to positions measured from home.
Presents the link to the running sum as a proposal, not an established finding.

pools.title: A Compass in the Brain, and Place Cells
pools.covers: reading §9.3.1, §9.3.2 · lecture 9.3 slides a_compass_in_the_brain, rings_you_can_see, place_cells

items.stem: What is a head-direction cell?

options.text: A cell that fires when the animal’s head points in one direction, whatever the animal is doing and wherever it is.
options.why: Correct. Each head-direction cell prefers one direction, and different cells prefer different directions, so together they cover the whole circle.

options.text: A cell that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way the animal’s head is facing.
options.why: That is a place cell, which fires for a location rather than a heading. A head-direction cell fires for one direction of the head, wherever the animal is.

options.text: A cell that fires at many places across the animal’s surroundings, laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles.
options.why: That is a grid cell, in the medial entorhinal cortex. A head-direction cell fires for one direction of the head, wherever the animal is and whatever it is doing.

options.text: A cell that fires when the animal is close beside a wall or another edge of its surroundings, as it moves along that edge.
options.why: That is a border cell, which marks an edge of the space. A head-direction cell fires for one direction of the head, wherever the animal is.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A cell that fires when the animal’s head points one particular way, whatever the animal is doing and wherever it is”.

options.text: head-direction cell
options.why: Correct. Head-direction cells with different preferred directions together cover the whole circle. They were found in rats in the 1980s.

options.text: place cell
options.why: A place cell fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it is facing. That is a location, not a direction of the head.

options.text: grid cell
options.why: A grid cell fires at many places, laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles across the floor. It marks positions, not a direction of the head.

options.text: ring attractor
options.why: A ring attractor is a circle of units whose single bump of activity marks a heading. It describes how a heading can be kept, not a single cell that fires for one direction.

items.stem: A cell is recorded in a rat exploring a square box. The cell fires strongly whenever the rat’s head points north, whether the rat is walking along the south wall, grooming in the middle, or sniffing in a corner. When the head points any other way, the cell is nearly silent. What kind of cell fits the description?

options.text: A head-direction cell, since it fires for one heading whatever the rat is doing and wherever it is.
options.why: Correct. The cell’s firing depends on which way the head points and on nothing else about where the rat is or what it is doing. That is the definition of a head-direction cell.

options.text: A place cell whose field covers the whole box, since it fires in every part of the box that the rat visits.
options.why: A place cell fires in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces. The recorded cell is the reverse: it fires anywhere in the box, but only for one heading.

options.text: A grid cell, since it fires at many separate places in the box rather than at only one place in it.
options.why: A grid cell fires at many places laid out on a triangular lattice, whatever the heading. The recorded cell fires anywhere, but only when the head points north.

options.text: A border cell, since the rat’s head points toward one of the walls of the box each time the cell fires.
options.why: A border cell fires when the animal is along a wall. The recorded cell fires in the middle of the box as well, and only when the rat’s head points north.

items.stem: Head-direction cells lie along a chain of structures running from the brainstem, through the thalamus, to the cortex beside the hippocampus. If structures low in the chain, near the brainstem, are damaged, what happens to the head-direction signal in the thalamus and the cortex?

options.text: The signal is abolished in both, because damage low in the chain abolishes the signal in every stage above it.
options.why: Correct. The structures higher in the chain depend on those below them for the head-direction signal, so damage low in the chain removes it above.

options.text: The signal continues in both, because each structure along the chain keeps its own heading signal without the others.
options.why: The structures along the chain do not keep independent headings. Damage low in the chain abolishes the signal in the structures above it.

options.text: The signal continues in both but drifts within minutes, as it does in darkness, until a familiar landmark pulls it back.
options.why: Drift corrected by landmarks is what happens in darkness, when the signal is still kept going. Damage low in the chain does more than that: it abolishes the signal above.

options.text: The signal is lost in the thalamus, while the cortex beside the hippocampus keeps it going from landmarks in view.
options.why: Landmarks correct a heading signal but do not supply one on their own. Damage low in the chain abolishes the signal in every structure above it, the cortex included.

items.stem: What keeps a rat’s head-direction signal going from moment to moment?

options.text: Signals of turning from the semicircular canals, which sense rotation, so a heading is added up from turns.
options.why: Correct. The semicircular canals of the vestibular system sense how the head rotates, not where it points. So the heading has to be built up from the turns.

options.text: Signals from the semicircular canals that report directly which way the head points, much like a compass needle does.
options.why: The semicircular canals sense rotation of the head, not where the head points. A heading has to be added up from the turns they report.

options.text: A familiar landmark kept in view, which sets every cell’s preferred direction afresh at each moment.
options.why: A familiar landmark corrects the signal when it drifts, and the signal keeps going in darkness without one. What keeps it going is the signal of turning.

options.text: Counts of the animal’s own steps, which give the distance it has traveled along each heading as it goes.
options.why: Steps give distance, not direction. The head-direction signal is kept going by signals of turning from the semicircular canals.

items.stem: In rats whose vestibular organs had been destroyed, head-direction cells in the thalamus kept firing, but not for any one heading, and the direction signal never came back. A familiar card stayed in view on the wall the whole time. Why could the card not restore the direction signal?

options.text: Without any sense of the rats’ turns, there was no heading left for the card to correct.
options.why: Correct. A landmark pulls a drifting heading back into line, but a heading has to exist first. With the turn signal gone, there was nothing for the card to correct.

options.text: Destroying the vestibular organs also damaged the rats’ vision, so the card on the wall could no longer be seen.
options.why: The card stayed in view throughout. The trouble was not seeing the card but having no heading for it to correct, since the heading is built from turns.

options.text: The rats stopped moving about the room, so the cells received none of the turns a heading depends on.
options.why: The rats still moved about and found food. What was lost was the signal of turning from the vestibular organs, so there was no heading for the card to correct.

options.text: A card takes about 8 minutes to gain control of the cells, and the rats were recorded before it could.
options.why: A card does take about 8 minutes to gain control in a new room, but the direction signal never came back at all. With no turn signal, there was no heading for the card to correct.

items.stem: A rat’s head-direction cells are recorded in a room with a familiar card on one wall. While the rat is out of the room, the card is moved a quarter turn around the room, to the next wall. What happens to the cells’ preferred directions when the rat returns?

options.text: Every cell’s preferred direction turns with the card, all of them together, so the set still covers the circle.
options.why: Correct. A familiar landmark controls the heading signal. When the card is rotated, every cell’s preferred direction rotates with it, all together.

options.text: Each cell’s preferred direction turns by a different amount, so the cells no longer cover the whole circle.
options.why: The cells do not scatter. They behave as one heading signal, so when the card is rotated, every preferred direction rotates with it, together.

options.text: The preferred directions stay where they were, since the cells are kept going by turning rather than by landmarks.
options.why: Turning does keep the signal going, but a familiar landmark corrects it. When the card is rotated, every preferred direction rotates with it.

options.text: Only the cells that preferred the card’s direction turn with it, while the others keep their old directions.
options.why: The cells act together rather than one at a time. When a familiar card is rotated, every cell’s preferred direction rotates with it, all together.

items.stem: A rat watches as an experimenter moves a familiar card from one wall to another. Afterward, the card no longer controls the rat’s head-direction cells. According to the lecture, why does the card’s loss of control make sense?

options.text: A landmark is worth using to correct a heading only if it stays put, and the rat has seen that the card does not.
options.why: Correct. In the lecture, the finding is tied to a principle about correcting a running estimate: a landmark helps only if it stays where it is. A card the rat has seen move fails that test.

options.text: The cells always follow the signal of turning over a landmark, and the moved card now disagrees with the turns.
options.why: Head-direction cells do follow a familiar landmark: when a card is moved while the rat is away, every preferred direction rotates with it. The card lost control because the rat saw it move.

options.text: Only distant landmarks can correct a heading, and a card small enough to be carried around is too close to do it.
options.why: A card on the wall does control the cells when it has not been seen to move. It lost control here because the rat saw that it does not stay put.

options.text: The cells are corrected only by landmarks the rat has never encountered, and a card it has watched is now familiar.
options.why: It is familiar landmarks that pull a drifting heading back. The moved card lost control because the rat saw it move, and a landmark is useful only if it stays put.

items.stem: Rat head-direction cells are said to behave like a ring attractor. What about their behavior fits that description?

options.text: Turns update a single heading signal, and stable landmarks correct that signal when it drifts.
options.why: Correct. A ring attractor keeps one heading, slides it when the animal turns, and is pulled back by a recognized landmark. Rat head-direction cells behave that way.

options.text: Each cell fires in one part of the room, and together the cells cover the whole floor of the room.
options.why: That describes place cells, which mark locations. The ring-attractor behavior is one heading signal updated by turns and corrected by stable landmarks.

options.text: Several patterns of different sizes, each repeating across the floor, combine to pin down a single place.
options.why: That is the proposal of repeating codes for position, which grid cells may fit. The ring-attractor behavior is one heading signal updated by turns and corrected by landmarks.

options.text: The cells lie in a circle in the tissue, each one beside the cells that prefer neighboring directions.
options.why: In the rat, the cells are not laid out in a circle. The ring is a way of arranging them on paper, and what fits a ring attractor is how they behave.

items.stem: Both the rat and the fruit fly keep a heading signal that behaves like a ring attractor. How does the ring in the rat differ from the ring in the fly?

options.text: In the rat the ring is a way of arranging cells on paper by preferred direction; in the fly it can be seen in the tissue.
options.why: Correct. Rat head-direction cells are not laid out in a circle, though they behave as a ring would. In the fly, neurons tile a doughnut-shaped structure, and the bump can be seen moving around it.

options.text: In the rat the ring can be seen in the tissue; in the fly it is a way of arranging cells on paper by preferred direction.
options.why: That reverses the two. The fly’s ring is a doughnut-shaped structure in its brain, while rat head-direction cells are arranged in a ring only on paper.

options.text: In the rat the ring is updated by turns and corrected by landmarks; in the fly it follows turns but ignores landmarks.
options.why: The fly’s bump does follow a landmark: as a fly on a ball turns, the bump turns with a landmark it can see. The difference is whether the ring is visible in the tissue.

options.text: In the rat the ring keeps following turns in darkness; in the fly it stops moving as soon as the lights go out.
options.why: In darkness the fly’s bump keeps following its turns, drifting slowly. The difference between the two is whether the ring can be seen in the tissue.

items.stem: A fruit fly walking on a ball is in complete darkness. It stands still for twenty seconds and then turns sharply to its left. What does the bump of activity in its ring of neurons do?

options.text: It stays still while the fly stands still, then moves around the ring with the turn, drifting slowly over time.
options.why: Correct. In darkness, the bump follows the fly’s turns with slow drift, and when the fly stands still the bump stays still too, sometimes for more than 30 seconds.

options.text: It vanishes in the darkness, since with no visible landmark the ring has no heading for a bump to mark.
options.why: The bump does not need a landmark to exist. In darkness it keeps following the fly’s turns, drifting slowly, and stays still when the fly does.

options.text: It stays still while the fly stands still, and through the turn as well, since only a visible landmark moves it.
options.why: A visible landmark is not the only thing that moves the bump. In darkness it follows the fly’s turns, with slow drift.

options.text: It spreads around the whole ring while the fly stands still, then gathers into one bump again once the fly turns.
options.why: At any moment, the activity forms a single bump. While the fly stands still, the bump stays where it is rather than spreading out.

items.stem: A fruit fly walking on a ball faces a screen with a visible landmark. The landmark is suddenly moved to a new position on the screen, though the fly has not turned. According to the lecture, what does the bump of activity in the fly’s ring do?

options.text: It jumps to a new position on the ring, following the landmark’s jump with no turn by the fly at all.
options.why: Correct. The bump turns with a landmark the fly can see, and when the landmark jumps, the bump jumps with it. So the bump moves with a visible landmark as well as with the fly’s own turns.

options.text: It stays where it was, since the bump follows only the fly’s own turns and the fly has not turned at all.
options.why: The bump does follow the fly’s turns, but it also follows a landmark the fly can see. When the landmark jumps, the bump jumps too.

options.text: It slides slowly toward the landmark’s new position over several minutes, as a card takes control of a rat’s cells.
options.why: A card takes minutes to gain control of a rat’s cells in a new room, but that is a different finding. In the fly, the bump jumps when the landmark jumps.

options.text: It splits into two bumps on the ring, one for the landmark’s old position and one for its new position.
options.why: At any moment the activity in the fly’s ring forms a single bump. When the landmark jumps, that one bump jumps with it.

items.stem: Larval zebrafish were held by the head during recording, with the tail free to swim. A patch of activity in a ring of hindbrain neurons tracked each larva’s summed turns for minutes, and vision made no difference. Where does the heading come from?

options.text: From copies of the larva’s own swim commands, since the held head did not turn and vision did not matter.
options.why: Correct. With the head held, there was no rotation of the head to sense, and vision made no difference. What remains is efference copy, copies of the commands that move the tail.

options.text: From the vestibular organs, which sense the head turning each time the larva swims to the left or the right.
options.why: The vestibular organs sense rotation of the head, but the larvae were held by the head, so it did not turn. The heading came from copies of the swim commands.

options.text: From landmarks the larva picks out by vision, which pull a drifting patch back to the right place on the ring.
options.why: Vision made no difference to the patch, so landmarks seen by the larva were not keeping the heading. It came from copies of the larva’s swim commands.

options.text: From a heading set once at the start of recording and kept unchanged, since a held larva cannot turn at all.
options.why: The patch did not stay put: it slid as the larva swam left or right and tracked its summed turns. Those turns were known from copies of the swim commands.

items.stem: The fruit fly’s ring and the larval zebrafish’s ring each keep one bump of activity that follows the animal’s turns. In the recordings, how do the two rings differ?

options.text: The fly’s bump turns with a landmark the fly can see; in the held larva, vision made no difference to the patch.
options.why: Correct. The fly’s ring follows both its turns and a visible landmark. In the zebrafish recordings, vision made no difference, and the heading was kept from copies of the swim commands.

options.text: The fly’s bump ignores landmarks the fly can see; in the held larva, the patch follows visible landmarks rather than turns.
options.why: That reverses the role of vision. The fly’s bump turns with a visible landmark, while in the held larva vision made no difference to the patch.

options.text: The fly’s bump follows its turns only in the light; in the held larva, the patch follows its turns in darkness as well.
options.why: The fly’s bump also follows its turns in darkness, drifting slowly. Where the two differ is in the role of vision: it made no difference in the held larva.

options.text: The fly’s bump drifts slowly in darkness; in the held larva, the patch tracks the summed turns with no drift whatsoever.
options.why: Both drift. The larva’s patch tracked its summed turns for minutes, drifting slowly. Where the two differ is that vision made no difference in the held larva.

items.stem: One way to keep a single bump of activity on a ring is for each unit to excite its near neighbors while all units feed a shared inhibition. How does the wiring of the larval zebrafish’s heading ring compare?

options.text: It is a different wiring that does the same job: each neuron inhibits the opposite direction, so one patch is active.
options.why: Correct. In the zebrafish, each neuron’s output crosses the ring to inhibit neurons tuned to the opposite direction. That is a different wiring from neighbors exciting and sharing inhibition, and it does the same job.

options.text: It is the same wiring in a different animal: neighbors excite one another and all feed a shared inhibition, so one patch is active.
options.why: The zebrafish ring is wired differently. Each neuron inhibits the neurons tuned to the opposite direction, across the ring, and that also leaves only one patch active.

options.text: It is a different wiring that does a different job: each neuron inhibits the opposite direction, so two patches face each other.
options.why: Inhibiting the opposite direction does not produce two patches. Activity at one direction suppresses the directions across from it, so only one patch can be active at a time.

options.text: It is a different wiring that cannot keep one patch by itself, so the larva relies on vision to pick out the right patch.
options.why: The cross-ring inhibition does keep a single patch, and vision made no difference in the recordings. Activity at one direction suppresses the directions across from it.

items.stem: The fruit fly and the larval zebrafish keep their headings with a similar arrangement of neurons. According to the reading, how is that similarity best read?

options.text: As a likely case of convergent evolution, the same problem solved separately in insects and in vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. The researchers read the similarity as shared principles of circuit design, not shared ancestry. According to the reading, a heading signal arising separately in insects and vertebrates is a likely case of convergent evolution.

options.text: As a homology, a ring inherited by both animals from a common ancestor that already kept its heading this way.
options.why: The researchers read the similarity as shared principles of circuit design, not as shared ancestry. The heading signal likely arose separately in insects and in vertebrates.

options.text: As a mismatch of method, since the two rings do not behave alike and only drawings of them look similar.
options.why: The two rings do behave alike: each keeps one bump or patch that follows the animal’s turns and drifts slowly. The similarity is read as a likely case of convergent evolution.

options.text: As evidence that insects inherited their heading ring from the early vertebrates that came before them.
options.why: Insects are not descended from vertebrates, and the researchers read the similarity as shared design, not shared ancestry. It is taken as a likely case of convergent evolution.

items.stem: What is a place cell?

options.text: A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it faces.
options.why: Correct. Each place cell fires in one part of the surroundings, its place field, and together the place cells cover the whole space.

options.text: A cell that fires when the animal’s head points in one direction, wherever the animal is and whatever it is doing.
options.why: That is a head-direction cell, which fires for a heading rather than a location. A place cell fires in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces.

options.text: A cell in the medial entorhinal cortex that fires at many places, laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles.
options.why: That is a grid cell, which fires at many places on a triangular lattice. A place cell, in the hippocampus, fires in one part of the surroundings.

options.text: A cell in the entorhinal cortex that fires when the animal is along a wall or another edge of its surroundings.
options.why: That is a border cell, which marks an edge of the space. A place cell, in the hippocampus, fires in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it is facing”.

options.text: place cell
options.why: Correct. Place cells were found when the rat hippocampus was recorded from, and together they cover the whole space.

options.text: place field
options.why: A place field is the part of the surroundings in which a place cell fires. It is a region of space, not the cell itself.

options.text: grid cell
options.why: A grid cell, in the medial entorhinal cortex, fires at many places on a triangular lattice rather than in one part of the surroundings.

options.text: head-direction cell
options.why: A head-direction cell fires when the head points in one direction, wherever the animal is. A place cell fires in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces.

items.stem: What is a place field?

options.text: The part of the surroundings in which one particular place cell fires, whichever way the animal faces.
options.why: Correct. Each place cell has its own place field, and together the place cells cover the whole space.

options.text: A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it faces.
options.why: That is a place cell. Its place field is the part of the surroundings in which it fires, a region of space rather than the cell.

options.text: The whole space that an animal’s place cells cover when the fields of all of them are put together.
options.why: Together the place cells do cover the whole space, but a place field is the part of the surroundings in which one place cell fires.

options.text: The one direction of the head for which a head-direction cell fires, wherever the animal is in its surroundings.
options.why: That is a head-direction cell’s preferred direction. A place field is a part of the surroundings, the part in which one place cell fires.

items.stem: A rat’s place cell fires whenever the rat is near one corner of a familiar box. The experimenters then remove the landmarks around the box and change the lighting, and the cell still fires near the same corner. What can be concluded about place cells?
tags: place cells as a running sum

options.text: Their firing is not simply a response to what the animal senses, since the field outlasts the changes.
options.why: Correct. Place fields survive the removal of landmarks and changes in the lighting. Place cells do not simply respond to what the animal senses.

options.text: Their firing is set by the walls of the box alone, since the walls were the one thing in the scene left unchanged.
options.why: Walls matter most, but they are not the whole story. In a stretched box, fields stretch by only about half as much, a compromise between the walls and the distance run.

options.text: Their firing depends on which way the rat is facing, since the rat turns toward the corner each time it arrives.
options.why: A place cell fires in its field whichever way the animal is facing. Firing that depends on the heading belongs to head-direction cells.

options.text: Their firing is fixed from birth, so that nothing the rat senses or does can ever shift any of its place fields.
options.why: Place fields can change. They stretch when a box is stretched and change near a barrier put across a familiar maze. Because the field outlasts the loss of landmarks, place cells cannot be simply sensory.

items.stem: A rat runs along a familiar straight track from a start box, past landmarks beside the track. The start box is then moved partway along the track. Cells that fire early in each run now fire at their usual distances from the new start box. Cells that fire later in the run fire at their usual places relative to the landmarks. Which procedure does this pattern fit?
tags: place cells as a running sum

options.text: A running sum of the distance run from the start, which landmarks correct as the run goes on.
options.why: Correct. On a track, place cells at first fire by the distance run from the start, before landmarks correct them. That is the running sum corrected by landmarks.

options.text: A response to the landmarks beside the track alone, which is why the fields stay put when the start box moves.
options.why: Landmarks do correct the later fields, but place cells do not simply respond to what the animal senses. The early fields moved with the start box, at their usual distances from it, though the landmarks stayed put.

options.text: A fixed sequence of moves from the start box, which the landmarks along the track play no part in correcting.
options.why: The later fields line up with the landmarks, so landmarks do correct the estimate. The early ones follow the distance run, the running sum before correction.

options.text: A home vector pointing back to the start box, which gives the way to every other place along the track.
options.why: A home vector points back to one place, the start, and gives no information about the way to any other place. The pattern fits a running sum of distance, corrected by landmarks.

items.stem: Two changes are made to a familiar box in which a rat’s place cells have been recorded. In one, the box is stretched lengthwise. In the other, a single small object is added. How do the place fields respond to each change?

options.text: Stretching the box makes the fields stretch by about half as much; the small object barely moves them at all.
options.why: Correct. Walls matter most. In a stretched box, fields stretch by about half as much, a compromise between the walls and the distance run, while a single small object barely moves them.

options.text: Stretching the box makes the fields stretch exactly as much as the box; the small object barely moves them at all.
options.why: The small object does barely move the fields, but they stretch by only about half as much as the box. That is a compromise between the walls and the distance run.

options.text: Stretching the box barely moves the fields at all; the small object pulls every nearby field toward itself.
options.why: That reverses the two. Walls matter most, so stretching the box stretches the fields by about half as much, while a single small object barely moves them.

options.text: Stretching the box makes the fields stretch by about half as much; the small object makes every cell fire somewhere new.
options.why: The stretching half is right, but a single small object barely moves the fields. It is the walls that matter most.

items.stem: A rat is trained to run around a circular track in one direction only, always clockwise. How would its place fields be expected to change with the training?

options.text: They would stretch backward, extending against the direction in which the rat runs around the track.
options.why: Correct. Place fields depend on how the animal moves. In rats trained to run one way along a track, fields stretched backward, against the direction of travel.

options.text: They would stretch forward, extending ahead in the direction in which the rat runs around the track.
options.why: The fields do stretch, but backward, against the direction of travel. Place fields depend on how the animal moves.

options.text: They would shrink evenly on both sides, since the rat passes each spot from one direction only.
options.why: One-way running does not shrink the fields evenly. In rats trained to run one way, fields stretched backward, against the direction of travel.

options.text: They would stay as they were, since place fields depend only on where the rat is and not on how it moves.
options.why: Place fields depend on how the animal moves as well as on where it is. On a one-way track, fields stretched backward, against the direction of travel.

items.stem: A barrier is put across one part of a maze that a rat already knows well, so the rat can no longer move through that spot. Which of the rat’s place fields change?

options.text: The fields near the barrier change, while the fields far from the barrier stay as they were.
options.why: Correct. Place fields depend on how the animal moves. When a barrier was put across a familiar maze, fields near the barrier changed while distant ones did not.

options.text: The fields across the whole maze change at once, since the blocked maze has become a different place to the rat.
options.why: Place cells can reorganize all at once in a new room, but a barrier in a familiar maze changed only the fields near it. Distant fields stayed as they were.

options.text: The fields stay as they were, since a familiar maze keeps the same place fields when one path is closed.
options.why: Place fields depend on how the animal moves, so closing a path does change some of them. The fields near the barrier changed, while distant ones did not.

options.text: The fields far from the barrier change, while the barrier itself anchors the fields close to it.
options.why: That reverses the result. The fields near the barrier changed, where the rat’s movement was altered, and distant ones did not.

items.stem: The predictive map is a proposal for what the hippocampus does. How do its results compare with the place fields seen in recordings?

options.text: It reproduces fields stretching backward on a one-way track and the change near a barrier, but not field size near a goal.
options.why: Correct. The predictive map reproduces both findings about movement and place fields. It does not reproduce the size of fields near a goal, and it remains a proposal.

options.text: It reproduces fields stretching backward on a one-way track and the change near a barrier, and field size near a goal as well.
options.why: The predictive map does reproduce the two findings about movement, but not the size of fields near a goal. That exception stays with the proposal.

options.text: It reproduces the size of fields near a goal, but not fields stretching backward on a one-way track or the change near a barrier.
options.why: That reverses the fit. The predictive map reproduces the backward stretching and the change near a barrier, and it is field size near a goal that it does not reproduce.

options.text: Recordings have confirmed it in full, settling that the hippocampus stores which places follow which, and how soon.
options.why: The predictive map is a proposal, tested in simulations. It reproduces two findings about place fields but not the size of fields near a goal, so nothing is settled.

items.stem: What is the hippocampus?
tags: place and response in the brain

options.text: An old part of the pallium, with counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, needed to find places defined by surroundings.
options.why: Correct. In mammals, its cells include place cells. Rats with damage to it can still swim to a platform they see, but cannot find a hidden one defined only by the room.

options.text: Part of the basal ganglia, needed for learning to repeat a movement, such as a turn, whatever location the movement leads to.
options.why: That describes the striatum. Rats with striatal damage find a hidden platform but not a visible one, the reverse of rats with damage to the hippocampus.

options.text: A cortex that feeds the hippocampus, and whose medial part contains cells firing on a triangular lattice.
options.why: That describes the entorhinal cortex, which lies beside the hippocampus and feeds it. The hippocampus is an old part of the pallium, needed for finding places defined by their surroundings.

options.text: A doughnut-shaped structure in the middle of an insect’s brain, whose neurons form a ring that marks the heading.
options.why: That is the fruit fly’s heading ring. The hippocampus is an old part of the vertebrate pallium, needed for finding places defined by their surroundings.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “An old part of the pallium, with counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, whose cells in mammals include place cells, and which is needed for finding places defined by their surroundings”.
tags: place and response in the brain

options.text: hippocampus
options.why: Correct. Rats with damage to the hippocampus still swim to a platform they can see, but cannot find a hidden one defined only by the room around the pool.

options.text: entorhinal cortex
options.why: The entorhinal cortex lies beside the hippocampus and feeds it. Its medial part contains grid cells, not place cells.

options.text: dentate gyrus
options.why: The dentate gyrus is one region of the mammalian hippocampus, and no counterpart to it in reptiles or birds has been agreed. The definition is of the whole structure.

options.text: striatum
options.why: The striatum, part of the basal ganglia, is needed for learning a response such as a turn. Rats with striatal damage show the reverse of the hippocampal pattern.

items.stem: Rats are tested in a pool in two ways. In one, they swim to a platform they can see. In the other, they must find a hidden platform whose position is defined only by the room around the pool. How do rats with damage to the hippocampus compare with rats with damage to the striatum?
tags: place and response in the brain

options.text: Hippocampal damage spares the visible platform and impairs the hidden one; striatal damage does the reverse.
options.why: Correct. Rats with hippocampal damage still swim to a platform they can see but cannot find one defined only by the room. Rats with striatal damage show the reverse.

options.text: Hippocampal damage impairs the visible platform and spares the hidden one; striatal damage does the reverse.
options.why: That swaps the two structures. Finding a place defined only by the room needs the hippocampus, so it is hippocampal damage that impairs the hidden platform.

options.text: Both kinds of damage impair the hidden platform, and neither of them makes any difference to the visible one.
options.why: Only hippocampal damage impairs the hidden platform. Rats with striatal damage show the reverse pattern, so each structure is needed for a different task.

options.text: Hippocampal damage impairs both of the platforms; striatal damage makes no difference to either of them.
options.why: Rats with hippocampal damage still swim to a platform they can see. And striatal damage does make a difference: it does the reverse of the hippocampal pattern.

items.stem: In a plus-shaped maze, silencing the hippocampus and silencing the striatum have different effects on what rats have learned. What can be concluded from the two results together about place learning and response learning?
tags: place and response in the brain

options.text: Rats learn both, each depending on a different structure, and the setting decides which tendency is stronger.
options.why: Correct. Each kind of learning depends on its own structure. That fits what had been found in experiments on behavior: both tendencies are present, and the setting decides which is stronger.

options.text: Rats are place learners by nature, and a learned turn is a sign that the hippocampus has stopped working.
options.why: Intact rats learn a turn too, with more training, and that learning depends on the striatum. Neither tendency is the rat’s nature; the setting decides which is stronger.

options.text: Rats learn a response first and a place after long training, each depending on a different structure.
options.why: The order is the other way around. In the plus-shaped maze, rats first learn where the food is, and with more training learn a turn.

options.text: Both kinds of learning depend on the hippocampus, and the striatum moves the body along whichever path is chosen.
options.why: Silencing the striatum removes the learned turn, so response learning depends on the striatum. Place learning is the kind that depends on the hippocampus.

items.stem: A rat has been trained for a long time in a plus-shaped maze, long enough that it now repeats the trained turn. On a test, it is started from the arm opposite its usual start, so the trained turn would lead to the wrong arm. Its striatum is silenced for the test. Where would the rat be expected to go?
tags: place and response in the brain

options.text: To the arm where the food has been, since silencing the striatum removes the turn but not the hippocampal place learning.
options.why: Correct. Silencing the striatum removes the learned turn. The rat also learned where the food is, and that place learning depends on the hippocampus, which is still working.

options.text: Down the arm the trained turn leads to, since a turn learned over long training comes to depend on the hippocampus.
options.why: A learned turn depends on the striatum, not the hippocampus, and silencing the striatum removes it. What remains is the place learning that depends on the hippocampus.

options.text: Down the arm the trained turn leads to, since silencing the striatum removes what the rat learned about the place.
options.why: That swaps the two structures. Silencing the striatum removes the turn, and the place learning, which depends on the hippocampus, is left.

options.text: Into the arms at random, since silencing the striatum removes what was learned about the place and the turn alike.
options.why: Silencing the striatum removes the turn only. Place learning depends on a different structure, the hippocampus, so the rat can still go to where the food has been.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what happened to head-direction cells in rats whose vestibular organs were destroyed. Then explain why a familiar card on the wall failed to bring the direction signal back.
items.answer: The vestibular organs include the semicircular canals, which sense rotation of the head rather than where the head points, so a heading has to be added up from turns. When the vestibular organs were destroyed, head-direction cells in the thalamus stopped signaling direction within a day. They kept firing, but not for any one heading, and the direction signal never returned. A familiar card stayed in view the whole time, but a landmark corrects a heading that drifts. With no signal of turning, there was no heading for the card to correct.
rubric: Says the semicircular canals sense rotation of the head, not where it points, so a heading has to be added up from turns.
Says that after the lesion the cells kept firing but no longer for any one heading.
Says the direction signal never came back, even with a familiar card in view.
Says a landmark corrects a heading, and without the turn signal there was no heading for the card to correct.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why rat head-direction cells are said to behave like a ring attractor. Use what happens to their signal in darkness and when a familiar card is moved. Then say in what sense the rat’s ring exists.
items.answer: In a ring attractor, turns update a single heading and a recognized landmark pulls a drifted heading back. Rat head-direction cells do both. In the dark, their signal keeps going, kept up by turns, but it drifts within minutes, and a familiar landmark pulls it back. When a familiar card on the wall is rotated, every cell’s preferred direction rotates with it, all together, as one heading signal would. But the rat’s cells are not laid out in a circle in the tissue. The ring is a way of arranging them on paper, by the direction each one prefers, and the cells behave as such a ring would.
rubric: Says turns update a single heading signal, which keeps going in darkness.
Says the signal drifts in darkness and a familiar landmark pulls it back.
Says that when a familiar card is rotated, every cell’s preferred direction rotates with it, together.
Says the rat’s cells are not laid out in a circle; the ring is an arrangement on paper by preferred direction.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe what silencing the hippocampus and silencing the striatum do to rats in a plus-shaped maze. Then explain what can be concluded from the two results about whether rats learn places or responses.
tags: place and response in the brain
items.answer: In a plus-shaped maze, rats first learn where the food is, and with more training they learn a turn. Silencing the hippocampus with a drug removes the place learning, and silencing the striatum removes the learned turn. So rats learn both places and responses, and each kind of learning depends on a different structure. That fits what had been found in experiments on behavior. Rats are not place learners or response learners by nature. Both tendencies are present, and the setting decides which one is stronger.
rubric: Says rats first learn where the food is and, with more training, learn a turn.
Says silencing the hippocampus removes the place learning and silencing the striatum removes the turn.
Concludes that rats learn both places and responses, each depending on a different structure.
Connects this to the behavioral finding that both tendencies are present and the setting decides which is stronger.

pools.title: Grid Cells, Border Cells, and the Circuit

items.stem: What is the entorhinal cortex?

options.text: The cortex beside the hippocampus that feeds it and receives its output, and whose medial part contains grid cells.
options.why: Correct. The entorhinal cortex lies next to the hippocampus and feeds it, and the hippocampus sends its result back there. Grid cells are found in its medial part.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives input from the cortex beside it and spreads that input across many more cells, few of them active at once.
options.why: Spreading input across many more sparsely firing cells describes the dentate gyrus, which receives its input from the entorhinal cortex. The entorhinal cortex is the cortex beside the hippocampus that feeds it.

options.text: An old part of the pallium, with counterparts in fish, reptiles, and birds, whose cells in mammals include cells that fire in one part of the surroundings.
options.why: An old part of the pallium whose cells include place cells is the hippocampus itself. The entorhinal cortex is the cortex beside it, which feeds it and receives its output.

options.text: The part of the basal ganglia that learning a turn depends on, so that silencing it removes the turn while leaving learning the food’s place intact.
options.why: Learning a turn depends on the striatum, part of the basal ganglia. The entorhinal cortex is the cortex beside the hippocampus, which feeds it and contains grid cells in its medial part.

items.stem: What is a grid cell?

options.text: A cell in the medial entorhinal cortex that fires at many places, at the corners of equilateral triangles across the surroundings.
options.why: Correct. A single grid cell fires at many places, and those places form a regular triangular pattern that covers the whole floor.

options.text: A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way the animal happens to be facing.
options.why: Firing in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal faces, describes a place cell in the hippocampus. A grid cell fires at many places, at the corners of equilateral triangles.

options.text: A cell in the entorhinal cortex that fires when the animal is along a wall or other edge of its surroundings, such as one side of a box.
options.why: Firing along a wall or other edge describes a border cell. A grid cell, in the medial entorhinal cortex, fires at many places laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles across the floor.

options.text: A cell that fires when the animal’s head points in one direction, whatever the animal is doing and wherever in the surroundings it is.
options.why: Firing for one heading, wherever the animal is, describes a head-direction cell. A grid cell fires by where the animal is, at many places on a triangular pattern.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A cell in the medial entorhinal cortex that fires at many places, laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles across the animal’s surroundings”.

options.text: grid cell
options.why: Correct. A grid cell fires at many places, and the places form a regular triangular pattern across the whole floor.

options.text: place cell
options.why: A place cell is in the hippocampus, and it fires in one part of the surroundings, its place field. A cell that fires at many places on a triangular pattern is a grid cell.

options.text: border cell
options.why: A border cell is in the entorhinal cortex, but it fires along a wall or other edge. A cell that fires at many places on a triangular pattern across the floor is a grid cell.

options.text: head-direction cell
options.why: A head-direction cell fires when the head points in one direction, wherever the animal is. A cell that fires at many places on a triangular pattern is a grid cell.

items.stem: What is a border cell?

options.text: A cell in the entorhinal cortex that fires when the animal is along a wall or other edge of its surroundings.
options.why: Correct. A border cell marks an edge of the space, firing along a wall.

options.text: A cell in the medial entorhinal cortex that fires at many places, laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles across the floor.
options.why: Firing at many places on a triangular pattern describes a grid cell. A border cell, also in the entorhinal cortex, fires along a wall or other edge.

options.text: A cell in the hippocampus that fires when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it is facing.
options.why: Firing in one part of the surroundings describes a place cell in the hippocampus. A border cell fires along a wall or other edge of the surroundings.

options.text: A cell that fires when the animal’s head points in one direction, whatever the animal is doing and wherever it is.
options.why: Firing for one heading describes a head-direction cell. A border cell fires by where the animal is relative to the edges of the space, along a wall.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A cell in the entorhinal cortex that fires when the animal is along a wall or other edge of its surroundings”.

options.text: border cell
options.why: Correct. A border cell fires along a wall or other edge, marking the edges of a space.

options.text: grid cell
options.why: A grid cell is also in the entorhinal cortex, but it fires at many places across the whole floor, at the corners of equilateral triangles. A cell that fires along a wall is a border cell.

options.text: place cell
options.why: A place cell is in the hippocampus, and its place field can lie anywhere in the surroundings. A cell in the entorhinal cortex that fires along a wall is a border cell.

options.text: head-direction cell
options.why: A head-direction cell fires for one heading, wherever the animal is. A cell that fires when the animal is along a wall is a border cell.

items.stem: Border cells and the related boundary cells both respond to the walls of a space. How do the two kinds of cell differ?

options.text: A border cell fires when the animal is along a wall, while a boundary cell fires when a wall lies at a particular distance and direction from the animal.
options.why: Correct. A border cell fires along the wall itself. A boundary cell fires when a wall lies at a particular distance and direction from the animal, which need not be right beside it.

options.text: A border cell fires when a wall lies at a particular distance and direction from the animal, while a boundary cell fires when the animal is along a wall.
options.why: The two descriptions are swapped. A border cell fires along a wall, and a boundary cell fires when a wall lies at a particular distance and direction from the animal.

options.text: A border cell fires when the animal is along a wall, while a boundary cell fires at many places laid out on a triangular pattern lined up with the walls.
options.why: The border-cell half is right, but firing at many places on a triangular pattern describes a grid cell. A boundary cell fires when a wall lies at a particular distance and direction from the animal.

options.text: A border cell fires when the animal is along a wall, while a boundary cell fires at a particular distance from the starting point, wherever the walls lie.
options.why: The border-cell half is right, but boundary cells respond to walls, not to the distance from the start. A boundary cell fires when a wall lies at a particular distance and direction from the animal.

items.stem: A researcher records grid cells one after another while moving an electrode from the top of a rat’s medial entorhinal cortex toward the bottom. What should happen to the grid spacing along the way?

options.text: The spacing should grow, in steps, so the cells fall into a few groups, each with its own spacing and orientation.
options.why: Correct. Grid spacing grows from the top of the entorhinal cortex to the bottom, and the growth comes in steps. Within one rat, grid cells fall into a few groups, each with its own spacing and orientation.

options.text: The spacing should grow smoothly, so that each cell has a slightly wider spacing than the cell recorded just above it.
options.why: Spacing does grow toward the bottom, but not smoothly. Neighboring grid cells share spacing and orientation, and the growth comes in steps, so the cells fall into a few groups.

options.text: The spacing should shrink, and in steps, so that the cells fall into a few groups, each narrower than the group above it.
options.why: The steps and the groups are right, but the direction is reversed. Spacing grows from the top of the entorhinal cortex to the bottom, up to about 3 meters.

options.text: The spacing should stay the same throughout, while the orientation of the grid turns a little with each step downward.
options.why: Spacing does not stay the same. It grows from the top of the entorhinal cortex to the bottom in steps, and each group of grid cells has its own spacing as well as its own orientation.

items.stem: Grid cells from several groups in one rat were recorded in a familiar box, and then the box was made shorter. Cells in the larger groups stretched their grids to fit the shorter box, while cells in the smallest group barely changed. What does the result show about the groups?

options.text: The groups can respond independently of one another, rather than all changing together as a single unit.
options.why: Correct. One group refit its grids to the shorter box while another barely changed, so the groups can respond independently.

options.text: The grids of every group are set by the walls alone, so all of the groups were refit to the shorter box together.
options.why: The groups were not all refit. Cells in the smallest group barely changed, which is what shows that the groups can respond independently.

options.text: The groups always change together, so the smallest group must have stretched by an amount too small to be measured.
options.why: If the groups always changed together, the smallest group would have stretched along with the others. It barely changed, so the groups can respond independently.

options.text: The smallest group stopped firing in a grid pattern, so only the larger groups were still keeping a grid in the shorter box.
options.why: The cells of the smallest group barely changed, which means their grids stayed much as they were. The result shows that the groups can respond independently.

items.stem: A pattern that repeats across the floor fixes an animal’s position only within one repeat, much as a clock’s minute hand gives the minute but not the hour. If grids are such repeating codes, why does it matter that grid cells come in several groups with different spacings?
tags: grid cells and the running sum

options.text: Patterns of different sizes, combined, could pin down a single place, which no one group’s pattern can do on its own.
options.why: Correct. On the leading hypothesis, grids are repeating codes for position. One repeating pattern fixes position only within one repeat, but several patterns of different sizes, combined, pin down a single place, and the groups supply patterns of different sizes.

options.text: Each group could cover a different part of the floor, so that together the groups reach places that no single group’s grid reaches.
options.why: A grid cell fires at many places across the whole floor, so no group is limited to one part of it. What several sizes add is that, combined, they can pin down a single place.

options.text: Groups with wider spacing could fire more near the walls, so that together the groups mark where the edges of the space lie.
options.why: Marking edges is what border cells do. Each grid is a regular pattern across the whole floor, and what several sizes add is that, combined, they can pin down a single place.

options.text: A single pattern already fixes position exactly, so the extra groups could serve as spare copies in case one of the groups failed.
options.why: A single repeating pattern does not fix position exactly. It fixes position only within one repeat, which is why patterns of several sizes, combined, are needed to pin down a single place.

items.stem: Within one rat, grid cells fall into a few groups, each with its own spacing. How does each group’s spacing compare with the spacing of the group before it?

options.text: It is about 1.4 times as wide, so the spacings grow in steps of roughly the same proportion.
options.why: Correct. Each spacing is about 1.4 times the one before, and the most thoroughly recorded animals have four or five groups.

options.text: It is about twice as wide, so the spacing doubles from each group to the next one down.
options.why: The spacings do grow in steps, but each one is about 1.4 times the one before, not twice it.

options.text: It is about the same, so the groups differ from one another only in the orientation of their grids.
options.why: Each group has its own orientation, but also its own spacing. Each spacing is about 1.4 times the one before.

options.text: It is about 3 meters wider, so the spacing grows by a fixed distance from group to group.
options.why: About 3 meters is roughly how large the spacing gets at the bottom of the entorhinal cortex. Each spacing is about 1.4 times the one before, a proportion rather than a fixed distance.

items.stem: An engineer gives a robot several patterns that repeat across the floor like tiles, each of a different size. Each pattern slides along as the robot moves, driven by signals for the robot’s speed and direction. On the leading hypothesis about the rat’s brain, which cells would correspond to these patterns?
tags: grid cells and the running sum

options.text: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex, each firing at many places laid out at the corners of equilateral triangles.
