options.why: Correct. The leading hypothesis is that grids are repeating codes like the robot’s patterns, and that grid cells may keep the running sum of position.

options.text: Place cells in the hippocampus, each firing in one part of the surroundings, whichever way the animal happens to be facing.
options.why: A place cell fires in one part of the surroundings, so its firing does not repeat across the floor. The repeating codes are hypothesized to be grids, which fire at many places.

options.text: Border cells in the entorhinal cortex, each firing when the animal is along a wall or other edge of the space.
options.why: A border cell marks an edge of the space rather than repeating across the floor. The repeating codes are hypothesized to be grids, which fire at many places across the whole floor.

options.text: Head-direction cells along a chain from the brainstem to the cortex, each firing when the head points in one direction.
options.why: A head-direction cell fires for a heading, not for where the animal is, so it gives nothing that repeats across the floor. The repeating codes are hypothesized to be grids.

items.stem: On the leading hypothesis, grid cells may keep the running sum of an animal’s position. Which observation counts against a simple version of that hypothesis?
tags: grid cells and the running sum

options.text: Grids break up when travel is interrupted, and distort in oddly shaped rooms.
options.why: Correct. Grids that break up when travel is interrupted, distort in oddly shaped rooms, and stretch when a box is stretched are evidence against a simple version of the hypothesis.

options.text: Grids appear within the first minutes after the animal enters a place it has never been in.
options.why: Grids do appear within minutes in a new place, but that is not among the evidence against the hypothesis. What counts against a simple version is that grids stretch, distort, and break up.

options.text: Grids survive when the landmarks around the animal are removed from the box.
options.why: Grids do survive the removal of landmarks, and a running sum kept from the animal’s own movement needs no landmarks, so that observation fits the hypothesis. What counts against a simple version is that grids stretch, distort, and break up.

options.text: Some entorhinal cells combine the animal’s head direction, speed, and grid firing.
options.why: Such cells combine the inputs that models of the running sum need, so they fit the hypothesis rather than count against it. What counts against a simple version is that grids stretch, distort, and break up.

items.stem: Suppose that in the young of some mammal, place cells already fire by distance traveled, days before any grid cells appear. The young also find their way home by path integration before grid cells appear. What idea would that finding count against?
tags: grid cells and the running sum

options.text: The idea that grid cells are the only route by which place cells come to track the animal’s position.
options.why: Correct. Place cells that track distance before grid cells exist must be getting there by some other route. The same finding in rat pups counts against grid cells being the only route to place cells, while leaving open a role for grid cells.

options.text: The idea that grid cells play any part at all in keeping the running sum of position in adult animals.
options.why: The finding shows that place cells can track distance without grid cells, not that grid cells play no part in adults. Grid cells as keepers of the running sum remains the leading hypothesis.

options.text: The idea that the young can keep any running sum of their own position before grid cells appear.
options.why: The young in the example already find their way home by path integration, so they do keep a running sum. What the finding counts against is grid cells being the only route to place cells.

options.text: The idea that place fields are corrected by landmarks, since the young’s place cells followed distance traveled instead.
options.why: Place cells that first fire by distance traveled fit a running sum that landmarks later correct. What the finding counts against is grid cells being the only route to place cells.

items.stem: On the leading hypothesis, grid cells may keep a running sum of the animal’s position. Grid firing drifts, and touching a wall corrects the drift. Why does that pattern fit the hypothesis?
tags: grid cells and the running sum

options.text: A running sum gathers error as the animal moves, and a fixed feature such as a wall can reset it, as a stable landmark resets a drifting estimate.
options.why: Correct. Every small error stays in a running sum, so the sum drifts. A feature that stays where it is, such as a wall, can correct it, which is how landmarks correct a drifting estimate of position.

options.text: A running sum gathers no error as the animal moves, so a grid that drifts must be following the walls rather than following the animal’s own movement.
options.why: A running sum does gather error, since every small error in heading or distance stays in the sum. Drift corrected by a wall is what a running sum corrected by a fixed feature would show.

options.text: A wall works as a beacon, and an animal keeping a running sum finds its way back to the start by steering toward a beacon.
options.why: Steering toward a beacon is a separate procedure, which needs no running sum. The wall matters here because a fixed feature can reset a sum that has drifted.

options.text: A wall is the nearest cue, and the nearest cue corrects a running sum whether or not the cue stays where it is.
options.why: Nearness is not what matters. A landmark is worth using to correct the sum only if it stays where it is, and cues an animal has seen move lose their control. A wall corrects the drift because it is a fixed feature.

items.stem: In people, brain scans show a sixfold pattern in entorhinal activity during navigation in a virtual space. How does that evidence compare with recordings from single cells?

options.text: The scan pattern is an indirect signal, expected if many grid cells share an orientation, while a single-cell recording measures one cell’s firing.
options.why: Correct. The sixfold pattern is what many grid cells sharing an orientation would produce, but it is not a recording of grid cells. Single cells with grid-like firing have also been recorded in people.

options.text: The scan pattern is a direct recording of grid cells, while a single-cell recording shows only that a cell fires, not where the person is when it fires.
options.why: The scan pattern is the indirect evidence, not the direct one. It is expected if many grid cells share an orientation, but it is not a recording of grid cells.

options.text: The scan pattern shows place cells firing in the hippocampus, while a single-cell recording is the only evidence of entorhinal activity in people.
options.why: The sixfold pattern is in entorhinal activity, and it is what many grid cells sharing an orientation would produce. It is an indirect signal rather than a recording of any cell.

options.text: The scan pattern shows border cells firing along the virtual walls, while a single-cell recording shows the triangular pattern of grid cells.
options.why: The sixfold pattern is expected from grid cells sharing an orientation, not from border cells. It is an indirect signal, not a recording of any one kind of cell.

items.stem: What is CA1?

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives the output of CA3, as well as direct entorhinal input, and sends the result back toward the entorhinal cortex.
options.why: Correct. CA1 receives CA3’s output and is also reached directly by the entorhinal cortex. With the subiculum, CA1 sends the result back to the entorhinal cortex.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives input from the dentate gyrus and the entorhinal cortex, and whose cells excite one another as well as sending output onward.
options.why: Cells that excite one another, with input from the dentate gyrus and the entorhinal cortex, describe CA3. CA1 receives the output of CA3 and sends the result back toward the entorhinal cortex.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives entorhinal input and spreads it across many more cells that fire sparsely, before passing it on to the next region.
options.why: Spreading entorhinal input across many more sparsely firing cells describes the dentate gyrus. CA1 comes later in the loop, receiving the output of CA3.

options.text: The cortex beside the hippocampus that feeds the hippocampus and receives its output, and whose medial part contains the grid cells.
options.why: The cortex beside the hippocampus is the entorhinal cortex, where the loop starts and ends. CA1 is a region of the hippocampus that sends the result back to it.

items.stem: What is CA3?

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives input from the dentate gyrus and the entorhinal cortex, and whose cells excite one another as well as sending output to CA1.
options.why: Correct. CA3 receives input from the dentate gyrus and directly from the entorhinal cortex. Its cells excite one another, each contacting about 5% of the rest, and it sends its output to CA1.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives the output of another hippocampal region, along with direct entorhinal input, and sends the result back to the entorhinal cortex.
options.why: Sending the result back to the entorhinal cortex describes CA1, which receives the output of CA3. CA3 comes before CA1, and its cells excite one another.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives entorhinal input and spreads it across many more cells that fire sparsely, before passing it on to the next region of the loop.
options.why: Spreading input across many more sparsely firing cells describes the dentate gyrus, which then passes its input to CA3. CA3 receives that input, and its cells excite one another.

options.text: A neighboring region beside CA1 that, together with CA1, sends the result of the loop back to the entorhinal cortex, where the loop began.
options.why: Sending the result back alongside CA1 describes the subiculum, a neighboring region at the end of the loop. CA3 is earlier in the loop, receiving input from the dentate gyrus and the entorhinal cortex, and its cells excite one another.

items.stem: Suppose the connections from the dentate gyrus to CA3 were cut in a rat. By which routes could input from the entorhinal cortex still reach CA1?

options.text: Directly, and also by way of CA3, since entorhinal axons reach CA3 and CA1 as well as the dentate gyrus.
options.why: Correct. Entorhinal axons reach the dentate gyrus and CA3, and the entorhinal cortex also reaches CA1 directly. With the dentate gyrus cut off from CA3, both of the other routes to CA1 remain.

options.text: By no remaining route, since entorhinal input passes through the dentate gyrus before it can reach CA3 or CA1.
options.why: Entorhinal input does not have to pass through the dentate gyrus. Entorhinal axons also reach CA3 directly, and the entorhinal cortex reaches CA1 directly as well.

options.text: By way of the subiculum, since the subiculum passes entorhinal input forward from the cortex into CA1.
options.why: The subiculum is on the way out of the loop, not the way in. With CA1, it sends the result back to the entorhinal cortex.

options.text: Directly but not through CA3, since CA3 receives its input from the dentate gyrus and would now receive none.
options.why: The direct route to CA1 does remain, but CA3 does not depend on the dentate gyrus alone. Entorhinal axons reach CA3 directly, so the route through CA3 remains too.

items.stem: What is the dentate gyrus?

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives entorhinal input and passes it on to CA3, spread across many more cells that fire sparsely.
options.why: Correct. The step into the dentate gyrus spreads the entorhinal input across many more cells, few of them active at a time, before it passes on to CA3.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus whose cells excite one another, each contacting about 5% of the rest, and which sends its output on to CA1.
options.why: Cells that excite one another and send output to CA1 describe CA3. The dentate gyrus comes before CA3, spreading entorhinal input across many more sparsely firing cells.

options.text: The region of the hippocampus that receives the output of CA3 and direct entorhinal input, and sends the result back toward the entorhinal cortex.
options.why: Receiving CA3’s output and sending the result back describe CA1, near the end of the loop. The dentate gyrus is near the start, receiving input from the entorhinal cortex.

options.text: The cortex beside the hippocampus that feeds it and receives its output, and whose medial part contains the grid cells.
options.why: The cortex beside the hippocampus is the entorhinal cortex, which feeds the dentate gyrus. The dentate gyrus spreads that input across many more sparsely firing cells.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The region of the hippocampus that receives input from the entorhinal cortex and passes it on to CA3, spread across many more cells that fire sparsely. It is thought to keep similar places apart”.

options.text: dentate gyrus
options.why: Correct. The dentate gyrus spreads entorhinal input across many more sparsely firing cells, and it is thought to keep similar places apart.

options.text: CA3
options.why: CA3 is the region the dentate gyrus passes its input on to, and its cells excite one another. The region that spreads the input across many more cells is the dentate gyrus.

options.text: CA1
options.why: CA1 receives the output of CA3 and sends the result back toward the entorhinal cortex. The region that spreads entorhinal input across many more cells is the dentate gyrus.

options.text: entorhinal cortex
options.why: The entorhinal cortex is the cortex beside the hippocampus that supplies the input. The region of the hippocampus that receives it and spreads it across many more cells is the dentate gyrus.

items.stem: In the rat, about 200,000 entorhinal cells feed about a million dentate cells. What does the step from the entorhinal cortex into the dentate gyrus do to its input?

options.text: It spreads the input across many more cells, few of them active at a time.
options.why: Correct. The step expands the input into many more cells, and dentate cells fire more sparsely than the cells elsewhere in the loop, so few of them are active at a time.

options.text: It narrows the input onto fewer cells, so that many entorhinal cells converge on each dentate cell.
options.why: The dentate gyrus has many more cells than the entorhinal cells that feed it, about a million against about 200,000. The step spreads the input out rather than narrowing it.

options.text: It spreads the input across many more cells, most of them active at the same time.
options.why: The input is spread across many more cells, but dentate cells fire sparsely. Few of them are active at a time.

options.text: It passes the input on unchanged, from each entorhinal cell to one dentate cell.
options.why: A one-to-one step could not reach about a million dentate cells from about 200,000 entorhinal cells. The step spreads the input across many more cells, few of them active at a time.

items.stem: The step from the entorhinal cortex into the dentate gyrus has the same arrangement as the insect mushroom body. What do the two share?

options.text: In both, a small number of input channels fan out onto many more cells, few of them active at a time.
options.why: Correct. In the insect mushroom body and in the step into the dentate gyrus, input spreads from a few channels onto many more cells that fire sparsely.

options.text: In both, a large number of input channels converge onto a few cells, each of them active most of the time.
options.why: The arrangement runs the other way. In both, a few input channels fan out onto many more cells, and few of those cells are active at a time.

options.text: In both, a ring of cells keeps a single bump of activity, which slides around the ring as the animal turns.
options.why: A ring with a single bump that slides as the animal turns describes a ring attractor for heading. The shared arrangement is a few input channels fanning out onto many more sparsely active cells.

options.text: In both, each cell excites its neighbors, each contacting about 5% of the rest, so that activity spreads among them.
options.why: Cells exciting one another, each contacting about 5% of the rest, describe CA3. The shared arrangement is a few input channels fanning out onto many more sparsely active cells.

items.stem: Input reaches the hippocampus through both the medial and the lateral entorhinal cortex. How do the two streams of input differ?

options.text: The stream through the medial part is more spatial, and the stream through the lateral part is about objects and context.
options.why: Correct. A more spatial stream comes through the medial entorhinal cortex, where grid cells are found, and a stream about objects and context comes through the lateral entorhinal cortex.

options.text: The stream through the medial part is about objects and context, and the stream through the lateral part is more spatial.
options.why: The two streams are swapped. The more spatial stream comes through the medial entorhinal cortex, where grid cells are found, and the stream about objects and context through the lateral.

options.text: The stream through the medial part is about heading alone, and the stream through the lateral part is about distance traveled.
options.why: The lateral stream is about objects and context, not distance. The medial stream is the more spatial one, and it is not limited to heading.

options.text: Both streams are spatial, and the two differ only in which region of the hippocampus each one reaches first.
options.why: Only one of the two streams is mainly spatial. The stream through the lateral entorhinal cortex is about objects and context.

items.stem: Researchers silence the lateral entorhinal cortex of a rat while leaving its medial entorhinal cortex working. According to the reading, which input to the hippocampus would be most reduced?

options.text: The stream of input about objects and the context they appear in.
options.why: Correct. Input about objects and context reaches the hippocampus through the lateral entorhinal cortex, so silencing the lateral part would reduce that stream.

options.text: The more spatial stream of input, including the input from grid cells.
options.why: The more spatial stream comes through the medial entorhinal cortex, where grid cells are found, and the medial part is still working. The lateral stream is about objects and context.

options.text: The output that CA1 and the subiculum send back toward the entorhinal cortex.
options.why: CA1 and the subiculum send output out of the hippocampus, not input into it. The input that comes through the lateral entorhinal cortex is about objects and context.

options.text: The heading signal from head-direction cells, kept going by turns of the head.
options.why: Heading is spatial, and the more spatial stream comes through the medial entorhinal cortex. The stream through the lateral part is about objects and context.

items.stem: Reptiles and birds have a hippocampus in the same place as mammals. How does its circuit compare with the mammalian loop?

options.text: Its two or three parts are connected back and forth rather than mostly one way, and no part of it is agreed to match the dentate gyrus.
options.why: Correct. The loop through the dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1, running mostly one way, is the mammalian form. In reptiles and birds, the parts are connected back and forth, and none is agreed to match the dentate gyrus.

options.text: Its parts form the same one-way loop as in mammals, with a dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1, but with far fewer cells in each of them.
options.why: The reptile and bird hippocampus does not share the mammalian loop. Its parts are connected back and forth, and no part of it is agreed to match the dentate gyrus.

options.text: Its two or three parts are connected mostly one way, as in mammals, but it has no connection to the thalamus or to the cortex above it.
options.why: The reptile and bird hippocampus is connected to the thalamus, to the septum below it, and to the cortex above it. What differs is that its parts are connected back and forth.

options.text: Its parts include a dentate gyrus even larger than the mammalian one, and that region is connected back and forth with the other parts.
options.why: The parts are connected back and forth, but no part of the reptile and bird hippocampus is agreed to match the dentate gyrus at all.

items.stem: Suppose a vertebrate’s hippocampus turns out to have three parts, each sending connections to the other two and receiving connections back from them. None of the three parts spreads its input across many more sparsely firing cells. Which circuit does the three-part hippocampus resemble most closely?

options.text: The hippocampus of reptiles and birds, whose two or three parts are connected back and forth, with no part agreed to match the dentate gyrus.
options.why: Correct. In reptiles and birds, the parts of the hippocampus are connected back and forth rather than mostly one way, and none is agreed to match the dentate gyrus. The mammalian loop runs mostly one way and has a dentate gyrus.

options.text: The hippocampus of mammals, whose parts form a loop through which input runs back and forth among the dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1.
options.why: The mammalian hippocampus does form a loop, but input runs through it mostly one way, from the entorhinal cortex through the dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1 and back. Its dentate gyrus also spreads input across many more sparsely firing cells.

options.text: The hippocampus of mammals, whose CA3 cells excite one another, so that each part of the loop sends connections back to the parts before it.
options.why: CA3 cells do excite one another, but that is excitation within CA3, not connections running back between the parts. The mammalian loop as a whole runs mostly one way, and it includes a dentate gyrus.

options.text: The insect mushroom body, in which a small number of input channels fan out onto many more cells, few of them active at a time.
options.why: Fanning out onto many more sparsely active cells is what the mushroom body shares with the step into the dentate gyrus. None of the three parts here does that, and parts connected back and forth match the reptile and bird hippocampus.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, state the leading hypothesis about what grid cells do. Then describe two kinds of evidence against a simple version of the hypothesis: evidence from the grids themselves, and evidence from rat pups. Say what the evidence from rat pups does and does not count against.
tags: grid cells and the running sum
items.answer: The leading hypothesis is that grids are repeating codes for the animal’s position, and that grid cells may keep the running sum of position. The idea is a hypothesis, not a settled finding. One kind of evidence against a simple version comes from the grids themselves. Grids stretch when a box is stretched, distort in oddly shaped rooms, and break up when travel is interrupted. A second kind comes from development. Rat pups find their way home by path integration, and their place cells track distance traveled, before grid cells appear. The evidence from pups counts against grid cells being the only route to place cells, but it does not show that grid cells play no part in keeping the running sum.
rubric: States the hypothesis: grids are repeating codes for position, and grid cells may keep the running sum, presented as a hypothesis rather than a fact.
Gives evidence from the grids themselves: stretching in a stretched box, distorting in oddly shaped rooms, or breaking up when travel is interrupted (one is enough).
Gives the developmental evidence: in rat pups, path integration and place cells tracking distance come before grid cells appear.
Says the developmental evidence counts against grid cells being the only route to place cells, without ruling out a role for grid cells.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain in what sense the hippocampal loop of the rat is “the mammalian form”, by comparing it with the hippocampus of reptiles and birds.
items.answer: In mammals, the parts of the hippocampus form a loop with the entorhinal cortex, and input runs through it mostly one way. Input goes from the entorhinal cortex to the dentate gyrus and CA3, from CA3 to CA1, and from CA1 and the subiculum back to the entorhinal cortex. Reptiles and birds also have a hippocampus, in the same place, connected to the thalamus, the septum, and the cortex. But its two or three parts are connected back and forth rather than mostly one way, and no part of it is agreed to match the dentate gyrus. So the one-way loop through a dentate gyrus is the form the hippocampus takes in mammals, not a plan every vertebrate shares.
rubric: Describes the mammalian loop as running mostly one way, from the entorhinal cortex through the dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1, and back to the entorhinal cortex.
Says reptiles and birds also have a hippocampus, in the same place as in mammals.
Says the parts of the reptile and bird hippocampus are connected back and forth rather than mostly one way.
Says no part of the reptile and bird hippocampus is agreed to match the dentate gyrus.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe two kinds of evidence that people have grid cells, and explain why one kind is weaker than the other.
items.answer: One kind comes from brain scans. During navigation in a virtual space, people’s entorhinal activity shows a sixfold pattern, which is what would be expected if many grid cells shared an orientation. But the sixfold pattern is an indirect signal, not a recording of grid cells, since a scan measures the activity of a whole region rather than of single cells. The other kind comes from people with electrodes placed in the brain to treat epilepsy, in whom single cells with grid-like firing have been recorded. A recording from a single cell measures that cell’s firing directly, so it is the stronger of the two.
rubric: Describes the brain-scan evidence: a sixfold pattern in entorhinal activity during navigation in a virtual space.
Says the sixfold pattern is expected if many grid cells share an orientation.
Says the scan pattern is an indirect signal, not a recording of grid cells.
Describes the single-cell evidence: cells with grid-like firing recorded in people with electrodes placed in the brain to treat epilepsy.

pools.title: Many Maps, and Which Thing Was Where

items.stem: What is remapping?

options.text: The reorganization of place cells when an animal moves to a different environment, with some cells firing in new places and others falling silent.
options.why: Correct. Remapping happens all at once when a rat is moved to a new room. One rat kept separate maps for eleven rooms, so one set of place cells can keep many maps.

options.text: The slow drift of place fields within one familiar environment, as a running sum of position gathers error until landmarks bring it back into line.
options.why: A running sum does drift, and landmarks do correct it, but that is a correction within one map. Remapping is the all-at-once reorganization of place cells in a different environment.

options.text: The recovery of a whole stored map of a familiar environment when only some of its landmarks remain, so that the place fields stay where they were.
options.why: That is pattern completion, applied to a place, which CA3 shows when some landmarks are removed. Remapping is the reorganization of place cells in a different environment.

options.text: The turning of every head-direction cell’s preferred direction together when a familiar card on the wall is rotated to a new position in the room.
options.why: That is a landmark correcting the heading signal, and it concerns head-direction cells. Remapping is the reorganization of place cells when an animal moves to a different environment.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The reorganization of place cells when an animal moves to a different environment, with some cells firing in new places and others falling silent”.

options.text: remapping
options.why: Correct. Remapping is what place cells do in a new room: some fire in new places, and others fall silent, all at once.

options.text: reorientation
options.why: Reorientation is recovering which way one is facing, and where one is, after becoming disoriented. The reorganization of place cells in a different environment is remapping.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Pattern separation is making overlapping inputs less alike, which the dentate gyrus is thought to do. The reorganization of place cells in a different environment is remapping.

options.text: place field
options.why: A place field is the part of the surroundings in which one place cell fires. The reorganization of many place cells in a different environment is remapping.

items.stem: Researchers record a set of place cells while a mouse explores its usual testing box. Then they carry the mouse to a box in a different room. In the new box, some of the same cells fire in new places, and others fall silent. What can be concluded from the change in the place cells?

options.text: The same set of place cells has formed a separate map for the new box, and the map of the old box can be kept alongside it.
options.why: Correct. The change is remapping. Place cells reorganize all at once in a new place, and the maps of different places are kept apart: one rat kept separate maps for eleven rooms.

options.text: The map of the old box has been erased and replaced, so the place cells will need a new map of the old box when the mouse returns.
options.why: The cells did reorganize, but remapping does not erase the old map. One rat kept separate maps for eleven rooms, so the maps of different places are kept side by side.

options.text: The new box offers fewer landmarks, so CA3 has filled in the old box’s map from the few cues that it shares with the new box.
options.why: Filling in a stored map from part of it is pattern completion, and it keeps place fields where they were. Here the fields changed, which is remapping, a separate map for a new place.

options.text: The mouse has lost track of which way it faces, and the old fields will come back once it recovers its heading in the new box.
options.why: Losing and recovering a heading is reorientation. A box in a different room is a different environment, and the reorganization of place cells there is remapping, a separate map.

items.stem: What does pattern separation mean?

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell the inputs apart.
options.why: Correct. The dentate gyrus is thought to separate places in this way, so that two similar places can be given different maps.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so a familiar input with pieces missing is matched.
options.why: That is pattern completion, which CA3 shows when some landmarks are removed and its place fields stay intact. Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike.

options.text: Weighting several estimates by their reliability, so that they combine into a single better estimate.
options.why: That is cue combination, a way of correcting a drifting running sum. Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart.

options.text: Reorganizing place cells in a new environment, so some fire in new places and others fall silent.
options.why: That is remapping, which is what place cells are seen to do in a new room. Pattern separation is a process, making overlapping inputs less alike, and remapping involves more than that process.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart”.

options.text: pattern separation
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation is the job the dentate gyrus is thought to do for places, keeping similar places apart.

options.text: pattern completion
options.why: Pattern completion runs the other way: it recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

options.text: remapping
options.why: Remapping is the reorganization of place cells in a different environment, something place cells are seen to do. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Cue combination weights several estimates by how reliable each is, and so makes them into one. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

items.stem: Pattern separation and pattern completion are both described for the hippocampus. How do the two processes differ?

options.text: Separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, as the dentate gyrus is thought to do for similar places. Completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it, as CA3 does when some landmarks are removed.
options.why: Correct. Separation keeps similar places apart, and the dentate gyrus is thought to do it. Completion keeps a familiar place on its own map when some landmarks are missing, and CA3 shows it.

options.text: Separation recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it, as the dentate gyrus is thought to do for similar places. Completion makes overlapping inputs less alike, as CA3 does when some landmarks are removed.
options.why: The two definitions are swapped. Separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, and completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it.

options.text: Separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, as CA3 does when some landmarks are removed from a box. Completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it, as the dentate gyrus is thought to do for places.
options.why: The definitions are right, but the regions are swapped. The dentate gyrus is thought to do the separating, and CA3 keeps place fields intact when some landmarks are removed.

options.text: Separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, as the dentate gyrus is thought to do for similar places. Completion builds a new map for a new room, as CA3 does when the animal is moved somewhere new.
options.why: Building a new map for a new room is remapping, not completion. Completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it, as when CA3 keeps place fields intact with some landmarks removed.

items.stem: The dentate gyrus is thought to keep similar places apart by pattern separation. How does remapping relate to pattern separation in the dentate gyrus?

options.text: Remapping involves more than separation: grid and head-direction cells shift together into a new alignment, and silencing entorhinal input causes remapping.
options.why: Correct. Remapping is not only separation. Grid cells, head-direction cells, and input from the entorhinal cortex take part in it too.

options.text: Remapping is the same thing as separation: both terms name the work of dentate cells, which respond to small changes in a box that CA3 cells ignore.
options.why: Dentate cells do respond to small changes that CA3 cells ignore, and that is evidence for separation. But remapping also involves grid and head-direction cells and input from the entorhinal cortex.

options.text: Remapping is the opposite of separation: it recovers a whole stored map from part of the map, as CA3 does when some landmarks are removed from a box.
options.why: Recovering a stored pattern from part of it is pattern completion. Remapping is a reorganization of place cells, and it involves more than separation, including grid and head-direction cells.

options.text: Remapping happens only among place cells: grid cells and head-direction cells keep one and the same alignment in every room while the place cells reorganize.
options.why: When place cells remap, grid cells and head-direction cells shift together into a new alignment. Remapping reaches beyond the place cells, which is one reason it is not only separation.

items.stem: A rat sits in a box it knows well, and nothing about the box changes. Researchers then silence the input to the rat’s hippocampus from the entorhinal cortex. What happens to its place cells?

options.text: They remap: some fire in new places and others fall silent, though the box itself has not changed.
options.why: Correct. Silencing input from the entorhinal cortex causes remapping. That is one reason remapping is not only pattern separation in the dentate gyrus.

options.text: They keep the familiar map, since remapping happens only when the room or its landmarks change.
options.why: Moving to a new room does cause remapping, but it is not the only cause. Silencing input from the entorhinal cortex causes remapping in a box that has not changed.

options.text: They keep the familiar map, since CA3 recovers the stored pattern from whatever input still reaches it.
options.why: CA3 does recover a stored map from part of it when some landmarks are removed. But silencing input from the entorhinal cortex causes remapping, not a recovered map.

options.text: They all fall silent at once, since place cells cannot fire without input from the entorhinal cortex.
options.why: Silencing input from the entorhinal cortex does not silence every place cell. It causes remapping, in which some cells fire in new places and others fall silent.

items.stem: Suppose the input from the dentate gyrus to CA3 is blocked in a rat. The rat is returned to a room it already knows, and later put in a new room much like that familiar room. According to the reading, what would CA3 be expected to do?

options.text: Recall the map of the familiar room as usual, but fail to keep a separate map for the similar new room.
options.why: Correct. CA3 needs input from the dentate gyrus to keep maps separate, but not to recall a map it already has.

options.text: Fail to recall the map of the familiar room, but keep a separate map for the similar new room as usual.
options.why: The two halves are reversed. CA3 does not need dentate input to recall a map it already has, but it does need that input to keep maps separate.

options.text: Recall the familiar map and keep a separate map for the new room, since CA3 never depends on the dentate gyrus.
options.why: CA3 does recall a map it already has without dentate input. But it needs that input to keep maps separate, so the similar new room would not get a map of its own.

options.text: Fail both to recall the familiar map and to keep a new one apart, since all its input passes through the dentate gyrus.
options.why: CA3 also receives input directly from the entorhinal cortex, and it recalls a map it already has without dentate input. What it loses is the ability to keep maps separate.

items.stem: About the dentate gyrus and pattern separation, what has been found, and what is still a model?

options.text: Dentate cells respond to small changes in the shape of a box that CA3 cells ignore, but whether their sparse firing does the separating is still a model.
options.why: Correct. Dentate cells respond to changes that CA3 cells ignore, and damage to the dentate gyrus impairs telling apart places that differ only slightly. Whether the sparse firing of dentate cells is what does the separating is still a model.

options.text: Dentate cells respond to small changes in the shape of a box that CA3 cells ignore, and their sparse firing has been found to be what does the separating.
options.why: Dentate cells do respond to small changes that CA3 cells ignore. But whether their sparse firing does the separating is still a model, not a finding.

options.text: CA3 cells respond to small changes in the shape of a box that dentate cells ignore, and whether the firing of CA3 cells does the separating is still a model.
options.why: The regions are swapped. Dentate cells respond to small changes in the shape of a box that CA3 cells ignore.

options.text: Dentate cells respond to small changes in the shape of a box that CA3 cells ignore, and CA3 needs input from the dentate gyrus to recall a map it already has.
options.why: CA3 needs dentate input to keep maps separate, not to recall a map it already has. And whether sparse dentate firing does the separating is still a model.

items.stem: In one experiment, a square box was changed step by step toward a circle while a rat’s place cells were recorded. What did the place cells do?

options.text: They kept the square’s map through the first steps, and then switched all at once to the circle’s map.
options.why: Correct. That is how a set of cells with a few stable states would behave. The choice between maps can be seen in the place cells.

options.text: They shifted their fields a little at each step, so the map changed smoothly along with the shape of the box.
options.why: A smooth change would follow the box step by step. Instead, the cells kept the square’s map for a while and then switched all at once, like cells with a few stable states.

options.text: They switched to the circle’s map at the very first step, as soon as the box was no longer a square.
options.why: The cells did not switch at the first change. They kept the square’s map for a while, and only then switched all at once to the circle’s map.

options.text: They fell silent one by one as the box changed, until none of the cells from the square’s map still fired.
options.why: Cells falling silent is part of remapping, but it did not happen one by one. The cells kept the square’s map for a while and then switched all at once to the circle’s map.

items.stem: As a box is changed step by step from a square toward a circle, a rat’s place cells keep one map and then switch all at once to another. What can be concluded from the all-at-once switch?

options.text: The cells behave like a set with a few stable states, keeping a slightly changed box on the square’s map up to a point, then giving it a new map.
options.why: Correct. The switch is the choice of which map an animal is on, seen in cells. A changed place is matched to its stored map until it differs enough to get a map of its own.

options.text: The cells track the box’s shape directly, so their fields move by about the same amount at each step of the change from the square to the circle.
options.why: Fields that moved at each step would mean the cells were following the shape smoothly. The cells kept the square’s map for a while instead, then switched all at once.

options.text: The cells make the overlapping inputs of each step less alike, giving each slightly changed box a separate map of its own as the change goes on.
options.why: Giving each step its own map would be separation at each step. The cells kept one map across the first steps and switched only once, like cells with a few stable states.

options.text: The cells recover the whole square map from part of it at each step, so the circle’s map does not form, however round the box becomes in the end.
options.why: Recovering a stored map from part of it is pattern completion, which CA3 shows when some landmarks are removed. In the changing box, the cells did not stay on the square’s map. They switched, all at once, to the circle’s map.

items.stem: A rat’s place cells have a stable map of a familiar box. One day, several of the cues around the box are taken away, and the place fields in CA3 stay where they were. Which process fits what the CA3 place cells did?

options.text: Pattern completion, recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, applied to a place.
options.why: Correct. CA3 keeps place fields intact when some landmarks are removed, recovering the familiar box’s whole map from the cues that remain.

options.text: Pattern separation, making overlapping inputs less alike, so a later stage can tell them apart.
options.why: Pattern separation keeps similar places apart, and the dentate gyrus is thought to do it. Keeping the same map with some cues missing is pattern completion.

options.text: Remapping, reorganizing the place cells so that some fire in new places and others fall silent.
options.why: Remapping would move the fields, and here they stayed where they were. Keeping the same map with some cues missing is pattern completion.

options.text: Reorientation, recovering which way an animal is facing, and where, after it is disoriented.
options.why: Nothing in the case disoriented the rat. CA3 keeping the familiar map when some cues are gone is pattern completion, recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it.

items.stem: Rats were moved between two boxes with different cues, and mice between a real box and a virtual one, while their place cells and grid cells were recorded. What changed from one room to the other, and what was kept?

options.text: The place fields moved and the grids shifted, yet a place cell tended to fire where the same grid cell was active in both rooms.
options.why: Correct. Remapping changes the place fields and shifts the grids, but it keeps something: the tie between a place cell and a grid cell tended to survive the move.

options.text: The place fields moved while the grids stayed put, so a place cell’s field fell on different grid locations in the two rooms.
options.why: The grids did not stay put; they shifted along with the place fields. And a place cell tended to fire where the same grid cell was active in both rooms.

options.text: The place fields moved and the grids shifted, and no relation between a place cell and a grid cell survived from one room to the other.
options.why: The place fields did move and the grids did shift. But a relation survived: a place cell tended to fire where the same grid cell was active in both rooms.

options.text: The grids shifted while the place fields stayed put, so each place cell kept firing in the same spot in both of the rooms.
options.why: The place cells remapped between the two rooms, so their fields moved. What was kept was a tendency for a place cell to fire where the same grid cell was active.

items.stem: One model of the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex had predicted that, across rooms, a place cell would tend to fire where the same grid cell was active. What feature of the model leads to that prediction?

options.text: Entorhinal cells code layout in the same way in every room, and hippocampal cells tie that code to what is sensed in each room.
options.why: Correct. If the layout code is shared across rooms and each place cell ties into it, a place cell should keep its relation to a grid cell even as both shift.

options.text: Entorhinal cells code a separate layout for every room, and hippocampal cells copy each layout with no regard to what is sensed.
options.why: A separate layout for every room would give no reason for a place cell to keep its relation to a grid cell. In the model, entorhinal cells code layout the same way in every room.

options.text: Hippocampal cells code layout in the same way in every room, and entorhinal cells tie that code to what is sensed in each room.
options.why: The roles are swapped. In the model, entorhinal cells code layout the same way in every room, and hippocampal cells tie that code to what is sensed in each room.

options.text: Entorhinal and hippocampal cells both code layout in the same way in every room, so neither set of cells changes between rooms.
options.why: In the experiment, the place cells remapped and the grids shifted, so both sets of cells changed. In the model, hippocampal cells tie a shared layout code to what is sensed in each room.

items.stem: Across two rooms, a place cell tended to fire where the same grid cell was active. The correlation was 0.322 across 115 pairs of cells in seven rats, and 0.273 across 64 pairs in four mice. How is that relation best described?

options.text: As modest: a tendency found in both rats and mice, well short of a place cell always firing on the same grid cell’s locations.
options.why: Correct. The relation was modest. Remapping keeps something, but only as a tendency, with correlations of 0.322 in rats and 0.273 in mice.

options.text: As strong: in both rats and mice, nearly every place cell fired on the same grid cell’s locations in each of the two rooms.
options.why: Correlations of 0.322 and 0.273 are not a near-perfect match. The relation was modest, a tendency rather than a rule.

options.text: As absent: with correlations of that size, place cells and grid cells were in effect unrelated once the animals changed rooms.
options.why: Correlations of 0.322 and 0.273 are modest but not zero, and the tendency appeared in both rats and mice. The relation was modest, not absent.

options.text: As limited to rats: the rats showed the tendency, but in the mice no relation between the place cells and the grid cells was found.
options.why: The tendency was found in both species: 0.322 across 115 pairs in seven rats, and 0.273 across 64 pairs in four mice. In both, the relation was modest.

items.stem: What does the hippocampus code about an object?

options.text: Little about the object in itself, and much about the place and the context the object was in.
options.why: Correct. A structure that keeps a map can keep more than places. Damage to the hippocampus spares a sense of familiarity and impairs learning where objects are.

options.text: Much about the object in itself, such as its shape, and little about where or in what context it was.
options.why: That reverses the account. The hippocampus codes little about objects in themselves and much about the place and context an object was in.

options.text: Mainly whether the object has been seen before, the sense of familiarity that damage to the hippocampus removes.
options.why: Damage to the hippocampus spares a sense of familiarity. What it impairs is learning where objects are, because the hippocampus codes the place and context an object was in.

options.text: Little about objects or their places, since its cells fire only for the animal’s own position in its surroundings.
options.why: Place cells do fire for the animal’s own position, but the hippocampus also codes the place and context an object was in. Damage to it impairs learning where objects are.

items.stem: A woman with damage to her hippocampus is shown a room with several objects in it. Later she is tested on the objects. Which pattern of results would be expected?

options.text: She finds the objects familiar, but has trouble remembering where in the room each object was.
options.why: Correct. Damage to the hippocampus spares a sense of familiarity and impairs learning where objects are. People with such damage have trouble remembering where several objects were in a room.

options.text: She remembers where in the room each object was, but no longer finds any of the objects familiar.
options.why: That reverses the pattern. Familiarity is spared by damage to the hippocampus, and memory for where objects were is impaired.

options.text: She neither finds the objects familiar nor remembers where they were, since both rest on her hippocampus.
options.why: Memory for where objects were does rest on the hippocampus, but a sense of familiarity is spared when the hippocampus is damaged.

options.text: She finds the objects familiar and remembers where they were, since the hippocampus serves only for finding the way.
options.why: The hippocampus is needed for more than finding the way. A structure that keeps a map also keeps where objects were, and damage to it impairs that memory.

items.stem: Rats become familiar with two objects in one setting and two other objects in a second setting. When an object from the first setting turns up in the second, the rats explore it longer. Why does the longer exploring count as memory for which thing was where, rather than for the object alone?

options.text: The object and the setting are both familiar, so only their pairing is new, and the longer exploring is evidence that the rats remembered the pairing.
options.why: Correct. Nothing about the object or the setting is new on its own. And damage to an input of the entorhinal cortex removes the preference while sparing ordinary recognition.

options.text: The object is new to the rats in the test, so exploring it longer is a sign of ordinary recognition that an object has not been seen before.
options.why: The object is not new. The rats saw it in the first setting, so only its turning up in the second setting is new.

options.text: The second setting is new to the rats in the test, so the longer exploring is a response to a setting they have never been in before.
options.why: The second setting is familiar too. The rats had already explored two other objects there, so only the object’s turning up in that setting is new.

options.text: Ordinary recognition of a familiar object produces the preference, since damage that removes the preference also removes recognition.
options.why: Damage to an input of the entorhinal cortex removes the preference while sparing ordinary recognition. So the preference rests on memory for the pairing, not on recognition alone.

items.stem: In one recent study of food-caching chickadees, what was found in the birds’ hippocampal cells?

options.text: Each hidden seed was marked by activity in its own group of cells, and the same activity returned when the bird came back for the seed.
options.why: Correct. Each hidden seed was marked by activity in its own group of hippocampal cells, and the same pattern of activity came back when the bird returned to that seed.

options.text: All hidden seeds were marked by activity in one shared group of cells, which fired whenever the bird hid or found any seed at all.
options.why: The seeds were not marked by one shared group. Each hidden seed was marked by activity in its own group of hippocampal cells.

options.text: Each hidden seed was marked by activity in its own group of cells, but different activity appeared when the bird came back for the seed.
options.why: Each hidden seed was marked by activity in its own group of cells, but the activity did not change. The same activity returned when the bird came back for the seed.

options.text: No hippocampal cells responded to hidden seeds, since the hippocampus codes the bird’s own place rather than the places of things.
options.why: The hippocampus codes much about the place an object was in. In the chickadees, each hidden seed was marked by activity in its own group of cells.

items.stem: Two views of what the hippocampus is for put space and memory in different orders. How do the map-first view and the memory-first view differ?

options.text: On the map-first view, the hippocampus served first as a map, and memory for what happened where grew out of that. On the memory-first view, memory came first, and space is one relation among many.
options.why: Correct. The map-first and memory-first views are two of three. On the remaining view, the same circuit suits both equally, and none of the three is chosen.

options.text: On the map-first view, memory for what happened where came first, and the map grew out of that memory. On the memory-first view, space came first, and memory is one relation among many.
options.why: The two views are scrambled. On the map-first view, the map came first and memory grew out of it. On the memory-first view, memory came first and space is one relation among many.

options.text: On the map-first view, the hippocampus served first as a map, and memory for what happened where grew out of that. On the memory-first view, memory came first, and space is handled by other structures.
options.why: The map-first view is right as stated, but on the memory-first view, space is not handed elsewhere. Space is one relation among many that memory relates.

options.text: On the map-first view, the hippocampus served first as a map, and memory for what happened where grew out of that. On the memory-first view, the same circuit suits maps and memory equally.
options.why: A circuit that suits both equally is a separate view, not the memory-first view. On the memory-first view, memory came first, and space is one relation among many.

items.stem: A student writes that, according to the reading, the hippocampus began as a map, with memory for what happened where growing out of it later. Is the student’s summary accurate?

options.text: No. The comparative evidence gives the map-first view its weight, but partly through what was tested, and that view is one of three left open.
options.why: Correct. No view is chosen. The comparative evidence gives the map-first view its weight, but nearly all comparative work has looked at memory for places.

options.text: Yes. The comparative evidence from fish, reptiles, and birds settles the question for the map, since every species tested has place memory.
options.why: The comparative evidence does give the map-first view its weight, but it settles nothing. Nearly all of that work has looked at memory for places, and no view is chosen.

options.text: No. In the reading, the conclusion is that memory came first, and that space is only one relation among many that memory relates.
options.why: Memory first is one of the three views, not a conclusion. None of the three is chosen, and the comparative evidence gives the map-first view its weight.

options.text: No. In the reading, the conclusion is that the same circuit suits maps and memory equally well, so neither of the two can have come first.
options.why: A circuit suited to both equally is one of the three views, not a conclusion. None of the three is chosen.

items.stem: In goldfish, turtles, and birds, damage to the hippocampal region impairs memory for places. Those lesion results fit the view that the hippocampus began as a map. Why do the results not settle the question?

options.text: Nearly all comparative work has looked at memory for places, so the evidence is partly a matter of what was tested, and other kinds of memory were rarely looked for.
options.why: Correct. The comparative evidence gives the map-first view its weight, but partly through what was tested. Other kinds of memory were rarely looked for.

options.text: The animals compared are living cousins rather than ancestors, so nothing at all can be learned from them about what an ancestral hippocampus did.
options.why: They are living cousins, but comparing them is how an old ability is inferred. When distantly related species share a capacity, the simplest reading is that their common ancestor very probably had it.

options.text: The region damaged in fish lies on the side of the forebrain, not at its inner edge, so it is not the same region as the mammalian hippocampus.
options.why: The fish’s region does lie on the side, but because the fish forebrain folds outward. The region is agreed to be the same region across these animals.

options.text: Damage in these animals also removes the ability to follow a visible cue to a goal, so the impairment is not specific to memory for places.
options.why: Damage to the region spares cue-following. Goldfish, turtles, and birds with such damage still learn a goal marked by a cue, as rats do.

items.stem: A rat given a shock moments after entering a box learns little fear of the box, while a rat that explored the box first learns a lot. What happens when the exploring rat’s hippocampus is silenced during its exploration?

options.text: The head start from exploring is removed, so exploring the box first no longer helps the rat learn fear of it.
options.why: Correct. The hippocampus is needed to learn from exploring. Without it during the exploration, the rat gains no head start.

options.text: The head start from exploring is kept, since the hippocampus is working again by the time of the shock.
options.why: The hippocampus is working at the time of the shock, but the learning from exploring happened earlier. Silencing the hippocampus during the exploration removes the head start.

options.text: The rat learns more fear than a normal explorer, since a box that was not learned seems more threatening.
options.why: Silencing the hippocampus during exploration does not add fear. Silencing removes the head start that exploring the box first would have given.

options.text: The head start is kept, since the exploring itself, not the hippocampus, is what gives the rat its head start.
options.why: Exploring does give the head start, but only when the hippocampus is working during it. Silencing the hippocampus during exploration removes the head start.

items.stem: A rat that explored a box before being shocked in it learns much more fear of the box than a rat shocked moments after entering. Silencing the hippocampus during the exploration removes that head start. Why does the result count as latent learning, located in tissue?

options.text: The rat learned about the box while exploring, though nothing showed in its behavior. The learning appeared once the shock gave a reason to use it, and it needs the hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. Latent learning does not show in behavior when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it. Because silencing the hippocampus during exploration removes the head start, that learning depends on the hippocampus.

options.text: Exploring let the rat learn a turn that leads out of the box. The turn showed once the shock came, and the hippocampus is the structure needed for learning such turns.
options.why: Learning a turn is response learning, and silencing the striatum, not the hippocampus, removes it. What the rat learned while exploring was the box itself, shown only later.

options.text: Exploring made the box familiar to the rat. That familiarity alone produced the extra fear, so the hippocampus is the structure needed for a sense of familiarity.
options.why: Damage to the hippocampus spares a sense of familiarity. What the hippocampus is needed for here is the learning during exploration that showed only once the shock came.

options.text: The rat learned about the box while exploring, and the learning showed at once in how it moved. The hippocampus is needed for learning to show in behavior right away.
options.why: Learning that shows at once in behavior is not latent. Latent learning does not show when it happens, and appears later, once there is a reason to use it, as when the shock came.

items.stem: Novelty releases dopamine in the hippocampus. From which two sources does that dopamine come?

options.text: The ventral tegmental area and the locus coeruleus.
options.why: Correct. The ventral tegmental area is a source of dopamine in the midbrain. The locus coeruleus is the main source of norepinephrine, and its axons release dopamine as well.

options.text: The ventral tegmental area and the dentate gyrus.
options.why: The ventral tegmental area is one source. The dentate gyrus is part of the hippocampus itself, the region that passes entorhinal input on to CA3. The second source is the locus coeruleus.

options.text: The locus coeruleus and the medial entorhinal cortex.
options.why: The locus coeruleus is one source. The medial entorhinal cortex sends the hippocampus spatial input, but the second dopamine source is the ventral tegmental area.

options.text: The prefrontal cortex and the ventral striatum.
options.why: In people, the frontmost part of the prefrontal cortex is engaged in directed exploration, and in monkeys the value of exploring has been recorded in the ventral striatum. The two sources of novelty dopamine in the hippocampus are the ventral tegmental area and the locus coeruleus.

items.stem: The ventral tegmental area and the locus coeruleus both release dopamine in the hippocampus when an animal encounters something new. How do the two sources differ?

options.text: The ventral tegmental area is a source of dopamine in the midbrain; the locus coeruleus is the main source of norepinephrine, and its axons release dopamine as well.
options.why: Correct. Both release dopamine in the hippocampus, and neurons in both become more active when an animal encounters something new. They differ in what else they are: the locus coeruleus is also the main source of norepinephrine.

options.text: The ventral tegmental area is the main source of norepinephrine, and its axons release dopamine as well; the locus coeruleus is a source of dopamine in the midbrain.
options.why: The two descriptions are swapped. The locus coeruleus is the main source of norepinephrine, and the ventral tegmental area is a source of dopamine in the midbrain.

options.text: The ventral tegmental area becomes more active when an animal encounters something new; the locus coeruleus becomes more active only once a place has grown familiar.
options.why: Neurons in both sources become more active when an animal encounters something new. That shared response is why both count as sources of novelty dopamine.

options.text: The ventral tegmental area sends dopamine only to CA3 in the hippocampus; the locus coeruleus sends dopamine to every part of the hippocampus except CA3.
options.why: The locus coeruleus does send input to CA3: silencing that input blocks the memory of a new setting. The two differ in what they are: the ventral tegmental area is a source of dopamine in the midbrain, and the locus coeruleus is the main source of norepinephrine.

items.stem: In mice learning a new maze, stimulating either dopamine input to the hippocampus made the new place map steadier. Silencing the locus coeruleus input to CA3 blocked the memory of a new setting. Which conclusion is supported by the mouse results?

options.text: Dopamine input can steady a new place map and supports memory of somewhere new; whether that dopamine drives exploring is left open.
options.why: Correct. Both results concern the map and the memory of a new place, not whether the animal explores.

options.text: Dopamine released by novelty is what drives the animal to explore a new place; in the experiments, mice without the inputs explored less.
options.why: Novelty does release dopamine in the hippocampus, but the mouse results concern maps and memory, not whether the animal explores.

options.text: Dopamine released by novelty is how the brain detects that a place is new; the experiments identified which cells first register a new place.
options.why: How the brain detects that a place is new is less settled. The mouse results concern what dopamine does for maps and memory once it is released.

options.text: Dopamine released by novelty comes from two inputs with separate jobs; in the experiments, one input built maps and the other kept memory.
options.why: Why the hippocampus has two dopamine inputs is not known. And stimulating either input made the new map steadier, so no such division of jobs was found.

items.stem: Which question about novelty and dopamine in the hippocampus is still not answered?

options.text: Why the hippocampus receives dopamine from two separate inputs rather than from only one.
options.why: Correct. Why the hippocampus has two dopamine inputs is not known. How the brain detects that a place is new is also less settled.

options.text: Whether novelty releases any dopamine in the hippocampus at all, or only norepinephrine.
options.why: Novelty does release dopamine in the hippocampus, from the ventral tegmental area and the locus coeruleus. What is not known is why there are two inputs.

options.text: Whether neurons in either dopamine source become more active when an animal finds something new.
options.why: Neurons in both sources become more active when an animal encounters something new. What is not known is why the hippocampus has two such inputs.

options.text: Whether silencing the locus coeruleus input to CA3 affects the memory of a new setting.
options.why: Silencing that input blocks the memory of a new setting, in mice. What is not known is why the hippocampus has two dopamine inputs.

items.stem: What are dopamine neurons in monkeys reported to respond to?

options.text: The chance of early information, and novelty, with a response that fades as things become familiar.
options.why: Correct. Dopamine neurons in monkeys are reported to respond to both, and the response fades as things become familiar. If so, the idea of a prediction error extends to information and novelty.

options.text: Familiar rewards only, with a response that grows stronger as the same reward is given again and again.
options.why: The reported response is to novelty and to the chance of early information, and it fades rather than grows as things become familiar.

options.text: The direction of the head, with a response that drifts in darkness until a familiar landmark comes into view.
options.why: That describes head-direction cells, which signal heading. Dopamine neurons in monkeys are reported to respond to the chance of early information and to novelty.

options.text: Novelty only when a reward follows, with no response to information that changes nothing about the reward.
options.why: The reported response includes the chance of early information, even though learning early changes nothing about what the monkey gets. Novelty draws a response too.

items.stem: A rat’s place cells have a stable map of a familiar square box. In a short paragraph, answer three questions. What do place cells in CA3 do when some of the box’s landmarks are removed? What do place cells do when the box is changed step by step toward a circle? And how are the two behaviors related?
items.answer: When some landmarks are removed, CA3 keeps the place fields intact. Keeping the fields is pattern completion: recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, applied to a place. When the box is changed step by step toward a circle, the place cells keep the square’s map for a while. Then they switch all at once to the circle’s map, which is how a set of cells with a few stable states would behave. Both are the choice of which map the animal is on, carried out by cells. With landmarks missing, the cells stay on the stored map. When the box has changed enough, they switch to a different map, rather than changing smoothly with the box.
rubric: Says CA3 keeps place fields intact when some landmarks are removed.
Names that as pattern completion, recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it.
Says the place cells kept the square’s map for a while and then switched all at once to the circle’s map.
Says the switch is how cells with a few stable states would behave, or calls it the choice of map seen in cells.
Relates the two: completion keeps the stored map when part of the input is missing, while enough change calls up a different map.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the three views of what the hippocampus is for. Then explain why the comparative evidence from fish, reptiles, and birds does not settle which view is right.
items.answer: On one view, the hippocampus served first as a map, and memory for what happened where grew out of that. On another, memory came first, and space is one relation among many. On a third, the same circuit suits both equally. The comparative evidence gives the map-first view its weight, since damage to the hippocampal region impairs memory for places across many vertebrates. But that evidence is partly a matter of what was tested. Nearly all comparative work has looked at memory for places, and other kinds of memory have rarely been tested. None of the three views is chosen.
rubric: States the map-first view: the hippocampus served first as a map, and memory for what happened where grew out of it.
States the memory-first view: memory came first, and space is one relation among many.
States the third view: the same circuit suits both equally.
Says the comparative evidence gives the map-first view its weight.
Says nearly all comparative work has looked at memory for places, so the evidence partly reflects what was tested.

items.stem: In a few sentences, say where the dopamine that novelty releases in the hippocampus comes from. Then say what experiments in mice found the dopamine does, and which questions remain open.
items.answer: Novelty releases dopamine in the hippocampus from two sources. One is the ventral tegmental area, a source of dopamine in the midbrain. The other is the locus coeruleus, the main source of norepinephrine, whose axons release dopamine as well. Neurons in both become more active when an animal encounters something new. In mice, stimulating either input while the animal learned a new maze made its new place map steadier. Silencing the locus coeruleus input to CA3 blocked the memory of a new setting. These results concern maps and memory, not whether the animal explores. How the brain detects that a place is new is less settled, and why the hippocampus has two dopamine inputs is not known.
rubric: Names the two sources: the ventral tegmental area and the locus coeruleus.
Says neurons in both become more active with something new.
Says stimulating either input made a new place map steadier, or that silencing the locus coeruleus input to CA3 blocked memory of a new setting.
Says the results concern maps and memory, not whether the animal explores.
Says how novelty is detected is less settled, or that why there are two inputs is not known.

pools.title: Older Than Mammals, Growing a Map, and What the Chapter Concludes
pools.covers: reading §9.3.7, §9.3.8, §9.C · lecture 9.3 slides older_than_mammals, what_mammals_elaborated, growing_and_changing, an_old_map_in_a_new_animal

items.stem: Goldfish trained in a maze were tested again after damage to one region of the forebrain. What did the damage do to their performance?

options.text: They chose the rewarded place less often, about at chance from new starting points, yet learned a cue-marked goal as well as before.
options.why: Correct. Before the damage, the fish chose the rewarded place about 85% of the time; after it, about 60–65%, and about chance from starting points they had never used. Learning a goal marked by a visible cue was untouched. The damage impaired the place strategy and spared cue-following.

options.text: They learned a goal marked by a visible cue much less well than before, yet still chose the rewarded place from new starting points as often as before.
options.why: This reverses the result. The damaged fish lost much of their ability to find a place defined by the room around them, and kept their ability to learn a goal marked by a visible cue.

options.text: They lost both abilities to about the same degree, choosing near chance whether the goal was a place in the room or a spot marked by a visible cue.
options.why: The two abilities came apart. A goal marked by a visible cue was learned as well as before the damage, while finding the rewarded place fell, to about chance from new starting points.

options.text: They chose the rewarded place as often as before, since in fish that forebrain region plays no part in finding places, unlike the hippocampus of a rat.
options.why: The damage did affect them: choices of the rewarded place fell from about 85% to about 60–65%. That region is the fish’s counterpart of the hippocampus, and damaging it impairs finding a place by its position, as in rats.

items.stem: In a grid of feeders, goldfish with damage to one forebrain region found the rewarded feeder as well as intact fish did. Then the cues near the goal were removed, and only the damaged fish fell behind. How had the damaged fish been finding the goal?

options.text: They had been steering to a cue near the goal, which hid their weaker place-finding until the nearby cues were taken away.
options.why: Correct. The damage impaired finding a place by its position and spared cue-following. While cues sat near the goal, steering to them was enough, and the damage stayed hidden. With the cues gone, the intact fish, which could still find the place by its position in the room, did better than the damaged fish.

options.text: They had been finding the goal by its position in the room, and taking away the nearby cues disturbed the layout they relied on.
options.why: Finding a place by its position is the ability the damage impaired. The intact fish, which still had that ability, kept succeeding without the nearby cues. So the damaged fish’s earlier success must have come from the cues.

options.text: They had been repeating a fixed sequence of turns through the grid, which the removal of the nearby cues happened to interrupt.
options.why: Taking away cues near the goal does not interrupt a sequence of turns. The damaged fish kept up with the intact fish only while those cues were present, which points to steering toward a nearby cue.

options.text: They had lost the ability to learn a goal marked by a cue as well, which the removal of the nearby cues finally brought to light.
options.why: Damaged goldfish learned a goal marked by a visible cue as well as they had before the damage. Cue-following was the ability that survived the damage; finding a place by its position was the one that did not.

items.stem: Turtles with damage to the region corresponding to the hippocampus were given more training on a rewarded place. They relearned it, but only while they could see the part of the room behind the goal. How were they most likely finding the place?

options.text: They behaved as if matching a stored view of the goal’s surroundings, which can be matched only near the goal.
options.why: Correct. A stored view of what the surroundings look like from the goal is a snapshot, and a snapshot works only where those surroundings still look much as they did. Depending on a view of the room behind the goal is what we would expect of a turtle matching a snapshot. A turtle that knew where the place lies in the room would not need that view.

options.text: They had regained the place strategy completely, since the damaged region recovered over the course of the extra training.
options.why: A turtle that had fully regained the place strategy would not need one particular view to succeed. Their success depended on seeing the part of the room behind the goal, which points to matching a view.

options.text: They were steering to a visible cue at the goal, which damaged turtles could still learn as easily as intact turtles could.
options.why: Damaged turtles did still learn a goal marked by a cue. But here the goal was a place in the room, and what they needed was a view of the room behind it, as if matching a stored view.

options.text: They were keeping a running sum of their own turns and steps from the start, which needs no view of the room at all.
options.why: A running sum of the animal’s own movement needs no view of the room. These turtles succeeded only while they could see the part of the room behind the goal, so a view was what they used.

items.stem: In goldfish, turtles, birds, and rats, damage to a corresponding region of the forebrain impairs finding a place by its position and spares the ability to follow a cue. What is this pattern evidence for?

options.text: That these regions are homologs, inherited from a common ancestor, doing the same job in each of the four lines.
