options.why: Correct. The same damage producing the same split in animals this distantly related is evidence of homology: the region and its job very probably go back to a common ancestor. It is evidence rather than proof, and which part of the region matches which is still argued.

options.text: That these regions arose separately in each line, by convergent evolution, because each line faced the problem of finding places.
options.why: Convergence is the simpler reading when similar abilities rest on brain parts that are not counterparts, as with insects and vertebrates. Here the regions correspond, and damage does the same thing in each, which points to a shared origin.

options.text: That finding a place by its position first appeared in mammals, while the other animals solved their tasks by following cues.
options.why: Goldfish, turtles, and birds are all impaired at place-finding when their region is damaged, so the intact animals were using it. The ability is shared widely among vertebrates and is not new in mammals.

options.text: That following cues and finding places both depend on this one region, so that damage to it impairs the two strategies equally.
options.why: The damage impairs place-finding and spares cue-following, so the two strategies do not depend on the region equally. That split is the very result being explained.

items.stem: According to the lecture, the reasoning used to date an ability by comparing living animals applies to brain tissue too. Suppose the same lesion result is found in goldfish and in rats. Why would the result in goldfish and rats say more about the age of the region and its job than the same result in rats and mice alone?

options.text: Goldfish and rats are far more distantly related, so a region and job shared by both are likely to be far older.
options.why: Correct. When distantly related species share a capacity, homology is the simplest reading, and the more distant the species, the older the capacity is likely to be. Applied to tissue, a lesion result shared by goldfish and rats very probably goes back to a common ancestor that lived in water, long before mammals.

options.text: Goldfish and rats are far more distantly related, so the same result in both is more likely to have arisen twice, by convergence.
options.why: Convergence is the simpler reading when similar abilities rest on brain parts that are not counterparts. Here the regions correspond, and damage does the same thing in each. Greater distance points to an older shared origin, not to convergence.

options.text: Goldfish are simpler animals than rats, so a result found in goldfish shows the region and its job in their first, unchanged form.
options.why: Living goldfish are cousins of mammals, not their ancestors, and their brains have kept changing too. What the comparison gives is the age of the shared ancestor, not an unchanged early form of the region.

options.text: Goldfish live in water, so a result found in goldfish shows the region began as a help for swimming rather than for finding places.
options.why: Damage to the goldfish’s region impairs finding a place, just as in rats, so the job is the same in both. Living in water bears on where the common ancestor lived, not on what the region was for.

items.stem: In mammals, the hippocampal region sits at the inner edge of the forebrain. In goldfish, its counterpart sits on the side. Why?

options.text: In ray-finned fish, the forebrain develops by folding outward instead of inward, which moves the region to the side.
options.why: Correct. The embryonic forebrain of ray-finned fish folds outward rather than ballooning inward. The outward folding moves the counterpart of the hippocampus to the lateral part of the pallium, so the same region ends up in a different position.

options.text: In ray-finned fish, the hippocampal region was lost, and a region on the side of the forebrain took over its job by convergence.
options.why: The region was not lost. Damage to the region on the side has the same effect as damage to the hippocampus in rats, and its position follows from how the fish forebrain develops.

options.text: In ray-finned fish, the forebrain folds inward more deeply than a mammal’s does, which pushes the region out toward the side.
options.why: The direction is the other way. In ray-finned fish the forebrain folds outward instead of inward, and the outward folding is what moves the region to the side.

options.text: In ray-finned fish, the region moves to the side in adulthood, as the fish learns the layout of the water around it.
options.why: The region’s position is set as the forebrain develops in the embryo, by folding outward. It has nothing to do with what an adult fish learns.

items.stem: A student argues that the goldfish’s lateral pallium cannot be the counterpart of the mammalian hippocampus, because it lies on the side of the forebrain rather than at its inner edge. What is the best reply?

options.text: Its position follows from the fish forebrain folding outward, and damage to it has the same effect as damage in rats.
options.why: Correct. In ray-finned fish the forebrain folds outward instead of inward, which moves the counterpart of the hippocampus to the side. Position alone does not settle whether two regions correspond, and the lesion results match those in rats.

options.text: The student is right, since a region that does the same job from a different position must have arisen separately, by convergence.
options.why: A difference in position has a developmental explanation here, the outward folding of the fish forebrain. And damage to the region impairs finding a place by its position, as in rats, which is evidence of a shared origin.

options.text: The position does not matter, since any forebrain region with cells that fire by head direction is a counterpart of the hippocampus.
options.why: Head-direction cells lie along a chain of structures from the brainstem, through the thalamus, to the cortex. Firing by head direction does not by itself mark a region as the hippocampus’s counterpart.

options.text: The region is on the side in fish only because the fish hippocampus grew too large to fit at the inner edge of the forebrain.
options.why: Size is not the explanation. The region ends up on the side because the forebrain of ray-finned fish folds outward instead of inward as it develops.

items.stem: How do the spatial cells recorded in the goldfish’s lateral pallium compare with the spatial cells recorded in rats?

options.text: Goldfish cells fired by head direction, near walls, or with swimming speed, but none had a place field or a grid.
options.why: Correct. Of 132 cells recorded in freely swimming goldfish, 31 fired by head direction, 11 near the walls of the tank, and 43 with swimming speed. None had a place field or a grid, both of which rats have. The cells match the lesions, with differences.

options.text: Goldfish cells had place fields and grids much like a rat’s, but none of them fired by the direction of the head.
options.why: This reverses the recordings. Goldfish cells did fire by head direction, 31 of 132, while none had a place field or a grid.

options.text: Goldfish cells showed no spatial firing of any kind, so the lesion results in goldfish have no counterpart in their cells.
options.why: Goldfish cells did fire spatially, by head direction, near walls, and with swimming speed. It was place fields and grids that were missing.

options.text: Goldfish cells fired in grids across the tank, but none had a place field, so in fish grid cells appeared before place cells.
options.why: No goldfish cell had a grid. Grid cells have so far been found only in mammals: rats, mice, bats, monkeys, and people.

items.stem: In tufted titmice, songbirds that store food, most excitatory hippocampal cells are place cells, much as in rats. What follows about place cells in mammals?

options.text: Place cells are not unique to mammals, so they are not what sets the mammalian hippocampus apart.
options.why: Correct. Birds have place cells too, so place cells are not what is new in mammals. Grid cells, by contrast, have so far been found only in mammals, though that is a statement about what has been recorded so far.

options.text: Place cells are unique to mammals, and the titmice’s cells are look-alikes of another kind, since a bird’s brain lacks a hippocampus.
options.why: Birds do have a hippocampus, in the same place as a mammal’s, and it is agreed to be the same region. Place cells in titmice mean place cells are not unique to mammals.

options.text: Place cells must be built from grid cells, so titmice must have grid cells that have simply not been recorded yet.
options.why: Rat pups have place cells that track distance traveled before their grid cells appear, which counts against grid cells being the only route to place cells.

options.text: Place cells go with storing food, since zebra finches, which do not store food, turned out to have no place cells.
options.why: Zebra finches do have place cells, though fewer: 48 of 179 cells, against 321 of 538 in titmice. The researchers offer the link to storing food only as speculation.

items.stem: A 2017 review found no spatial cells reported in reptiles. What is the right way to read the review’s result?

options.text: As an absence of evidence: none had turned up by then, and a newer study could change the picture.
options.why: Correct. Finding no reports of spatial cells is not the same as finding that reptiles lack them. The statement is tied to the date of its review. And turtles do learn places, with a corresponding region that damage impairs.

options.text: As evidence of absence: reptiles lack spatial cells, so their hippocampal region must work unlike that of fish and of birds.
options.why: No reports is not the same as a finding that the cells are missing. The review’s result is an absence of evidence, and a newer report would change it.

options.text: As evidence that reptiles cannot find places by their position, since without spatial cells nothing could support doing so.
options.why: Turtles do learn a rewarded place, and damage to their corresponding region impairs it. Not having recorded spatial cells in reptiles says nothing against that.

options.text: As evidence that spatial cells first appeared in mammals, so that the spatial cells of fish and birds must have arisen separately.
options.why: Head-direction cells have been recorded in goldfish and quails, and place cells in titmice. Spatial cells are not confined to mammals, and the reptile result is only an absence of evidence.

items.stem: As far as the evidence goes, which of these does the mammalian brain have with no agreed counterpart in reptiles or birds?

options.text: A dentate gyrus, the part of the hippocampus that spreads its input across many sparsely firing cells.
options.why: Correct. As far as the evidence goes, mammals have a dentate gyrus, and no part of the reptile or bird hippocampus has been agreed to match it. The hedge matters: the claim is about what has been agreed, not a proof that nothing corresponds.

options.text: Head-direction cells, which fire when the animal’s head points in one direction, wherever the animal is.
options.why: Head-direction cells are not unique to mammals. About one hippocampal cell in eight in quails is a head-direction cell, and goldfish have them in the lateral pallium.

options.text: Place cells, which fire when the animal is in one part of its surroundings, whichever way it is facing.
options.why: Place cells are not unique to mammals. In tufted titmice, most excitatory hippocampal cells are place cells, much as in rats.

options.text: A hippocampus with ties to the septum below it, as well as to the thalamus and to the cortex above it.
options.why: Reptiles and birds have a hippocampus in the same place, connected to the thalamus, the septum, and the cortex. In mammals, the ties to the septum are in fact weaker.

items.stem: As far as the evidence goes, how does the mammalian hippocampus compare with the hippocampus of reptiles and birds?

options.text: The mammal’s has more parts, several with more than one layer of cells, that pass signals mostly one way.
options.why: Correct. In reptiles and birds, the hippocampus has two or three parts connected back and forth. The mammal’s has more parts, passing signals mostly one way. It also has stronger ties to the neocortex, weaker ones to the septum, and an entorhinal cortex with its grid system beside it.

options.text: The mammal’s has fewer parts, each with a single layer of cells, that pass signals back and forth between them.
options.why: This reverses the comparison. The two or three parts connected back and forth belong to reptiles and birds. The mammal’s hippocampus has more parts, passing signals mostly one way.

options.text: The two are built alike, part for part, and differ only in that the mammal’s contains place cells and the bird’s does not.
options.why: Titmice have place cells much as rats do, so place cells are not the difference. The difference is in how the region is built: more parts, a dentate gyrus, and signals passing mostly one way.

options.text: The mammal’s has more parts that pass signals mostly one way, and its ties to the neocortex are weaker than a bird’s.
options.why: The first half is right, but the ties go the other way. The mammalian hippocampus has stronger ties to the neocortex and weaker ones to the septum below it.

items.stem: Comparing the hippocampal region across fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals, what is agreed, and what is still argued?

options.text: That it is the same region in each line is agreed; which of its parts matches which is argued.
options.why: Correct. The region is agreed to be the same region across these animals. Which part matches which is argued, and one reviewer suggests that memory for many places arose in birds and mammals partly in parallel.

options.text: That its parts match one for one in each line is agreed; whether it is the same region at all is argued.
options.why: This reverses the two. That it is the same region is the agreed part. How its parts correspond, such as what in a bird matches the dentate gyrus, is what is argued.

options.text: That it arose separately in each line is agreed; whether it does the same job in each line is argued.
options.why: The region is agreed to be shared, not separate. And damage to the region impairs place-finding and spares cue-following in fish, turtles, birds, and rats alike.

options.text: That it is the same region in each line is agreed; whether damage to it impairs place-finding in fish is argued.
options.why: The lesion result in goldfish is clear: choices of the rewarded place fell, to about chance from new starting points, while cue-following was spared. What is argued is how the parts correspond.

items.stem: Titmice and rats both have hippocampal place cells, and both can remember many places. Does it follow that their memory for many places was inherited, part for part, from their common ancestor?

options.text: No, not necessarily: the region is agreed to be shared, but which part matches which is argued, and memory for many places may have arisen partly in parallel.
options.why: Correct. A shared region does not mean every part and every ability was shared. One reviewer suggests that memory for many places arose in birds and mammals partly in parallel, and the mammal’s dentate gyrus has no agreed counterpart in birds.

options.text: Yes: because the region is agreed to be the same in both lines, every ability it supports must already have been present in their common ancestor.
options.why: A shared region can be reworked in each line after the lines part. Which part matches which is argued, and memory for many places may have arisen partly in parallel.

options.text: No: the place cells of birds and of mammals sit in unrelated brain regions, so any resemblance can only be a case of convergence.
options.why: The bird’s hippocampus and the mammal’s are agreed to be the same region. What is argued is how their parts correspond, not whether the region is shared.

options.text: Yes: place cells have been found in every vertebrate tested so far, so memory for many places must be as old as the vertebrates.
options.why: Goldfish cells fire by head direction, near walls, and with speed, but none had a place field. And no spatial cells have been reported in reptiles, though that is an absence of evidence.

items.stem: In rat pups, the spatial cells appear in a particular order. Which kind comes first, and which comes last?

options.text: Head-direction cells come first, and grid cells come last.
options.why: Correct. Head-direction cells are adultlike at about two weeks, around the time the eyes open. Border cells and place cells follow, and grid cells appear last, at about 20 to 21 days.

options.text: Grid cells come first, and head-direction cells come last.
options.why: This reverses the order. Head-direction cells are adultlike at about two weeks, and grid cells appear last, at about 20 to 21 days.

options.text: Place cells come first, and head-direction cells come last.
options.why: Place cells are present at 16 to 17 days, after head-direction cells have become adultlike at about two weeks. Head-direction cells come first, not last.

options.text: Grid cells come first, and place cells come last.
options.why: Grid cells are the last to appear, at about 20 to 21 days. Place cells are present before them, though they are the slowest to mature, into the sixth week.

items.stem: A rat pup is 18 days old. Going by when each kind of spatial cell appears in rat pups, which would we expect to find in its brain?

options.text: Head-direction cells, border cells, and place cells that are still maturing, but no grid cells yet.
options.why: Correct. Head-direction cells are adultlike at about two weeks. Border cells are present by about 17 days, and place cells at 16 to 17 days, though they keep maturing into the sixth week. Grid cells do not appear until about 20 to 21 days.

options.text: Head-direction cells and grid cells, but no place cells or border cells, which appear only after the grids.
options.why: Grid cells come last, at about 20 to 21 days, so an 18-day pup has none yet. Place cells and border cells are already present by then.

options.text: All four kinds, head-direction, border, place, and grid cells, each of them already as mature as in an adult.
options.why: Place cells are present but keep maturing into the sixth week, and grid cells have not yet appeared at 18 days.

options.text: Grid cells only, since they appear first and the other spatial cells are later built from their firing.
options.why: Grid cells appear last, not first. And rat pups have place cells that track distance traveled before any grid cells appear.

items.stem: Before their grid cells appear, what can rat pups already do?

options.text: Find their way home by path integration, with place cells that track the distance traveled.
options.why: Correct. Pups home by path integration, and their place cells track distance traveled, before grid cells appear at about 20 to 21 days. That counts against grid cells being the only route to place cells.

options.text: Little of a spatial kind, since without grid cells a running sum of position cannot yet be kept.
options.why: Pups do keep track of where they have gone before grid cells appear: they home by path integration. And their place cells already track distance traveled.

options.text: Find their way home only by the smell of the nest, since no place cells are present yet.
options.why: Place cells are present at 16 to 17 days, before grid cells appear. And the pups home by path integration, not only by smell.

options.text: Keep a heading only, since head-direction cells are the sole spatial cells present before grids.
options.why: Head-direction cells do come first, but border cells and place cells are present before grid cells too. And pups already home by path integration.

items.stem: A student holds two hypotheses: grid cells keep the running sum of position, and place cells get their positions only from grid cells. Which finding in rat pups counts against the second hypothesis?

options.text: Pups home by path integration, and the pups’ place cells track distance traveled, before any grid cells appear.
options.why: Correct. If place cells got their positions only from grid cells, place cells could not track distance before grid cells existed. In pups they do, which counts against grid cells being the only route to place cells.

options.text: Head-direction cells are adultlike at about two weeks, before the other spatial cells, and act together as one ring.
options.why: That is true, but it concerns the heading signal, not where place cells get their positions. It neither supports nor counts against place cells depending only on grid cells.

options.text: Place cells are the slowest of the spatial cells to mature, and are still maturing into the sixth week after birth.
options.why: That is true, but slow maturing says nothing about whether place cells depend on grid cells. The finding that bears on that is place cells tracking distance before grids appear.

options.text: Grid cells mature almost at once after they first appear, at about 20 to 21 days, unlike the slow-maturing place cells.
options.why: That is true, but how fast grids mature does not bear on whether place cells need them. Place cells tracking distance before any grids exist is what counts against that.

items.stem: Researchers followed 79 men through the three to four years of training to become London taxi drivers. What did they find in the hippocampus?

options.text: The 39 who qualified gained gray matter in the back part of the hippocampus; those who failed, and a control group, did not.
options.why: Correct. Only the qualifiers gained. The same men were followed over time, but they were not randomly assigned to train. The qualifiers also trained more hours a week, and a predisposition cannot be ruled out.

options.text: All 79 trainees gained gray matter in the back part of the hippocampus, whether or not they went on to qualify in the end.
options.why: The gain was found only in the 39 who qualified. Those who failed did not gain gray matter, and neither did the control group.

options.text: The 39 who qualified gained gray matter throughout the hippocampus, and so did the control group, though by a smaller amount.
options.why: The gain was in the back part of the hippocampus, and only in the qualifiers. The control group, like those who failed, did not gain.

options.text: The trainees who failed gained the most gray matter, since they spent the most hours each week struggling with the streets.
options.why: It was the qualifiers who gained, and the qualifiers who trained more hours a week. Those who failed did not gain gray matter.

items.stem: A journalist describes the taxi-driver study as proof that learning a city’s streets makes the hippocampus grow. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: Trainees were not randomly assigned, the qualifiers trained more hours a week, and a predisposition cannot be ruled out.
options.why: Correct. The same people were followed over time, so the gain was seen within the qualifiers. But they were not assigned at random. Something about the men who went on to qualify, or their extra hours, could explain the gain.

options.text: Different men were compared at one moment in time, so no change within a single person over the training could be seen.
options.why: The same men were followed over time, which is the design’s strength. Its weakness is that they were not randomly assigned to train.

options.text: The qualifiers lost gray matter rather than gaining it, which is why they got worse at recalling a complex drawing afterward.
options.why: The qualifiers gained gray matter in the back part of the hippocampus. They also got worse at recalling a complex drawing, but that is a separate finding, not a loss of gray matter.

options.text: The control group gained as much gray matter as the qualifiers did, so the training itself made no difference to anyone.
options.why: The control group did not gain gray matter, and neither did the trainees who failed. Only the qualifiers gained.

items.stem: In the taxi-driver study, researchers followed the same trainees over time, but did not assign them to train at random. What does each of these two features mean for what can be concluded?

options.text: Following the same men shows the gain across training; without random assignment, a predisposition or extra hours could explain the gain.
options.why: Correct. According to the lecture, following the same people over time is a strength of the study. But the trainees were not assigned to train at random, and the qualifiers trained more hours a week. A predisposition cannot be ruled out, so the gain cannot be firmly credited to the training.

options.text: Following the same men rules out any predisposition; without random assignment, the gain in gray matter might not be real at all.
options.why: Following the same people over time does not rule out a predisposition; only random assignment would. And the gain itself was measured. What is uncertain is its cause.

options.text: Following the same men made a control group unnecessary; without random assignment, the qualifiers could not be compared with anyone.
options.why: There was a control group, which did not gain gray matter. And the qualifiers were compared both with the controls and with those who failed.

options.text: Following the same men makes the study randomized in effect; without random assignment, only the drawing result is in doubt.
options.why: Following people over time is not the same as assigning them at random. The missing random assignment leaves the gray matter result open to other explanations, not only the drawing result.

items.stem: How does finding the way change in later life?

options.text: Path integration is particularly vulnerable, and strategies using a map decline more than those using the body’s own frame.
options.why: Correct. In aging, keeping a running sum of one’s own movement is particularly vulnerable. And strategies that rely on a map decline more than strategies that work in the body’s own frame, such as a remembered sequence of turns.

options.text: Path integration is spared in later life, and strategies that use the body’s own frame decline more than those that use a map.
options.why: This reverses both halves. Path integration is particularly vulnerable in aging, and strategies that use a map decline more than those in the body’s own frame.

options.text: Path integration improves with experience, and strategies that use a map decline only once path integration itself has failed.
options.why: Path integration does not improve in aging; it is particularly vulnerable. And map strategies decline more than body-frame ones, not only after path integration fails.

options.text: Every way of finding the way declines equally, so no strategy holds up better in later life than any other does.
options.why: The decline is not even. Path integration is particularly vulnerable, and strategies that use a map decline more than those that use the body’s own frame.

items.stem: An older adult tries two tasks in a familiar neighborhood. In one, the person works out a new shortcut between two well-known places from knowledge of the layout. In the other, the person repeats a learned sequence of turns relative to the body: left at the first corner, then right. Compared with a younger adult, on which task would we expect the larger decline?

options.text: On the shortcut, since strategies that use a map decline more in aging than those that use the body’s own frame.
options.why: Correct. Working out a new shortcut from the layout uses a map, and map strategies decline more in later life. Repeating turns relative to the body works in the body’s own frame, which holds up better.

options.text: On the turns, since strategies that use the body’s own frame decline more in aging than those that use a map.
options.why: This reverses the finding. In aging, strategies that use a map decline more than strategies that use the body’s own frame.

options.text: On both equally, since aging slows every way of finding the way by about the same amount in each person.
options.why: The decline is not even across strategies. Map strategies decline more than body-frame ones, and path integration is particularly vulnerable.

options.text: On the turns, since a remembered sequence of turns depends on memory, while a shortcut is worked out on the spot.
options.why: A shortcut is worked out from a map, which also has to be remembered. And it is map strategies, not body-frame ones, that decline more in aging.

items.stem: A dog has walked a large park many times, always along the same few paths. Which of these feats is one that only the highest of the six kinds of knowledge about location allows?

options.text: Cutting across a lawn it has never crossed, to reach a gate hidden behind trees from where it stands.
options.why: Correct. Reaching a known place by a route never taken needs knowledge of where places lie relative to one another. Only that kind lets an animal go from anywhere to any place it knows, including by a new route such as a shortcut or a detour.

options.text: Running straight back to where its walk began, after a long and winding ramble through the park in the dark.
options.why: Getting back to the start from anywhere is the fifth kind of knowledge, the way back to the start. It needs no knowledge of where places lie relative to one another, and it leads to one place only.

options.text: Heading for a tall flagpole that it can see from far off, standing right beside the gate it wants to reach.
options.why: A flagpole beside the goal is a beacon, and using one is the second of the six kinds. A beacon helps only from where it can be sensed, and the dog needs to know only that the flagpole is near the goal.

options.text: Following its usual path from the bench to the gate, past the fountain, along the hedge, and around the pond.
options.why: Following a familiar path is the fourth kind, a route. A route can lead from far away, but only along its own path, so it does not let the dog take a way it has never taken.

items.stem: To reach a place it cannot sense, an animal has to know four things, and six kinds of knowledge about location can supply three of them. Which of the four is left over?

options.text: Which place is worth going to now, which depends on the animal’s state as well as on what it knows.
options.why: Correct. The six kinds of knowledge supply where the animal is, where the goal is, and which way to go. Which place is worth going to depends on the animal’s state, such as hunger or thirst, as well as on what it knows.

options.text: Where the animal is now, which depends on its own movement as well as on what it knows about the ground.
options.why: Where the animal is now is one of the three that the kinds of knowledge supply. The one left over is which place is worth going to, which depends on the animal’s state.

options.text: Where the goal lies, which depends on what the animal can sense as well as on what it remembers of the goal.
options.why: Where the goal is lies within what the six kinds of knowledge supply. The one left over is which place is worth going to now.

options.text: Which way to go, which depends on the shape of the ground as well as on what the animal knows of the goal.
options.why: Which way to go is one of the three the kinds of knowledge supply. The leftover is which place is worth going to, set partly by states such as hunger.

items.stem: A hiker in thick fog keeps track of position by counting paces and noting each compass turn. Every so often, a distinctive boulder looms out of the fog. How should the hiker use these two sources?

options.text: Together: the count covers the gaps between boulders, and each boulder recognized corrects the error the count has built up.
options.why: Correct. Animals rarely rely on one source alone. A running sum of one’s own movement keeps going between landmarks but drifts. A recognized, stable landmark can correct that drift, so each source makes up for the other’s weakness.

options.text: The pace count alone, since it keeps going between boulders, while a boulder glimpsed in thick fog could easily be mistaken for another one.
options.why: Landmarks can look alike, but the pace count drifts, with nothing in it to show how far. Ignoring the boulders would leave that drift uncorrected.

options.text: The boulders alone, since a pace count drifts, and a source that drifts gives no information worth keeping at all.
options.why: A drifting estimate is still informative between landmarks, where nothing else is available. The boulders correct the count; they do not replace it.

options.text: Each in turn, relying on the count in fog and on the boulders in clear weather, without ever combining the two.
options.why: The point of having both is to combine them, here in the same fog: the count fills the gaps, and each recognized boulder corrects the count.

items.stem: A running sum of an animal’s own movement and a stable landmark can each correct errors in the other. How do their weaknesses differ, so that each source can correct the other?

options.text: The sum keeps going between landmarks but drifts, with nothing to show how far; the landmark gives a drift-free fix, but only where recognized.
options.why: Correct. Each small error in heading or distance stays in the running sum, and nothing in the sum reveals how large the error has grown. A stable landmark gives a position independent of that history, but only where it can be sensed and recognized. So each covers the other’s weakness.

options.text: The sum gives a drift-free fix, but only where it is recognized; the landmark keeps going between fixes but drifts, with nothing to show how far.
options.why: This reverses the two. The running sum is the source that drifts and keeps going between landmarks. The landmark gives a fix free of drift, but only where it can be sensed.

options.text: The sum and the landmark drift in the same way and by the same amount, so combining the two cancels their errors exactly.
options.why: They fail in different ways, which is why combining them helps. The sum drifts; a stable landmark does not, but it can be out of sight or look like another landmark.

options.text: The sum points to any place the animal knows, from anywhere; the landmark points only back to the animal’s starting point.
options.why: This has the running sum backward. A home vector from a running sum points to one place, the start. A landmark helps wherever it can be recognized.

items.stem: Why do animals settle for rules of thumb when deciding whether to keep exploring?

options.text: No best answer to the trade-off between exploring and exploiting can be computed in a realistic world.
options.why: Correct. In a realistic world, options are many and much is unknown, so no general best answer to the trade-off can be computed. Every animal, and every machine, has to settle for rules of thumb.

options.text: Exploring never yields more than exploiting does, so a simple rule is enough to keep an animal near what it knows.
options.why: Exploring can yield more in the long run, which is the whole point of the trade-off. Its value lies in what it teaches, if there is time to use it.

options.text: Animals cannot remember what earlier trips found, so they cannot weigh a known option against an unknown one.
options.why: Remembering what earlier trips found is what lets an animal exploit a known option at all. The difficulty is that no best answer can be computed in a realistic world.

options.text: A best answer can be computed, but only by a machine, since a brain is too slow to finish the calculation in time.
options.why: Machines face the same limit. No general best answer can be computed in a realistic world, so animals and machines alike settle for rules of thumb.

items.stem: A crow has just eaten its fill. It then spends several minutes turning over leaves in a corner of its aviary it has never explored. Nothing there has ever been food, and no smell of food comes from it. What does the crow’s behavior illustrate?

options.text: Animals also seek information that no reward depends on, beyond what they need for food or for the way home.
options.why: Correct. Animals explore to find food and to learn the layout of a place, but they also seek information that no reward depends on. That is curiosity, a drive to gain information for its own sake.

options.text: Animals keep exploiting a patch already known to be decent, even well after their hunger has been satisfied.
options.why: Exploiting means taking an option already known to be decent. This corner is unexplored and has never held food, so the crow is not exploiting anything.

options.text: Animals that are full still forage as if hungry, since a full stomach does not change what a stimulus is worth.
options.why: Internal states such as hunger do change what a stimulus is worth. A full crow searching where food has never been is seeking information, not food.

options.text: Animals follow a gradient of smell toward a source of food, even one they cannot yet see or reach.
options.why: No smell of food comes from the corner, so there is no gradient to follow. The crow is seeking information that no reward depends on.

items.stem: A young animal lives where predators are rare for now. Why can it not simply wait to learn where places lie relative to one another until it needs an escape route?

options.text: Knowing where places lie has to be learned before it is used, which means exploring beforehand and giving up known meals for information that may never be needed.
options.why: Correct. Knowing where places lie relative to one another has to be learned before it can be used, and learning it means exploring. So the knowledge has to be built in advance, by giving up known meals for information that may never be needed.

options.text: Knowing where places lie can be worked out on the spot from a running sum of the animal’s own movement, so nothing about the layout has to be learned in advance.
options.why: A running sum points back to one place, the start, and gives no information about the way between other places. Knowing where places lie has to be learned before it is needed.

options.text: Knowing where places lie is present in the hippocampus from birth, so waiting to learn it would neither gain the animal anything nor lose it anything at all.
options.why: Knowing where places lie has to be learned, and learning it means exploring. Such knowledge is not present from birth, even if the tissue that keeps it is.

options.text: Knowing where places lie builds up by itself along the familiar paths the animal already takes, so no exploring beyond those paths is ever required of it.
options.why: Familiar paths are routes, which work only along their own path. Knowing where places lie relative to one another means going where the animal has not been.

items.stem: The goldfish’s lateral pallium and the rat’s hippocampus are taken to be the same region, inherited from a common ancestor. How does the region differ between the two?

options.text: In the goldfish it lies on the side of the forebrain, with cells responding to heading, walls, and speed; the rat’s has a dentate gyrus and a grid system beside it.
options.why: Correct. The region is the same in each line but has been reworked in each. In the goldfish it lies to the side, and its cells respond to heading, walls, and speed, without place fields or grids. In the rat it is a hippocampus with a dentate gyrus, and an entorhinal grid system beside it.

options.text: In the goldfish it is needed for following cues rather than for finding places; in the rat it is needed for finding places rather than for following cues.
options.why: The job is the same in both. Damage impairs finding a place by its position and spares cue-following, in goldfish as in rats.

options.text: In the goldfish it contains place cells and grid cells; in the rat it contains head-direction cells, with no place cells or grid cells of its own.
options.why: This reverses the recordings. Goldfish cells fire by heading, near walls, and with speed, but none had a place field or a grid. Rats have place cells and grid cells.

options.text: In the goldfish it sits at the inner edge of the forebrain, with a dentate gyrus; in the rat it sits on the side, with no grid system beside it.
options.why: This reverses the two. The fish forebrain folds outward, which moves the region to the side. The dentate gyrus and the grid system belong to the rat.

items.stem: Caching birds keep many hiding places apart, although no part of their hippocampus is agreed to match the dentate gyrus, the part thought to keep similar places apart in mammals. What does the caching birds’ case illustrate?

options.text: The same problem can be solved with different parts, which fits the view that what the hippocampus does has changed less than how it is built.
options.why: Correct. One reviewer’s summary is that across reptiles, birds, and mammals, what the hippocampus does has changed much less than how it is built. Caching birds solve the problem of keeping places apart, and how they do it is not yet known.

options.text: The structure is what has stayed constant, which fits the view that how the hippocampus is built has changed less than what it does.
options.why: This reverses the summary. The job, keeping track of places, has stayed much the same, while the way the region is built differs from one line to another.

options.text: The dentate gyrus plays no part in keeping similar places apart in mammals either, since birds manage the job without one.
options.why: In mammals, damage to the dentate gyrus impairs telling apart places that differ only slightly. That birds manage without one shows the job can be done by other parts, not that the dentate gyrus does nothing.

options.text: Caching birds must find their seeds by following cues, since a hippocampus with no dentate gyrus cannot keep track of positions.
options.why: Chickadees with damage to the hippocampus hide food normally but rarely find it again, and titmice have many place cells. The bird’s hippocampus does keep track of places, by means not yet known.

items.stem: According to the reading, what did the early mammal need in order to find its way home?

options.text: An old map, put to harder use by a warm body that needed more food.
options.why: Correct. The tissue that does the work of finding places is older than mammals. What changed for the early mammal was how hard that tissue was used. A warm body needed a great deal of food, found in poor light, with a trip home at the end.

options.text: A new map, built on place cells that first appeared in early mammals.
options.why: Place cells are not new in mammals; tufted titmice have them much as rats do. And the region that keeps the map is older than mammals.

options.text: A keener nose, able to sense its nest from anywhere in its range.
options.why: The animal was out of smell of its nest, so nothing at the nest could reach it. The problem was reaching a place it could not sense.

options.text: No map at all, since its running sum could lead it to anywhere it knew.
options.why: A running sum points back to one place, the start. And the region that keeps a map was already old, inherited and put to harder use.

items.stem: For the vertebrate brain as a whole, the demands on an animal barely changed over half a billion years, while the structures that met those demands were rebuilt several times. Which of these results fits that pattern?

options.text: In goldfish and rats, damage to a corresponding forebrain region impairs finding places by position, though the region is built differently in each.
options.why: Correct. The demand, reaching a place by its position, is shared by goldfish and rats, and the region that meets it is inherited. But it has been reworked in each line: on the side of the forebrain in the fish, with a dentate gyrus and a grid system in the rat.

options.text: Rats go to a place in rooms full of distinct objects, and repeat a turn in plain rooms, so the setting decides which tendency wins out.
options.why: That is true of rats, but it is about which strategy one animal uses in different settings. It says nothing about old demands met by structures rebuilt across lineages.

options.text: Head-direction cells appear before grid cells in rat pups, so the parts of the map are put in place in a fixed order.
options.why: That is true of rat pups, but it concerns development within one animal. The pattern in question is about demands that stayed the same while structures changed across lineages.

options.text: Taxi trainees who qualified gained hippocampal gray matter, so a structure grows within one lifetime to meet a new demand.
options.why: That is a change within one person’s life in response to a new demand, and a predisposition cannot be ruled out. The pattern in question is an old demand met by structures rebuilt over evolutionary time.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe what damage to a corresponding region of the forebrain does in goldfish, turtles, birds, and rats. Explain why that lesion result is evidence that the region is older than mammals. Then name two features that, as far as the evidence goes, the mammalian hippocampal region has and reptiles and birds do not.
items.answer: In all four kinds of animal, damage to the corresponding region impairs finding a place by its position, while sparing the ability to find a goal marked by a cue. Goldfish, for example, fell to about chance from new starting points, yet learned a cue-marked goal as well as before. When distantly related animals share a region that does the same job, the simplest reading is homology: the region and its job were inherited from a common ancestor. An ancestor shared with goldfish lived long before mammals. That is evidence, not proof, and which part matches which is still argued. As far as the evidence goes, mammals have a dentate gyrus with no agreed counterpart in reptiles or birds. Their hippocampus also has more parts, passing signals mostly one way, and an entorhinal cortex with a grid system beside it.
rubric: Says damage impairs finding a place by its position while sparing the ability to follow a cue or find a cue-marked goal.
Says the same result in such distantly related animals is evidence that the regions are homologs, inherited from a common ancestor and doing the same job.
Keeps a hedge: the lesion result is evidence rather than proof, or which part matches which is argued, or the mammalian features apply “as far as the evidence goes”.

Names two of: a dentate gyrus; more parts, passing signals mostly one way or with several layers of cells; an entorhinal cortex with its grid system; stronger ties to the neocortex and weaker ones to the septum.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe what researchers found in the hippocampus when they followed London taxi trainees through their training. Then explain why we cannot conclude that the training itself caused the change.
items.answer: Researchers followed 79 men through three to four years of training to learn the city’s streets. The 39 who qualified gained gray matter in the back part of the hippocampus, while those who failed, and a control group, did not. Following the same men over time is a strength, since the change was seen across the training. But the men were not randomly assigned to train. The qualifiers also trained more hours a week, and some predisposition in the men who went on to qualify cannot be ruled out. So the gain is consistent with training changing the hippocampus, but training has not been shown to cause it.
rubric: Says the trainees who qualified gained gray matter in the hippocampus (the back part), and those who failed and the controls did not.
Says the same people were followed over time (the design was longitudinal).
Says the trainees were not randomly assigned to train.
Names a rival explanation: the qualifiers trained more hours a week, or a predisposition cannot be ruled out.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what it means to say that the early mammal did not need a new map, but an old one put to harder use. Use the evidence from damage to the corresponding brain region in other vertebrates, and say what was harder for the early mammal.
items.answer: In a goldfish, a turtle, a bird, and a rat, damage to a corresponding forebrain region impairs finding a place by its position. All four can still find a goal marked by a cue. That region is the same region in each line, inherited from a common ancestor, so the tissue that does this work is older than mammals. The region has been reworked in each line. In a goldfish it sits on the side of the forebrain, and in a rat it is a hippocampus with a dentate gyrus and a grid system beside it. Finding the way fits the pattern seen for the vertebrate brain as a whole, where the demands barely changed while the structures that met them were rebuilt. What was harder for the early mammal was the use. A warm body needed a great deal of food, found in poor light, and the animal then had to get back home.
rubric: Says damage to the corresponding region impairs finding a place by its position, but spares finding a cue-marked goal, in animals as distant as goldfish and rats.
Says the region is inherited from a common ancestor, so the tissue is older than mammals.
Says the region has been reworked in each line, with an example (on the side in fish; dentate gyrus or grid system in mammals).
Says what was harder was the demand: a warm body that needed more food, found in poor light, with a trip home.
Links the case to the pattern of old demands met by rebuilt structures, or says the demand stayed while the structures changed.

items.stem: On the radiating paths, each rat is trained along the roundabout route once, the route is then blocked, and a fan of twelve paths is offered. Path 6 ends nearest the old food box, paths 4 and 5 lie beside the blocked route, and the lamp stands on its post behind the food box. With The lamp set to in place, which of the six rats took path 6?

options.text: The healthy rat and every hidden rat but one, the rat following a route, which took paths 4 and 5 beside the blocked route.
options.why: Correct. With the lamp in place, H and the hidden rats following a beacon, a snapshot, or a map all took path 6, and so did the rat with damage to the hippocampus. Only the route rat went elsewhere, to paths 4 and 5. In this room, heading for the lamp and heading for the goal are nearly the same thing, and four different programs and the healthy rat ended up on the same path. A new route is therefore not proof, on its own, of knowing where places lie: a beacon can produce the same result. The programs follow their strategies every time, while in the original experiment only 19 of 53 rats took the path nearest the food box.

options.text: The healthy rat and the hidden rats following a beacon, a snapshot, or a map; the rat with damage to the hippocampus took paths 4 and 5.
options.why: Without its map, the rat with damage to the hippocampus is left with a beacon and a route, and its route does lead to paths 4 and 5. With the lamp in place, though, the damaged rat took path 6, as the beacon rat did. Only the route rat went to paths 4 and 5.

options.text: The healthy rat, the hidden rats following a beacon or a map, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus; the snapshot rat showed no preferred path.
options.why: A snapshot can be matched only near the goal, so it is natural to expect the snapshot rat to show no preference at the table where the fan begins. With the lamp in place, though, the snapshot rat took path 6. The snapshot rat lost that path when the lamp was switched off. Only the route rat went elsewhere, to paths 4 and 5.

options.text: Only the hidden rats following a beacon, a snapshot, or a map; the healthy rat took paths 4 and 5, beside the blocked route.
options.why: The healthy rat took path 6 as well, and so did the rat with damage to the hippocampus. The rat that took paths 4 and 5 was the one following a route, which repeats its trained turns.

items.stem: On the radiating paths, every rat is run with The lamp set to in place, and then again with it switched off. Which rats took a different path with the lamp off from the path they had taken with it in place?

options.text: The beacon rat, the snapshot rat, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus; H, the map rat, and the route rat kept theirs.
options.why: Correct. With the lamp in place, every rat but the route rat took path 6. With the lamp off, the beacon rat and the snapshot rat showed no preferred path in nearly every run, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus joined the route rat on paths 4 and 5. H and the map rat kept to path 6, since a map contains where the food box lay relative to the room as a whole. The route rat took paths 4 and 5 under both settings. A snapshot can be matched only near the goal, and with the lamp gone the snapshot rat had nothing it could match from the table where the fan begins.

options.text: Only the beacon rat, which had nothing left to head for; H and the other four hidden rats all kept the paths they had taken before.
options.why: The beacon rat did lose its path once the lamp it headed for was gone. The beacon rat was not the only one. The snapshot rat, which had taken path 6 with the lamp in place, showed no preferred path with the lamp off. The rat with damage to the hippocampus moved from path 6 to paths 4 and 5.

options.text: The beacon rat and the rat with damage to the hippocampus; the snapshot rat kept to path 6 by matching the look of the room.
options.why: The rat with damage to the hippocampus did change, from path 6 to paths 4 and 5. The snapshot rat changed too. A snapshot can be matched only near the goal, and with the lamp off the snapshot rat showed no preferred path from the table where the fan begins.

options.text: The beacon rat and the snapshot rat; the rat with damage to the hippocampus kept to paths 4 and 5 under both settings.
options.why: The beacon rat and the snapshot rat did both lose path 6. The rat with damage to the hippocampus changed as well. With the lamp in place the damaged rat took path 6, as the beacon rat did, and only with the lamp off did it fall back on its route, to paths 4 and 5.

items.stem: On the radiating paths, every rat is run with The lamp set to moved across the room. What did the healthy rat, H, and the hidden rat with damage to the hippocampus each do?

options.text: H stayed on path 6, nearest the old food box, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus followed the lamp to path 1.
options.why: Correct. With the lamp moved, H stayed on path 6, as the map rat did, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus followed the lamp to path 1, as the beacon rat did. The damaged rat is the healthy rat without its map, so it keeps a beacon and a route. With the lamp in view, the damaged rat headed for the lamp rather than repeating its route, wherever the lamp stood. Only with the lamp switched off did the damaged rat take paths 4 and 5.

options.text: H and the rat with damage to the hippocampus each followed the lamp to path 1, since each heads for a beacon in view.
options.why: The damaged rat did follow the lamp to path 1. H has a beacon too, but it also has a map of the room, and it stayed on path 6, nearest the old food box, as the map rat did.

options.text: H stayed on path 6, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus took paths 4 and 5, falling back on the turns of its trained route.
options.why: Without its map, the damaged rat is left with a beacon and a route, and its route does lead to paths 4 and 5. The damaged rat took those paths only with the lamp switched off. With the lamp moved across the room and still in view, the damaged rat headed for the lamp instead, to path 1.

options.text: H followed the lamp to path 1, and the rat with damage to the hippocampus took paths 4 and 5, beside the blocked route.
options.why: H, with its map intact, stayed on path 6. The damaged rat, left with a beacon and a route, followed the lamp to path 1. Paths 4 and 5 are where the damaged rat went with the lamp switched off, when only its route was left.

items.stem: In the recording box, the bump’s offset from the rat’s true heading, in degrees, is printed in The recording, the panel beside the view. Once the white card had taken control, with the lights on, what did that offset do over a minute of driving?

options.text: It stayed near one value, set when the card’s input was learned, not by the true heading, wandering only a few degrees.
options.why: Correct. Once the card had control, the offset wandered by about 4 to 5° over a minute and otherwise stayed put. Its value is arbitrary. The ring has no built-in north: the bump starts wherever it settles, and the card’s input is learned onto whichever upper-ring units are active when the card is seen. So the card keeps the bump steady at that alignment, not at the true heading. A heading is useful if it stays put relative to the room; it does not have to match the true direction.

options.text: It stayed near 0°, wandering only a few degrees, since the white card pulls the bump back onto the rat’s true heading whenever it drifts.
options.why: A landmark corrects a heading, but it can pull the bump back only to the alignment at which its input was learned. The ring has no built-in north, so that alignment is arbitrary. The offset sat at a steady value fixed while the card’s input was learned, and nothing in the model makes that value 0°.

options.text: It drifted steadily away from its starting value, by more degrees each minute, as every noisy turn signal added error.
options.why: Drift that keeps adding up is what happened in the dark, with the card out of sight: after five dark minutes the bump stood as much as 105° from where it had been. In the light, the card corrected the drift, and the offset wandered by only about 4 to 5° over a minute.

options.text: It swung widely each time the rat turned away from the card, and settled back only when the card was in view again.
options.why: Turning away from the card does not undo the heading. The turn signal keeps sliding the bump as the rat turns, and the card’s input corrects only slow drift, so the offset stayed close to one value whichever way the rat faced.
